Up on the tower the lantern jumped. It went up, and sideways, and then it dropped. It fell straight down the front of the tower, turning over, a little yellow spark. It went out before it hit anything.

And something else came down after it.

I only saw it for a second, against the sky, where the cloud was thin. Something long and dark came away from the top of that tower, from under the little roof. It leaned out and it went. It didn't fall the way the lamp had. It turned as it came down, slowly, with its arms out. It dropped behind the roof of the stables, on the far side, where the ground fell away to the creek.

I didn't hear it land. It was too far.

"Christ alive," said the boatman.

I couldn't speak. Above the stables, on the tower, there was one figure left under the roof, on the right-hand side of the bell. It was the big one, the woman. She had her arm up.

* * *

"I'm away," the boatman said. He was already bending to the post. "I don't know what you lot have got going over here and I don't want to know. I never see you. I never come."

"Wait."

"I'll wait for nothing. That's guns." He'd thrown off the line. The launch began to come away from the staging by itself, not fast, and I saw that the water was moving. It had been dead still five minutes before. Now there were little creases in it round the piles. The slack was over. It was going out. "You tell Vane, if you see him, I come and I waited, and that's four hundred pound I'm owed whether or no. And you can tell him the other feller says he'll want a word. Now stand off my rope."

I had a hand on his gunwale. I don't know what I thought I was going to do. I think I wanted to go with him. I think for about one second I wanted more than anything on earth to step down into that boat and be taken round to Harwich with the thermos flask, and never find out what was lying behind the stables.

He didn't argue. He picked something up off the bottom boards and swung it. It was a boathook, six feet of ash with a brass end. It got me across the forearm and then, coming back, on the hip, and I sat down on the jetty in three inches of sea. He wasn't angry about it. He did it the way you'd clear a fender. By the time I'd got up on one knee the launch was ten yards off and turning, with the engine opened up and the lantern coming down off the mast, and he was a shape hunched over the tiller.

I've read a lot of books, since, where the private detective has a fight on a wharf. He takes a couple and gives a couple and somebody goes in the drink. I'd like to have given you one of those. I got hit twice with a pole by an oysterman of sixty who then went home. That's the only fight I had that night. I'd been knocked cold by a pianist before that. I told you at the start that I used to be good.

I got up. My arm was dead to the shoulder. I went back along the wall.

* * *

I ran some of it. I'd not have said I could. I ran along the top of that bank with the tide beginning to slide away on my right hand, and the black gap of the spinney coming up. All the way I was watching the tower. There wasn't any light on it now. The woman stood up there alone against the cloud.

I didn't go through the trees. I kept to the wall, round the outside. The wall bent in behind the stable block, and I remembered from the afternoon that the creek came in there, the fleet they called it, through a brick sluice under the bank, and ran along the back of the buildings.

I came round the bend and I was above it.

It was a ditch in the daytime, I suppose, twenty feet of mud with a trickle down the middle. It was full now. It was a strip of black water as wide as a road, lying between the back wall of the stables and the bank where I stood. The tower went straight up from the far edge of it. And it had begun to run. The whole length of it was sliding along, smooth and quiet, toward the sluice and the sea, with bits of straw and foam on it turning round as they went.

There was something in it.

It was sixty yards up from me, near the foot of the tower, when I first saw it, and I took it for a log. It was long and dark and low in the water, coming down slowly, a little sideways. The moon was behind a cloud. I stood on the bank and waited for it to come on.

The cloud went by. The light came down on the fleet like someone drawing a curtain.

It was a man. He was lying on his face. His arms were out from his sides and his legs were together, straight, and he rode high, with his back out of the water. He had a black jacket on. It had come up round his shoulders with the wet, and I could see the white of a shirt cuff at the end of one sleeve, and the back of a dark head. He came down that creek on the first of the ebb like a man asleep on a lilo. As he passed under where I stood he turned a little, the way the straw was turning, and I saw the white of a collar.

I went down the bank. I went down it on my backside in the mud, and got to the edge with one foot in. I reached. He was twelve feet out. I hadn't a stick or a rope. I put my other foot in and the bottom wasn't there. It just went. I was in to the thigh, and it was like standing in cold porridge with a hand round your ankle. I grabbed the grass and hauled myself back. I've never learned to swim. They don't teach you in Poplar.

So I knelt on the bank and watched him go. I'll put that down plainly, the same as the other.

At two o'clock somebody fired a twelve-bore twice. At a quarter past, a man in a dinner jacket went down the fleet on the ebb, face down, in no hurry.

He went under the bank through the sluice, into the dark, and I heard the water take him on the other side. That was the sea, out there. It was going out, and it wouldn't be back till the afternoon.

I knelt there. I thought, well, there he goes. That's Edmund Vane. They brought him up from the ice house and took him up the tower and put him over, into the one piece of water on the island that'd carry him clean away. I'd seen them do it. I'd seen him fall, from the Hythe, with his arms out. I couldn't think why they'd carried a dead man up forty feet of ladder to do it. I couldn't think who'd shown a lamp, or who'd fired a gun, or what at. None of it would come straight. But I'd seen what I'd seen. An hour ago I'd looked at a dead man in a black jacket at the bottom of some steps, and now I'd looked at a dead man in a black jacket going out to sea. It didn't cross my mind that there could be two of them.

I'd worked it out, you see. A detective is a man who can't leave two things lying next to each other without joining them up.

Behind me, over the stable roof, from the direction of the house, I could hear music.

I thought it was my head. I got up and climbed the bank and listened. It was real. It was thin and scratchy and it came and went on what was left of the wind. It was a waltz.

## 6. The Odd Hour

The front door of Compline House was standing wide open.

I came round the end of the stables onto the gravel and that was what I saw. Eighty yards of dark with the wet shining on it, and at the far end a tall doorway full of yellow light, both halves of the door folded right back against the stone, and nobody on the step. They'd opened it and left it. You could have driven a hearse in.

I crossed toward it slowly. I wasn't being careful. I'd gone past careful. I was wet to the thigh on one side and to the knee on the other, and I had a head like a cracked bell and an arm I couldn't lift. I'd just watched a man go out to sea. And somewhere on that gravel as I walked, or in the trees, or in one of those black outhouses at my back, was somebody with a twelve-bore who'd already used it twice. I ought to have felt that between my shoulders. I didn't much care.

The music got louder as I came. It was a gramophone, an old one, the kind with a horn; you could hear the needle. A big sugary waltz with a lot of fiddles in it.

I stopped at the edge of the light, short of the step, and looked in.

I've said the hall was a stone room with a fireplace and a dozen tall clocks. They'd filled it with candles. There must have been fifty; on the table, on the stairs, along the top of the panelling, on the hoods of the clocks themselves. The fire was built up. The Font stood where it had stood, with the light sliding about on the watches in it. All the long brass pendulums were going behind their little windows, out of step, and winking as they went.

In the middle of the floor two people were dancing.

One of them was the old man. He had his dinner jacket on and his white hair standing up and the eyeglass swinging on its cord. He was holding himself as straight as a guardsman, and he was waltzing. He wasn't shuffling. He was doing it properly, the turn and the reverse and the long step, the way they were taught it before the first war. His left hand was out, holding hers. His right was flat in the small of her back. His face was lifted, and his eyes were shut.

The woman he was dancing with wore a long grey silk dress.

I'll say what I saw and then I'll say what I think. She was a woman of middle height, slim, with dark hair done up on her head. The dress was an evening dress, old-fashioned, cut low at the back, and it was the grey of a pigeon's breast. When they turned and the skirt swung out, the candles ran up and down the folds of it like water. She had her head a little on one side. I knew that dress and I knew that tilt of the head. I'd stood in front of both of them for ten minutes that afternoon, at the end of the long gallery, in a gold frame.

They came round. I saw her face over his shoulder. Grey eyes.

I told myself it was the daughter. I'm telling you now it was the daughter. It couldn't have been anybody else. She was the right height, and her hair was dark, and if there was a white streak in it, well, the candles were on the other side. She'd put on her mother's frock. Why she'd do that on that night, in front of that old man, I couldn't have told you. But families do worse.

I'd like it noted, though, that I stood outside that door for a full minute and wasn't sure. I'd seen one woman in two places at five to one. I'd watched a man with a lamp on a tower an hour after I'd looked at his corpse. By that time, if she'd walked out of the hall straight through the wall, I'd have written it down with the time beside it and gone on.

Nobody was looking at them. That was the queer part. Or they were, but sideways, the way they'd looked at the empty chair at dinner. Dame Octavia Prowse was planted in a big chair by the fire with a glass, with her chin sunk on her chest, staring into the coals. Fenn was at the hall table, bent over, writing something on a long sheet of paper with a fountain pen, and stopping to read it through. The vicar was on a settle with his head back, asleep, and somebody had put a cushion under it. The cropped girl was sitting halfway up the stairs. She had on a man's overcoat, buttoned up to her chin, with her boots sticking out of the bottom of it, and her face was in her hands. No boy with her.

On the hall table, next to the Font, next to Fenn's elbow, where no one seemed to be taking any notice of it, there was a thing I couldn't make out at first. It was a square grey heap, with something on top that shone. Then I got it. It was an army blanket, folded back. And standing in the middle of the blanket, with all the candles in its glass, was the clock. The big dial, the five little ones, and the moon.

I shut my eyes and opened them. It was still there.

I'd tied that clock up in a tea chest at twenty to twelve. I'd watched its owner dead at a quarter past one and missed it from the landing. At a quarter to two I'd gone down twelve steps and found the place where it and he had been. I'd walked six hundred yards along a wall to ask a boatman if he had it. And it was on the hall table, with a party going on round it.

Then I saw her. She was standing by herself at the back of the hall, under the biggest of the clocks, where the light was good. She'd done what I told her. She had the green dress on, dry or near enough, and her hair combed, and her shoes, both of them. She stood with her hands together in front of her and her back straight, and she was watching the old man dance with the woman in grey. Her face was white and it was perfectly composed. You'd have said she was a woman at a party, a little tired.

I'd told her to stand where everybody could see her. She must have felt me there, outside, in the dark. She turned her head, slowly, and looked straight out through the open door at where I was. I don't know if she could see me. She looked for a second or two. Then she looked back at the dancers. She'd been on a stage, and she knew better than to look at the wings.

The record came to the end. The needle went round and round in the groove with a noise like someone breathing. The old man stood still in the middle of his hall, holding the woman, with his eyes shut.

"There," he said. I heard him from the step. "There, my dear. You see. It's quite all right. We had the time after all."

She kissed him and went, quickly, toward the back of the hall. I didn't see where. The nurse got the old man to a chair. And the nephew, who'd been sitting on the stairs with a plate, got up and crossed the floor to her. He stood bent right over her, tall as he was, with his big pink hands going, saying something very fast and low, and stopping, and starting again. She was looking up at him without any expression at all. As I watched she nodded, once. He straightened up as if someone had given him a present.

* * *

I didn't go in by that door. I've never felt less like walking into a room.

I went round the side, past the dark dining-room windows where I'd stood at midnight in a flowerbed, and in at the kitchen yard. The back door was open, as she'd said. There was a lamp burning on a long scrubbed table, and a range with the fire door ajar and a red glow behind it, and the carcass of the goose in a pan. There was nobody about. I stood on the mat and dripped. The kitchen clock on the wall said twenty-two minutes to two. That would have been a lie half an hour ago. It was now, by Act of Parliament, more or less the truth. I'd got to stop thinking like that.

I looked for the nail by the range. It was there, a big one, driven into the bricks. Nothing on it. Her keys were still hanging in the ice-house gate.

I was looking for a drink, mostly. But a room tells you things when it's empty, and I went round that one. There was a stone sink with a wooden plate rack. One plate had been taken off the rack and laid on the draining board, a big oval dish, a good one, with nothing on it. Beside it stood a round thing under a cloth. I lifted the cloth. It was a copper mould, a tall one, shaped like a dome, with a lid. A pudding mould. It was empty and clean, and it was warm from the room.

On the table somebody had dumped a tray of little glass plates, dirty, with cream and bits of sponge on them. I counted. Thirteen. Twelve had been scraped clean and one hadn't been touched. They'd even given her a helping of that.

So somebody had fetched out a dish to turn a moulded pudding onto, and then served a trifle instead. The mould had never been filled, or it had been filled and emptied and washed. I thought about a silver serving spoon in wet straw, with a crest on it. I had one wheel, a spoon, a pair of slippers, the cook's keys and an empty pudding mould. I've done a few crosswords since, in the home, of an afternoon, and I know now what you do with a set of clues like that: you stop looking for something clever. I picked up the cloth and put it back over the mould. I felt the answer brush past me in that kitchen. I heard it go out of the door behind me, and I let it.

There was a brandy bottle on the dresser, the cooking stuff. I had some from the neck.

Off the kitchen was a stone passage, and off that a door with a slatted panel in it. I opened it because it was there. It was the pantry: shelves, crocks, a ham in a cloth on a hook, a marble slab. In the wall at the back was a square hatch with a rope hanging in it, a lift for sending dishes up. On the floor underneath the slab, shoved in anyhow, with its lid beside it and a length of sash cord trailing, was a plywood tea chest with tin edges.

It was empty. There was nothing in it but a pillowcase.

So they'd unpacked it here. They'd carried the box in from the ice house to the kitchen, into the pantry, and opened it, and taken the thing out and carried it through to the hall and stood it on a table on its blanket, for anyone to see. *Who* had? It wasn't a way to steal a clock. It wasn't a way to hide one. I leaned on the marble and tried to think like Edmund Vane's murderer, and like Ronnie Sears, and like a wife, and I couldn't make any of them do it.

It didn't occur to me to think like a man who'd been sent to fetch the pudding.

* * *

When I went up the back passage and through the baize door into the hall, the dancing was over and the company had thinned out. The gramophone was shut. The woman in grey had gone, and so had Celia. The girl had gone from the stairs. Dame Octavia hadn't moved, and the vicar slept on. The nephew was at the fire, alone, pouring himself something, and humming. The front door was still open on the night, and the candles nearest to it were streaming sideways.

Leo Vane was standing by himself in front of one of the tall clocks.

It was on the left of the fireplace, plainer than the rest, a long narrow case of dark wood with a glass door the whole length of the front. He had the door open. Inside, where the others had a pendulum going to and fro, this one had a pendulum hanging dead. It wasn't going. I'd come past it, I suppose, a dozen times that day, and couldn't have told you whether it was or not. He was looking at something in the bottom of the case. As I came up he put his hand in, and touched it with the tips of his fingers.

It was the weight. A cylinder of dull grey metal a bit bigger than a tin of beans, hanging on a line off a pulley, low down, where it had run to the end of its drop.

I'd come to ask him about the clock on the table. I'd come, I suppose, because he was the one who'd hired me, and it was gone two, and he'd said he would know by one. I stopped a yard behind him. I had no idea what I was going to say.

He turned his head. The glass was in his eye.

"You've been in the water," he said.

"Yes, sir."

"That's unwise. It was a spring tide and a surge on it. High water was at eight minutes to one. I have that from the Thorne, which is never out, not by a minute in the year, whatever they print on their cards." He took his fingers away from the lead and rubbed them together, slowly, looking at them. "Are you the man?"

"I'm the man Mr Fenn sent."

"Then you are late. You were to tell me by one."

"I know who took your clocks, Mr Vane."

"So do I," said Leo Vane. "I've seen to it."

It's a small thing, how a man says four words. I'd have passed over it from most people. But he said it the way he'd have told me he had put a new spring in something. A job done, and done properly. Then he looked at his fingers again.

I looked too. I couldn't help it. There was candlelight all down that side of him. His hand was clean. But the cuff of his shirt, the right one, where it came out of the black sleeve, wasn't. The edge of it was brown. There was a stain on the linen the size of a half-crown and a few more, smaller, going up toward the link, like drops off a brush. I've seen that colour a good many times, on a good many shirts, when it's had an hour or two to dry.

"You've hurt yourself," I said.

"I?" He turned the wrist over and considered it. "No. No, I don't believe so. That will be Edmund."

There are times when everything in a room gets very clear and small, as if you were looking down the wrong end of a telescope. I remember the noise of the fire. I remember the nephew humming.

"What will be Edmund, sir?"

"He was in the ice house, you know. He had her clock in a box, like groceries. I asked him why. I asked him quite civilly. I've been waiting all the year to ask him why." His voice was thin and reasonable. "He laughed. He said, 'It's a copy, you old fool. They're all copies. There's nothing in this house that isn't.' And I had this in my hand. I don't recollect why I had it in my hand. I must have taken it off to stop the clock. One stops the clocks when there is a death, you know, it was always done. So I must have known beforehand. That's the part I can't get straight."

He put his hand into the case again and lifted the weight an inch on its line and let it down. It was heavy. You could see the cord go taut.

"Fourteen pounds," he said. "Lead, in a brass jacket. Mr Vulliamy's, for the regulator. I struck him here." He touched his own left temple, above the eye, with one long forefinger. "He went down the steps. I heard him go. I killed him, you know. At ten minutes to twelve. I looked at the dial as I came in; every clock in the hall said it."

He'd got the right temple. I mean the left, the correct one. I'd looked at it by a lighter for a minute at a quarter past one, and it had gone in where it should have gone out.

"Mr Vane—"

"And now I haven't." He smiled at me. It was the smile of a clever child. "That's what's so very interesting. You should write that down; you had a notebook. At one o'clock the hour came back. I had calculated that it would, and it did, and I've been through it a second time, and it has all gone differently. Margot came down. She didn't go out on the Wade at all. I gave her the tide, properly this time, to the minute, and she's gone to put her shoes on." He glanced round the hall as if to be sure nobody else could hear, and lowered his voice. "I haven't been out to see about Edmund yet. I am going directly. But you may take it from me that he will be perfectly well. It doesn't happen the second time. That's the whole principle."

I stood there. I've interviewed some mad people. There was a woman in Hackney who'd been getting messages from her gas meter. But I've also interviewed a good many men who told me a thing that was sixty per cent raving, and in the middle of it was a fact, with a time on it and a place, and the fact checked. You learn to hear the difference. The raving comes loose and wanders. The fact stays where it's put.

Ten minutes to twelve by the hall clocks. That was ten to one by my watch. He'd named the ice house and the box, and the left temple, and the steps. And there was that cuff.

And I had a woman's kiss on my mouth, a woman who'd sat on a hearthrug and told me, *I did that. Nobody pushed him. You needn't look for anybody.*

They couldn't both have. Could they? She gives him enough dope to drop a horse. He walks out of the house on his own legs half an hour later; she'd said so herself, and been surprised at it. He goes down to the spinney. And somebody follows him there. It's not a boatman or a moneylender's man. It's his own father, eighty-one years old, in his evening pumps, with a lump of lead off a clock swinging in his hand.

Then the gate. I'd wondered about the gate. *A man doesn't shut himself in a hole he means to come out of.* No. But a man who has just done a thing like that, and walks away from it, pulls the door to behind him. Anybody would. He wouldn't even know he had done it.

It fitted. God help me, it fitted better than hers.

I was going to ask him. I had my mouth open. I was going to say, *Mr Vane, who else was there? Who moved him?* But I saw that I'd lost him. His eyes had gone past me to the open front door and the dark. He was listening to something.

"It's stopped," he said. "The Jack's stopped. He should have done the quarter." He frowned. "I must go across. I've the Reconciler to see to, and it's all coupled through the going train, and if he has jammed—" He began to walk. He went by me as if I were a hatstand. At the door he checked, and put a hand on the stone, and looked back into his hall, at the candles and the clocks.

"You might tell my wife where I've gone," he said. "If she asks."

Then he went out, down the step, onto the gravel, in his thin shoes. I watched him as far as the light went. A long white-haired old man going off slowly toward the stables.

I let him go. I'd like that known, as well. An old man of eighty-one, off his head, was going out alone at half past two in the morning, toward a place where somebody had been letting off a shotgun. I stood and watched. I've got no excuse. I was thinking about his cuff.

"Excuse me." It was the nurse. She had come up beside me without my hearing. She was a small pale thing, and that close I could see she was shaking, very slightly, all over, like a wire with a current in it. "Have you seen Mr Vane? I only turned my back. I was asked something and I only turned my back for a minute."

"He was here," I said. "He was looking at this clock."

She looked at the clock. She looked at the open case, and the still pendulum, and the grey weight at the bottom of its line. I saw her look at that weight and I saw her stop shaking.

She didn't say anything. She put out her hand and shut the long glass door, gently, till the catch clicked.

"Thank you," said Miss Quaile, and went away toward the stairs. She hadn't asked me where he'd gone, and I hadn't told her. I'd file that, I thought. If I ever opened the cabinet again.

* * *

Fenn found me in the library. I'd gone there because it was dark and had a chair in it. The fire was nearly out. The glass case stood on its table in the window with the baize cloth over it, covering nothing.

He came in with a candle and shut the door and set the candle down on the mantelpiece. He stood with his back to the grate and his hands behind him. He had a long envelope sticking out of his breast pocket.

"You look as though you had been in a road accident, Mr Cade."

"I was. Somebody's son ran into me."

"I shan't ask." He meant it. "Mr Vane wished to be told the name of a person before one o'clock. He was not told. May I ask whether you are now in a position to tell it to me?"

"Edmund."

"Yes." There wasn't a flicker.

"He lifted the Thorne out of that case at about twenty past eleven, when the lights went. He put it in a tea chest and carried it to the ice house. I saw him. I saw the clock in the chest. There was a boat due at the Hythe at a quarter to two, sent by a moneylender in Southend called Sears, to whom he owes a hundred and eighty thousand pounds. He's had thirty clocks out of this house in four years, not eleven. That's what you paid for." I had the back of my head against the leather of the chair. It was the only way I could keep the room level. "The boat came. I talked to the man in it. He's gone, without the clock. The clock is on the table in the hall."

"I am aware of that," Fenn said. "I was present when it arrived."

I sat up. It cost me something.

"You were what?"

"I was in the hall, with the rest of the company, at one o'clock. Mr Vane had opened the door. There was a clap of thunder, or so I took it to be, two claps, and some little confusion; Miss Quaile cried out. And into the midst of this came Mr Pargeter, from the kitchen passage, carrying a wooden box. He appeared to be under the impression that it contained a pudding." Fenn said it with no more expression than he'd used for the family tree. "He set it on the table and removed the lid with something of a flourish. I believe he had prepared a few words. It contained what you have seen."

"The *nephew* had it?"

"Mr Pargeter."

"Where the hell did the nephew get it?"

"I did not enquire. I formed the view, Mr Cade, some hours ago, that this was not a night upon which to enquire into anything. I am sixty-seven years of age, and I have a wife."

I got my head back onto the leather. A pudding. I thought about the empty mould under its cloth. The spoon. The saucer with the candle on the third step. One wheel.

It's hard to describe how I felt. Something was trying to come up, from a long way down, and it was nearly there. It felt like a laugh. I was afraid of it. I thought, if I once let that come up, I'll never be able to take anything seriously again, and there's a man dead.

"What did the old man say? When he saw it?"

"He looked at it for some moments through his glass. He said, 'Ah. The Copy. I wondered where I had put it.' He then observed that it had stopped. And he thanked Mr Pargeter, and said that it was very thoughtful, but that he believed we had been promised an ice."

"The copy."

"That was the word he used."

"He told me a few minutes ago that Edmund said the same thing to him. That it was a copy. That everything in the house was."

"Did he." Fenn looked at the covered case in the window. "I should not place too much reliance, Mr Cade, on anything Mr Vane has said since midnight. Nor, I regret to say, since about 1991. He is capable of telling you with great exactness the day on which he acquired that clock and what he paid for it. He is equally capable of telling you that his wife has gone upstairs to change her shoes."

"There's a mark," I said. "On the real one. A sprig of thorn. Scratched under the left foot of the dial. I looked for it this afternoon."

"And?"

I didn't answer him straight off.

"The light was bad," I said.

Fenn inclined his head. He didn't say anything. He reached into his breast pocket, beside the long envelope, and brought out a smaller one, and held it out to me between two fingers.

"What's that?"

"A cheque. Three days at two hundred pounds, and fifty for expenses. You will find it in order."

"I've done one day."

"You have done all that will be required." He waited until I'd taken it. "I shall tell you how matters stand, and then, if you'll forgive me, I shall go to bed. In the course of the last hour Mr Vane addressed his family. He was, for perhaps ten minutes together, entirely himself; more so than I have seen him in three years. He said that he had asked a question at dinner, and that he no longer wished to have it answered. He said the matter of the clocks was closed. He said that whoever had taken them had no doubt had need of them, and that he had been a poor father to anyone who had been driven to it, and that it was all to go on the Hour's account and not be spoken of again. He then desired me to take down a codicil to his will, which I did, and which has been properly witnessed, and which does not concern you." He touched the long envelope. "My instructions from my client, therefore, are that you found nothing. There was no enquiry. A gentleman from Pemberton's came to count the clocks and was detained by the tide. That is what I shall say if I am asked, and I should be obliged if you would say the same."

"There's more to it than clocks, Fenn."

"I daresay."

"A man's dead."

He didn't jump. I'll give him that. He stood on the hearthrug with the candle behind him and his face in shadow. It was quite a time before he spoke.

"Which man?"

"Edmund Vane."

"You have seen him?"

"At a quarter past one, in the ice house, at the bottom of the steps, with his head stove in. Through the gate. And at a quarter past two in the creek behind the stables, on his face, going out with the tide."

"Through the gate," Fenn said. "And in the creek. I see. You did not, on either occasion, lay a hand upon him?"

"I couldn't get to him."

"No. Then you have not, in the sense in which a coroner would understand the words, got a body."

"He's not in the house, is he? Go and look for him. Go and knock on his door."

"I shall do nothing of the kind. Edmund has not slept a night through in his own bed on this date in twenty years. He walks about. He has been found in the morning in the stable, and in the boathouse, and on one occasion in the vicar's car." Fenn took his hands from behind his back and looked at them. "Mr Cade. I engaged you because I was told that you had once, at considerable cost to yourself, declined to go along with a falsehood. I thought the better of you for it. I think the better of you now. But I will ask you to consider your position. By your own account you have been struck on the head. You've been drinking; so have we all. It is dark, and you don't know the place. You saw something through a gate by, I assume, a match, and something else in the water by moonlight. And upon that you propose to tell me, at the age of eighty-one, that Leo Vane's son is dead? Tonight, of all nights? When he has just forgiven him?"

"I propose to tell the police. At twenty-five to six, when the road dries."

"That is your right. I should not dream of preventing you." He picked up his candle. "I would only observe that if a man has gone into the sea off the Ness on the ebb of a spring tide, the sea will bring him back in its own time, without the least assistance from either of us. It always does. And that when it does, everyone in this house will be asked where they were, and what they saw. I shall say that I was in the hall, taking down a codicil. I wonder what you'll say. I wonder who you would be obliged to mention."

He knew. He didn't know what, exactly. He'd stood in that hall for an hour and watched Celia Vane come in at the garden door at ten to one with her hair wet, and take up a place under a clock, and not move. He'd watched an old man come in from the dark with a clock-weight. He'd been the family's solicitor for forty years. He knew there was something, and where it was, and that was as much as he wanted. I'd met a hundred like him. They'd tell you they never asked a client whether he did it, and they'd tell you it was a principle.

"You'd rather not know," I said. "You told me that on Wednesday."

"I told you that I act for the family, Mr Cade. All of the family." He opened the door. "Good night. There's a decanter on the table behind you. I should have the whisky; the brandy in this house has been rather unreliable this evening."

* * *

I had the whisky. I sat in the dark with it and Fenn's cheque. Six hundred and fifty pounds, to have found nothing.

I'd been in that house eleven hours. I counted up. I'd had two clients. One of them had just paid me off and told me the job had never existed. The other was a widow, and I'd stood in a brick well and told her so, twice. I had two confessions. The wife said the drug had done it, and showed me the bottle. The father said the weight, and showed me his cuff. They couldn't both be the whole of it, and each of them, I'd have sworn, was telling me what they believed. There'd been a body, and somebody had moved it. I'd got a clock worth a million pounds that might be worth nothing. There was a shotgun out there I couldn't account for at all, and a boy with a cricket bat, and somebody in slippers. And somebody had shown a dead man's signal from the top of a tower.

I've known cases with nobody in the frame. I never had one before where everybody was trying to get into it.

At some point the clock in the stable tower struck. I heard it through the open front door, down the length of the hall. The big bell, twice. Two o'clock by the house, three by the watch on my wrist. No. Two by both. I'd forgotten to put it back. I never did put it back, not that night. I went on being an hour ahead of the lot of them till the morning.

There was something wrong with the striking. I sat and worked out what it was. There'd been no little bell first. All night it had gone *ting-tang* four times over before the hour, and that time it hadn't. Only the big one, twice, slow, out of nowhere. The old man had said it: *the Jack's stopped*. I thought of the little roof up there, and the one figure left under it with her arm up.

The door opened. I knew who it was before I saw her. That scent came in ahead of her.

She shut the door and stood against it, exactly as she had at eleven in the other room. She had no candle. There was only what was left of the fire.

"You said you'd tell me first," Celia Vane said.

So I told her. I told her about the boat, and one man in it, and him gone. I told her about the light on the tower and the shots, and what came down. I told her what I'd watched go under the wall at a quarter past two. I didn't make it gentle, because there wasn't a gentle way. She listened to all of it without a sound. When I got to the creek she slid down the door until she was sitting on the floor with her knees up. She put her forehead on them.

I didn't tell her about the old man's cuff.

I've asked myself why. I had it ready. It would have been a kindness, of a sort, to say to her: it may not have been your bottle. It may have been a piece of lead, and you needn't carry it. I didn't say it. I think it was because I wasn't sure, and you don't hand a woman a thing like that unless you're sure. I'd like to think so. But I know what I am. If she hadn't done it, she wouldn't need me, and I think that was in it too.

"Then he's gone," she said, into her knees. "There isn't even anything to find in the morning."

"Not here. Somewhere down the coast, in a day or two."

"And they'll say he drowned."

"He went out drunk and he went off the wall. Twelve people saw how he was at dinner. It's a better story than the ice house, as it happens. Nobody has to explain a locked gate." I heard how that sounded. I went on anyway. "There's blood on the straw down there. I'll see to that before it's light. And your cook's keys."

She lifted her head.

"Why did they bring the clock into the house?"

"I don't know. The nephew had it. He thought it was a pudding."

"Toby?" She stared at me, and then she made a sound that was half a laugh. "Oh, God. Toby. Of course he did." She wiped her face with the heel of her hand. "And Leo says it's a copy."

"Leo says his wife's upstairs changing her shoes."

"Yes."

"Is it a copy?"

"I don't know," said Celia Vane. "I never could tell one from another. I hated every one of them." She was quiet. Then she said, in a different voice, slower: "Does it matter? If the man who's paying for it thinks it's the real one?"

I looked at her across the dark room. I think I'd known since the fourth stair that it would come to this.

"Sears has still got to be paid," she said. "He doesn't stop because Edmund's dead. You know him; I don't. Does he stop?"

"No."

"He'll come to the estate. He'll come to Leo. He'll come to Kit." She got up off the floor. She came across to the chair and knelt down in front of it and put her two hands on my knees, and I could feel the cold of them through the wet cloth. "Harry. That clock's sitting on the hall table with a blanket round it, and nobody in this house wants it. Leo's just told everyone he doesn't care who took what. There's a man in Southend who'll wipe out a hundred and eighty thousand pounds for it and give something over. Edmund fixed the price. It's all arranged; it's only the boat that's gone. You've got a car."

"You want me to drive a stolen clock to Ronnie Sears."

"I want you to drive me. I'll do the rest. I'll telephone him from a box. I know the number, I've heard it often enough. You needn't see him. You needn't see anyone." Her hands tightened. "I can't stay here. I can't be in this house when they find he's gone. I can't sit at that table at breakfast and watch them start to wonder, and Imogen looking at me, and the boy. I'll go mad. I'll say something. Take me with you when the road opens. Please."

"And after?"

"I don't know about after. I told you, I do a day at a time."

I've got to be fair to myself, just once. I knew what it was. I knew a woman who's on her knees to you at three in the morning isn't there because of your eyes. I knew I'd be driving off that island at dawn with a dead man's wife and a dead man's clock in the boot, a few hours after he'd gone out on the tide. And I'd be doing it under the nose of a solicitor who had just told me, in so many words, that he'd remember it.

But I could feel her hands. And I thought of that card from Sears, in the drawer at Leigh, six years old. I thought, he'll take it. He'll take a copy for a million and never know, and I'll have sold it to him. It was the only way I was ever going to get to laugh at him.

"Six o'clock," I said. "By my watch. Be in the yard. Bring a coat of your own."

She put her head down on my knees. I put my hand on her hair. It was still damp.

We stayed like that. Out in the hall the clocks went on, all hundred and eleven of them. The Odd Hour was over. They'd told me nothing in it would count.

## 7. Harwich

I did what I'd said I would do before it was light. I'm putting it down because I said I'd put down all of it.

At about four I went back to the spinney with a stable lantern I'd found and the cook's kitchen saucer in my pocket. The gate was as we'd left it, wide, with her ring of keys hanging. I went down the steps for the third time that night. I took the straw where his head had been and the straw round it, a double armful, and carried it up and out and along to the wall, and threw it into the sea. I went back and scrubbed the bottom step with a handful of sacking and meltwater until the smear was gone and the hairs with it. I raked the rest of the straw about with my foot so that there wasn't the shape of a man in it any longer. Then I broke a few pieces off the ice with the iron bar and let them lie on the wet, where he'd been, to melt.

It took me twenty minutes. I've spent longer destroying evidence that didn't matter. When it was done I stood at the bottom with the lantern and looked round. It was a round brick room with ice in it. There was nothing there to say anyone had died.

I took the keys out of the lock and pulled the gate shut and heard the tongue drop. I hung the ring on its nail by the kitchen range, with the red wool to the front, and stood the saucer on the draining board by the empty dish. The serving spoon I put in the sink.

Nobody saw me. There was a light under the door of the servants' hall, and somebody snoring behind it. Out in the scullery passage, as I came through, I thought I smelled cigarette smoke, fresh, and there was a plate on the kitchen table that hadn't been there at half past two, with some bones on it, and a tumbler. Somebody had been in and eaten cold goose with his fingers. I looked at the plate. I thought, the boy. The boy's come in from wherever he's been hiding and had his supper. I felt sorry for him.

I can tell you to the minute when that plate was used, and who by. I've been told since. I didn't know it then. I rinsed the tumbler under the tap and stood it on the rack with the others. I was tidying up.

* * *

It began to get light about a quarter past six. It was a dirty yellow light, low down in the east behind the stables, and the tower stood up against it. I'd been sitting in the Granada in the yard since half past five with the engine running and the heater on, trying to stop my teeth.

I'd looked up at the tower when I came out. I'll admit I looked. There was one of them up there under the little roof. The woman. She stood on the right of the bell in her painted gown with her hammer up by her shoulder. Somebody's shawl was still on her, soaked, hanging straight down. On the left, where the little man had been in his black jacket, there was a post and a bit of iron sticking up, and the sky.

I sat in the car and looked at that gap. I'd seen something come off that tower at two o'clock, with its arms out. I'd seen where it had come from. I knew there'd been two wooden people up there at midnight and there was one now. All three of those things were in my head together, in the front seat of a Ford. I had an hour to put them side by side.

I don't know what to tell you. I've sat in the day room at the home with the telly on and gone back to that hour in the car, and I've wanted to reach in through the window and take myself by the collar. But I'd seen a face at the bottom of the ice-house steps. I'd seen it by a flame, twelve feet off, and it was a man's, and I knew whose. After that the thing in the creek was Edmund Vane, to me, and it stayed Edmund Vane. Whatever had happened to a wooden dummy on a clock could wait. I think I thought the gun had brought it down. I think I thought, well, somebody shot the Jack, that's another one for the file. I didn't follow it over the edge and ask where it had landed.

That's the last of them. I've given you every chance I had that night to get it right and what I did with each one. There won't be any more.

At ten to six the vicar's Morris came round from the coach house with the nephew at the wheel, crouched over it like a man driving a pram. The old clergyman was in the passenger seat in a rug, asleep still, or again. The nephew saw me and stopped and got out. He came across the yard in the half-dark with his hands in his pockets. He'd lost the hopeful look. He looked about fifteen.

"I say," he said. "Mr Cade. Might I have a word? Only I gather you're by way of being a sort of detective. Kit says. And I think I'd better own up to somebody, and I'd rather it was a professional."

I wound the window down. I thought, here it comes. The box. He's going to tell me where he got the box.

"It was me," he said.

"What was?"

"The clock. What Uncle Leo said at dinner. One of you is robbing me. I mean, it wasn't *robbing*, I never meant to take it out of the house. But there was a little one in my room, on a sort of table, with a handle on top, and I caught it with my elbow, changing. And then I trod on it. Getting it out from under the bed. There was a noise like someone stepping on a budgerigar." He took his hand out of his pocket. He was holding a fistful of brass: a bent plate, some wheels, a spring that had got out and was hanging down like a bit of bracken. "I've had it on me all night. I couldn't think where to put it. I kept thinking he was looking at me. Do you suppose it was one of the good ones?"

I looked at what was in his hand. I'd spent Friday night with photographs of the good ones.

"It's a ten-pound carriage clock," I said. "They sell them in Woolworth's."

"Oh, *thank* God." He actually swayed. "You've no idea. I've been through absolute torment. I nearly confessed during the syllabub."

"I saw."

"Did you? Gosh." He put the wreckage away. He stood there, shifting his feet on the gravel, and didn't go. "There's another thing, actually. Rather worse. I don't know whether I ought to mention it."

"Then don't."

"No. Only I can't find him to apologise, and we're off now, the vicar's got early service, and I shouldn't like him to think I'd just—" He stopped. He looked at the tower, and then at the ground. "It was the wheel, you see. On the cobbles. They aren't built for it."

The Morris's horn went. A thin little parp. The vicar had woken up.

I'd had no sleep and I was waiting for a woman. I had a stolen clock in a blanket on the back seat, because I'd walked into the hall at five and picked it up off the table in front of a sleeping dame and nobody had said a word. I had no room in my head for a boy's second confession about another piece of the furniture.

"Write him a letter," I said.

"Yes. Yes, I suppose I could do that." He looked relieved. "I'll write to Edmund from town. He'll have cooled off by then. Well. Cheerio. I'm awfully glad about the Woolworth's."

He loped back to the Morris and they went off round the end of the stables, toward the Wade, at about nine miles an hour.

I wound the window up. He'd said the name. *I'll write to Edmund.* It went past me. I thought, poor young fool, he doesn't know yet. I watched his tail lights out of sight and I felt sorry for him too. I was sorry for everybody that morning.

* * *

She came at six. She came out of the garden door in a camel coat with a headscarf on, and a small case in her hand, and dark glasses, though the sun wasn't up. She had flat shoes. She got in beside me without a word and looked over her shoulder at the thing on the back seat. Then she faced front.

"Did anyone see you?" I said.

"Mrs Pask. She was lighting the range. She said, 'You're never going out, madam, at this hour.' I said I had a headache and Mr Cade was running me to the chemist's in Maldon."

"On a Sunday."

"She didn't say anything. She just looked at me." Celia Vane folded her gloved hands in her lap. "She had her keys back. She was holding them. She said, 'Somebody's been at my nail.'"

I put the car in gear.

We went out under the arch of the stables and down a track with the sea wall on one hand, and came to the ramp where the Wade went off the island. The tide was a long way out. You wouldn't have known it had ever been in. There was the mud again, miles of it, shining pink and yellow where the light caught it, and the birds walking about. The road lay across it, wet and black.

I drove out onto it. Neither of us spoke. I had it down to fifteen miles an hour, for the weed.

Halfway over we came to the dip, and the plank bridge, and the black box on its legs beside the bridge. I slowed for the planks. I looked at the box as we came up to it, the way you look at anything on an empty road.

The door of it was open. It was swinging a little on its hinges. And the ladder up the post was wrong. I'd noticed that ladder on the way in, and thought somebody should see to it. There'd been rungs all the way down, the bottom ones gone soft. Now there weren't. From about the height of a man's chest to the ground there was nothing but the two uprights, and where each rung had been socketed in there was a stub, snapped off short. The wood in the breaks was white. It hadn't had time to go grey.

On the shingle at the foot of the post, half sunk, was a child's torch. It was a small one, red plastic. The tide had been over it.

I saw that. I say so because it's the one thing I've got to show for twenty years of being trained to see. I saw four broken rungs and a toy torch on the Wade at ten past six on the Sunday morning, and I've never been able to do anything with them. They weren't in my case. I had a dead man and a widow and a clock. There wasn't any child. There'd been no child in that house, and nobody had been out on the road in the night; nobody could have been, there was six feet of water on it. Somebody's kid had dropped a torch there in the summer, and the storm had finished the ladder.

"What is it?" she said. I'd nearly stopped the car.

"Nothing."

I took us over the planks and on.

Where the Wade came up onto the mainland, I looked across at the farm under the wall. There was smoke from the chimney. In the yard stood the grey horse. It had a rug thrown over it and its head was down, and it was wet; its legs were black with it to the belly, and steam was coming off its back in the cold. There was nobody with it. A lamp was burning in a downstairs window of the house.

"Whose is that?" I said.

She turned her dark glasses to it and away.

"The Garrows'," she said. "It's nothing to do with us."

I filed it. For the last time. Then we were up on the wall and through Thorney Staithe, where there wasn't a soul about and the street lights were back on, burning away in the daylight.

* * *

She telephoned from a box outside a shut garage near Manningtree. I sat in the car and watched her do it. She had the number by heart. She talked for about two minutes with her back to me and her head bent. She came out and got in and said, "Parkeston. The car park by the quay. Half past eight."

"That was Sears?"

"That was somebody who said he'd tell him. He rang me back." She took her glasses off and rubbed her eyes. In the daylight she looked every hour of it. "He laughed. He said, 'Tell Mrs Vane Ronnie's always pleased to do business with a lady.'"

"Did you tell him about your husband?"

"I said he'd been taken ill."

"And me?"

"I said a friend was driving me."

I let that go. I said, "When we get there, you stay in the car. I'll hand it over. I want to see his face."

"No. Harry. No. You said you needn't see anyone. He'll know you, you said so, and then it's all—he'll think it's a trap. He'll think you're still a policeman." She put her hand on my arm, the one the boathook had found. "Let me do it. It's my husband's debt. It's the last thing I can do for him. Please."

I'd like to say I argued more than I did.

Parkeston Quay on a Sunday morning in October is a mile of wet tarmac with a railway line down one side and a ferry down the other. The boat was in. She was a big white thing with a blue funnel, and there were lorries going up into the back of her. It was twenty past eight. The car park was half empty. I pulled up at the far end, by a chain-link fence with rags of polythene blown against it, where I could see the way in.

"I could do with a coffee," she said. "I'm so cold. There's a place in the terminal. Would you?"

I looked at her. She looked back. Her eyes were steady and tired and they were thinking about something a little way behind me.

"Two sugars," she said.

Now, I knew. I'm not going to pretend I didn't. I'd sent men for coffee myself. I sat with my hand on the door, and I knew that if I got out of the car and walked two hundred yards to that terminal and stood in a queue, I'd come back to something different.

I've had twenty-five years to ask why I went. I think it's this. I was tired, and it was her husband's clock, and her husband's debt, and her life. If she wanted to do it with me out of the way, then she'd weighed me up and decided, and she'd probably got it right. And there was a bit of me that didn't want to see Ronnie Sears's face after all. I was afraid of what I'd see there. I thought he'd be pleased to see me.

I went and got the coffee. There were five people in the queue. I carried two paper cups back across the car park with the lids on, and I could see from a long way off.

The Granada was where I'd left it. Both the back doors were open. There was nobody in it and nothing on the back seat. Thirty yards off a big dark Jaguar was pulling away toward the exit, taking it slowly over the ramps. I saw the back of a man's head in the rear window, a wide head, with grey hair cut short. I'd have known that head across a football ground. There was a grey blanket beside him on the seat.

She wasn't in the Jaguar.

I found her with my eyes a few seconds later. She was a long way off, at the foot of the passenger gangway, a small figure in a camel coat and a headscarf, with a case. A man in uniform was looking at something she'd handed him. A ticket. He gave it back. She started up the gangway.

She stopped halfway. She turned round, and looked back along the quay at the car park. She'd have seen me. I was the only thing standing still in it, a man by a Ford with a cup in each hand.

She didn't wave. She lifted one hand, in its glove, as far as her shoulder, and held it there. Then she went on up and in through the door in the side of the ship.

I stood there till the coffee was cold. Then I drank both of them, sitting on the bonnet. Hers had the two sugars in.

On the passenger seat, where she'd been, there was an envelope. She'd written *Harry* on the front in eyebrow pencil. There was four hundred pounds inside it in twenties. I counted it. Double what Fenn was paying, she'd said, for one day. She'd kept her word to the pound. There wasn't a note.

*He's quite good at notes*, she had said. She wasn't. I've wondered since whether that was the better way to be.

* * *

They found him on the Monday afternoon. A man digging for bait came on him at low water on the Ray Sand, seven miles down the coast from Compline. I read it in the *Evening Echo* on the Tuesday, half a column on page five. *Body on beach is missing landowner.*

A detective inspector called Brand came down to Leigh to see me on the Thursday. He was a decent enough bloke, young. He didn't know who I was, or he was polite about it. He sat on my one chair and had tea out of my one good cup. I gave him what Fenn and I had agreed to give, which was nothing. Pemberton's, the valuation, the tide. I'd dined, and I had turned in early with a headache; I'd fallen on some steps in the dark when the lights failed, which accounted for the dressing. I'd left at first light. Yes, I'd given Mrs Vane a lift to Harwich. She'd asked me. She said she was going to a sister in Holland for a few days and was upset about a quarrel with her husband. No, I hadn't seen Mr Edmund Vane after the port. He'd been drinking heavily. He'd seemed to have something on his mind.

He wrote it all down. He said, "You were in the job, I believe, Mr Cade?"

"A while ago."

"You'll know I've got to ask. Did you hear anything in the night? Any kind of disturbance?"

"The wind."

"Nothing like a shot?"

I looked at him. "A shot?"

"We've a witness in the village says he heard a gun go off twice, over on the Ness, round about two. Likely nothing. They're always after duck out there." He shut his book. "It's only that the deceased had some pellet wounds. In the shoulder. Fresh."

I kept my face still. I'd had a lot of practice that week.

I went to the inquest. It was held in December, at Maldon, in a room over the magistrates' court with a radiator that knocked. I sat at the back. The family were there, what was left of them. The boy was in a black tie and looked about forty. Imogen Vane sat very upright, and next to her, to my surprise, was a lean brown man in a suit that didn't fit him, with a hat on his knee. Fenn was there. They'd left the old man at home. The nurse was at the end of a row by herself, as white as paper, twisting a handkerchief. The nephew wasn't called. Nor was I. There was no Mrs Vane. She'd sent an affidavit from an address in Rotterdam.

A pathologist read from a sheet. I've heard a great many of them read. He'd a flat Scots voice.

The deceased was a well-nourished man of fifty-two. The cause of death was drowning; there was sea water in the lungs and the stomach, and diatoms in the marrow, and I needn't go on. He had been alive when he went into the water. He'd been in it approximately thirty-six hours.

I heard that. *He had been alive when he went into the water.* I sat on a hard chair at the back of that room with my hat in my hands. I felt my whole case go, like a ladder with the bottom rungs out of it.

The man went on. There was more.

There was a depressed fracture of the left temporal bone, consistent with a single blow from a heavy blunt object of small surface, or with a fall against a projecting edge. It had been sustained some hours before death. I thought of a lead weight in a brass jacket, hanging at the bottom of its line. There was a second injury, a large contusion over the occiput, the back of the head, which was separate and somewhat later. There were eleven pellets of number five shot in the left shoulder, the left side of the neck and the back of the left ear, fired from a distance and from below; the wounds were superficial. There was chloral hydrate in the blood, in a quantity that the witness would call substantial. And alcohol.

The body was clothed in evening trousers, a dress shirt and braces, and one sock. There was no jacket. There were abrasions to the palms of both hands, and to the inner sides of the forearms, with tarred wood fibres in them, as though the deceased had been gripping something for a long time.

The coroner was an old solicitor with half-glasses. He looked at the sheet for a while when it was finished. He said that in thirty years he had not seen a man arrive at his own death by so many roads at once. He said that the deceased had evidently been struck, and drugged, and shot at, and had fallen or been struck a second time, all on the one night. And none of it had killed him. What killed him was the sea. There was no evidence before the court to show how he came to be in it. The family could offer none. He was not satisfied that it was an accident and he was not satisfied that it was anything else. He recorded an open verdict, and he hoped that somebody's conscience would one day supply what the evidence did not.

He looked round the room when he said that. He looked along the rows over his glasses. I've sat in a few courts, and I can tell you, he might have been looking at anybody. Every single person in that room dropped their eyes. I did. I saw the nurse do it, and the boy, and the daughter. I saw the brown man in the bad suit look down at his hat. Fenn studied his papers.

There wasn't one of us looked back at him. I noticed that. I wondered about it for years, what the rest of them had to look down for.

* * *

I've got one more thing to tell. It was the second week of January.

There were two of them, and they came in the afternoon, when I'd just got back with the paper. One was young and had a neck wider than his head. The other was getting on, a thin man in a car coat with a cough. They were quite civil. The thin one asked if I was Mr Cade and I said I was. He said Ronnie would like to ask me something, and they'd been told to ask it for him.

They took me down to the garages behind the flats. The young one did the work. He was good at it. He did the ribs first and left the face till later. The thin one stood and smoked.

When I could listen, the thin one squatted down by me on the concrete. He said, "It's a wrong 'un, Harry."

I said I didn't know what he meant. That got me another one.

"The clock," he said. "The million-pound clock. Ronnie had a feller over from Geneva to look at it, for a customer. Flew him in. The feller's there two minutes, with a little glass. He turns it over. He says, 'Where's the thorn?' Ronnie says, 'What thorn?' The feller says it's a very nice thing. It's worth eight or nine thousand of anyone's money, as an example of the English craft revival. Made about 1965." He coughed. "Ronnie give that woman sixty grand cash in a car park on top of what her old man owed him. On your say-so."

"I never said anything."

"You was driving."

"I didn't know. I looked for the mark. The light was bad."

"That's what Ronnie thought you'd say," the thin man said. "He says he don't reckon you're bright enough to've been in on it. He says you'd have run. That's why you're only getting this." He stood up. His knees cracked. "He wants to know where the real one is."

"I don't know."

"And the woman."

"I don't know. I swear to God I don't. She went up a gangway."

He looked down at me for a bit. Then he nodded to the young one, and I got the face.

It was three weeks before I could go out. I lay on the bed in Leigh and looked at the ceiling, the way I used to, and thought about her.

I thought about whether she'd known. I went over it and over it. There was the way she'd said, *Does it matter? If the man who's paying thinks it's the real one?* She'd asked me that straight out, in the library, kneeling. Did a woman who knew she was passing a dud say that out loud? Or was it just exactly what she would say, so that afterwards I'd remember she'd as good as told me? I can't decide. I've had her both ways, all these years, and I've had her true in the morning and false at night.

I think now she didn't know. I think she took the old man at his word about a copy as much as I did, which is to say not at all. She thought she was selling her husband's father's clock to pay her husband's debt and buy herself a start. And she had the sense to be on a ship by the time anyone looked underneath. She left me standing there because somebody had to be. It wasn't personal. It's what I'd have told her to do, if I'd been advising her.

And the real one? Fenn wrote to me that spring. One line, typed. *You may care to know that the article of which we spoke has been found, in the clock room of the stable tower, where the late Mr Vane had apparently placed it some months since, and has been identified beyond doubt.* The late Mr Vane. The old man had died in March. So it had been up there the whole time, forty feet above my head, while I lay on a horse rug underneath it listening to the big clock cut bread. He'd hidden it himself, and forgotten. Or he hadn't forgotten. I'll never know that either.

I had one card from her. It came two years after, with a Portuguese stamp. It was a picture of a tram. On the back, no signature, in a hand I'd only ever seen once, in eyebrow pencil on an envelope:

*It isn't the right time here either.*

* * *

That's all of it. I've put it down in the order it happened to me, and I've given you the time off my own wrist for every part. I haven't made myself look any better than I was. You'll have seen that.

I know what the pathologist said. I was there. *Alive when he went into the water.* I've turned it every way there is. I've told myself the old man hit him, and I've told myself she doped him. Then somebody carted him out of that ice house, and somebody put shot in him, and somebody put him in the fleet. And through all of that he had some flicker left in him, deep down, that a lighter couldn't show and a doctor could. So it was the sea that finished it. That's how I've had to leave it. It makes five or six people in that house a party to it, one way and another. And I've got no names for half of them.

It's not good enough. I know that. I never closed it.

But I'll say this, and then I've done. I stood at that gate. I put my arm through the bars with a flame in my hand and I looked at him for the best part of a minute. He was at the bottom of twelve steps with his feet higher than his head, and his eyes were open and the light was in them and they didn't move. I'd done it for twenty years. I knew my job when I knew nothing else. They can read me whatever they like off a sheet of paper.

Edmund Vane was dead at a quarter past one by my watch. I'd swear to it. I've sworn to worse.

# PART TWO {.part}

::: {.parttitle}
The Compline Business

*from* Mostly My Fault *by Toby Pargeter*
:::

## Editor's Note {.note}

Tobias Pargeter is a wine merchant, and at the time of writing is alive, solvent, and married for the third time, in that order of likelihood by his own account. In 2003 he had three hundred copies printed, at his own expense, of a volume of reminiscences called *Mostly My Fault*, which he distributed, the flyleaf says, "to friends, creditors, and wives, where these could be told apart." What follows is the eleventh chapter of that book, complete. He broke it into seven sections and I have kept his divisions and his headings.

It began life as an after-dinner story. I have spoken to several people who heard him tell it in the nineteen-nineties, at wine-trade suppers and at two weddings, and they agree that it was the best thing he did and that it ran about twenty-five minutes, and that he always stopped at the same place. The printed chapter does not stop there. It goes on for some two pages more, and those two pages were never part of the performance. His wife, the current one, told me that he wrote them in a single evening and would not have the book printed without them.

You will observe that Mr Pargeter is a comic writer and that he knows it. I ask you not to hold that against his evidence. A man who is trying to make you laugh has a strong motive to describe exactly what people did, because that is where the laughs are. He is, on matters of fact, the most scrupulous witness of the six. I have checked him against the dimensions of the stable yard, the weight of the object in question, and the recollections of Gail Pask, who is now Mrs Gail Thurlow and keeps a garden centre near Tiptree, and I have not caught him out once.

His watch was in the Font from seven o'clock. Every time he gives is house time, and most are from the clock on the kitchen wall. That clock was kept eight minutes fast. Mrs Pask set it so herself, every Monday, on the principle that a dinner which thinks it is late will come up on time, and she told nobody. Mr Pargeter did not know it. Nor, when he looked at the same clock an hour later, did Mr Cade.

You have just read that a man was dead. You are about to read that he was not. I remind you of what I said at the start, and I ask you to put a finger on the place.

## 1. In Which I Arrive by Sea

Let me say at once, for the benefit of the nervous reader, that nobody died. I am in a position to know, having carried the body.

I put that first because the story I am about to tell has a house on an island in it, and a storm, and a family dinner at which the host rose to accuse his nearest and dearest of a crime. Any reader who has been properly brought up will be feeling for the light switch at this point, and counting the guests. I know the kind of book you mean. My Aunt Hilary reads nothing else. I can only say that I was there, from five in the afternoon until a quarter to six the next morning, and that the worst thing that happened in my sight to any person under that roof was that a clergyman fell asleep. There was also an incident with a wheelbarrow, which I shall come to. Nobody could call it fatal.

It was my mother's idea. Most of the really bad ones were.

I should explain how I stood in the autumn of 1994. I was twenty-nine, and the wine trade had got hold of me in the way that the sea gets hold of some families. I had no gift for it, but all my friends were in it. I had recently been let go by a firm in St James's, quite amicably, after a misunderstanding about a pallet of Sancerre. I was living in two rooms in Fulham on what remained of a legacy from my grandmother. I had, however, an Opportunity. A man I had met at a tasting, a Bulgarian with a beautiful overcoat, was in a position to supply four hundred cases of a red wine from the Thracian valley at a price that would have made a Frenchman weep. All that was needed to secure it was five thousand pounds by the end of the month. I had three hundred and twelve.

I laid this before my mother over lunch. She heard me out. Then she said, "You must go and see your Uncle Leo."

"I haven't got an Uncle Leo."

"Of course you have. Granny's brother. The clock one. He's rolling in it, and he's never done a thing for any of us. He must be nearly dead. He has a party every October for the family and we're always asked and none of us ever goes, because it's in a swamp. I shall write and say you're coming."

"But I don't know him."

"All the better," said my mother. "He'll have nothing against you."

So I went. I think it was Napoleon who said he would rather have a lucky general than a clever one. My mother has always had the same view of sons, and I have been a steady disappointment to her on both counts.

* * *

I had at that time a motor car, an MG Midget in a shade the makers called Flame. It was nineteen years old. I had bought it from a man in the trade who was emigrating, and I have often wondered since whether that was why. It had a number of ways of expressing itself. There was a knock that meant the weather was going to change. There was a smell of hot toffee that came on at about sixty, and one learned to respect it. And there was a habit, in the wet, of simply ceasing. It didn't cough or struggle about it. It stopped, the way a horse stops at a ditch it has thought about, and no amount of language would shift it till it had dried out.

I mention this because it rained all the way from Chelmsford.

My mother's letter had produced a reply, on thick paper, from a Mrs Edmund Vane. It said that they would be delighted, that the road was tidal and I must on no account try to cross before a quarter past five, and that I should bring a dinner jacket and not expect to sleep. I thought that last a hospitable touch at the time.

I will not describe the country. Mr Cade, who was also of the party, and of whom more later, once told me it reminded him of the inside of a filing cabinet, and I can't improve on that. The Midget, for once, had gone like a bird. I reached a village at twenty to five and a sea wall at a quarter to, and from the top of the sea wall I looked down upon my uncle's drive.

It was just coming up out of the sea. There was a road, of a sort, lying on the mud like something dropped, with sticks either side of it, and it went away into the murk toward a lump with trees on. A good deal of water was still lying about on it. Beside the road at the top of the slope was a notice board, which I read with close attention. It said that one should on no account cross within three hours of high water, and that the sea came in faster than one could walk.

There was a card with the times. Road closed, it said, from 8.40 a.m. until 4.12 p.m.

I looked at my watch, which was the Mickey Mouse one, of which also more later. It was ten to five. The road had therefore been open, by the estate's own figures, for thirty-eight minutes. Mrs Vane's quarter past five I put down to a hostess's natural caution. One expects a certain amount of water on a road that has recently been the sea. I let in the clutch with a light heart. It did not occur to me to read the small print at the bottom of the card. It never has. I am told this is how they get you with timeshares.

For those who have not driven on a causeway, I can report that it is very like driving on a road, but that one's opinion of the road keeps changing. For the first two hundred yards I thought it rather jolly. There were birds. For the second two hundred I noticed that the surface was not so much wet as provisional. Then I came to a place about halfway over where the whole thing went down in a dip, to cross a sort of creek by a bridge made of planks, and the dip was not there. Where it should have been there was a sheet of water about the size of a tennis court, with the two rows of sticks marching down into it and out the other side.

I took it at speed. I had been told that one should. The Midget went into that water like a labrador, with a great fan of spray on either side. It found the bridge, more by its luck than my judgment, came out on the far side, went up the slope for about its own length, and ceased.

I knew that silence. I had heard it on the Hammersmith flyover and outside a registry office in Reigate. I sat for a moment with my hands on the wheel. Then I got out, into about eight inches of the North Sea, put up the bonnet, and looked at the engine, which is what one does. I have never known what I was looking for. There was steam coming off it and the smell of toffee.

It was now, by Mickey, three minutes to five. I lit a cigarette and leaned on the wing and looked about me, and it was then that I noticed the creek.

It was going under the plank bridge like an express train. There was foam on it. Bits of weed were going by at the pace of a man running for a bus. I am a Londoner, and the only tide I had ever had to do with was the one at Putney, which is a gentlemanly affair. I looked at that water, and I looked at the sea, which appeared to be on every side of me, and I asked myself a simple question. Was it coming in, or going out?

I had no idea. I don't know how one tells. I stood in it, in a yellow pullover, with the dusk coming down, and all at once the notice board came back to me with terrible clearness. *Faster than you can walk.* I looked at my watch again. I looked at the thirty-eight minutes I had been so pleased with, and wondered for the first time whose minutes they were.

I should like to say that I acted with decision. What I did was walk round the car. I walked round it several times, briskly, as though the trouble might be on the other side. I tried the starter. I spoke to the car quite frankly about its past. I thought of pushing, and discovered what every Midget owner discovers in the end, that it is a very small car until you try.

Beside the bridge there was a wooden hut on four posts, about fifteen feet up, with a ladder. I had taken it for something to do with birds. It now came to me, with the force of revelation, what it was actually for. I splashed across to it and got a foot on the bottom rung.

The bottom rung came off.

It did not break, exactly. It gave a sort of sigh and came away at one end, and hung there by a nail. I looked at it. I looked at the one above, which was the colour of a mushroom and about as firm. I am six foot three and at that period I weighed thirteen stone. It was plain that whoever had built that ladder had had a smaller refugee in mind.

I pushed the rung back into its socket. I don't know why. One does. It seemed rude to leave it. It stayed there, more or less, with the nail sticking out, looking perfectly sound to anybody who didn't put a foot on it. I have had that rung on my conscience since. I once woke in the night thinking of it. But I am getting ahead of myself.

I was standing at the foot of that hut, with the sea over my shoes, composing in my head the paragraph that would appear in the *Essex County Standard*, when I heard an engine.

* * *

It was a tractor. It was coming toward me from the island end, very slowly, pushing a bow wave. A young man was driving it. He was thin and dark and he had a cigarette in the exact centre of his mouth. Behind him, standing on the drawbar with her hands on his shoulders, was a girl with no hair.

I say no hair. She had the kind one sees on a tennis ball. She was wearing army boots and a man's dress shirt and she was laughing so much she could hardly stand. As they came up she pointed at me and shouted something, and the young man took the cigarette out of his mouth.

"Are you the wine one?" he called.

I said I was Toby Pargeter, and that I thought we ought to hurry, because of the tide.

"Kit. This is Saskia. We saw you from the tower." He stopped the tractor and regarded me. "What about the tide?"

"Well. It's coming in. Isn't it?"

"It's going out."

"Oh," I said.

"It's been going out since half past one. You could sit there till nine o'clock tonight and not wet your knees. You've just come twenty minutes before it had finished, that's all. Didn't you read the bottom of the card?" He jumped down, up to his shins, with a rope. "Compline time. An hour behind yours. Grandfather won't have the other sort on the place. Nobody reads it. In the spring they turn up an hour late and we go out for them in the punt. In the autumn they turn up early and sit in the Rill with their bonnets up. He says it teaches people to finish a sentence."

"I thought I was going to be drowned."

"Sass had a bet you'd try the Perch," said Kit. "I owe her a fiver. Did the ladder hold?"

"Not altogether."

"No. Father's been going to see to that since I was at school." He was already under my front bumper. "You'd not have drowned. But another ten minutes sitting in that and you'd have had salt in everything, and then you'd have a garden ornament. Sass, get the jacket off the hook, I want the hook."

The girl reached under the back of the tractor and unhooked a black dinner jacket, of all things, which had been hanging there like a dead rook. She put it on over the shirt. It came down to her knees.

"We've been dressing the Jacks," she said to me, as if that explained it. "This one's spare. Your car's a really horrible colour, did you know?"

"It's called Flame."

"It's called a mistake." She had a wide, gappy grin. I liked her at once, in the way one likes a dog that has just knocked one over.

Kit Vane had got the rope round something. He did it with about two movements, without looking. He had extraordinary hands, like a surgeon's, and he kept the cigarette going throughout. I have never been able to tie anything, including my own tie, without a mirror and a run at it.

"Get in and steer," he said. "Don't brake. Don't do anything clever."

"I never do anything clever."

"No," he said, looking at the Midget. "I can see that."

So I arrived at Compline House backwards. That is to say I was towed, at the end of twenty feet of rope, through the retreating sea, behind a tractor, steering a dead car with the hood down.
