I think of him still sitting on that table with a goose bone, saying, "Hallo, it's the pudding."

But I know what a large contusion over the occiput is. I was there. I heard it. It sounded like a melon dropped on a kitchen floor.

He was awake afterwards. I hold on to that. He spoke to me in the yard, and he was sitting up an hour and a half later, eating and talking, in the best spirits I ever saw in him. I've asked two doctors, without saying why. I asked them at dinner, as a general question. They both said the same. A man can take a blow like that and walk about for hours. He can feel perfectly well. He can feel unusually well, they said; rather light, as if a weight had been lifted. And then, quite suddenly, his balance may go, or he gets sleepy, or he doesn't quite know where he is.

*I feel as if somebody had taken a hundredweight off my back,* he said. *I suppose it's concussion.*

Some time after a quarter past two, my cousin Edmund went down to the water. Nobody knows why. Nobody saw him go. I think he went to look at the tide. I think he was dizzy, and that he was dizzy because of me.

Mrs Pask had the barrow. She knew the ground and was taking it round the block, slowly, picking her way. I was twenty-nine, and I felt a fool walking alongside with a box. I said, "Do let me," and took hold of a handle.

I only wanted to help. That's what I said to her at the time, on the cobbles. It's what I have said to myself ever since, and it's true, and it doesn't alter the outcome in the least. I caught the pudding, and I dropped the man. If I'd let the box go and held on to the barrow, he'd have slid out onto his feet, or onto his backside, and sworn at me, and I'd have a broken clock on my conscience and nothing else.

I never told anyone. I never told the man Cade, who would have known what to do with it. I never told Hester in the tea shop, though I had it ready. She said there was a thing she had done that night which she thought about every day, and I very nearly said, so have I. I should like to know what hers was. It cannot have been as bad.

I notice that I began this chapter by saying that I had carried the body. I wrote that sentence a long time ago, for a different purpose. It was the first line of the after-dinner version, and it always got a laugh, because the audience knew that the body was going to sit up and ask for goose. I've left it where it was. It is still true. I didn't know how true when I wrote it.

Nobody died that night in my sight. I can swear to that. When I shut the baize door he was alive.

But it was mostly my fault. I've thought so for nine years. I called the whole book that so that I could put this chapter in it.

# PART THREE {.part}

::: {.parttitle}
The Grey Room

*by Hester Quaile*
:::

## Editor's Note {.note}

Hester Mary Quaile wrote this in the summer of 1995, in three red exercise books, at a hospital in York where she was then a patient. A doctor there, a Dr Imrie, had asked her to set down what had happened to her at Compline, in order, without stopping to decide whether she believed it. She told me that it was the best advice she was ever given and that she has passed it on to a great many people since.

She did not write it for print. She became a writer afterwards; under her initials she has published five novels, every one of which has a house in it, and she is alive and well and lives on the north-east coast with a view of the sea that she says she chose on purpose. When I asked whether I might use the exercise books she took a week to answer. Then she said yes, on one condition, which was that I should not correct them.

I have not corrected them. That includes the places where she and I both now know that there is another explanation for what she saw. You will find that she knows it too, in the writing itself. She was a trained nurse and a careful person, and I do not think there is a single page on which she fails to tell you what a sensible woman would conclude. She tells you, and then she tells you what she saw.

I am not going to say which of those you should prefer. I will say that I have stood in the long gallery at Compline at midnight, in October, and that I would not have stayed to take notes.

Two practical matters. Miss Quaile arrived at Compline three weeks before the night in question, and so she alone of the six gives you the house as it was beforehand. I have let that stand at its full length, since without it you will not understand what the others walked into. And her times are house times, read from the clocks round her, of which there was always one in sight. She had been told on her first day to put her own watch back an hour. She did so, and never changed it again while she lived there.

You will meet in these pages a conversation you have read once already, in Mr Pargeter's account. I have compared the two versions word for word. They agree.

## I. The Crossing

Dr Imrie says that I am to begin at the beginning and that I am not to explain. I have told him that I do not know where the beginning is. He says that in that case I am to begin with the first thing I saw, and so I shall begin with the water.

I came to Compline on the first day of October, in the afternoon, by the bus from Maldon. It set me down at the end of a village street with my one case and went away. I had been told that I should be met. No one was there. There was a church with a squat flint tower and a row of cottages with their doors shut, and beyond the last cottage the road ran up onto a green bank and seemed to end in the sky.

I walked up it. I am from Whitby, and I was brought up within the sound of the sea, and I had thought when I took the post that the sea at least would be no stranger to me. But our sea at home is a thing that stands up. It comes at the cliff and breaks, and you may hate it or love it, but you know where it is. From the top of that bank I looked for the sea and could not find it. There was a grey plain running out to a grey horizon, without a wave on it or a rock, and I could not tell what was land and what was not. A line of thin poles went away across it, getting smaller. There were birds crying. It was absolutely flat, and yet as I stood I had the plain sensation that I was looking down into something, as one looks down into a well.

Far out, at the end of the poles, there was a dark rise with trees on it, and among the trees a roof.

I have asked myself since whether I felt anything then. It would be easy to say that I did. I have read the kind of book in which a young woman comes to a house and knows at the first sight of its chimneys that she will suffer there, and I despised those books when I was a girl, because it seemed to me that a person with any sense would turn round. I can only say that I did not turn round. I had eleven pounds, and a reference, and nowhere else to go. And I will be truthful, since that is the whole purpose of this. What I felt, looking at that roof across the flats, was not dread. It was relief. I thought: it is a long way from anywhere, and there will be no one there who knows.

There was a notice at the top of the slope, and I read it through, to the end, as I read everything. It gave the hours when the road was closed. At the foot, in red, it said that all times were Greenwich Mean Time. I looked at my mother's watch. I worked out that I had the best part of three hours, and then I picked up my case and went down the slope onto the sea bed and began to walk.

They call it the Wade. It is nine hundred yards, and I counted my steps for the first part of it, from an old habit of the wards, where one counts everything. The surface was shingle and broken stone, and there was weed on it, still wet. Either side the mud lay shining, with small creeks winding through, and in the creeks the water was moving, though I could not have said which way. No sound came from the land behind me. I have never been in a place so wide that felt so much like a room.

Halfway over, the road dipped to cross a deeper channel on a bridge of planks. Beside the bridge stood a wooden box on four tall legs, black with tar, with a ladder against it and a small shut door. I stopped and looked at it. I knew what it must be for. I thought of someone climbing that ladder in the dark, with the water coming, and sitting in that box through the night to listen to it go by underneath.

I thought: someone has done that. I do not know why I was so sure. But I had been a nurse for five years. When one comes onto a ward at night one learns to tell, without being told, in which bed there has been a death. It is nothing one sees. The bed is made up fresh, and it has a kind of attention about it. That box on its legs had it.

I walked on rather faster. I did not count any more.

* * *

The house does not show itself until one is almost upon it. The road comes up off the flats between banks, and turns, and there is a sweep of gravel, and one sees it all at once and too close, as one sees a face that has come up beside one in a crowd.

It is a long house, and low, and it is not all of one age. The middle is very old, of narrow brick the colour of dried blood, with stone round the windows. A plain grey front has been put across this, like a mask, with tall sashes and a pillared door. At one end a later wing runs back, with pointed gables. There are a great many chimneys. The trees round it all lean one way, away from the sea, with their branches streaming, as though they had been caught in the act of running from it and fixed there.

Opposite the front door, across the gravel, is a range of stables with an arch through the middle, and above the arch a square tower with a clock. I looked at the clock, naturally, to see the time. It said ten minutes to three. My watch said ten to four.

I thought it had stopped. Then, while I looked, I saw the long hand move. And above the clock face, under a little tiled roof, I saw that there were two people standing, and looking down at me.

I have been told since that everyone who comes to Compline has that moment, and that the family think it rather a joke. They are figures of carved oak, as large as life, a man and a woman. They stand either side of a bell, and each has a hammer. The man strikes the quarters and the woman the hours. They have been there two hundred years and are called Jack and Jenny, and children are held up to wave to them.

I did not wave. I stood with my case on the gravel and looked at the woman. She is the taller. She wears a gown painted grey, with long sleeves, and her face is painted too, though the weather has taken most of it, so that there is only the suggestion of eyes. Her right arm is lifted, with the hammer, as high as her shoulder. She does not look at the bell. She looks out, over the yard, toward the house and the Wade beyond it, and I thought she had the look of a woman who has been waiting for someone longer than is reasonable, and who has made up her mind to it.

I do not know how long I should have stood there. A door banged, and a girl of sixteen or seventeen in an apron came running round the end of the house and said that I must be the nurse, and that they had been going to send Kit with the car, only nobody had told Kit. She took my case from me. Her name was Gail. She said that I was to come in by the kitchen, since the front was only opened for company, and that her auntie would give me my tea.

"Does it always say the wrong time?" I asked her. I meant the tower.

She looked up at it, and then at me, as though I had asked whether the grass was always green.

"That's the right time," she said. "That's Compline time. It's all the rest that's wrong."

* * *

I was given my tea in the kitchen by a Mrs Pask. She was the cook, and I came to respect her more than anyone else in that house, though I do not think she ever quite approved of me. She was a broad, short, silent woman with strong arms. She watched me eat a piece of bread and butter as though she were making up her mind how long I should last.

"You'll have been told about the old gentleman," she said.

I said that Mr Fenn had told me he was eighty-one, and that his memory was failing, and that he walked at night.

"He walks," said Mrs Pask. "He don't sleep above three hours, and then he's up. He'll be all over. The Shop, that's his workshop, down under. The long gallery. Out to the stable to wind the tower. Out on the wall. It's the wall we don't like. He's no notion of the cold, and he's no notion where his feet are, and there's a fifteen-foot drop to the saltings. You're to keep him off the wall."

"How am I to keep him off it?"

"I don't know," she said. "That's what you're for."

She told me the hours. I was to sit with him from ten at night until six in the morning. He had a sleeping draught at ten, one spoonful in water, from a bottle that I must keep on a tray and let no one else touch. In the daytime I might sleep until noon. After that I was to make myself useful with the papers.

"What papers are those?"

"Mrs Vane's. Her letters and such. There's a deal of them, in the morning-room desk and in boxes, and they've never been touched. Mr Vane wants them put in order. He says she'll be vexed to come home and find them in a muddle." Mrs Pask looked at me steadily. "She's dead. She's been dead twenty years this month. You're not to tell him so."

"Does he not know it?"

"Some days. Some days he knows it as well as you or me, and them's the bad days. Other days she's gone up to change, or she's over at the farm, or she's just this minute left the room. He'll ask you has she come in. You say, not yet, sir. That's what we all say. It does no harm, and it saves him having it to hear new."

I said nothing. I had my own opinion about that. I have been a nurse, and I have seen what is done to old people by those who lie to them out of kindness, and I had made a private rule that I would not do it. But I had been in the house for a quarter of an hour, and it was not the time.

"And you'll want to put your watch right," said Mrs Pask. "Back an hour. Mr Edmund'll tell you the same. You'll go mad else."

I took off my mother's watch and put it back an hour, there at the kitchen table. It was a small thing to do. I have thought about it a great deal. I think that it was the moment I came to belong to that house, and that I did it with my own fingers, because I was asked.

I should say that it is not only a matter of the clocks. One can alter a watch. But for the whole of the three weeks that followed I lived an hour behind the rest of the country, and I found that it did something to me that I had not foreseen. I had no wireless. I saw no newspaper until it was a day old. When I thought of my mother in Whitby sitting down to her tea, I had to remember that she had sat down to it an hour ago; and by degrees I stopped thinking of her. It was as though the house stood a little way back from the present, in a place that the present had already left. Everything that happened in the world had happened by the time it reached us. I do not know how to say it better than that. At Compline it was always slightly too late.

* * *

There are a hundred and eleven clocks in the house. I was told the number on my first evening by Mr Edmund Vane, who said that I should not try to count them, as it had driven a housemaid out of her mind in 1931.

I heard them before I saw them. Gail took me up by the back stairs to a small room on the first floor, next to the old gentleman's, and left me to unpack, and when she had shut the door I stood still and listened. I had been hearing it, I found, ever since I came into the kitchen, without attending to it, as one hears rain. It came through the walls and up through the floor. It was a ticking; but there were so many, at so many different paces, that they made together a kind of soft continuous rustle with a pulse in it. I thought of a great many people in a dark room, whispering.

And every quarter of an hour the house spoke. I learned to wait for it. One clock would begin, somewhere below, and then another on the stairs, and a third, in no order, each with its own voice. There were small sharp ones and deep slow ones and one, in the long gallery, that had a cracked note like a cough. No two struck together. It would take a full minute for the hour to pass through the house from one end to the other, like a rumour, and when the last of them had done there was always a moment's pause before the tower clock answered from across the yard. One could hear the big bell, and one knew that it was the grey woman, bringing down her arm.

I thought, that first night, that I should never sleep in it. As it happened I was not required to.

I met the family at dinner. I shall not say much of them here, since they will come in their places. There was a Mrs Edmund Vane, who was fair and handsome and tired, and who spoke to me kindly and forgot me the moment her head was turned. There was her husband. And at the head of the table there was the old gentleman, my patient, to whom I was presented as "Miss Quaile, who has come to help with Mother's papers."

He rose. He was very tall. He took my hand in both of his and bent over it and looked into my face through a magnifying glass that he wore on a cord, and I stood and was looked at.

"You've been on nights," he said.

"Yes, sir. For four years."

"It shows about the eyes. It is the same with watchmakers; we lose the use of daylight." He let go my hand. "You are a nurse, and they have told you that I'm to be watched. Don't trouble to deny it. They think I don't know. I know a great deal that I'm not supposed to, and then I forget it, which is very convenient for them." He smiled. He had a smile of great sweetness, like a child's. "I shall try not to be a nuisance. I should be obliged if you would not lie to me. Everyone else does."

"I shan't lie to you, Mr Vane."

"No," he said. "I don't believe you will. You have that sort of mouth." And then, turning to the empty place on his right, which I had not understood until that moment, he said in exactly the same tone: "Margot, this is the young person. She says she will not tell me lies. We shall see how long she keeps it up."

There was a chair there, drawn back, and a place laid. He waited, with his head a little bent, as one waits for a reply. Then he nodded and sat down.

I looked round the table. Mrs Vane was looking at her plate. Her husband was looking at me.

He was a big dark man in his fifties, heavy, with a handsome ruined face and a glass in his hand. I had been conscious of him ever since I came into the room, as one is conscious of a fire. He looked at me across the candles while his father spoke to the empty chair, and he lifted one eyebrow, very slightly. It was not mockery. It was the look that one gives to a new member of the staff on a difficult ward, over the head of a patient. It said: yes, it is as bad as you think, and you will get used to it, and I am sorry.

I looked down. I felt the colour come into my face, and I was angry with myself. I had come to that house to be nobody. It was not in my plans to be seen, and by him least of all.

* * *

I sat up that night for the first time in the room they call the Admiral's, where Mr Vane sleeps.

It is a large room on the first floor at the front, with three windows looking east across the gravel to the stables. There is a great bed with curtains. There were seven clocks in it then. I had given him his draught at ten, the one spoonful in water, and he had drunk it down obediently and thanked me, and by half past he was asleep on his back with his long hands folded on the sheet, like a figure on a tomb.

I sat in a low chair by the fire with a shaded lamp and a book, which I did not read. It was very quiet, apart from the seven clocks. The wind had fallen. I had left one curtain a little drawn back, as I always do, since I cannot bear to be shut in a room at night without some sight of the sky. Through the gap I could see the top of the tower with its two figures, black against the stars.

I should explain why I do not sleep at night. Dr Imrie knows; he has had it all from me, and it took him four months. I shall put it here in a few lines, since it belongs with the rest, and then I need not come back to it.

I was a staff nurse at a hospital in Scarborough, on a women's medical ward. I had been on nights for the best part of four years, by my own wish. In the March of last year I had charge of the ward, alone, with one auxiliary. There was a patient in the end bed, a Mrs Aske, who was seventy-six and had been admitted with her chest. She was not thought to be in danger. She was to be looked at every half hour. At three in the morning I sat down at the desk to write up the charts. I had been awake for twenty-two hours, as I had been to my father's that day, and I put my head on my arm for a moment.

It was twenty past four when I lifted it. I went down the ward at once. Mrs Aske was lying half out of the bed. She had tried to reach the bell, and it had fallen, and she had tried to reach it on the floor. She had been dead, they told me afterwards, about three-quarters of an hour. Her hand was still stretched out.

There was an inquiry, and I was not dismissed. They said that the staffing had been at fault and that I had an unblemished record. They were very fair. I resigned on the day the finding was read to me, and I have not worked in a hospital since.

I do not think that I shall ever be able to describe to anyone what that hand was like. But I can say what it did. Since that night I have not been able to sleep in the dark. I lie down, and I begin to go, and at the edge of it I see the ward and the end bed, and I am awake with my heart going like a hammer. I can sleep in daylight, with the curtains open and the sounds of people about. So I looked for night work, of the private kind, where there would be only one patient and I could sit by him and never close my eyes. I answered an advertisement in *The Lady*. That is how I came to be in the Admiral's room at Compline on the first night of October, with an old man asleep and seven clocks going.

I thought it would suit me very well. I had only to stay awake and watch, and I had no fear of failing at that. I knew I should never again do the other thing.

* * *

He woke at a quarter past one. He woke all at once, with no confusion, and sat up and put his feet to the floor.

"Mr Vane," I said. "It's the middle of the night."

"I know what it is." He was feeling for his slippers. "It's a quarter past one. I must go across. There is the tower to wind; it's a thirty-hour movement, and I let it go yesterday."

"It can be wound in the morning."

"It cannot. It'll be down by four, and she will lose the hour." He stood up. He looked about him, with a troubled face. "Where is my wife?"

I had known that it would come. I had not thought that it would come on the first night.

I stood up too. I put my book down on the chair. I was a good deal frightened. I had a rule and I had promised it to him at the dinner table, in front of his family, and I could see, very clearly, the easy thing. *She has not come in yet, sir.* It would have cost me five words, and he would have nodded, and I could have led him back to bed.

"Mr Vane," I said. "Do you want me to tell you the truth?"

He looked at me. In the lamplight his eyes were extraordinarily pale.

"You said that you would."

"Your wife is dead. I'm very sorry. She died twenty years ago. She was drowned."

I waited for it to break on him. I have told people that kind of thing before, in the small hours, in my uniform, and I have held them afterwards. I was ready for him to cry out. I was ready for him to fall, and I had moved near enough to catch him.

He did none of those things. He stood quite still by the bed, in his nightshirt, and I saw his face change. It did not crumple. It settled. It was like watching a man who has been looking everywhere for something find that he has had it in his hand.

"Yes," he said. "On the Wade. In the Odd Hour. I had put the clocks back before dinner, to save a scramble, and so she had the wrong time for the tide." He said it over to himself, like a lesson. "I knew that. Thank you. I knew it, and then I didn't. It gets away from me. It goes round a corner, and I'm left standing with the feeling that there's something I have forgotten to do." He put a hand on the bedpost. "They tell me she is upstairs. I go up, and she is not. Then I think she's angry with me, and is hiding. That is a great deal worse, you know. It is much worse than her being dead."

"I should think it must be."

"You'll tell me again? When I ask?"

"Every time."

"I shall very likely be rude."

"I've been shouted at before, Mr Vane."

"I daresay you have." He looked at me for a moment longer. Then he reached out, as naturally as a child, and patted my cheek. "You're a good girl. You have had some great trouble; I don't know what, and I shan't ask. It has made you truthful. It takes people that way or it takes them the other." He drew himself up. "And now I must wind the tower, because if I do not she'll lose her hour, and I've lost her enough."

I could not stop him. I did not think that I had the right. I put his dressing gown on him, and his overcoat over it, and found his shoes, and I lit a lantern and went with him.

We went down through the sleeping house, and out at the side door, and across the gravel under the stars. He walked slowly, with his hand on my arm. He told me as we went that the tower clock had been made by his great-great-grandfather in 1790, and that the Jacks had been carved by a man from Ipswich who did ships' figureheads. That was why Jenny looked out to sea, he said. She had been meant for the bow of a ship, and the ship had never been built.

He climbed the ladder-stair in the harness room by himself. I went up behind him with the lantern, to be under him if he fell. At the top there is a chamber, eight or nine feet square, with the great iron frame of the clock in the middle and a pendulum as long as a man swinging through a slot in the floor. It was bitterly cold. There are louvres in the walls and the wind comes straight through. A door on one side opens onto the leads, where the figures stand.

He wound it with a crank handle as long as his arm. It took him a quarter of an hour, with rests. I offered to do it and he would not let me. I stood and held the light.

When it was done he leaned on the frame, breathing. He looked at the door to the leads.

"Would you care to see her?" he said. "You'll not have been so near."

I did not want to. I should like that to be written down. I had no wish in the world to open that door. But he had it open before I could speak, and the night came in, and I went and stood on the sill.

She was a yard from me. I had only seen her from the ground. I had not understood how large she was. She is nearly six feet, and broad, and carved from a single trunk, and the grain of the oak runs up through her like sinew. They had painted her gown grey, long ago, and the paint has crazed all over into fine lines like the skin on old hands. Her face was turned away from me, outward. Her arm was up.

I held the lantern a little higher. And I had the most distinct impression that she had only just turned her head. It was nothing that I saw. It was what one feels on coming into a room where the talk has stopped.

"She strikes the hours," said Mr Vane behind me. "And he the quarters. So she has a great deal of time to stand, between. I have often thought that it was hard on her. I asked my father when I was a boy what she thought about, all that while. He said she was counting. He said that Jenny was counting up all the hours she had struck, and that when she got to the end of the sum she would come down."

"What did he mean by that?"

"I have no idea. He was a silent man, and it was a great many words for him. I've never forgotten it." He was looking past me, at the grey figure, with great affection. "My wife is painted in a gown of that colour. I chose it. She laughed at me; she said I wanted her to match the clock. She was quite right. I did."

The works behind us gave a whirr and a clank. I stepped back, quickly, into the chamber. A rod moved in the frame. Out on the leads, with a creak of old iron, the small figure on the far side of the bell lifted his hammer and struck, twice, and the note went out over the yard.

It was half past one. The woman did not move. It was not her turn.

I got him back to his bed by two, and he slept till seven. I sat in the low chair by the fire. I had drawn the curtain right across this time, over the gap.

I have said that I thought the work would suit me. I thought so still. But I had learned something on that first night which I had not known when I walked across the Wade with my case. I had believed that I was coming to a place where no one knew me, and where I might watch and never be looked at.

I had been in the house nine hours. I had been seen three times: by an old man with a glass, by his son across a table, and by a thing on a tower that was made of wood.

In the morning, when Gail brought me a cup of tea, I asked her what was in the room at the end of the long gallery. I had passed the door on my way down. It was the only one on that floor that was shut.

"That's the Grey Room," she said. "That was hers. That's kept locked."

"Who has the key?"

"Miss Imogen has one, but she's in Scotland. And there's one somewhere of Mr Vane's, only he's lost it." She put the tea down. "You don't want to go in there, miss. Nobody does. Auntie says it's just as she left it, with her frocks in the cupboard and her brushes on the table. Her shoes are still by the bed. She'd took them off, see, that night. She went out to the Wade in her stockings."

## II. The Watches

I had three weeks of that life before the night came, and I am to set them down, Dr Imrie says, although nothing happened in them. I have told him that a great deal happened. It was only that none of it could be seen.

My days went like this. I left Mr Vane at six, when Gail came up with his tea, and went to my bed in the little room next door and slept with the curtains open until the light was strong. At noon I got up. In the afternoons I sat in the morning room on the garden side of the house, at a desk that had been his wife's, and sorted her papers into heaps. At ten I gave him his draught and took my chair by the fire. Between one and two in the morning, on most nights, he woke, and then we walked.

I came to know the house in the dark better than I ever knew it by day. He went where he pleased and I went with him, a pace behind, with the lamp. We went down to the Shop, where he would stand at his bench and pick up a tool and look at it, and lay it down exactly where it had been. We went along the long gallery. We went across to the tower every night to wind the great clock, and I learned to stand with my back to the door that opened on the leads.

He talked. I think that he had not been listened to for some years, except as one listens to a child, and when he found that I answered what he had said and not what was convenient, he opened to me like a book that has been long shut. He told me about the going of clocks. I did not understand a tenth of it. But I understood, after a time, what it was to him. He believed that there was a true time, which was the sun's, and that a good clock was a kind of honest witness to it, and that a man who kept one in order was doing a small right thing in the world, every day, by which others might set themselves.

"And then they passed the Act," he said to me, one night, on the stairs. "In the year 'sixteen, when I was three years old. They said the clocks should all be moved an hour forward in the spring, and so they were, and so they have been ever since. Do you understand what that is? It is a lie agreed upon. The sun stands where he stood. Noon is when he crosses the meridian of the place; that is what the word means. And forty million people look at their watches and say it is one o'clock."

"It gives them lighter evenings, Mr Vane."

"It gives them nothing. There is exactly as much light as before. They have only chosen to get up earlier and to call it something else, so as not to notice." He was quite calm about it; he had been angry for so long that it had worn smooth. "I put up with it for fifty-eight years. I changed the clocks in this house every spring and every autumn, like a good citizen, and I made a ceremony of the autumn for my wife's sake, because she liked a party. And on the night of the autumn change in 1974 it killed her."

"How did it kill her?"

"She went by the clock in the hall. She thought she had an hour more than she had." He stopped, with his hand on the rail. "I had put them back early. Before dinner. It is a long business, a hundred and eleven clocks, and I had always done it at the Hour, with the family, and that year I was tired, and I thought, I will get it over. So that when she looked at the hall clock and it said two, the world's clocks said three, and the tide goes by the world. She walked out onto the Wade with a quarter of an hour in hand, believing that she had an hour and a quarter. And I had done it. With these hands. To save myself a scramble."

"You couldn't have known that she would go out."

"No. I did not know that. I didn't know why she went, for a long time. They kept it from me. And then I did know, and then I forgot again, and now I'm not perfectly sure." He looked down at me, and his face was puzzled and gentle. "I think that she was going to someone. I think that is what I knew. Was she?"

"I can't tell you, Mr Vane. I never heard."

"No. You weren't here. I must ask Edmund. Edmund will know; he was always about, on that night." He went on down the stairs. "I have never changed a clock in this house since. Not one. I told them that the Act might do as it liked on the other side of the water, but that at Compline we should keep the hour that killed her, since it was the true one. And I've owed her the other ever since."

"Owed her?"

"The hour. The one I took. A man who takes an hour from his wife owes it to her; that is simple bookkeeping. I've been twenty years thinking how it was to be paid." He nodded to himself, in the dark. "I believe that I've found a way. I shall show you, one night. It wants only the occasion."

I thought it was his illness speaking. I had been told that he was confused. I was to learn that he was never less confused than when he talked like that, and that he meant every word precisely.

* * *

It was in the long gallery that he liked best to walk, and it was there, on my second night, that he took me to see her.

The gallery runs the whole length of the first floor on the west side, a hundred feet or more, with windows along one wall that look toward the Wade. It is panelled, and the floor is of wide boards that have sunk in the middle, so that one walks in a kind of shallow trough. There are clocks at intervals. At the far end, on the end wall, facing down the length of it, hangs the portrait.

I had seen it by day and had thought it a good picture of a handsome woman. I had not seen it by a single lamp, coming toward it from a hundred feet away, with an old man on my arm who was saying, "She will be so glad that you have come."

One sees the dress first. It is grey silk, and whoever painted it loved to paint silk; it has a light of its own. It comes out of the dark before the face does. Then the bare shoulders, and one hand resting on a chair-back, and last of all the face, which is not beautiful and is very much alive. The mouth is a little open. The eyes are grey, like the gown, and they are looking at you. I know that it is said of every portrait. I can only report that I moved from one side of the gallery to the other, on the pretext of trimming the lamp, and that I did not get away from them.

"There," said Mr Vane. "Margot, this is Miss Quaile. I told you of her."

He stood before the picture with his hands behind him. I stood a little to one side. Beneath the frame a tall clock was going, the one with the cracked voice. It was the only sound.

"She is laughing at me," he said presently. "You see it? She had just said something. I was in the room, and I had told the painter that he was not to make her look like a duchess, and she said, 'Leo wants me to look like something that keeps good time.' And the fellow caught it. I have never known how. He was not a clever man in any other way."

"She looks very kind."

"She was not especially kind. She was amused. It is a different thing, and wears better." He put out a hand and touched the bottom of the frame, lightly. "She was amused by me for thirty years. I don't think that I ever once amused anybody else. I used to hear her laugh in another part of the house and know that I had done something, or had been reported as doing it. I didn't mind. I found that I rather missed it, when it stopped."

"When did it stop?"

He considered. "Some while before the end. A year. Two. She was still kind to me then. That was how I knew."

I looked up at the face. I have said that I do not hold with the kind of book in which the heroine feels things. But I was a nurse, and I had been trained to look at faces for what they would not say. I thought, looking at Marguerite Vane, that she was a woman who had been waiting for a long time for someone to ask her a question. Nobody had. She had gone on being amusing in the meantime.

I thought too, and I am ashamed of it, that she was looking at me as one looks at a girl who has come to take a place in the household, to see how she would do.

We went back along the gallery. At the door that was shut he stopped, as he did every night, and laid his palm flat against the wood.

"She is asleep," he would say. Or, "She's not come up yet." Or once, on a bad night, "Why has she locked it? What have I done?" And on that night I said, "Mr Vane, she is dead," and he leaned his forehead on the panel and wept, and afterwards thanked me.

I never passed that door, in those three weeks, without feeling that there was someone on the other side of it who knew I was there.

* * *

I must write about Mr Edmund Vane. Dr Imrie says I have been going round it.

I have said that he looked at me across the table on my first evening, and that I was angry at being seen. I told myself that it was nothing, and that he was a man who had looked at a great many women. I daresay that was so. He was fifty-two. He had a wife. He drank from the middle of the morning and was never, in the time that I knew him, what could be called sober, though he was also never what could be called drunk. He carried it as he carried his bad leg, with a kind of impatient ease. Everyone in the house except his father spoke of him in the same tone, half exasperated and half protective, as one speaks of a large dog that has killed a hen.

He came into the morning room on the fourth or fifth afternoon. I was at the desk with a box of letters. He stood in the doorway with his glass.

"So you're the archivist," he said. "What are you finding?"

"Bills, mostly. Seed catalogues. Mrs Vane kept everything."

"She did. She kept every bus ticket. She said she liked to know where she'd been." He came across and looked over my shoulder. I could smell the whisky, and tobacco, and under those something clean, like cold air. He picked a photograph out of the heap. It was of a small boy on a pony, scowling. "Good God. That's me. I was eight. That animal bit me a minute later, and she laughed so much she dropped the camera."

"You look very fierce."

"I was frightened out of my wits. I've always looked fierce when I'm frightened; it has got me a reputation I haven't earned." He put it down. He looked at the heaps I had made, each with its label, and at my hands. "You're a neat creature. You do that the way my father does a movement. Everything laid out in the order it came off."

"It's how I was taught to do a dressing trolley."

"You were a hospital nurse, Fenn says. Why did you stop?"

I had been asked that by Mr Fenn, and by the agency, and I had an answer that I gave, about wishing for a change. I opened my mouth to give it. I do not know what happened. I think it was only that he had asked, and stood waiting, as though he would be interested in whatever I said.

"A patient died," I said. "In the night. I'd fallen asleep."

He did not say that he was sorry, or that I must not blame myself. He put his glass down on the corner of the desk.

"How long were you asleep?"

"An hour and twenty minutes."

"And she'd rung for you."

"She'd tried to."

"Did you tell them? That you'd slept?"

"I told them all. I told the night sister, and the matron, and the inquiry. I told her daughter."

"What did the daughter say?"

"She said, 'You poor girl.'" I had never told anyone that part. "I think I could have borne it if she had hit me."

He was silent. He had gone to the window. It looks out on what was once a garden, and beyond it the old glasshouse they call the orangery, with half its panes gone and a vine grown through the roof.

"Then you're a better man than I am, Miss Quaile," he said. "You told them."

I did not understand him. I said, "What did you do?"

He laughed. It was not a happy sound. "I? I woke up. That was all I ever did. I woke up, and it was getting light, and I walked home." He turned round and took up his glass again, and he was the large careless person that everyone knew. "Don't mind me. I talk nonsense in October. It's the equinox. Go on with your bus tickets. And Miss Quaile."

"Yes, Mr Vane?"

"Don't get fond of us. We're not a good investment. Ask my wife."

He went out. I sat with my hands in my lap. After a time I found that I had been looking at the photograph of the scowling child for some minutes. I put it in the heap that was labelled *Photographs, family, before 1955*.

I did get fond. I shall say it once and plainly and then leave it. I had not meant to. I was twenty-six, and plain, and had never been much noticed by anyone, and he had asked me a true question and listened to a true answer. I do not think it takes more than that. He never touched me, except once, by accident, at the dinner table on the last night, when his sleeve brushed my wrist. He never said a word to me that his wife might not have heard. But when he came into a room I knew it with my back turned. I found that I was listening, all day, among the hundred and eleven clocks, for the sound of an uneven step.

I have wondered whether she knew. The woman in the gallery. I used to feel, going past, that the amusement in her face had a different quality on some nights. I thought that she was saying to me, *Yes. I know. He was mine first, and I did him no good either.*

* * *

There was a second time, and it was at night.

It would have been the twelfth or thirteenth of the month. Mr Vane had slept through, as he did perhaps one night in four, and at three in the morning I went down to the kitchen to make myself tea. I was coming back through the hall with the cup when I saw that the library door was open. There was no light inside. But there was the smell of a cigarette.

I should have gone on up the stairs. I stood at the door instead.

He was sitting in a chair that he had drawn up to the table in the window. There was a little moon. On the table stood the great clock under its glass, the one they call the Thorne, which is the chief treasure of the house; I had been shown it and told what it was worth. Someone had taken off the cloth that covered it at night. The moon was on its face. All its small hands were going about, and he was sitting in front of it with his elbows on his knees, watching, as a man might sit and watch a fire.

"Come in, Miss Quaile," he said, without turning. "I knew your step. You walk like someone trying not to wake a ward."

I came in a little way. "I didn't know anyone was up."

"I'm always up, this month. I haven't slept through an October night in twenty years. I walk about. I sit. Sometimes I come and look at this." He nodded at the clock. "Do you know what it does?"

"It tells the tide."

"It tells everything. That's what he was after, old Thorne. He wanted one machine that would say where the sun was, and where the stars were, and the moon, and how high the water stood on the bar out there, all at once and for ever, with no one to touch it. And he very nearly did it. It's the cleverest thing I've ever seen made by a man. I helped my father put it together, the last two years. I was sixteen. I cut the moon's train." He drew on his cigarette, and I saw his face for a moment in the glow. "I've hated it ever since I was thirty-two."

"Why?"

"Because it knew. That night. It was standing here in this window, saying the tide to the minute. High water such a time. The Wade shut from such a time. It had it right. It always has it right. And nobody came and looked at it." He let the smoke go. "She did, I think. Mother. She was the only one who ever really used it; she said it was the one clock in the house that told you something you needed to know. She'd have looked. She knew exactly how long she had."

I stood very still. I was holding the cup in both hands.

"Your father thinks that she was misled by the hall clock," I said. "He thinks that he had put it back too soon and that she was an hour out."

"I know what my father thinks."

"Is it not true?"

"He did put them back early. That part's true." He was quiet for so long that I thought he would say no more. "It's a comfortable thing to believe, isn't it? That she made a mistake about the time. It's nobody's fault but a clock's. I've let him believe it for twenty years. He's built his whole life on it since; he's turned this house into a monument to it. And every one of these damned things that ticks is telling him, all day, it was the hour, Leo, it was the hour."

"And it wasn't?"

He turned his head then. I could not see his eyes.

"You're a truthful girl," he said. "My father says so. He says you won't lie to him. It's rather hard on the rest of us; we've got out of the way of it." He stubbed out the cigarette. "I'll tell you this much, since you told me yours. My mother never made a mistake about a tide in her life. She was born on this coast. She could tell you the state of the water by the smell. Whatever happened to her on the Wade that night, it wasn't arithmetic."

"Then what was it?"

"I woke up," Edmund Vane said. "I told you. And it was light."

He stood, heavily, and took the green cloth from the chair-back and laid it over the glass case. The little moving hands went out. At the door he paused beside me. He was a head and a half taller than I am. He looked down, and for a moment I thought that he was going to say something else. I do not know what I should have done if he had.

"Go and drink your tea, Miss Quaile," he said. "It'll be cold. Everything in this house gets cold while one's thinking about it."

He went away across the hall. I heard his step on the stairs, the one and then the other.

I did not sleep that day at all. I lay on my bed with the curtains open and watched the light move on the ceiling. He had told me that he had hidden something for twenty years, and that it was to do with his mother's death, and that he had been asleep when he should have been awake. He had told me as one tells a fellow sufferer. I should have felt the weight of it. What I felt, God forgive me, was that there were now two of us in the house.

* * *

On the night of the fifteenth, Mr Vane showed me how the debt was to be paid.

He woke at one. He was very clear that night, and brisk, and in a hurry. He would not walk in the gallery. He said that we must go across at once, since there was work to do and only a week to do it in, and he had me carry a canvas roll of tools that he took from the Shop.

We climbed to the clock chamber in the tower. It was a still night, with frost. He did not go to the winding handle. He went to a cupboard built into the corner of the chamber, a tall narrow one of old deal that I had taken for part of the wall, and he opened it with a key from his dressing-gown pocket.

"Hold the light there," he said.

There was something standing in the cupboard, on a shelf at the height of his chest, with a cloth over it. He drew the cloth away.

It was a clock. I thought for an instant that it was the Thorne itself, and that he had carried it across in the night. It had the same broad white dial and the same ring of small ones, and the same painted moon. But I had seen the Thorne under its glass in the library not six hours before, when I went through to fetch a book. So I knew that this must be the other. I had been told that there were copies. Gail had said that he had made a twin to the great clock, years ago, to teach himself how it went, and that it lived in a cupboard somewhere.

This one was going. I could hear it, under the slow saw of the tower works. And it was joined to them. From its back there ran two thin rods of bright new brass, through holes bored in the side of the cupboard, across a yard of air, to the iron frame of the great clock, where they ended in a little cage of wheels that had been clamped to one of the arbors. The brass was clean and yellow. Everything else in that chamber was two hundred years old and black. It looked like new growth on a dead tree.

"There," he said. He was breathing quickly. "I began it in September. I've done the most of it at night, since they think I am asleep. It's nearly complete. I have only to cut the last pinion, and set her to the year."

"What is it, Mr Vane?"

"I call it the Reconciler. It is a differential, of a kind. You'll not follow the train, and you needn't." He touched one of the rods with a fingertip, and it sang, faintly. "You know what happens on the night. At one o'clock by this house, the world puts its clocks back. It has run on for seven months an hour ahead of the truth, and it comes back, all at once, and agrees with us. It is two o'clock out there, and then it is one. Do you see? There's an hour that they have had, and now they are to have it again."

"Yes."

"Where does it come from?" He looked at me as a teacher looks at a slow pupil. "An hour is a real thing. It cannot be made from nothing. In March they take one, and say that it did not happen. In October they are given one back. It must be kept somewhere in between. I have thought about this for twenty years. It is kept, Miss Quaile. It is held over. And on the night, at the stroke, it is paid out again to everyone in England, and they sleep through it. They waste it. They turn over in their beds."

I said nothing. The frost was coming through the louvres. Out on the leads, a yard from the cupboard, behind the shut door, I knew that the grey woman was standing.

"I do not intend to waste mine," he said. "This house has never taken the false hour. So when the true one is paid back, we are not owed it. It goes past us. It has gone past us for twenty years, on this night, like a train through a station at which it does not stop. But I believe that it may be caught. That is what this is for. The great clock keeps our time, and the Thorne keeps the sun's, and the stars', and at the instant that the world's time falls back upon ours there is a difference between them of one hour exactly, and the Reconciler will take it up. It will take up the slack. Like a fusee." His hands moved, showing me. "And then I shall have it. I shall have an hour that is not on any clock. I shall go back through it. And I shall give her the tide properly."

"Give her—"

"I shall tell her the right time. I shall say, 'Margot, the clock in the hall is wrong; I put it back before dinner. It is three, not two. You have only a quarter of an hour.' And she'll not go. Or she will go by the punt. Or she'll run." He was smiling. His face was lit from below by my lantern, and it was the face of a man who has found, after long calculation, that the sum comes out. "She will get across. I have only to tell her. It is such a small thing. I have had the words ready for twenty years."

I have nursed people who believed that they were being poisoned by their relations, and one who believed that she was the Queen. I had been taught that one does not argue. I stood in that freezing chamber and looked at an old man's beautiful new brasswork, which had been made with more skill than I shall ever have at anything, to do a thing that could not be done. I found that I was not thinking of what I had been taught. I was thinking of a hand stretched out along a hospital floor. I was thinking that if someone had come to me with a machine and said, *You may have that hour and twenty minutes again*, I should not have asked how it worked.

"Mr Vane," I said. "I don't believe that it can be done."

"No," he said kindly. "You are a truthful girl, and you say what you think. I should be disappointed if you didn't. But you'll hold the lamp for me all the same, while I cut the pinion."

I held the lamp. He worked for two hours, with a file no thicker than a needle, on a wheel that I could have hidden under my thumbnail. His hands were perfectly steady. Once, behind us, the works gave their whirr and the quarter struck outside, and I felt the grey woman listen to it.

When he had finished he covered the clock with its cloth and locked the cupboard.

"You will not speak of this," he said. "Edmund would take it down. He means well. He doesn't understand what is owed."

I gave him my word. I have kept it until now.

* * *

I come to the diary.

I had worked through the desk by the nineteenth. It is a pretty desk, of rosewood, with a great many small drawers, and I had emptied them one by one and found nothing that could not have been read aloud in a drawing room. There were her household books. There were letters from her children at school. There was a bundle of tide tables, one for each year from 1946, which she had bought at the chandler's in Maldon; she had marked them in pencil, in a small upright hand, with rings round certain nights and now and then a single letter. I did not know then what the letter stood for. It was an A.

On top of the desk there stood a clock. It was a little French thing of gilt metal, in the shape of a drum held up by two cupids, such as one sees in the windows of antique shops. I had dusted round it for a fortnight. It did not go. It was the only clock in the whole of that house which did not, and I had come to be almost fond of it for that.

I asked Mr Vane about it, one night, on the stairs.

"That is Margot's," he said. "It was her mother's. It stopped in the year we were married and she would never let me touch it. She said that one clock in this house should be allowed to be wrong." He smiled. "She said it was a comfort to her. She said that when she was tired of being told the time, she went and looked at the one that had given up."

On the afternoon of the nineteenth I lifted it down to polish the desk beneath. It was heavier than I expected, and it rattled.

I turned it over. There is a round door in the back of such clocks, of brass, with a little catch, through which one reaches the bell. I do not know why I opened it. I think it was only that everything else in that desk had been opened, and I am a tidy person.

There was no bell. There was no movement of any kind; the drum was empty. It had been taken out, long ago, and the case kept. And pushed into the hollow, curled round to fit, there was a small book.

It was a pocket diary, bound in red cloth, such as one buys at a stationer's. The year was stamped on the cover in gilt. It was 1974.

I sat down in her chair. I held it shut on my knee for some time. The room was quite silent; there is a clock in the corner, but I did not hear it. Through the window I could see the orangery, with its broken panes, and the vine.

I knew that I ought not to read it. I had been engaged to put the papers of a dead woman in order. That does not give one leave to read what she had hidden inside a clock. And I knew whom I ought to take it to. It belonged to her husband.

But I thought of the old man in the tower with his file and his brass rods, building a machine to carry a message to his wife. *You have only a quarter of an hour.* And I thought of his son in the dark library, saying that it was not arithmetic.

One of them was wrong about how she had died. I had in my hand, in all likelihood, the means of knowing which. And whichever it was, I should have to go on telling the old man the truth when he asked me for it, at one in the morning. I had promised. I did not see how I could promise that and choose not to know.

That is what I told myself. I have since thought of another reason, which does me less credit. I wanted to know what Edmund had done. I wanted to know whether it was worse than what I had.

I looked up, before I opened it. I had the feeling that I was observed. There was no one in the doorway. There was no one in the garden. But the morning room is directly beneath the south end of the long gallery, and I knew very well what hung on the wall above my head.

I opened the book at the ribbon.

## III. The Red Book

It was written in pencil, in the small upright hand that I knew from the tide tables. There was a week to an opening, and for most weeks she had written no more than a few lines. Some were empty. I read it through from January, sitting in her chair, and the light went from the garden while I read.

I am going to copy out some of it. Dr Imrie has asked whether I think I have the right, and I have told him that I do not, but that I cannot make what followed understood without it. I have the book still. I have it by me as I write. I did not make these entries up, though I have sometimes wished that I had.

*Jan. 3. Frost. L. in the Shop from six till midnight with the Copy; he has got as far as the moon. He came up to bed and told me the equation of time for an hour. I told him the equation of marriage, which is that one of us talks and the other is supposed to be asleep. He said, "Quite so," and went on. I do love him. It is like loving a cathedral. One is very proud and it is cold about the feet.*

*Jan. 19. Rode over to Saltcote on the ebb. A. was dipping. He came across the yard with his sleeves rolled and sheep on him and said, "Well, Daisy." Ten years in March. I am fifty-three and when he says that I am nineteen. It is ridiculous. I told him so. He said he'd never claimed to be anything else.*

I stopped there, the first time. I looked at the bundle of tide tables on the desk, with the ringed nights and the letter A. I understood them then. They were the nights when the Wade lay open in the small hours, and a woman might cross and come back before the house was awake.

I thought of the old man on the stairs. *I think that she was going to someone. Was she?*

I went on.

*Feb. 8. Edmund has finished the lunar train for L.'s Copy. Eleven weeks' work, and I never saw anything so fine; it is like lace. He brought it up to show me before he took it down. L. looked at it through his glass for a quarter of an hour and said, "It will serve." E. went out and did not come in to dinner. I said to L. afterwards, could you not have told him it was good? He said, "He knows it is good. I should not have said it would serve if it were not." It is quite useless. He thinks that praise is a sort of inaccuracy.*

*Mar. 2. E. drinking. Celia came to me. I said, he is thirty-one, I can't smack him. She said, he would mind you. I don't think it is true. I think I am the thing he minds about, which is different. I made too much of him when he was small, to make up for L., and now he can't stand unless someone is looking.*

*Apr. 21. Summer time began last month and L. has finally finished putting the clocks on. He does it like a man burying relations. Every year he says the same: "It is a lie, Margot, by Act of Parliament." I said, darling, it's only an hour. He said, there is no such thing as only an hour.*

*May 30. Imogen home. She is twenty-four and looks at pictures all day and thinks I don't see where she goes in the evenings. She goes where I go. Young Tom Garrow is back from the agricultural college, brown as a nut, and can't string three words together, and she comes in with straw in her hair and her face shining. Like mother, like daughter. God help the Vanes, we can't keep off that farm. I ought to speak to her and I've not the face.*

*June 14. A. says, come away. He's said it before. This time he had it worked out. There's a place in Suffolk his cousin wants to give up; Tom can have Saltcote. He said, "I'm fifty-seven, Daisy. I'd like to eat my breakfast with you before I'm past chewing." I laughed. Then I went and sat on the sea wall for an hour and didn't.*

*July 9. Told L. I was tired. He said, "You should rest." He was regulating the gallery clock. I stood behind him for five minutes. If he had turned round and asked me one single question I'd have told him the whole of it and stayed. He said, "She is gaining four seconds a week. I can't account for it."*

There was a good deal more through the summer. I shall not copy it all. She wrote about her garden, and a horse, and a quarrel with Dame Octavia Prowse over a jumble sale. She was very funny. I found that I was smiling as I read, and then that I had stopped. One could see it coming, week by week, in the spaces between the jokes. The entries about her husband grew kinder and shorter.

*Sept. 20. Told A. yes.*

That was the whole of the entry. It had been written hard; the pencil had gone through the paper.

*Sept. 28. It will be the night of the Hour. It must be. I started that nonsense, in '51, to make them talk to each other, and I've stood in that hall every year since and made them say their piece, and never once said mine. I'll say it this year. I'll tell L. to his face, in the Hour, when by my own rule he can't hold it against me, and then I'll go. It is cowardly to use the rule. But I've earned one cowardice. I'll not creep out by the back in the dark like a housemaid.*

*Oct. 11. Imogen knows. She walked in on me sorting my jewel case. She's not a fool. I told her all of it; I thought, she of all people. She went white. She said, "With Tom's father? You?" She seemed to think I'd stolen it from her. I suppose I had. She said, what about Papa. I said Papa would notice in about a week, when the gallery clock wanted winding. That was unkind and not true and she knew it. We both cried. She has promised to say nothing. She says she'll come with me as far as the farm.*

*Oct. 22. A. will be at the Wade head from one, with the lantern and the mare. He says he'll show the light the whole time so I can walk to it. He says he'll come out and meet me. I said no. I said, I'm going to walk off this island on my own feet and you're going to stand there and watch me come. He said, "You always were a hard woman, Daisy." He was crying. Sixty next year, with hands like spades.*

And then the last.

I shall give it entire. It filled the space for the Saturday and ran over onto the Sunday and down the margin. It was dated the twenty-sixth of October. It had plainly been written in more than one sitting, with different pressures of the pencil.

*Sat. Oct. 26. The Thorne says low water twenty-eight minutes past midnight by the sun, and the Wade good until a quarter past two. So by the summer clocks, which is what everyone but L. will be keeping till the Hour, that's low at 1.28 and shut at 3.15.*

*I'll go at one. That's by my watch, and I mean to keep it on my wrist and trust nothing else, because L. has just been in to say he has put all the hall clocks back already, this afternoon, before dinner, "to save a scramble at the Hour." So the house says six now, and the world says seven. He was rather pleased with himself. It'd be like him to drown me by being efficient. But I am not such a fool about water as that, and I shan't look at a clock in this house tonight. One by my wrist. That gives me two hours and a quarter to do a walk of fifteen minutes. I could do it on my knees.*

*I shall tell L. at half past twelve. I've got it by heart. Then up for my coat. I shall go in my stockings; the Wade eats shoes. I'll leave them by the bed where he'll see them. He'll know then that I meant it and didn't fall in a ditch.*

*Later. Edmund has been in. He knows. Imogen told him; they had a row at tea about something else, and it came out, poor child, she was beside herself. He stood in that doorway, the size of a wardrobe, and cried like a boy of six. He said, "You can't. You can't leave me with him." I said, darling, you're thirty-two, you've a wife and a child of your own. He said, "If you go I'll come after you. I'll bring you back. I'll carry you." I said, then you'll get your feet wet.*

*It was the wrong thing to say. I'm always saying the amusing thing and it is always the wrong one. He has gone down to drink himself brave.*

*I'll not put it off. If I put it off for E. I'll put it off for ever; he'll see to that. He must learn to stand up without me watching. Tonight is as good a night to begin as any.*

*It is a quarter to eight by the house and they are waiting dinner. I can hear Leo in the hall, telling someone the time.*

*I'm fifty-four years old and I am going to walk across the bottom of the sea to a man with a lantern. I ought to be ashamed. I've looked for it, and I can't find that I am.*

*One by my wrist.*

There was nothing after that. The pages for November were clean. In the space for the twenty-seventh, the Sunday, someone had begun to write a word, in the same pencil, and had only made the first stroke of a letter.

* * *

I do not know how long I sat there. When I looked up the room was nearly dark.

I am a methodical person and I made myself be methodical. I took a sheet of paper and I wrote down what the book said and what it did not.

It said that Marguerite Vane had not been deceived. Her husband had put the clocks back early, as he believed, and it had killed nobody. She had known of it. She had written it down, with a joke, and had resolved to go by her own watch. She had known the hour of the tide to the minute, from the clock in the library. She had allowed herself two hours and a quarter to cross a causeway that I had walked, with a case, in under twenty minutes.

A woman who sets out at one, to do a quarter of an hour's walk, is not caught by a tide that comes at a quarter past three.

So something had kept her. Something had held her on the Wade, or between the house and the Wade, for two hours. And there was a sentence written in the margin. *If you go I'll come after you. I'll bring you back.*

I thought of him at the morning-room window. *I woke up, and it was getting light, and I walked home.*

I folded the sheet of paper and put it in the red book. I put the red book in the pocket of my dress. I set the little gilt clock back in its place on the desk, with its door shut, and it looked as it had always looked, like a thing that had given up.

Then I went and stood under the portrait.

I had not planned to. I found that I had climbed the stairs and walked the length of the gallery, in the dusk, and that I was standing before her with my hand in my pocket. The cracked clock ticked under the frame. She looked down at me with her mouth a little open.

I said, aloud, "I have read it."

I am not a person who speaks to pictures. I can only say what I did.

I said, "He doesn't know. Your husband. He thinks that it was his clock. He has thought so for twenty years, and he's breaking his heart over it, and he is making a machine in the tower so that he can tell you the time. And your son knows that it wasn't, and has let him. What am I to do?"

I do not say that she answered. The light was going, and I was overwrought, and a painted face will take any expression that one brings to it. But I had looked at that portrait on twenty nights. I knew it as I knew my own hands. And I say that as I stood there the amusement went out of it. I thought that for a moment the woman in the grey gown looked at me as one looks at a servant who has opened a letter.

I turned and went back down the gallery. I did not run. But I felt the whole way that I was followed, and I did not look behind me.

* * *

I kept it for three days. I am not proud of that. I gave Mr Vane his draught and sat with him and walked with him, with the book in my pocket. On the Thursday night he asked me whether his wife had come in. I told him that she was dead. He said, "Yes, the clock, I had put it back," and I said nothing. It was the first lie I had told him. I told it by holding my tongue, and I found that a lie of that kind is quite as heavy as the other.

By the Saturday I knew that I could not go on. It was the twenty-second. The house had been turned upside down since the morning, for the dinner. I had slept late, and badly. When I came down at noon there were strange coats in the hall, and Gail told me that a gentleman had come from the insurance and was going round the clocks, and that Mrs Vane was in a state, and that I was to keep out of the kitchen.

I went to look for Mr Edmund.

He was in the library. It was a little after two. He was standing at the tray with his back to me, pouring from a decanter, and when he turned and saw who it was his face did what it always did. It lightened, briefly, as though someone had opened a shutter. I had seen it do that for no one else. I had been living on it for a fortnight.

"Miss Quaile. You're up early. It's hardly dark."

"I should like to speak to you, Mr Vane."

"That sounds like a notice to quit. Don't say he has bitten you." He saw that I did not smile. He put the decanter down. "What is it?"

I had thought of a great many ways to begin. In the end I took the book out of my pocket and held it where he could see it.

He knew it. That was the first thing. I had expected that I should have to explain what it was. He looked at the red cloth and the gilt figures, and all the colour went out of his heavy face and left it grey.

"Where did you get that?"

"It was in the gilt clock on her desk. The one that doesn't go. The works had been taken out."

"In the *clock*." He made a sound that was nearly a laugh. "Oh, God. Of course it was. The one place in the house my father would never open, because she'd asked him not to. I hunted for that book for a month. I had the floorboards up in her room." He had not taken his eyes off it. "Have you read it?"

"Yes."

"All of it?"

"To the end."

He sat down. He sat on the arm of a leather chair, quite suddenly, and the whisky slopped over his hand, and he did not notice.

"Then you know more than my father does," he said. "You know more than anyone alive but me."

"I know that she was not mistaken about the time. I know that she meant to leave at one, by her own watch, and that she knew the tide. And I know that you told her you would follow her." My voice was not steady. "I don't know what happened after that. It isn't written."

"No. She'd not have had the chance to write it."

"Mr Vane, I must ask you. Did you follow her?"

He looked up at me. I have thought about that look more than about anything else in my life, more than about Mrs Aske's hand. I had braced myself for anger. I had thought he might deny it, or tell me that it was none of my business, which was true. He looked at me as a man looks who has been carrying a heavy thing up a long stair, and has reached a landing, and found someone standing there.

"Yes," he said.

That was all. He did not go on. I waited, and the fire ticked, and behind me on its table the great clock went quietly under its glass.

"I'm not going to tell you the rest," he said at last. "Not because you've no right. You've as much right as anyone, now. But there are three people who should have heard it before you, and one of them's just been buried, and I'll not make it four by telling a stranger first." He rubbed his face with his dry hand. "What are you going to do with that?"

"It isn't mine. It was his wife's. I think I must give it to him."

"Do you know what it'll do to him?"

"I think it will tell him that he didn't kill her."

"It'll tell him she was leaving him. For Amos Garrow. A tenant. A man he's nodded to across a gate for fifty years. He's half known it, and he has spent twenty years not knowing it, very hard. He's built all this." He moved his hand, at the room, the house. "The hour. The clocks. It's a kind of church. He's the only worshipper, and it's dedicated to the proposition that it was all a mistake about the time. You'd pull it down."

"I should be telling him the truth. He asked me to. He asks me every night."

"He does. And you do. I've heard you." His mouth twisted. "I stood outside his door one night last week and heard you tell my father that my mother was dead. I've never had the nerve to do it in twenty years. I nearly came in and went on my knees to you."

I did not know where to look.

"I can't choose what is true, Mr Vane," I said. "I can only choose whether I say it. And I can't sit beside him another night with this in my pocket."

"No. No, I see that you can't." He was quiet. Then he held out his hand. "Let me look at it. The last page. I shan't keep it."

I gave it to him. He opened it at the ribbon. He read standing, with his head bent, moving his lips slightly, as a child reads. I watched him come to the part in the margin. I saw him stop. He stood for a long time without turning the page, and I looked away, since there are things that one does not watch.

"*Then you'll get your feet wet*," he said. His voice was very low. "Yes. That's what she said. She wrote that at about seven; I'd only just left her. I went down and drank a bottle of my father's port, straight off, in the gunroom." He shut the book. "I've wondered for twenty years what she thought of me, at the last. Whether she'd put it down. And there it is. *He must learn to stand up without me watching.*" He laughed, and it broke in the middle. "Well. I didn't, Ma. I'm sorry. I never got the trick of it."

He held the book out to me.

"I thought you'd want to keep it," I said.

"If I keep it I shall burn it. I've burned enough in this house. You're the archivist. You hold it." He put it into my hand, and for a moment his fingers were round mine, over the red cloth. They were quite cold. "Will you do something for me? I've no claim on you. But will you wait until tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow?"

"Tonight's the twentieth. He's been getting ready for it all the year. I don't know what he thinks is going to happen; he's got some notion, he's been up and down to that tower. Let him have it. Let him open his door and say his piece. And in the morning, when it's over, and they've all gone home, you bring him that book. I'll be there. I'll stand beside you while he reads it. And then I shall tell him the rest. What isn't in it. What happened on the Wade."

"You will tell him?"

"I give you my word. For what that's worth; ask anyone." He tried to smile. "I've been going to tell him every October for twenty years. I get as far as the door. I think perhaps I needed somebody to stand behind me and say, I can't sit beside him another night. I never had a sister who would. Imogen thinks she knows already, and what she thinks is nearly right, and worse than the truth, and she's never asked." He looked down at me. "You're a hard little thing, Miss Quaile. You're like a splinter. One doesn't know it's in till one tries to move."

I ought to have been offended. I felt my eyes fill.

"Tomorrow, then," I said. "After breakfast."

"After breakfast. In the Shop. He's always best down there, among his tools." He picked up his glass and looked at it and put it down again, untasted. I never saw him do that at any other time. "And if for any reason I'm not there—"

"Why should you not be there?"

"No reason. I've some business to see to tonight. A thing I've got to get rid of. It's nothing." His eyes went past me for an instant, to the table in the window, and I saw that same look of dislike that I had seen on him by moonlight. "If I'm not there, you give it to him anyway. And you tell him that Edmund said he was sorry, and that it wasn't the clock. Will you remember that? It wasn't the clock."

"I shall remember."

"Good girl," said Edmund Vane.

I went out. I have gone back to that room many times since, in my mind. He had said that he would tell his father in the morning. He had put his glass down. I thought that I had done a good thing, and that for once in my life I had spoken at the right moment. And I thought that on the next day the old man would know the truth, his son would be free of what he carried, and I should have been the means of it.

I see now what else I had done. I had told a man who had kept a secret for twenty years that by tomorrow he would have no secret. I had set a term to it. I had said, in effect, *You have until morning*, to a person who was known to disappear on that night of the year, and who had business to see to on the water.

I have asked Dr Imrie whether he thinks that a man might choose not to be there in the morning. He says that I cannot know. He says that I am to write down what occurred and leave the reasons. I am doing it. But I heard Edmund Vane say, *If for any reason I'm not there.* I heard that, and I went out of the room and shut the door.

* * *

I must now put down a thing that happened at about four o'clock that afternoon. I had thought of leaving it out. It does not belong with the rest, and I have never been able to make it belong. But I have been told to explain nothing, and so I am not entitled to choose.

I had gone up to the Admiral's room to see that the fire was laid and the tray set for the night. The old gentleman was in the Shop. I was alone on that floor. I had knelt down at the hearth to straighten the fire irons.

I heard a child singing.

It was quite soft and it was close. I thought at first that it was in the room with me. It was a thin, clear, tuneless voice, such as children have when they sing to themselves over a game, without knowing that they do it. I could not make out words. There was a line that went up, and one that came down, and then the first again.

I stayed where I was, on my knees. I looked round the room. There was the bed, with its curtains, and the seven clocks, and the window.

The singing went on. And I found where it was. It was coming down the chimney.

I put my head in under the mantel and listened. It was much plainer there. One could hear that there were words, though not what they were. And it came from above. The flue of that room goes up through the floor over it and joins another, as they do in old houses. I knew what was over it. I had been told on my second day, when I asked what the barred window was on the top landing. It was the old nursery, where Mr Edmund and Miss Imogen had slept as children, and it had been shut up since 1955.

I do not think that I was frightened, at first. I was a nurse. I thought only that there was a child in the house and that nobody had told me. I thought that one of the guests must have brought one.

I went up. There is a narrow stair from the end of the first-floor passage to the top landing, and it is uncarpeted. I went up it quietly. The landing was dim. There are three doors there, and the one at the end has a small square window beside it, set high, with two iron bars.

The singing had stopped. I did not know at what moment it stopped.
