I tried the door, and it was locked. I knocked, and I felt foolish doing it. I said, "Is someone there?" There was no answer. I put my ear to the panel. I could hear nothing at all. It was not the quiet of an empty room. I thought it was the quiet of somebody keeping quite still.

There was a keyhole, an old wide one. I stooped and looked.

I could see a strip of bare floor, and the lower half of a window with bars, and grey light. In the middle of the strip of floor there was a rocking horse. It was a big one, dappled, with a red saddle and most of its mane gone. It was facing me.

It was moving. It was only a little, a few inches forward and a few inches back, slowing as I watched. It was moving as a rocking horse moves after someone has got down from it.

I straightened up. My heart was going very hard. I stood with my hand flat on the door, as Mr Vane stood every night at that other door on the floor below.

There was a smell on that landing. I noticed it then. It was faint and sweet and sharp, and for a moment I could not think what it was, it was so out of place. It was oranges. It was the smell that is left on one's fingers when one has peeled a small orange, of the kind that is put into children's stockings at Christmas.

"You'll not get in there, miss."

I turned round so sharply that I struck my elbow on the wall. Mrs Pask was standing at the head of the stairs. She was out of breath, as though she had come up quickly, and she had flour to the elbows. I had never before seen her above the ground floor.

"I heard a child," I said. "Singing. I heard it in Mr Vane's chimney."

"That'll be the wind. That flue sings. It always has."

"There is no wind."

"There's always wind at Compline." She had her eyes on my face. They were small and brown and quite steady. "That room's been shut since Miss Imogen went to school. There's nothing in it but the horse and a few old toys and the damp."

"The horse was rocking. I saw it through the keyhole."

"It's the draught. Them floors are all on the tilt. You open a door downstairs and it'll go for an hour." She came a step nearer. She put herself, I saw, between me and the nursery door, not obviously. "There's no child at Compline, Miss Quaile. There's not been a child sleep in this house since 1955. You've been on your feet too many nights, and it's the day of the dinner, and everyone's on edge. You go and lie down for an hour."

"I smelled oranges."

Something moved in her face. It was gone at once.

"I've a box of satsumas in the kitchen for the table," said Mrs Pask. "It'll have come up the back stairs. Now you go down, there's a good girl, and let me get on. I've a goose."

I went down. I did as I was told, because I was told it by a sensible person, with flour on her arms, in a voice that had no doubt in it. I lay on my bed for an hour and I looked at the ceiling. I told myself that the flue sang, and the floors were on the tilt, and the smell had come up from the kitchen.

I will put down what I know. I know that the kitchen is at the other end of the house. I had been at Compline three weeks and had never once smelled cooking on the top landing. I know that the air that afternoon was as still as glass; the gale did not get up until dark. And I had listened to wind in chimneys all my childhood, on a cliff. It doesn't go up, and come down, and then go up again in the same place, like a child who has only learned the first two lines.

There is no child at Compline. I have that on the word of a woman who had lived there forty years and whom I never knew to say a thing she did not mean.

I heard one. I am not able to write anything else.

* * *

At twenty past five I carried the tray down to the pantry, to have a fresh glass put on it. On the turn of the main stair there was a young man standing in my way. He was very tall, and soaked to the skin, and was holding his shoes. He looked at me with his mouth open.

There was a small crab on his shoulder. It was alive. I told him of it. I do not know what else I said.

I mention him because he will come in again. I remember thinking, as I went on down, that he had a foolish kind face, and that he was the first person I had seen in that house in three weeks who did not seem to be listening for something.

At six I dressed Mr Vane. I got him into the evening clothes that had been laid out, which hung on him, and I tied his tie. He stood quite still for it, with his chin up, like a child.

"It is tonight," he said.

"Yes, Mr Vane."

"The twentieth. You have the count? I lose the count."

"It's twenty years tonight."

"Yes." He looked at himself in the glass. He put the loupe on its cord round his neck and settled it. "I finished the pinion. She is coupled and set. I went across at noon, when they thought I was at the bench, and I looked at her, and she is right." He turned from the glass and took my two hands. His were dry and warm and perfectly steady. "You'll stand by me at one. When I open the door. You are the only one of them who doesn't think me mad, or who has the grace to say so if she does. I shall want a witness."

"I'll stand by you."

"Whatever happens. You'll not leave me."

"No, Mr Vane."

I promised it. I had the red book in my pocket, under my hand. I had promised his son that I would keep it there until the morning. I thought it would be simple to keep both.

He gave me his arm, and we went down.

## IV. The Cry

I shall be quick about the dinner. Others were there who will have noticed more than I did. I sat through it with my hand going to my pocket, and saw very little beyond the two people on either side of me.

One of them was Mr Edmund. The other was no one.

They had put me next to the empty place. I had dined in the kitchen until that night, and had only seen it from across the room. I had not known what it would be to sit beside it. The chair was drawn back a hand's breadth from the table. There was a napkin, folded, and three glasses, and the candlelight stood in them. Mr Vane sat on the further side of it, at the head. Whenever he turned to speak to it he looked through the space where a face would be, and his eyes focused there. I mean that they did not look at the wall behind. They stopped short, at a distance of about two feet, and rested.

It was cold on that side of me. I am aware of what that sounds like. There was a window behind us, and the curtains moved all through dinner in the draught, and I had a bare forearm on the cloth. I do not say that it was anything but the window. I say that my right arm, which was toward Mr Edmund, was warm, and my left was cold to the elbow, and that when the girl leaned between us to set down a plate of soup at that place, I saw her shiver.

On my right he ate little and drank a great deal. He did not speak to me. He had said what he had to say in the library, and I understood that we were to be strangers until the morning. Once his sister, on his other side, said something to him in a low voice, and I heard a name, and I felt him go rigid from the shoulder to the wrist. Once he reached across me for the salt, and the cloth of his sleeve touched my arm, and I felt it in every part of my body. I looked at my plate. I thought that every person at that table must have seen. I think now that only one did, a heavy grey-faced man opposite who had been introduced as from the insurers. He watched us all as a cat watches a wainscot.

The old gentleman's speech I need not give. I knew a part of it before he made it. He had told me on the stairs, a week earlier, that someone was taking his clocks. He said that he had written to his solicitor, and forgotten, and remembered. I had not known that he would say it at his own table. He stood up to do it. I half rose, behind him, to be near if he should fall. His hands were pressed on the cloth, and I could see them from where I was. They did not shake until the very end.

"One of you has been robbing me," he said.

I felt the blood leave my face. I knew that he did not mean me. But I had in my pocket at that moment a thing of his wife's, that I had taken out of his house's one silent clock and kept from him for three days. And I had made a bargain over it that afternoon with his son. Everyone at that table went still when he said it. I think they were each looking into their own pocket. I was looking into mine.

He said that he would know by one o'clock. He said that whoever it was might come to him in the Hour and tell him why. And then his voice changed, and he said that he had not so many hours left that he could afford to waste the odd one, and I saw his hands begin to tremble on the cloth, and I had my arm under his before he was fully down.

"What is this?" he asked me, of his plate. It was a syllabub. I told him so. He turned to the cold place on his right. "Margot, did we order a syllabub?"

He waited for the answer. I watched his face while he listened. And he nodded, and took up his spoon.

I looked at Edmund then. I could not help it. He was not looking at his father, or at the chair. He was looking down the table at the grey-faced man, with a small hard smile. Then, as though he had felt my eyes, he turned his head, and the smile went.

He looked at me for one second. He looked like a man who had been told that the train he is waiting for has been taken off.

* * *

We went into the drawing room. I put Mr Vane in the wing chair by the fire, with the rug, and took the low stool beside him. It was a little before ten by the house. Outside the wind had risen; I could hear it in the chimney, and I listened to it, I confess, with attention. It did not sing. It made the noise that wind makes.

Young Mr Kit Vane played the piano. It was a piece of Schubert, slow, with a tune in it that came round and round. Mr Vane sat with his eyes shut and his hand moving on the rug, very slightly, beating a time that was not quite the music's. His daughter had gone to the window seat and drawn the curtain back. She was looking out toward the Wade, though there can have been nothing to see.

I had met her only the day before. She was a quiet, dark, guarded woman, with a white lock in her hair, and I had liked her, and been afraid of her. The first time she looked at me I had started. She has her mother's eyes. She has them exactly, the same grey and set the same. When she turned them on me in the hall and said, "You're the one who tells my father the truth," I had felt that the portrait had come down off the wall to say it.

At twenty past ten, in the middle of a bar, the lights failed.

The music stopped, and began again. Nobody cried out. They were used to it in that house. Someone said that it was the transformer. I sat in the dark with my hand on the old man's wrist, and felt his pulse go on, slow and regular. All through the house I could hear the clocks. They had not noticed.

The boy finished the piece. In the firelight I saw Mr Vane open his eyes.

"Thank you, Kit," he said. And then, in the same voice: "She has gone up. She always goes up after the Schubert, and takes her shoes off, and comes down for the Hour. Imogen, did you see her go?"

There was a pause. I had my mouth open. I had told him the truth on twenty nights and I was ready to tell it again, before them all.

"Yes, Papa," said Miss Vane from the window, without turning round.

"Was she tired?"

"A little."

I shut my mouth. I do not know why I let it pass. I think it was the way she said it. She did not say it as the others said such things, to keep him quiet. She said it as if she had seen.

Mrs Pask came in with lamps. People moved about. The gentleman from the insurers went out, and I did not see him again that night until much later. Young Mr Vane went out too, abruptly, with a white face. I put more coal on and sat down again.

At a quarter to eleven Edmund came in.

He had been out of doors. His hair was wet, though he had on a dry coat. He went to the tray by the piano and stood with his back to the room for some time. Then he went out again, and I heard his voice in the dining room, and other voices, and a laugh. When he came back, a little after eleven, his wife was with him. She sat down on a sofa at a distance from everyone, very upright. He took a chair on the far side of the hearth from his father and stretched his legs out.

I watched him. I had no right to, and I did. He was not as he had been at dinner. The hardness had gone out of his face. He looked easy, and almost sleepy. He yawned, and apologised to nobody, and yawned again. His eyelids were heavy. He rubbed at his eyes with his thumb and finger like a child kept up too late.

I thought it was the drink. He had been drinking since noon, and I had seen men go that way at the end of it, suddenly loose and mild. I am a nurse. I had sat by that tray in the Admiral's room every night for three weeks and measured out one spoonful. I had seen what the stuff does, to the eyes, and the jaw, and the hands. And I sat ten feet from Edmund Vane for twenty-five minutes, by firelight, and watched the same thing come over him, and did not know it.

At half past eleven he got up. He stood a moment with his hand on the chair-back, as if the floor had moved. He said, "I'm going to have a look at the generator." He said it to the room. His wife's head came up. She looked at him as a person looks who has dropped something down a well and is waiting to hear it land.

He went past me to the door. He did not look at me. He put his hand, in passing, on his father's shoulder. It rested there only an instant, and the old man did not wake.

That was the last time I saw him.

I must be exact about that. I have been told a number of things since by other people, as to where he was after that and what he did. Some of them I believe. But I am writing down only what I saw with my own eyes. I never saw Edmund Vane again after half past eleven that night, when he walked out of the drawing room with his hand trailing off his father's shoulder. I did not see him living, and I was not shown him dead. I saw something at one o'clock. I shall come to it. I do not know what it was.

* * *

It was only a minute or two afterwards that I heard the steps.

They were overhead. The drawing room is under the long gallery. I had sat in that room on other evenings and had heard, now and then, a board give as someone crossed above. That was a slow sound, one person walking. This was light and very quick. It began at one end and came the whole length of the ceiling, a patter, without a pause. I thought it was the sound that a child makes, running in stockinged feet down a long bare floor because it is there.

It stopped at the far end. It stopped just above my head, where the portrait hangs.

I looked round the room. Dame Octavia was asleep. Mr Fenn was nodding over a paper. Mrs Edmund Vane had got up and was standing by the door with her back to us, quite motionless, listening for something of her own. The clergyman had wandered away. None of them had raised their eyes.

But Miss Vane had. She had turned from the window at last. She was looking at the ceiling, and then she looked at me. I saw that she had heard it.

I got up. I went across to her.

"Miss Vane. I must go upstairs for five minutes. Would you sit by your father? He's asleep. He oughtn't to be left."

She did not answer at once. She had the look of a person who has been called back from a great way off. Her face was very white, and her eyes were wide and bright. I thought that she had been crying, or was about to.

"Yes," she said. "Of course. Go."

I ought to have seen that she was not attending. I ought to have waited until she had crossed the room and sat down in my place. I have been over it and over it. But the steps had stopped above the portrait, and I could not have stayed in that room for any consideration.

I took a candle from the mantel and went. As I shut the door I looked back. He was asleep in the wing chair, with the rug to his chin. His daughter was standing where I had left her, with one hand at her throat.

It was a little after half past eleven. I had promised him at six o'clock that I would not leave him. I had kept that for five hours and a half.

* * *

I did not reach the gallery. I had got to the first landing when I heard someone come pounding up behind me, and my name called. It was the tall young man who had had the crab.

"I think I've killed the vicar," he said.

I shall not write out what followed in the library; it was soon over. The old clergyman was in a chair by the fire, deeply unconscious. I took his pulse. I looked at his pupils. They were small, and they did not answer to the candle as they should. I put my face to his mouth, and I knew.

It has a smell. It is sweetish, and sharp, a little like pears that have gone over. One does not mistake it who has uncorked that bottle every night for three weeks. The young man gave me the glass that had been on the floor. I smelled it, and I put a drop on my tongue to be sure. It was brandy, and it was the Mixture.

I asked him where the glass had come from. I heard my own voice ask it, quite low and level.

He said the dining-room sideboard. He said that it had been Mr Edmund's. Mr Edmund had drunk about half of it and made a face and said that it was corked. Then he had left it, and the vicar had not liked to see it wasted.

I want to set down exactly what went through me. It did not come as a thought. It came as it comes on a ward when a bell rings in the night from the wrong bed, and one is running before one has understood.

The bottle was mine. I mean that it was in my charge. It was kept on a tray in the Admiral's room, and nobody else was to touch it. That had been said to me on my first day. I had carried it down myself at twenty past five, to the pantry, and carried it up again, and set it by the bed. I had not looked at it since. I had been at dinner for two hours, and in the drawing room for an hour and a half, and the Admiral's room had stood empty with its door unlocked. Anyone might have gone in.

Someone had gone in. They had taken the Mixture and put it in a glass of brandy, and given it to Edmund.

I thought of his eyes, by the fire. I thought of his hand on the chair. I had sat and watched him go under and had called it drink.

And he had drunk half. The vicar had had the other half and was insensible. Edmund was half as heavy again, and hardened to spirits, and it would be slower in him. But it would come. He had walked out of the drawing room ten minutes ago, to go out of doors, in a gale, on an island with a fifteen-foot drop all round it. He had business to see to on the water.

I asked the young man where Mr Edmund was now. He said that he had gone to see a man about a boat.

I told him what to do for the vicar. I told him twice. He was a good creature; he listened as if his life depended on it. I said that I must look at a tray. Then I went up those stairs faster than I have ever gone up any stairs, with my hand round the candle flame.

The door of the Admiral's room was shut. I opened it.

The tray was on the table by the bed, where I had left it. The spoon was there, lying across the saucer. The clean glass was there, upside down on its cloth.

There was no bottle.

I looked on the floor. I looked under the bed, and on the mantel, and the washstand, among the seven clocks. I knew that I should not find it. Whoever had taken it had not poured out a dose and put it back. They had taken it away with them. A bottle that had been new on Thursday, with enough in it to put an old man to sleep for sixty nights.

I stood with the candle in the middle of that room. I thought, quite clearly: this is the second time.

I had sat at a desk and put my head on my arm, and a woman had died reaching for a bell. I had sworn that I would never again fail to watch. I had taken night work so that I might sit by one patient with my eyes open and be sure. And I had gone down to a dinner, in a blue dress, to sit beside a man that I had no business to think of. I had left behind me, on a tray, in an unlocked room, the one thing in that house that could do harm.

I do not know who took it. I have never known. I have my own belief, and I have kept it to myself, since I had no proof and it could have done nothing but injury. But whoever's hand it was, the bottle was mine. I had left it there.

I went back down to the drawing room. I ran. I had it in my mind that I must find Edmund, and that first I must see that the old man was safe, since his daughter was with him and could be told, and could send her nephew out with a lamp.

The wing chair was empty.

The rug lay on the floor in front of it. The fire had sunk. Dame Octavia Prowse slept on her sofa. Mr Fenn sat with his paper on his knee and his spectacles pushed up. There was no one at the window. The curtain hung as she had left it, drawn back on the dark.

"Mr Fenn. Where is Mr Vane?"

He started awake. He looked at the chair.

"He was here a moment ago. He got up. He said—" He passed a hand over his face. "He said that he had a clock to stop. I supposed that Miss Vane was with him. Is she not?"

"When did Miss Vane go?"

"I couldn't say. Directly after you, I think. She went out rather quickly. I assumed that she was following you." He was getting to his feet, an old tired man in a dress shirt. "Miss Quaile, is anything wrong?"

I did not answer him. I could not have said it in fewer than a hundred words, and I had not the time for ten.

* * *

I looked for him as I had been trained to look for a patient who has got out of bed. One does it by rooms, in order, and one does not let oneself think.

I looked in the hall. There was no one there. The fire burned and the tall clocks stood round the walls. I noticed, as I went through, that one of them had stopped. It was the plain dark one to the left of the hearth, which he called the regulator and set all the others by. Its pendulum hung straight down behind the glass. In three weeks I had never seen it still. I marked it, as one marks a thing that is out of its place, and went on.

I went down to the Shop. A lamp was burning on the bench, low. His stool was pushed back. The tools lay in their rows. He was not there, and the air was cold, as if a door had been opened.

I went to the side door by the gunroom. It was unbolted. There was wet on the flagstones inside it, the marks of a man's feet, coming in or going out, I could not tell which. I opened the door and held my candle up, and the wind blew it out.

I stood in the doorway in the dark. The rain was driving past. Across the yard I could just see the stable block, and the tower, black. I called his name. The wind took it.

I thought: he has gone to the tower. He has gone to his machine. He said that he had a clock to stop.

I thought: I cannot cross that yard without a light. And I thought of the sea wall, which I was to keep him off.

I went back for a lamp. I am trying to give the order of it truthfully. I went back through the hall, to fetch the lamp that stood at the foot of the stairs. And as I took it up I thought that he might after all have gone to his room. He might have gone up by the back stair while I came down by the front. It would take me one minute to be certain, and if he were there I need not go out at all. I knew it was the cowardly choice. I went up the stairs.

His room was empty. I had left the door open, and the candle I had dropped was still lying on the carpet by the tray.

I came out onto the landing. I stood at the head of the main stair with the lamp in my hand. To my left, the long gallery ran away into the dark. Behind me was the narrow stair that goes to the top floor. Somewhere beneath me a clock that ran a little fast was gathering itself to strike. I looked at the dial of the one on the landing. It was five minutes to twelve.

And the child cried out.

* * *

I have been asked to describe it. I have tried, for Dr Imrie, a number of times.

It was above me. It was on the top floor, at the end, where the old nursery is. It came down the narrow stair as clearly as if a door stood open.

It was a child's voice. I am as sure of that as I am of my own name. It was not a woman's, and it was not an animal, or the wind, or a hinge. I have heard children cry in hospital at night, for their mothers, or from pain. This was neither of those. It was one cry, high and short, and it broke off. It was the sound a child makes that has seen something, and I thought that it had not been frightened for itself. It had seen a thing done.

Then there was nothing. I could hear the clocks.

I do not know how I got up those stairs. I remember the lamp swinging and the shadows of the banisters going round the wall like the spokes of a wheel. I remember that I was saying something aloud, and that it was, "I'm coming, I'm coming," as I used to say it down the length of a ward.

The nursery door was open.

I had tried it at four o'clock that afternoon, and it had been locked. Mrs Pask had told me that it had been shut since 1955. It stood open now, about a foot, and it was dark inside.

I pushed it wide and held up the lamp.

It was a long low room under the roof, with a sloping ceiling and the one barred window. There was a fireguard, and a cupboard painted with faded animals, and a table. There was the rocking horse in the middle of the floor. It was not moving. Its glass eye took the light.

Against the far wall there was a small iron bed.

It had been slept in. I should say that it had been lain on. There was an old eiderdown, pushed back in a heap toward the foot, and a pillow with no case. In the middle of the mattress was the hollow that a body leaves. It was a small one. I have made up a great many beds. I knew the size of the person who had made that hollow as well as if I had weighed it. It was a child of nine or ten.

I crossed the room and put my hand flat in it.

It was warm.

I cannot make that any less than it is. I held my palm there and counted ten, to be sure that it was not the heat of my own hand, and I moved it to the edge of the mattress, which was as cold as the room, and back. The hollow was warm, as a bed is from which someone has risen within the last few minutes.

"Where are you?" I said. I said it gently. "I'm not angry. I'm a nurse. Where have you gone?"

Nothing answered. I looked under the bed. I opened the painted cupboard, and there were a few broken toys, and a smell of mice. I looked behind the door. There was nowhere else in that room that a cat could have hidden.

I went round it then with the lamp, slowly, and I looked at everything, as I had been taught to look at a bedside.

There was a plate on the table. It had crusts on it, and the rind of a piece of cheese. Beside the plate there was a jam jar with an inch of water in it. And there was orange peel. It lay in a neat heap, in the small curled pieces that a child makes who has not yet learned to take it off in one. It was fresh. When I bent to it I smelled what I had smelled on the landing.

On the floor by the bed there was a sheet of paper. I picked it up.

It was a drawing, done in wax crayon. It showed a tall thin building with a pointed top, and near the top a circle with two lines in it for the hands of a clock. Above the circle, under the pointed roof, there were two figures. One was small and black. The other was larger, and had been coloured grey, heavily, with the crayon pressed hard, and it had one arm sticking straight up. Underneath, in pencil, in a child's square capitals, somebody had written:

THE MAN HITS THE LITTLE BELL.
THE LADY WAITS.

And lower down, smaller, as if it had been added afterward:

SHE IS LOOKING AT THE HOUSE.

I held that paper under the lamp. My hand shook so that I could hardly read it. I have it still. I kept it, with the red book. I have shown it to Dr Imrie, and he has looked at it for a long time and given it back to me without a word.

There was one thing more. By the door, on the bare boards, when I turned to go, the lamp showed me a mark. It was wet. It was the print of a shoe, a very small one, and it had come in from the landing. There was another beyond it, and a third, fainter, going toward the bed. Whoever had made them had been out in the rain, and had come back up the stairs running, and had not been in the room long.

I knelt and looked at the nearest. The sole had a pattern. It was a pattern of small stars.

I am a nurse and I do not make up evidence. I have put down what was in that room. There was a warm bed, and a plate, and peel, and a drawing, and three wet footprints with stars in them. A sensible woman, reading that list, will say that there was a child in the house. She will say that somebody had hidden a living child in the old nursery, for some reason of their own, and fed it. The child had got out, and seen something in the dark to make it cry, and run back, and run away again when it heard me on the stairs.

I have said all that to myself. I said it to myself then, on my knees on those boards. I should very much like to believe it.

But I had been in that house three weeks. I knew every person who slept in it and every person who had come to it that day, and there was no child among them. I had asked a truthful woman, who had been there for forty years, and she had looked me in the face and told me that there was no child at Compline. And I ask the sensible reader, in her turn, to tell me this. If there was a living child in that nursery, where did it go? I was on the stair within a quarter of a minute of the cry. No one passed me. There is no other way down from that landing.

There is no child at Compline. I heard a child cry out in the old nursery at five minutes to twelve. I found the bed warm, and nobody in it.

And it was Edmund's nursery. He had slept in that iron bed until he was thirteen. I thought of the photograph of the small boy on the pony, scowling because he was frightened. I thought, kneeling there, that I knew whose voice it had been. He had seen a thing done, a long time ago, and he was still up here at night crying about it, in the room where it had first been safe to.

I got to my feet. As I did so, I heard a sound on the landing. It was a soft rumble, in the wall, like ropes running. There is a hatch there, by the head of the stair, with a wooden door, where the nursery dinners used to be sent up from the kitchen. I pulled it open. The shaft was black, and a cold air came up it. The two ropes that hang there were moving. They were trembling, a very little, as a bell-rope trembles after the ringer has let go.

I let the hatch fall shut.

I had lost the old man. I had lost the bottle. Somewhere out in that gale a man was walking about with a sleeping draught in him that I had been set to guard. And I was standing on the top floor of the house, at midnight, in front of a hole in the wall, with a child's drawing in my hand.

Below me the first of the clocks began to strike twelve.

I took up the lamp and went down.

## V. The Gallery

The narrow stair from the top floor comes down beside the head of the main staircase. One stands there on a square landing, with the well of the hall on one hand and on the other the mouth of the long gallery.

I had the lamp. I had come down slowly, since my knees were not to be trusted. When I reached the landing I set the lamp on the bottom tread behind me, to have my hands free for the rail. So I was standing in my own shadow when I turned.

All through the house the clocks were telling midnight. I have said how they did it, each in its own time. The small quick one in the morning room had begun, and the hall clocks were taking it up, one by one, beneath me. In the gallery the cracked one had not yet spoken.

I looked along the gallery. I did so because I was afraid of it, and I had been taught as a child to look at what I am afraid of.

There was a light at the far end.

It was small and yellow, a single flame, and it was low down by the end wall, where the door of the Grey Room is. That door had been shut and locked for the whole of the three weeks that I had been in the house. I had seen the old man lay his hand on it every night.

The light moved. It came out from the wall into the middle of the gallery, and it began to come toward me.

I did not move. I do not think that I breathed. The gallery is a hundred feet long and the floor sags in the middle, so that the light seemed to come down a slope and up again. As it came I began to see what carried it.

First there was the gown. It was grey, and it shone. It took the candle flame all down its length and gave it back in long soft folds, like water running over a sill. I knew that grey. I had stood before it on twenty nights and tried to move out of the way of the eyes above it.

Then the bare shoulders, and an arm, lifted, holding a candle in a silver stick. The other hand hung at her side and had something in it. I saw what it was as she came nearer. It was a pair of shoes. She was carrying her shoes by the heels and walking in her stockings, and her feet made no sound at all on the old boards.

Then I saw the face.

She passed me at a distance of perhaps four yards. She did not turn her head. She was looking straight in front of her, at something a long way off, and her lips were parted, as if she had just said a thing or was about to. The candle was on the far side of her from me, so that her profile was dark against it and edged with light. I saw the line of her brow and her cheek. I saw the eye nearest to me, and it was grey. Her dark hair was piled up.

As she passed, the cracked clock at the end of the gallery, under the empty stretch of wall where the candle no longer reached, struck its first note.

As the clocks of Compline told midnight I saw Marguerite Vane come down the long gallery in her grey silk, and she had been twenty years in Thorney churchyard.

I have written that sentence as I first wrote it, in pencil, on the back of a temperature chart, two days afterward, when I could hold a pencil. I am not going to alter it now.

She went by. There is a second stair at my end of the gallery, a back one, that goes down to the garden passage and the door to the orangery. She turned to it. I saw the grey skirt gather and slip round the corner, and the light go down the wall after it. I heard nothing. I did not hear a step or a board.

There was a scent in the air where she had been. It was lavender, and camphor, and something else underneath, sweet and old, like a drawer that has not been opened for many years.

* * *

I shall now say what a sensible woman would conclude, as I have undertaken to do. Dr Imrie tells me that I am not obliged to. But I should think less of myself if I did not.

There was a living woman in that house who had those eyes. I have said so. I had met her the day before, and been startled. She was of the same height and build and colouring as the woman in the portrait, since she was her daughter. She had a key to the Grey Room; I had been told that on my first morning. She had been standing at the drawing-room window half an hour earlier in a state of great agitation, and she had left that room directly after I did.

A sensible woman will say that Miss Imogen Vane went upstairs and unlocked her mother's bedroom. She took her mother's gown out of the wardrobe and put it on, and came down the gallery carrying her shoes so as to make no noise. I did not see the white lock in her hair, but the candle was on the other side.

I have been told, since, by several people, that this is what happened. Miss Vane has told me so herself. She wrote me a kind letter in the spring, when she heard that I was ill. She said that she was very sorry to have frightened me, and that she had not known anyone was on the landing. She had had a reason for wearing the dress that night which had nothing to do with me.

I believe that she believes it. I have no wish to quarrel with her.

I can only say what it is that I am unable to get past. I had seen Miss Vane's face at dinner, and in the drawing room, and I should have known it anywhere. It is a closed, careful face. It is the face of a woman who has spent her life looking closely at things and keeping her opinion to herself. The face that passed me in the gallery was not careful. It was open, and alight, and a little amused, with the lips apart. It was the face in the portrait. I had studied that face more closely than I have ever studied a living one, and I saw it go by me in profile at four yards, by candlelight, and it had not changed by a line.

And she was carrying her shoes. Gail had told me, on my first morning, what the woman in the portrait had done on the night she died. *She'd took them off. She went out to the Wade in her stockings.* I did not know then that it was written in the red book, in her own hand. *I shall go in my stockings; the Wade eats shoes.* Miss Vane cannot have read that. No one had read it but her brother and I.

I do not say that there are no explanations. A daughter may walk as her mother walked. A woman of forty-four may look, for a moment, by one candle, on one night, as her mother looked at thirty-five. I know what grief and candlelight will do to a face.

But I will say this for my own judgment. I was not, at that moment, looking for a ghost. I had just come down from a room where I had found a warm bed and no child. I was thinking of a missing bottle and a missing old man, and of a man drugged and out of doors. If I had been asked what I most wanted to see in that gallery, I should have said Mr Vane, in his dressing gown, winding a clock. I had no thought to spare for the dead. And she came down the gallery to me all the same.

* * *

When I could move, I took up the lamp and went to the end of the gallery.

I did not want to. I went because of the door. I had seen the light come from it, and I had to know.

The portrait was in its place. I held the lamp up to it. I had been half afraid, I think, that I should find the frame empty. It was not empty. She stood there in her grey gown with her hand on the chair, as she had stood since 1956.

I looked at her for a long while. The paint was only paint. The silk had no light of its own, but was a flat grey-white, laid on with a brush, and I could see the strokes. The eyes did not follow me. I moved from one side to the other, with the lamp, and they stayed where the painter had put them, looking at a point in the middle of the floor.

It was a picture of a woman. For twenty nights it had been something else, and now it had gone back to being a picture. I can only put it as I felt it then. It was like looking in at the window of a house and knowing, from the stillness, that the person who lives there has gone out.

The door of the Grey Room stood open. There was a key in the lock, an old iron one, with a loop of faded ribbon through the bow.

I went in.

I had imagined that room for three weeks. I had thought of dust sheets and cobwebs, and a smell of decay. It was nothing like that, and it would have been easier if it had been. The bed was made, with a white counterpane. There was a dressing table in the window with a triple glass, and on it silver brushes laid out, and a comb, and a little china tray with hairpins in it. There was a book on the table by the bed, with a marker in it. It was a room that someone had left a few hours ago, meaning to come back.

Only the cold was wrong. It was the cold of a room that has had no fire in it for twenty winters, and it had got into the walls.

There was a clock on the mantelpiece. It was stopped. All through that house, in every room, there was something ticking; I had not been out of the sound of it since the first of October. In that room there was none. The hands stood at twenty-five minutes to four. I learned afterward that the old man had stopped it with his own hand on the morning they brought her home, and that it was the only clock at Compline he had ever stopped before that night.

By the bed, on the floor, side by side, there was a pair of shoes. They were grey satin, with a small heel, gone yellowish. They had been set down neatly, toes to the wall. They had stood there for twenty years, where she had left them for her husband to find.

So there were two pairs. I thought of that, standing over them. The woman in the gallery had carried her shoes in her hand. And here were the dead woman's shoes on the floor where she had left them.

I looked round, and I saw the rest.

The wardrobe door was open. It is a big mahogany one with a long glass. Inside there were dresses, a row of them, in cotton bags, pushed along the rail. One hanger hung by itself at the end. It was a padded one, covered in grey silk to match, and it was empty and swinging a little. On the floor of the wardrobe lay a cotton bag that had been pulled off and dropped.

And across the white counterpane, flung down, there was a black dress.

I knew it. I had sat two places from that dress at dinner for an hour and a half. On the carpet by the bed there were a pair of black evening shoes, kicked off, one on its side. On the dressing table one of the silver brushes had been moved out of its line. I went and looked. There were hairs in it. Most were dark. One was quite white.

I have said that I do not make up evidence, and I do not leave it out. There it was. A living woman had come into that room within the last half hour, and taken off a black dress, and put on a grey one, and brushed her hair with her mother's brush.

I stood and looked at the black dress on the bed. I thought that I ought to feel relieved. I had been frightened nearly out of my senses a few minutes before, and here was the explanation, lying on a counterpane.

I felt no relief at all. I was colder than I had been in the gallery.

I shall try to say why. On the stairs I had asked myself what I had seen. In that room I began to ask a different question. I asked what makes a quiet, guarded woman of forty-four go up alone, at midnight, on the twentieth anniversary, to a locked room, and take off her own clothes there, and put on her dead mother's. Why should she take off her own shoes and leave them, and carry another pair in her hand, when she could not know that that had been done before? And why had she gone down the gallery with that face?

I thought: she did not decide to do this. Nobody decides to do such a thing. She was standing at a window, and something came to her, and she went.

I had come to Compline with a poor opinion of the books in which the dead walk about in sheets. I still have it. I do not think that Marguerite Vane walked that night as a white thing with no one inside it. I think she had waited twenty years in that cold room for someone to come who was the right size.

I went out. I did not touch the black dress. I drew the door shut behind me, and I did not turn the key. It was not mine to turn.

* * *

I found Mr Vane in the hall.

I came down the main stairs with the lamp, at about ten minutes past twelve, and he was there. He was standing in front of the stopped regulator with its long door open. He had on his overcoat over his evening clothes. I had not put it on him. His white hair was dark with rain and flattened to his head. His thin shoes had left wet marks all the way from the gunroom passage.

On the settle by the fire, the old clergyman was laid out, asleep, on his side.

Mr Vane had something in his two hands. He was lifting it into the clock case, and it was heavy, and he could not find the hook. I saw that his hands were shaking. I had never seen them shake before, and I had watched him cut a wheel the size of a lentil.

"Mr Vane!"

He did not turn. "One moment," he said. "One moment, my dear. I must just put this back. It's very wrong to leave a regulator without its weight; the line will kink."

I set the lamp down and went to him. He had got the thing up to the pulley and it had slipped. I put my hands under his.

"Let me. Tell me where it goes."

"The hook. There. No, the bow goes over. So."

I took the weight from him. It was a cylinder of lead cased in brass, as thick as my wrist and about eight inches long, with a brass loop at one end. It was a great deal heavier than I expected. It was cold, and it was wet, and I supposed that was the rain. I lifted it and found the hook with the loop and let it hang. The line took the strain and creaked.

My fingers had come away with something on them. I did not look. I wiped them down the side of my dress, without thinking, as one does.

"Shall I start it?" I asked. The pendulum hung dead.

"No. No. Leave it stopped." He shut the long glass door himself, carefully, and stood with his palm against it. "One stops the clocks. When there is a death in the house. My mother did it for my father, and I did it for—" He lost the name. "It is the custom. They are not to go again until after the funeral."

"There has been no death, Mr Vane."

"Yes," he said. He turned round and looked at me. I have never seen a face so empty of everything but fact. "I have killed Edmund."

I thought that I had not heard him. Then I thought that I had, and that he was wandering. He often said things at night. He had told me once that he had left the gas on at a house in Clerkenwell in 1938.

"You've been out of doors," I said. "You're wet through. You've had a dream, or you have been walking in your sleep. Come to the fire."

"Miss Quaile." He said it quite sharply. "You undertook not to lie to me. I'll thank you not to begin by telling me that I'm mistaken as to where I have been. I have been to the ice house. I followed him there. He went out of the drawing room, and I saw his face as he went, and I thought, that is a man going to do a thing he's ashamed of. I've seen him go out so before. I got up and went after him. I took this from the case as I passed, to stop the clock. I don't recollect why I thought it should be stopped. I must have known."

"Mr Vane, sit down."

"He was on the landing at the top of the steps. He had a lamp. He had a box in his arms, and in the box was her clock. The Thorne. He had it in a blanket, like something he was going to drown." His voice was thin and exact. He might have been dictating. "I said, 'Edmund, it was you.' He said, 'Of course it was me, Father. Who else in this house could have done it?' I said, 'Why?' I asked him quite quietly. I've waited a year to ask him. And he laughed at me. He was not himself; his speech was thick and he could hardly stand. He said, 'It's a copy, you old fool. They're all copies. There's nothing in this house that isn't a copy of something. You've been winding fakes for four years and never knew it. You never knew anything. You never knew about her.'"

He stopped. His lips moved for a moment without sound.

"I asked him what he meant by that. He said, 'Ask the girl. Ask your nurse. She's got it in her pocket.'"

I put my hand to my pocket. I could not stop myself. The red book was there.

"And then he said the thing about the clock again. He said, 'It was never the clock.' He laughed. And I had this in my hand, on its line, and I swung it. I don't know that I meant to. It went of itself, like a pendulum." He touched his own left temple with one finger. "Here. He went backward, with the box. I heard him go down the steps, all of them. There are twelve. And then nothing. There was water dripping."

I had hold of his arm. I do not know when I had taken it.

"I stood there. I called to him. Then I thought, I must fetch Margot, she will know what to do. I came away. I pulled the gate to after me, because one always shuts that gate; the ice goes else. I came across the yard, and there was a child."

"A child?"

"Standing in the rain by the stable wall. A small girl, with dark hair. She was looking at me. I thought she was Imogen. I said, 'Go in, Immy, you'll catch cold.' She ran away." He frowned. "But Imogen's a grown woman. I can't account for that."

I could not speak. I thought of three wet footprints with stars in them.

"So you see," said Mr Vane, "that I have killed my son. It was at ten minutes to twelve. I looked at the dial as I came in, and every clock in this hall said the same."

* * *

I was a nurse for five years, and I have to say what a nurse did then.

I looked at him. I looked at his hands, back and front, for a cut. There was none. I looked at his shirt cuffs. The left was clean. On the right, where it came out of the black sleeve, there was a stain, and smaller ones running up toward the link. It was the size of a half-crown. It was red going brown.

I thought: he has fallen, out there, and has grazed himself where I cannot see. I thought: it is rust, from the gate. I told myself several things of that kind while I stood holding his wrist.

It was not that I disbelieved him. I should like that to be understood. I knew him too well by then. He was a man who could not have invented a thing to save his life; he had no gift for it. When he was confused he lost pieces of the world, but he did not make new ones. And he had given me a place, and a time, and a count of steps.

But I also knew something that he did not. I knew that Edmund had gone out of that drawing room with half a bottle of chloral in him. A man in that condition, struck on the head, at the top of twelve stone stairs, in a place as cold as a grave—

I said, "I must go to him."

"No." His hand closed on mine. It was astonishingly strong. "No. You promised. You said that you would stand by me at one."

"Mr Vane, if he is lying hurt—"

"He is not hurt. He is dead. I heard him go down." He was holding me with both hands now, and his face was working. "And it does not signify. Don't you see? It doesn't signify in the least. It is ten minutes past twelve. In fifty minutes the hour comes back, and I shall take it. I told you. I have her coupled and set. I shall go through it again, from twelve o'clock, and when I come to the ice house I shall not strike. It's perfectly simple. I had thought that I should need it only for Margot. I see now why I was made to build it. It was for both."

"That can't be done! I told you in the tower that it can't be done. He may be alive. He may be lying at the bottom of those steps with his skull broken, and every minute—"

"You'll not leave me."

"I must!"

I pulled my hands away. I had the lamp. I had taken two steps toward the gunroom passage.

I heard a sound behind me that I knew. I have heard it on a ward a hundred times. It is a small sound, like a sigh, and then the slither of cloth.

When I turned he was on the floor.

He had gone down all of a piece, as the very old do, without putting out a hand. He lay on the flagstones at the foot of the regulator with his long legs folded under him and his eyes half open. His face was the colour of putty and his lips were blue.

I do not remember crossing to him. I had him on his back and his collar open and my fingers on his neck before I knew that I had moved. The pulse was there, but it was thin, and it ran, and missed, and ran again. His skin was cold and wet. He had been out in a gale in thin shoes, at eighty-one, and had done whatever he had done, and walked back, and it had caught up with him.

I could not leave him then. I say it plainly. A nurse doesn't leave the patient who is on the floor in front of her to go and look for one who may be lying somewhere else. It is the first thing one is taught, and it is right. I got his feet up on a footstool. I loosened everything. I took the rug from the back of the settle, where the vicar lay, and I wrapped him in it, and I knelt on the stone with his head in my lap and counted his pulse against the big clock by the stairs.

I called out. I called for Mr Fenn, and for Mrs Pask, and for Gail. Nobody came. The drawing-room door was shut. The kitchen is down a flight and through a baize door, and I learned afterward that Mrs Pask was not in it, and that Gail had her shoes off by the range and heard nothing over the wind.

I counted. I thought: twenty minutes past twelve. I thought of twelve brick steps and water dripping. I thought of a child standing in the rain.

I had been set to keep two things safe in that house. I had left one of them, the bottle, for an hour and a half, and I had left the other for five minutes. I knelt on the floor of the hall with the old man's head on my knees, and I knew that between them my two absences had done it. I did not know yet what had been done. But I had left a drug where a hand could reach it, and it had made the son helpless. Then I had left the father alone, and he had got up and followed him with a weight.

I had come there so that I should never again be asleep when I was needed. I had been awake the whole time, and it had happened all the same.

* * *

He came round at about twenty to one.

His colour came back first. Then his eyelids moved, and he looked up at me, and I saw at once that it had gone. I mean the knowledge. His eyes were mild and clear and puzzled.

"Have I been asleep?" he said.

"You fainted, Mr Vane. You're in the hall. Lie still a moment."

"In the hall? How very odd. I don't remember coming down." He turned his head and saw the candles and the tall clocks. "Is it time? Have I missed it?"

"It's twenty minutes to one."

"Then there is time. Help me up, my dear. I mustn't be found on the floor." I got him into a chair. He sat with his hands on his knees, getting his breath. He looked at his wet shoes with surprise. "I have been out. Did I go out?"

I knelt by the chair. I looked into his face. He had asked me a question, and I had given him my word.

"Yes," I said. "You went out. You told me that you had been to the ice house."

"The ice house? Whatever for?"

I opened my mouth. I had it all ready. *You told me that you followed your son there and struck him with the weight of that clock, and that he fell down the steps.* I had told him on twenty nights that his wife was drowned. I had never spared him.

I could not say it. I had no rule for this. I did not know that it was true. If it was, I should be telling a man who had forgotten that he had killed his son. If it was not, I should be putting a horror into his head that had not been there. I looked at his mild face and I thought, for the first time since I came to that house, that there might be a thing worse than a lie.

"You didn't say," I told him. "You were very tired."

It was the second lie. I notice that I have kept count.

"Ah," said Mr Vane. He was satisfied. He looked across at the regulator. "That clock has stopped. How very vexing. It is never out. I shall look at it presently." His eyes went round the hall and came back to me, and brightened. "Has Margot come down?"

"Not yet, Mr Vane."

That was the third. I said it as they all said it. I heard my own voice.

People began to come in. It was nearly a quarter to one. Mr Fenn came from the drawing room with Dame Octavia on his arm, grumbling, and put her in the big chair. He carried bottles in from the pantry. Gail came up with a taper and began to light more candles, dozens of them, until the hall was as bright as a church. I got to my feet. My knees were stiff from the stone. There was a dark smear down the side of my blue dress, where I had wiped my fingers, and I held my hand over it.

I went to Mr Fenn. I spoke low.

"Mr Fenn. I can't leave Mr Vane; he has had a faint. But someone must go out to the ice house at once, with a light. I have reason to think that Mr Edmund is there, and that he's hurt."

He looked at me over his spectacles.

"What reason, Miss Quaile?"

"Mr Vane said so. Before he fainted. He has forgotten it since."

"Leo says a great many things."

"He said it very exactly."

"He is always exact. He told me last month with great exactness that I had died in 1987." But I saw that his face had changed. He looked old and wary. "Who is there to send? Kit is not to be found. I am sixty-seven and I do not know the way in the dark. The cook has vanished." He glanced round. "I will send Mr Pargeter, when he appears. He's young, and willing, and has nothing to do. Will that content you?"

It did not content me. But the old man had hold of my sleeve again and was asking me whether the door had been unbolted.

It was at that moment, at about ten minutes to one, that Mrs Edmund Vane came into the hall.

She came from the garden passage. She had on the green dress that she had dined in, and her shoes, and her fair hair was combed. But it was wet. It lay dark and flat against her head, and there was a leaf caught in it, behind her ear, that she had missed. Her face had no colour at all. She walked across the hall like a person carrying a full glass.

I went to her. I do not know what I meant to say. I think that I meant to ask her to go out to her husband.

"Mrs Vane. Have you seen Mr Edmund?"

She looked at me. Her eyes were quite blank.

"No," she said.

"I think that he may be ill. The bottle is gone from my tray. Mr Vane's sleeping draught. Someone has taken it out of his room, this evening, while we were at dinner, and has given a large dose of it to your husband in a glass of brandy. The vicar drank what he left, and is insensible." I was watching her face. "I think that Mr Edmund may be lying somewhere out of doors."

She did not ask me how I knew. She did not ask who would do such a thing, or exclaim, or put a hand to her mouth. Any woman would have done one of those. She stood and took it, as one takes a blow that one has seen coming for some time.

"Has someone," said Mrs Vane. Her voice was dry and very quiet. "Then he will be asleep, won't he? Somewhere. I shouldn't distress yourself, Miss Quaile. Edmund always turns up."

She went past me. She walked to the far end of the hall and took up a place by herself under the largest of the clocks, where the candles were thickest, and folded her hands in front of her, and stood.

I have said that I had no proof. I have none now. But I had seen her head come up in the drawing room, when he yawned, and her face when he went out. I had told her that her husband was drugged and lying out in a storm. She had answered me as though I had told her the time.

I knew then whose hand had been at my tray. I did not know why. I have never told anyone. She is gone abroad, I am told, and he is dead, and it was my bottle.

Mr Vane was tugging at my sleeve.

"It wants five minutes," he said. "Give me your arm. You'll stand on my left. You promised."

I gave him my arm. I thought: I will stand by him while he opens his door. It will take two minutes. And then, whatever he says, whoever holds me, I shall take a lamp and go to the ice house myself.

I walked him down the length of the hall to the great front door. His hand was steady again. He laid it on the bolt.

Behind us, one after another, the clocks began to strike.

## VI. The Tower

The front door of Compline faces east. From the step one looks across eighty yards of gravel to the stable arch, and above the arch the tower, with the clock face and the little roof.

Mr Vane drew the bolt. He took the two leaves of the door in his hands and folded them back against the wall. I stood at his left elbow, as I had promised. The night came in upon us, cold and wet, and the nearest candles lay over and went out.

The rain had stopped and the wind had dropped to nothing. There was a moon. It was low and white, behind a thin cloud, and it lit the gravel like frost. Everything was very clear and still. I could see each stone of the stable arch.

"Come in," the old man said, to the dark. "Come in, then. You're late."

I was not listening to him. I was looking at the tower.

There was a light on it. It was at the top, on the leads, under the roof where the figures stand. It was a lantern, and someone was holding it; it swung from side to side, slowly, in an arc, as a man swings a lamp to signal. It lit the underside of the tiles and the bell. It lit the grey woman on the right hand, all down one side, so that I saw her painted gown and her lifted arm.

And it lit a man.

He was standing to the left of the bell, where the small figure stands that strikes the quarters. I saw a white shirt-front and a black coat. I saw the light slide over a white cuff. He was in evening dress.

I knew that the Jack had been dressed for the night. I had been told so at tea; the young people had gone across with an old dinner jacket of Mr Vane's and a shawl. I knew therefore that there was a wooden figure on that tower in a black coat. I have never pretended that I did not know it.

But a wooden figure does not hold a lantern, and it does not swing one. There was something up there that moved. And as I stared, I saw that the black and white was not one shape but more than one. It shifted. A part of it came forward into the light and another part stayed back. I could not separate them. I can say only that on the left side of that bell, where for two hundred years there had been one small man of oak, there was that night more than he.

Behind me in the hall the last clock finished. There was a silence.

The tower clock began to strike. First came the four quarters on the small bell. I saw an arm rise and fall beside the lantern, four times, stiffly, and the light jerked with it.

Then the grey woman moved.

I had never seen her strike. I had always been in a room, or with my back to that door. Her whole arm came down from the shoulder, slowly, as a person brings down an axe, and the hammer met the great bell, and the note rolled out across the yard and over my head into the house.

It was one o'clock.

On that stroke, in the same instant, there was a flash of red in the darkness under the tower, down in the yard, and a noise like a door slammed in my face. And another.

The lantern leapt. It went up, and sideways, and fell. It fell straight down the front of the tower past the clock face, turning, and went out.

I saw the man go. The lantern was still in the air, and gave me its last light, and by it I saw the man on the left of the bell go backward. He did not crumple. He went all of a piece, slowly, with his arms out from his sides, like someone falling back into deep water. For a moment I saw the white of his shirt, tilted up toward the roof. Then he had gone over the far edge of the leads and there was nothing there.

On the first stroke of one a man in evening dress fell from the clock tower, and the grey woman beside him had her arm raised.

It was raised again. I saw that last, by the moon, when the lantern was out. She had struck, and her arm had gone back up to her shoulder, as it does, to wait for the next hour. She stood alone under the roof with the hammer lifted. She was not looking at the place where he had been. She was looking, as she always looked, across the yard at the house. She was looking at the open door, and at the old man, and at me.

I cried out. I did not know that I was going to. I had both hands at my mouth.

Mr Vane had not started. He stood in his doorway with his arms a little out, as he had held the doors, and his face was lifted to the tower, and he was quite calm.

"Ah," he said. "Yes. I thought there would be something to pay."

* * *

I should have run out. I know it. I had resolved five minutes before that as soon as the door was open I would take a lamp and go. I had now seen a man fall forty feet. I stood on the step and could not move.

It was his hand. He had taken hold of my wrist, without looking at me, and he held it down at his side as one holds a child at a kerb.

"Hush," he said, very low. "Don't tell them. They'd not understand the accounts."

"Mr Vane, there was a man—"

"I saw him. It is the debit. An hour is given back, and something is taken for it; I ought to have foreseen that. One cannot have an entry on one side only." He was nodding. "It is all right, my dear. It is all right now. I have it. I felt it come in at the door. Did you not feel it?"

"Somebody has fallen from the tower!"

I turned round to say it to the hall. I believe that I did say it. But my voice had gone to a thread, and they were all behind us, in the candlelight, and all talking, and not one of them had seen. I looked from face to face. Mr Fenn was saying that it was thunder. Dame Octavia said in her great voice that it was a twelve-bore and that somebody was after the duck. The cropped girl on the stairs said something, and there was a laugh. They had heard two bangs in the night and had explained them to one another before the echo died.

I stood with my back to the night and looked at them. And for a moment I felt the whole thing turn over, as one feels a boat turn.

I thought of the Jack. He was a wooden figure in an old dinner jacket, two hundred years on an iron pin, on the left side of that bell. Somebody below had fired a gun. I had seen black and white in a swinging light, at eighty yards, at night, and I had seen it fall. I had known all along that he was there.

I thought: that is what it was. Thank God. That is all it was.

But the lantern. Someone had held the lantern. A thing of oak does not swing a light to and fro.

I had my mouth open to say so. And through the baize door at the back of the hall, at that moment, the tall young man came in backwards, carrying a box, and said in a loud glad voice:

"Uncle Leo! The ice cometh!"

* * *

It was a wooden box with tin corners. He carried it the length of the hall and set it on the table and cut the cord. There was a grey blanket. He lifted something out of a pillowcase, with a flourish, and said a word in French.

It was a brass clock with a painted moon.

*He had a box in his arms, and in the box was her clock. He had it in a blanket, like something he was going to drown.*

The old man had said that to me an hour ago, by the stopped regulator, before he fainted. He had said that he struck his son, and that the son went backward down the steps with the box. I had half believed and half hoped. I had told myself that he lost pieces of the world but did not make new ones.

And here was the box, and the blanket. The young man said that it had been at the bottom of the steps.

It was true, then. Everything he had told me in the hall was true. Edmund had been in the ice house with that clock in his arms, and his father had come upon him there. And that box had been at the bottom of the steps because it had gone down them with a man.

I looked at Mrs Edmund Vane. She was standing under the tall clock with her hands folded. She was looking at the thing on the table. She did not look surprised. She looked as I have seen relatives look in a hospital corridor, when the doctor comes out and they can tell from the way he shuts the door.

Mr Vane had gone down the hall to it. He was bending over the clock with his glass. He said, "Ah. The Copy. I wondered where I had put it." He remembered nothing. He was pleased to see it. He thanked the young man, and said that we had been promised an ice.

I caught the young man by the sleeve as he went past me with the empty box.

"Mr Pargeter. Where is Mr Edmund?"

He went a deep red. He looked at the box, and at the floor, and at a spot above my head.

"I'm afraid I couldn't say," he said. "I promised." And then, in a rush: "He's all right, though. Honestly. I'll tell you presently. I can't now, I've got to put this away."

He went through the baize door. I stood where he had left me.

*He's all right.* He had been to the ice house. He had brought the box from the bottom of the steps. If there had been a dead man lying beside it he would not have come into the hall making a joke about ice. So Edmund had not been there. Or he had been there, and was not dead, and had got up.

Then where was he?

I looked out through the open door, at the tower. The grey woman stood alone under the roof.

* * *

I shall pass quickly over the next quarter of an hour. I was held in that hall by an old man's hand and by my own promise, and I was thinking of one thing only. But I must say what Mr Vane said, since I have heard that it was reported afterward, and that some people thought it showed his mind was gone. I thought it was the sanest thing I heard in that house.

He sat down in the chair by the door, with the rug over his knees, and I stood by him. He told his family that he had asked a question at dinner and no longer wanted the answer. He said that a clock was for telling a man how much time he had got, and that he owned a hundred and eleven, and they had only ever told him how much he had had. He said that if anything had been taken from him, it had no doubt been wanted more than he wanted it, and that he had been a father to whom a person could not come and ask. He would put it all on the Hour's account.

Then he called Mr Fenn to him and dictated a paper. I did not attend to it. I caught the name of the farm across the water. I heard him say, "I can't pay it to the man. I let him die without. I'll pay it to his name." I did not know what was owed, or to whom. I understood only that he was settling something, and that he did it like a man going through his pockets before a journey.

When that was done he shut his eyes, and I thought that I might go. I had drawn my wrist very gently out of his fingers. I had taken one step from the chair.

"Kit," he said, without opening them. "Wind the gramophone. I should like the Lehár."

The boy went to the corner. There was the sound of a handle turning, and a hiss, and then music, a slow waltz with violins. It was old, and sweet, and it filled the hall, and under it one could still hear the clocks.

I heard the girl on the stairs say her lover's name, in a gasp. I looked up.

She was coming down the main staircase.

She had one hand on the rail. She came a step at a time, in the candlelight, with the grey silk moving round her and her shoulders bare and her dark head up. She had put her shoes on. Her face was white, and wet, and there was a smile on it, a small steady one, as of someone who has made up her mind to be brave about a thing that is going to hurt.

I had seen her go down the back stair to the garden an hour before. I had stood in her cold room and looked at a black dress on the counterpane. I had told myself everything that a sensible woman tells herself. I had it all arranged in my head, the key and the hanger and the white hair in the brush. I knew as well as I knew my own name that the person on those stairs was Miss Imogen Vane, in a borrowed gown.

I am ashamed to say that it made no difference. My knees gave. I went back against the wall beside the door, and slid down it, and sat on the stone floor with my hands pressed flat on either side of me.

I saw Dame Octavia Prowse get up out of her chair, without help, which she had not done all night. I heard her say, "Oh, Daisy." I saw the boy at the gramophone with his hand out, and his mouth moving. I saw Mr Fenn bow his head, as a man does in church. Those were people who had known Marguerite Vane alive. They had dined with her, and quarrelled with her, and followed her coffin. They looked up at that staircase, and I saw in their faces that they did not doubt who was coming down.

Mr Vane had risen. He stood by his chair. The rug had fallen.

"You came back," he said. "Margot. You came back."

She crossed the floor to him. She put out her hand.

"Yes, Papa," she said. Then, lower, and I think that only he and I were near enough to hear it, "Yes, Leo. I came back."

They danced.

I have been asked by Dr Imrie what I felt, sitting on that floor. I have told him that I do not know the word. It was not fear, by then. The fear had been in the gallery. This was a thing that I had no right to be present at.

He held her as if she were made of glass. He had his eyes shut and his face lifted. He, who an hour before had lain on that same floor with his lips blue, led her round his hall, among his clocks, without a fault. And he talked to her. I heard some of it, each time they came by the door. He was telling her the tide.

"High water was at eight minutes to one," he said. "I have it from the Thorne. The Wade will not carry you on foot before half past four. But a horse may go at twenty minutes to three, and not a minute before, and he must swim at the Rill. Do you hear me, Margot? I had it wrong for you. The last time. I put the hall clock back and I never told you. I've got it right now. I have had twenty years to get it right."

"I hear you, Leo."

"You'll not go on foot."

"No."

"You'll wait for the horse."

"I'll wait."

"Then you will get across," he said. "You'll get across, my dear. That is all I wanted. I don't ask you to stay."

Her face was over his shoulder. I saw it when he said that. I saw what it did. I do not think that Miss Imogen Vane, by herself, could have looked like that at her father. There were two women in that face, and one of them was hearing a thing that she had waited twenty years to hear.

The record ended. The needle ran on in the groove. He stood still, holding her.

"There," he said. "There, my dear. You see. It's quite all right. We had the time after all."

She kissed him on the forehead. She took his face between her hands for a moment and looked at it. Then she turned, and went away quickly toward the garden passage. As she passed the place where I sat she looked down at me.

They were grey eyes, and they were full of tears. She knew me. She gave me a little nod, such as one gives to a nurse in a sickroom on the way out, that means *I leave him with you.*

I do not know to this day which of them it was that nodded.

* * *

I got up. I took the old man to his chair. He went like a child that has been promised something and been given it. He was smiling, and his eyes were closing.

I stood beside him and I looked through the door at the tower. There was nothing there. I knew what I had to do, and I was waiting only until he should be asleep.

It was then that the young man came across the hall to me. I have read what he has written of it, since. He was kind enough to send me the pages. He has put down what he said and what I answered, and I cannot find that he has changed a word. I shall therefore not go through it again. I shall say only what it was like from where I stood.

He told me that Edmund had been found at the bottom of the ice-house steps, drugged, with a wound on his head. He said that he and the cook had carried him to the stables and put him in the end loose box, under the tower, and that he had been left there asleep, at a quarter to one.

"Asleep," I said. "You left him asleep."

"Snoring like a grampus."

I looked at the tower. I had the whole of it then. It came together in my mind as quickly as a thing falls.

His father had struck him at ten minutes to twelve. He had lain at the bottom of those steps for half an hour. He had been lifted out, alive, and carried to the stable, and laid in straw at the foot of the tower stair. That was at a quarter to one.

And at one o'clock, fifteen minutes later, I had seen someone at the top of that tower with a lantern. I had seen a man in a black coat go backward over the edge.

"Then he woke," I said. "He woke, and he went up."

The young man said that it was impossible, with so much of the drug in him. He reminded me that I had said the vicar would be out for twelve hours. He was quite right. I had said so. It is what the dose would do, in an old man of nine stone.

I had sat by Edmund Vane at dinner. I had watched him drink for three weeks. I knew what he could carry, and how he could stand upright and speak clearly when another man would be on the floor. I thought: he woke in the dark, in the straw, with his head broken and that stuff in his blood. He did not know where he was or how he had come there. He saw the stair and climbed it, as he had climbed it when he was a boy and was unhappy. The girl had said so; I had heard her. *He goes up that tower when he's upset.* He took the lantern that hung in the harness room. He came out upon the leads, beside the grey woman, at the moment that she struck.

Dame Octavia had said that it was the Jack that fell. Perhaps the Jack did fall. I have told you that there was more than one shape on that side of the bell. But the Jack was not the only man in evening dress on that tower, and one of them had held the light.

The young man was still speaking. I heard him as one hears a person through a wall. He was saying that he would look after me. He said that whatever had happened that night, the glass, and the tray, and what I had seen, I need never say a word of it to anyone. He would say nothing himself. He asked me whether I would.

I looked at him. He had a round, anxious, honest face, and his hands were going. He had carried a hurt man up twelve steps because he thought it right. He had fetched me to the vicar. I thought that he was the only one in that house, that night, who had done nothing but try to help.

And he was offering me silence. I thought that was what he offered. The tray had been in my charge. The old man had been in my charge. I had failed in both, and a man was dead of it, and here was someone who knew a part and guessed more, telling me that it should go no further.

I said yes.

I have been told that he meant something else. He told me so himself, in a tea shop, with a ring in a box, and I have never been so sorry for anything. I had not heard what he asked. I had heard only that there was a way to stop thinking, and I took it.

* * *

Mr Vane woke. He spoke to the young man, and wrote something for him, and got up. He said that there was a clock stopped, and went across the hall to the regulator and opened the long door.

I followed a few steps. The heavy man from the insurers had come in from the back. He was wet to the thighs and there was blood dried on his face. He went and stood by Mr Vane, and they spoke together in low voices. I saw the old man touch the weight with his fingers. I saw him turn his wrist over and look at his cuff.

The young man said something to me about a clock that he had trodden on. I did not understand him.

When I looked again, Mr Vane had gone. The front door stood open. The heavy man was by himself in front of the regulator.

I went to him. I asked whether he had seen Mr Vane. He said that he had been there a moment since, looking at the clock.

I looked at the clock. The case was open. The pendulum hung straight. At the bottom of its line was the weight that I had lifted onto its hook two hours before.

There were fifty candles in the hall now. When I had held that thing in my hands I had had one lamp, standing on the floor behind me. I had felt that it was wet, and wiped my fingers.

It was not wet now. It had dried. Along one side of the brass, near the lower rim, there was a smear, as long as my finger, dull and dark, like varnish. In the smear there were hairs. There were four or five, stuck fast. They were short and dark, and one was grey.

I do not know what was in my face. The heavy man was watching it. He was the kind who does.

I shut the door of the case. I pressed it until the catch took. I said, "Thank you," and I walked away from him to the stairs.

I went up to my room and put on my outdoor shoes and my cloak. I took the lamp. I had finished with promises. The old man had gone out of the house again, alone, and this time I knew where.

* * *

I crossed the yard at about twenty minutes to two.

The moon was higher and very bright. The tide had turned. I could hear it going, behind the stables, a long soft sucking sound. I did not go to the tower door first. I went round the end of the block, by the track, to the back, where the ground falls to the creek they call the fleet.

It was full, and it was running out. It was black, and quite smooth, and it slid along under the wall of the stables with a speed that made me giddy to look at.
