If she went down to that yard, she would have to tell him. He would look at her, with those steady eyes, and she would have to say, *It was me. I told Edmund. And I hid, and let her go alone.* And then she would see his face change. She thought that she could bear anything but that.

So she had stayed behind the curtain. At a quarter past twelve he put his cap on, and turned, and walked out of the yard.

He left a letter with Dolly. It was one sheet, in pencil, in a round careful hand like a schoolboy's.

*I don't know what I done. If it is on account of my father and your mother I never knew of it till after. I would not have kept it from you. I will be at Saltcote till the 14th of November. Then I have took a passage. If you will come I will stay. If you send word I will stay. I will not come to the house again as I think it troubles you. T. G.*

She had read it standing at the scullery window. She had it still. It was in Edinburgh, in the lid of her workbox, with an iron ring that she had kept oiled for twenty years.

She did not send word. On the fourteenth she sat in her room all day with the door locked. On the fifteenth she packed, and went back to London, and did not come home again in October.

There had been one more. It came to the Institute, in the spring of 1976, forwarded from Compline. It had a Canadian stamp. Inside was a photograph, taken with a cheap camera. It showed a plain of yellow grass running away to the edge of the picture, and a line of mountains, very small, with snow on them. There was nothing else. No house, no figure. On the back he had written the name of a place, and then:

*It is all sky here. You would like the colour. T.*

She had looked at that photograph for a long time. She was a person whose business it was to look. She saw that he had stood in the middle of an empty country and tried to find something in it that he could give her, and that this was what he had found.

She had not answered. She had not known what to say that would be true and not unbearable. She told herself that she would write when she had found the words. She was still looking for them a year later. After that it was too late; one cannot answer a letter three years old.

Somebody had told her, in the 'eighties, that he had married. Dolly, she thought. It had come in a list of village news, between a wedding and a flood. *Young Tom Garrow's wed out there, his father says. A girl off a ranch.* Imogen had said, "I'm glad," and found, to her surprise, that it was true. She had been glad for him, and gone back to her flat, and taken off a decent man's ring.

* * *

Her father was in the Shop. She went down the stone steps at a quarter to eight and found him at his bench, under the window, with a thing in his hand no bigger than a sixpence.

"Papa."

He looked up. For an instant his eyes did not know her. Then they cleared, and he smiled, the slow sweet smile that he so seldom gave.

"Imogen. They said you were coming. I said, she never comes in October. Fenn must have written." He held up his cheek for her to kiss, like a child. His skin was as dry as paper. "You're thin. Are you working?"

"A Raeburn. A man in a red coat. Somebody cleaned him with soda in 1890 and took his eyebrows off."

"Can you put them back?"

"I can put back what I'm sure was there. Not more."

"That is honest. I'm glad to hear it. So few people will stop at what they are sure of." He turned the little wheel in his fingers, and she saw that it was newly cut, and bright. "I have been doing something of the kind myself. Not restoring. Making good. There was a thing I got wrong, a long time ago, and I've found a way to put it right. I shan't tell you. You would say that it couldn't be done. But you will see, tonight."

"What did you get wrong, Papa?"

"The time," he said simply. "I gave your mother the wrong time."

She stood beside him. She put her hand on his shoulder. It was all bone under the cardigan.

She had heard him say it for twenty years. Every time she came. *I put the clocks back early. She went by the hall clock. It was my doing.* And every time she had stood, as she stood now, with the truth in her mouth like a stone.

*It wasn't the clock, Papa. Edmund went after her. He kept her out there. I saw the lights. I saw him come back.*

She had never said it. To say it, she would have had to say the rest. *And he went because I told him.* She had kept silent to shield her brother, she told herself. It was a noble thing; one did not give one's brother to one's father. But she knew that it was not Edmund she was shielding.

So she let her father go on believing that he had killed his wife with a clock. She had let him turn the house into a shrine to it. She came twice a year, and kissed his cheek, and went away.

"You look like her this morning," he said. He was peering at her through his glass. "About the eyes. You have always had her eyes. I used to find it a comfort and now I find that I can't always tell." He touched her face, lightly. "Don't mind me if I call you by her name tonight. I do sometimes. Miss Quaile corrects me. It is very good of her, but one gets tired of being corrected."

"I shan't mind, Papa."

"No. You never minded things. You were the quiet one. Edmund made all the noise." He turned back to his bench. "He is unhappy, you know. He has been unhappy since he was thirty-two, and I've never found out why. I am not a man that people tell things to. Your mother said so. She said that I could hear a watch losing two seconds a week and couldn't hear my own children."

Imogen went up the steps. At the top she had to stop, and hold the rail.

* * *

She had meant to keep indoors. She had the whole day planned. She would look at the pictures in the dining room, which needed it. She would help Dolly with the silver. She would stay on the east side of the house, where the windows looked at the stables and not across the water.

At a quarter past eight she was standing at a window of the long gallery with her grandfather's telescope.

It was a ship's glass, of brass, in three draws, with the leather gone from the barrel. It had lain in that window seat since before she was born. As children she and Edmund had fought for it, to watch the shipping. She had not gone to look for it. She had been walking past, and her hand had lifted the seat, and there it was.

She told herself that she wanted to see the birds.

The tide was making. It had filled the creeks and was coming in over the flats from the north, grey and wrinkled, and the Wade lay across it like a road in a flood, with half an hour left to it at most. Across half a mile of mud and water the far shore stood up very clear in the cold light. She found the sea wall. She moved the glass along it, slowly, to the left. A tarred barn. Another. A black gable, with a chimney, and smoke.

The yard came into the circle, small and bright and shaking a little with her pulse.

There was the grey mare. She had her rug off, and she stood square and patient on the stones, with her head down. She was white now with age, white as a swan. And beside her, with his back to the glass, bent double, with one of her hind feet between his knees, was a man in a canvas coat.

Imogen stopped breathing.

She could see nothing of his face. She saw a hat, a wide one with a curled brim, pushed back. A lean back, with the coat tight across the shoulders. Long legs, in faded blue. He was working at the hoof with a rasp. She could see his elbow going. Every few strokes he stopped, and ran his thumb along what he had done, and bent again.

She would have known him among ten thousand, by that. He did it as he had done everything, slowly and completely, with his whole attention. He had drawn a foal so, with his eyes shut. He had kissed her so.

He let the foot down. He straightened, with a hand to the small of his back, the way a man does who is no longer twenty-three. He took off his hat and wiped his forehead on his sleeve. And he turned round.

She had been told that he had gone grey. She had not been told the rest. The round brown boy's face that she had carried about with her was gone. This was a man's face, long and spare and weathered, with lines cut deep on either side of the mouth, as though by wind. The brows had come down. It was a face that had spent twenty years looking at a great distance in a hard light.

But the eyes had not changed. She could not see their colour through the glass; she did not need to. She saw how they rested on things. He looked at the mare. He looked at the sky, a long measuring look, and she knew that he was reading the weather, and that there would be wind by dark.

And then he lifted his head and looked across the water at the house.

He looked straight at it. He stood with his hat in his hand and his eyes on Compline, and his face was perfectly still. It was not the way one looks at a view. She had seen that look on him once before, in a yard, in the rain, turned up toward a curtain.

She knew that he could not see her. She was a quarter of an inch of dark glass in a wall of windows, half a mile away. But the telescope brought him so near that she could have counted the buttons on his coat, and it seemed to her that his eyes came down the length of the brass tube and found her.

She stepped back from the window so sharply that the glass struck the frame.

Her heart was going like a bird's. She stood against the panelling with the telescope held to her chest. She was forty-four years old. She was a senior conservator, with a pension, and a flat, and a white streak in her hair. She was hiding from a man behind a wall for the second time in her life.

When she dared to look again, he had put his hat on. He was standing with his back to her. A car had come along the road on top of the sea wall, a big dull one, and stopped at the head of the ramp. A heavy man in a raincoat had got out and was reading the tide board. Tom was watching him.

She saw the stranger get back into his car and drive down onto the Wade, with the sea already at the stones. She saw Tom turn his head and follow the car with his eyes, the whole way across, until it was hidden by the point. Then he looked at the house again.

He stood a moment longer. He put his hand inside his coat, to his chest, as though to feel that something was there. He took the mare by the halter and led her into the barn.

Imogen closed the telescope. She laid it in the window seat and shut the lid.

She thought: he has not come home to bury his father and go away again. A man does not look at a house like that who means to leave it alone.

She did not know what he meant to do. She thought of a notice to quit, folded small, inside a shirt. She thought of her brother, who would be drunk by noon.

And she thought, with a clearness that frightened her, that whatever Tom Garrow had come back to settle with the Vanes, he had a right to settle it. The first account on the list was hers.

Behind her, at the end of the gallery, the cracked clock struck the half hour. Under the portrait the lamp had burned out. Her mother looked down the length of the floor at her, with her lips parted, as though she had just asked a question and would wait as long as it took for the answer.

## Chapter Three

She found Edmund in the gunroom at noon. He was sitting on the bench where they had sat as children to have their boots pulled off, with a tumbler beside him and an open letter in his hand. He put the letter in his pocket when she came in.

"Immy," he said. "The prodigal. I didn't believe Fenn when he said you'd come."

"I didn't believe Dolly when she said what you'd done."

"I've done a number of things. You'll have to narrow it down."

"Saltcote. A notice to quit. On the morning they buried him."

He looked at her blankly. Then she saw it reach him. He shut his eyes.

"Was it," he said. "Was that the day? Christ." He rubbed his face with his big hand. "I told Fenn the end of the week. I never looked at a calendar. I haven't looked at one since September. Was the boy there? Did he get it at the church?"

"He got it in Dolly's kitchen. He read it twice and put it in his shirt."

"Yes. He would. They never say anything, the Garrows. They just put it away somewhere and wait." He reached for the tumbler. "Don't look at me like that. It's a hundred and forty acres of grazing below the level of the sea, and the wall wants twenty thousand spent on it, and the old man paid the same rent in 1994 that his father paid in 1950 because Father never thought to put it up. There's a man who'll give me a hundred and ten thousand for it, for a holiday park. I owe more than that."

"How much more?"

"Enough."

"Edmund."

"Don't, Immy." He said it quite gently. "You've been in Edinburgh for twenty years, cleaning other people's pictures. You come down at Easter and in August and you look round at the damp and the dry rot, and you look at me. Then you go back. I don't blame you. I'd have gone if I could. But don't come home in October and ask me how much."

She sat down on the other end of the bench. There was a row of pegs opposite, with old coats on them, and under the coats a rack of guns. She remembered her brother teaching her to shoot, when she was ten and he was eighteen, out on the wall. He had put his arms round her from behind to hold the stock to her shoulder. He had been patient with her. He had been the kindest and funniest person she knew.

She looked at him now, sideways. He was fifty-two. He was heavy and grey and his hand was not quite steady on the glass. But he still had the long lashes, and the trick of looking up from under them, that had made every girl in the county stupid in 1962.

"The clocks," she said.

He went still.

"I looked at the Tompion in the hall this morning. The month-going one. It's Papa's copy. I knew it the moment I saw the dial; the silvering's too even. It hasn't had three hundred winters. And the bracket clock in the dining room. And the Knibb on the stairs." She kept her voice low. "I didn't look at the rest. I didn't want to know how many."

"When did you first see it?"

"Two years ago. At Easter. The little East in the morning room."

"And you said nothing."

"No."

"Why not?"

She could not answer him. She had asked herself the same thing. She had stood in front of that small clock for a quarter of an hour, knowing what she was looking at, and then she had gone in to luncheon and passed him the salt.

It was the habit of the house. That was all she could say for herself. One saw, at Compline, and one did not speak. She had seen her mother's lantern, and her brother's. She had seen him come up the lawn. Having kept silent about that, she had found that she had lost the right to open her mouth about anything else.

"I suppose I thought you must need it very badly," she said.

Edmund laughed, shortly. "That's what he'll say. You watch. If it ever comes out, that's what the old man will say. *I expect he wanted it more than I did.* It's the worst thing about this family. Nobody ever has the decency to be angry." He drank. "Well. It comes out tonight, or near enough. He's got a man in the house. A fat policeman in a blue suit, going round with photographs. He'll have the lot by dinner."

"What will you do?"

"I've made arrangements."

"What kind of arrangements?"

He turned his head and looked at her. She had the oddest impression that he was about to tell her. She thought that he wanted to, and that it was not only the clocks. Something else was just behind his teeth, something much older. His mouth opened.

"Immy," he said. "Do you ever—"

He stopped. She waited. She found that her hands had gone cold.

It was there. It was in the gunroom with them, as it had been in every room they had shared for twenty years. *I saw you come up the lawn.* She could have said it then, at noon, on a bench, with the coats looking on. She had only to open her mouth.

"Do I ever what?"

"Nothing." He looked away. The moment went, as it always had. "Do you ever think of getting married. That's all. You ought to. You're wasting yourself on dead Scotsmen."

"I'm forty-four."

"Mother was fifty-four." He said it very quietly, and then seemed to hear what he had said, and got up, too quickly, catching at the gun rack. "I hear young Lochinvar's come out of the west. Is that why you're here?"

"I came because Papa asked."

"Of course you did." He stood over her, swaying a little. He put out his hand and touched the white streak in her hair, just once, with one finger, as he had done when it first came, when she was fourteen and cried about it. "Go across, Immy. I mean it. Tomorrow, when the road dries. Go and knock at his door. One of us ought to have something out of that damned farm."

He went out. She heard his uneven step go away down the stone passage.

She sat on the bench. She thought: he knows that I know. He has always known. And he has just told me to go to Tom, as if he were giving me something back.

She thought that she had hated him for twenty years. She found, sitting there, that it was not so simple, and that she was crying.

* * *

The afternoon went. She kept away from the west windows.

She did what she had promised herself. She looked at the portraits in the dining room and found bloom on two of them. She cleaned her mother's silver brushes, on the kitchen table, with Dolly's whiting. Dolly herself was short and distracted and twice went up the back stairs with a covered plate and came down without it.

"Who's that for?"

"The cat," said Dolly.

"We haven't got a cat."

"We've one today."

At three she met Celia in the hall, arranging late roses in a bowl. Her sister-in-law looked up, and smiled, and the smile did not reach her eyes. She had been lovely once. She was still handsome, in a tired, guarded way, like a house with the shutters up.

"You look as though you had seen a ghost," Celia said.

"I've been looking through Grandfather's telescope."

"At Saltcote. Yes. Mrs Pask told me who was home." Celia snipped a stem. "I shouldn't, if I were you. This family's had quite enough out of that farm. Your mother. Now Edmund, with his caravans. You'd think there was nowhere else in England."

"Do you know what Edmund's arranged? For tonight?"

The scissors stopped.

"Why should he have arranged anything?"

"He told me he had."

"Did he." Celia put the rose into the bowl, very exactly. "Edmund arranges a great many things, darling. He arranged to make our fortune with a racehorse. Then he arranged it with a sea wall. I've given up asking." But her hand had begun to turn her wedding ring, round and round. "If he tells you any more, I should be glad to hear it. One likes to be kept informed. I am only his wife."

Imogen went up the stairs. On the first landing a girl in a dark blue dress was coming down with a tray. She was small and colourless and had a still, attentive face.

This would be the nurse.

"You're Miss Quaile," Imogen said. "You're the one who tells my father the truth."

The girl started so violently that the spoon rang on the tray. She stared. All the blood went out of her face.

"I'm sorry. I didn't mean to frighten you. I'm his daughter."

"I know," Miss Quaile said. Her voice was hardly above a whisper. "I know who you are. I beg your pardon. It was your eyes."

She went on down, holding the tray very level.

Imogen stood looking after her. *She tells him. He asks, and she tells him. Straight out.* The girl had been in the house three weeks. She had done every night what Imogen had failed to do in twenty years. It had cost her something, too, by the look of her.

She thought: I could go down to the Shop now. He is at his bench. I could say it in six words.

She went to her room instead, and lay on her bed, and watched the light go.

* * *

She put on the black dress. It was plain and well cut and she had owned it for ten years. She pinned up her hair. She did not look at herself for longer than it took.

The hall was full of firelight and people. She came down into it slowly. There was Fenn, who bowed. There was the vicar. There was old Octavia Prowse, enormous in black velvet, who took her by both shoulders and said, "You've your mother's bones. Why don't you dress like her? You look like a governess."

There was a tall pink young man, a cousin, who told her about a motor car. There was Kit, who kissed her cheek and said, "Aunt Immy. Thank God. Somebody sane." He had a girl with him, with a shaved head and a green silk dress, who looked round the hall at the clocks with frank delight. And there was Celia, coming down the stairs in the same green, and stopping, and going on.

There was a stranger by the wall with a glass. He was heavy and grey and watchful. This was the policeman. She went and spoke to him, since nobody else would. He told her that the Thorne made him feel poor.

"It makes everybody feel something," she said. And then, because Edmund was standing across the hall, and because she was so tired of saying nothing: "I clean paintings for a living, Mr Cade. I spend my days telling what's two hundred years old from what somebody put there last Tuesday. If you'd like a second opinion on anything in this house, you might ask me."

She saw him take it in. He had small, patient eyes.

It was the nearest she had come to speaking in twenty years. She did not know why she had done it. She thought that perhaps a thing which had been shut a long time must be opened a little way first, to see if the hinge would bear.

Then her father came in, on the nurse's arm, and stood at the Font, and stirred the watches with his finger. He made his old speech about the Act of Parliament. And at the end of it he looked round the hall with a puzzled face.

"Is Margot down?" he said.

Imogen was by the fire. She saw them all go still. She saw Edmund look into his glass.

She saw the nurse's lips part. The girl was going to tell him. She was going to say it, here, in front of the guests, in that clear low voice: *Mr Vane, your wife is dead.*

"She'll be along, Papa," Imogen said. "Come and sit down."

She did not know that she was going to. It came out of her mouth, the old lie, as easily as breathing. She saw Miss Quaile's eyes turn to her. There was no reproach in them. There was only a kind of recognition, as of one person noting which side another is on.

Her father nodded, satisfied, and let himself be led to a chair.

* * *

At dinner they put her beside Edmund.

She did not look at the empty place. She had sat at this table with that chair for twenty years of Easters and Augusts, and had learned to keep it at the edge of her eye. But tonight it was laid for the Hour, with the three glasses. Tonight she knew what dress hung in the wardrobe overhead, and she felt the chair on her skin all through the soup.

The talk went on round her. The pink cousin, on her left, told a story with a ferry in it. He was a nice boy. He had something in his pocket that rattled, and he kept one hand pressed over it. When she asked him gently how the wine trade was, he said, "Not awfully," and looked astonished at himself.

Her father carved the goose. She watched his hands.

"He could do that blindfold," she said to the cousin. "He used to, for us, at Christmas. Edmund could too. Edmund had the best hands of any of us."

She heard herself say *had*. On her right her brother filled his glass.

It was during the goose that she told him. She had not planned it. But she had seen a man through a telescope that morning who looked at this house as one looks at a debt. Edmund had made arrangements, and had been drinking since noon. She thought that he ought at least to know.

"Tom Garrow is at Saltcote," she said, very low.

His fork stopped.

"What?"

"He's been home a fortnight. For his father. I saw him this morning, in the yard."

"Where?" He had not lowered his voice. "Saw him where? Here?"

"Across the water. Through the glass. He buried Amos on Thursday. The funeral, Edmund. The day your notice came."

"He's got no business here." His face had gone dark. She could smell the whisky on him. "That farm's out at Lady Day. Fenn's served the notice. He can go back to his bloody cows."

"Edmund."

"Twenty years. And he comes back to stand at a graveside in a hat and look across at this house like—"

He stopped. The table had gone quiet. Even her father had looked up from his plate. Edmund picked up his glass and smiled round at them, the easy smile, the one he had always been able to find.

"A tenant of ours," he said, across the table, to the policeman. "Old Garrow, at the farm on the other side. Died a fortnight ago. The son's turned up from Canada to see what he can get."

"Lean man? Hat? Grey horse?" the policeman said. "I saw him this morning. By the road. He had a good look at me."

"I'll bet he did," said Edmund.

Imogen looked at her plate. She had a fork in her hand, and she kept hold of it.

*Like what?* She wanted to turn to her brother and ask it. *He looks across at this house like what, Edmund? What did you see in his face on Thursday, at the churchyard wall, that frightened you so?*

But she knew. Edmund had gone out onto the Wade twenty years ago after a woman who was walking to that farm, and the woman had not arrived. And an old man had waited at the far end with a lantern until the tide came. The old man was in the ground now. But the son had held his hand through the last night. *I don't know what was said.*

She thought: Tom knows something. Amos told him something, at the end. And Edmund is afraid of what it is.

She felt the cold go down her back.

* * *

Her father rose for the toast. He bowed to the empty chair. He said, "To absent time."

They stood. Imogen stood with them. She lifted her glass. She found that she could not say the words. She had said them every year of her childhood, in this room, with her mother laughing at the foot of the table. They had been a joke then. *Absent time, darlings; the hour we shan't get back till spring.*

Her lips moved. What she said, without sound, was *To Mother.*

Then her father said the other thing.

She heard it as one hears a sentence passed on someone else. *One of you has been robbing me.* She did not look at Edmund. She could feel him beside her, quite motionless, like a man standing in a river.

Her father's eyes went round the table. They came to her and rested, pale and clear. She looked back at him. She thought: he does not know me from Mother tonight, and he does not know his own son is a thief. And she had known both, for two years, and had passed the salt.

*I shall know which of you it is by one o'clock.*

She turned her head then. She looked at the place on his right, at the folded napkin, the three glasses with the candles in them, and the chair drawn a little back.

*You started this,* she said to it, silently. *You made the Hour. You stood in the hall every year and made us say what we thought. And the one year that it mattered, you were the only one who was going to tell the truth, and you never got the chance. We've none of us said a true word in this house since.*

*What am I to do?*

The chair did not answer. Her father sat down, and asked what was on his plate.

* * *

In the drawing room she went to the window.

She could not have sat with them. She pulled the curtain back and got into the window seat, with her knees up, as she had as a girl, and put her forehead to the glass.

This was the west side. The wind had risen with the dark, as she had seen him read that it would. It came across the flats in long gusts and shook the sash. There was no moon yet. There was nothing out there but the black. The tide had been over the Wade for more than an hour. Somewhere in front of her, under five feet of sea, was the road, and the Rill, and the Perch on its legs with the water going by.

Behind her Kit began to play.

It was the Schubert. He played it every year. Her mother had liked it, and had made Edmund learn it as a boy, and Edmund had taught it to his son. It was the only thing she had ever known Edmund to hand on. It went round and round, the same sad easy tune, like water going over a weir.

She looked for the light at Saltcote. There was none. The whole shore was dark. Then she remembered that the lamps in the room behind her had gone out, a while since, and that someone had said the whole of Thorney was down.

So he was sitting in the dark, too. With a child asleep, somewhere. With a folded paper in his shirt.

The music stopped, and she heard her father's voice.

"Thank you, Kit. She has gone up. She always goes up after the Schubert, and takes her shoes off, and comes down for the Hour. Imogen, did you see her go?"

She had her face to the glass. She was not thinking of what he asked. She was thinking of grey satin shoes on a cold floor, side by side.

"Yes, Papa," she said.

"Was she tired?"

"A little."

It was true. She had seen her go. She had watched her mother's lantern cross that lawn and go down to the Wade, twenty years ago tonight, from behind a vine. Her mother had been tired. She had been fifty-four, and had waited ten years.

Nobody spoke. The fire ticked. After a while people moved about, and somebody brought lamps. She did not turn round.

She did not know how long she sat there. An hour, perhaps. She heard Edmund come in, and go out, and come in again. She heard him yawn. She heard the clocks tell the half hour after ten.

It was a few minutes after that that she saw the light.

It was very small. It was on the far shore, low down, where the farm was. For a moment she thought that the electricity had come back. But it was the wrong colour. It was yellow, and it shook.

It moved. It came out from where the buildings must be, and along, and stopped. It stayed still for perhaps a minute. She could see it tremble in the wind.

Then it came down the ramp.

She knew that ramp. She knew to the foot where the land ended. The light came down the slope off the sea wall, steadily, and it reached the bottom, where the Wade began. It did not stop there.

It came on. It came straight out from the shore, toward her, along the line where the road lay. It was a yard or two above the water. It rose and dipped, slowly, with a rhythm that she knew.

Imogen put both her hands flat on the glass.

It was a lantern, on a horse. Someone was riding a horse out along the Wade.

She could not get her breath. The tide was at the three-quarter flood. There would be four feet of water on the road already, and a current setting north through the Rill that would take a man off his legs. No one crossed at that state. It had never been done. The Garrows themselves, who had farmed that shore since the wars with Napoleon, had a saying about it. *An hour and a half before, the Wade belongs to God.*

He knew that. He had known the tide all his life as other men know when they are hungry. He could not have made a mistake. He had looked at that water, in the dark, and smelled the wind, and known exactly how deep it was, and he had put the mare into it.

"Oh, you fool," she whispered. "Oh, my dear. Go back."

The light came on. She watched it as she had watched nothing in her life. It went under, once, behind a wave, and she heard herself cry out, and it rose again. It was a third of the way. It was nearly half.

It reached the place where the Rill must be, and it stopped.

She knew what he was doing. He was sitting the mare at the edge of the deep channel, with the sea up to her chest, letting her feel the ground go. There were six feet in the Rill at this state, and it ran like a mill race. The Clapper would be under. A horse could not walk it. She would have to swim, and be carried down, and find her feet again on the other side, if there was another side. If she was a hand's breadth out, she would miss the road, and there was nothing beyond but soft mud that would hold a horse until the water closed over her.

The mare was twenty years old.

The light stood still. It stood for so long that Imogen thought he had turned back, or was gone. Her nails were digging into her palms.

Then it dropped. It went down almost to the water. It moved sideways, quickly, to the right, as though something had taken hold of it and were sweeping it away toward the sea. It went thirty yards. It went forty.

And it steadied. It rose, slowly, a foot, and another. It began to come on again, lower now, and slower, slanting back toward the line.

He was through. Mab had found the road.

Imogen leaned her forehead on the glass and wept. She did not make a sound. The tears ran down and she let them.

She understood, watching that small stubborn light come up out of the sea, what she had been refusing to understand all day. He was not coming to deliver a letter. A man does not swim a horse through the Rill at night to speak to a solicitor. He was coming to the house where her brother was. He was coming with twenty years in him, and whatever his father had said. A Garrow put things away somewhere and waited, and then one day he came for them.

And she understood the other thing. She would go down to him. Nothing that he could say to her would be worse than the twenty years she had spent at a curtain.

The light went out of sight behind the point of the island, where the Wade came ashore below the orchard. The clock on the mantel behind her told twenty minutes past eleven.

She did not move at once. She could not have stood. She sat with her hands in her lap and got her breath, while the room went on behind her as if nothing had happened. She heard her brother say that he would have a look at the generator. She heard his step go out. It was half past.

Overhead, along the gallery, there was a sudden sound of running. It was light and quick, like a child's feet. She raised her eyes to the ceiling. It ran the whole length of the floor and stopped at the far end, above her head, where the portrait hung.

She thought, without surprise: yes. I hear you. I'm coming.

She turned from the window. The nurse was standing in front of her, very white, saying something. Would she sit by her father for five minutes. He was asleep; he ought not to be left.

"Yes," Imogen said. "Of course. Go."

She did not hear what she had promised. She saw the girl take a candle and go out. She saw her father asleep in the wing chair, with the rug to his chin. She saw Edmund's empty place by the fire, and Celia standing at the door like a woman listening at a keyhole.

She had the key in the pocket of her dress. She had put it there when she changed, not knowing why. Her fingers closed on it.

She went out of the drawing room quickly, without looking back. In the hall a tall young man came running and all but knocked her down. She hardly saw him. She went up the stairs with a candle in one hand and the old iron key in the other, and turned along the gallery, toward the lamp at the end.

## Chapter Four

The key turned. The cold of the room came round her.

She set the candle on the dressing table, where three flames looked back at her out of the triple glass. She did not give herself time to think. If she thought, she would stop. She would stand in the middle of the carpet for twenty years.

She unhooked the black dress and let it fall. She stepped out of her shoes. She stood in her slip, with the gooseflesh coming up on her arms, and opened the wardrobe.

It was at the end of the rail. She pulled the cotton bag off it and dropped the bag on the floor.

It went on over her head like cold water. She had been afraid that it would not fit, and then that it would. It fitted. It settled on her shoulders and at her waist as though it had been cut to her that morning. She had her mother's bones, Octavia had said. She did up the hooks at the side with fingers that would hardly obey her. The silk lay against her skin and began, slowly, to take her warmth.

There had been a reason. She had found it on the stairs, coming up, and she held on to it now. Her mother had taken off this dress, in this room, to go to a Garrow, and had not arrived. She had been stopped halfway. And Imogen, who was to have gone with her, had stayed behind a vine.

She was going down to him now. She would go as her mother ought to have gone, in the dress that had been left on its hanger. It was not for him to see. He had never seen it; he had never been inside this house. It was so that the dress should get there. She knew that it was not sensible. She was past sensible. She had been sensible since 1974.

She sat down at the glass. She took the pins out of her hair and put it up again, higher, as her mother had worn hers. She used her mother's brush. Three women looked at her out of the three mirrors, in grey, with bare shoulders. They had her mother's eyes. They were not careful.

She saw the white lock at her temple. She did not try to hide it. That was hers.

She could not wear her own black shoes. And she could not, she found, so much as touch the satin pair by the bed. Those were not to be moved. But on the floor of the wardrobe there were others, in a row, and among them some grey kid sandals with a low heel. She took them up. She would not put them on yet. The back stairs creaked, and the passage was stone.

*The Wade eats shoes,* her mother had said, laughing, on that bed.

Imogen took the candle in one hand and the sandals in the other. She went out, and drew the door to, and left the key in the lock. She did not want it any longer.

The lamp under the portrait had been lit again. She stopped beneath it for one moment. She looked up.

She had expected to feel like a thief. Her mother stood in the frame in the same silk, with her hand on the chair and her lips apart. And for the first time in twenty years Imogen looked into those eyes and did not see a question there. They had the look that her mother wore when somebody at last did the thing she had been waiting for them to think of.

"I'm going over," Imogen said. "I'm sorry it's so late."

Under the frame the cracked clock drew breath to strike.

She went down the gallery in her stockinged feet. The long floor was cold. All about her the clocks began to tell midnight, one after another, in the hall and on the stairs and behind the shut doors. She did not look to right or left. She passed the head of the main staircase without turning her head. She was looking at the dark arch of the back stair, and through it, in her mind, at a glasshouse with a vine.

She did not see anyone on the landing. She has been told since that someone was standing there. She is sorry. She would not, that night, have seen her own father.

* * *

The orangery was colder than the house and darker than the night.

She let herself in by the garden passage. The old door had dropped on its hinges and had to be lifted. Inside there was the smell. Wet earth, and rot, and something faintly sweet. She had not smelled it for twenty years, and it took the strength out of her knees.

The vine had gone on without her. It had been a great thing then. It was a monster now. The stem by the door was as thick as her waist, and it had gone up through the roof and along the ridge and down the far wall, and filled every pane that was left with brown leaves. Half of them had fallen. They lay in drifts on the brick floor, and the wind got in at the broken lights and turned them over. Up in the dark there were still bunches hanging, shrivelled black, that no one had picked.

The rain had thinned. She could hear it ticking on the glass.

She found the two upturned pots. They were where they had always been, in the corner by the stove pipe. She set the candle on one. She put her sandals on, at last, and stood up in them, and waited.

She did not know that he would come here. He might go straight to the house. He might go to the stables, to get the mare under cover. She had only the certainty that she had had at the window. He would have to bring the horse somewhere out of the wind, and this was the nearest roof to where the Wade came ashore, and he had known the way to it blind.

She was shaking. She told herself that it was the cold.

Through the wall, in the house, the last of the clocks finished. There was a silence. Then, from across the yard, slow and deep, the tower began. She counted the strokes. She had counted them from this corner on many nights, with her hand in his.

The twelfth had not died when she heard the hoofs.

They were on the brick path outside, slow and heavy and tired. There was a jingle. A voice said something low. The door at the far end, the wide one that the gardeners had used for the tubs, groaned and gave.

At midnight Tom Garrow was in the orangery with the rain on his shoulders and twenty years in his face.

He came in backwards, leading her. The mare filled the doorway, white in the dark, with her head down and the water running off her. He had a lantern hung from the saddle horn, turned low. He was soaked to the chest. His hat was gone; his hair lay flat and dark on his forehead. He had one hand on the mare's neck and was talking to her, as she had first heard him talk, a string of words with no gaps. *There. That's my old girl. That's the last of it. You're under a roof.*

He got her in, and turned to shut the door on the wind.

He saw the candle. He saw who stood beside it.

He stopped as though he had walked into a wall. All the colour went out of his brown face. His hand came up, slowly, the way a man's does who is not sure of what is in front of him.

"Mrs Vane," he said. It was a whisper.

She had not thought of that. She had not thought what it would be to him. He had been twenty-three. He had seen her mother a hundred times, across a yard, on a horse. And he was looking now, by one candle, at a woman in grey silk with her hair up, in the place where the Garrows had lost her.

"No," she said. "Tom. It's me."

She stepped forward so that the light fell on the white in her hair.

He looked at it, and at her face. She watched him find her in it, a piece at a time. The mare shook herself, and the bit rang.

"Imogen," he said.

He made it sound, as he always had, like the name of a place.

* * *

Neither of them moved. There were ten feet of brick floor between them, and dead leaves.

"Dolly said you were in Scotland," he said at last. His voice had deepened. There was something laid over it now, slow and flat, that was not Essex. "She said you never came home, this time of year."

"I never have. Until now."

"I'd not have come this way if I'd known. I'd not have frightened you."

"You didn't frighten me. I was waiting for you."

He took that in.

"I saw your light," she said. "From the drawing-room window. I watched you the whole way. I watched you put her at the Rill." Her voice shook. "You might have been drowned. Both of you. There's six feet in it."

"There's nearer seven. She swam it."

"She's twenty years old!"

"She knows that water better than I do. She was foaled beside it." He laid his hand on the mare's wet shoulder. "She went in of herself. I'd have turned her. I sat her on the edge of it and I thought, no, that's too much to ask, and she took the bit and went. I only had to stay on." His mouth moved, not quite a smile. "You named her right. There's something not canny about her."

Imogen laughed. It came out like a sob. She put her hand over her mouth.

He was looking at her. He looked at her face, and the dress, and her bare arms, slowly and completely, the way he looked at everything. She saw his eyes come to her left hand, and rest there, and go away.

"You've not changed," he said.

"I'm forty-four. I've a white streak like a badger and I wear spectacles to read."

"I said you've not changed. I never said you'd not got older." He wiped the wet from his face with his sleeve. "I have. I know it. I've seen myself in a shop window."

"You look like someone who has been out in the weather."

"That's about the size of it. There's a lot of weather, where I've been."

"I had your photograph. The yellow grass and the mountains."

"I didn't know if it would come to you."

"It came. I ought to have written. I looked at it for a year, trying to find something to say back that was good enough, and then it was too late." She took a breath. "Tom. I'm sorry about your father. I'm so very sorry."

"He was ready." His face closed. "He'd been ready a long time."

He turned from her. He began to see to the mare. He loosened the girth and lifted the saddle off and set it on the edge of a stone trough. He took a handful of dead leaves and began to rub her down, in long strokes, along the back and the quarters. She stood with her head hanging and let him. He did it with his whole attention.

Imogen watched his hands. They were the same hands. They were broader and scarred across the knuckles, and one of the fingers had been broken and set crooked.

Then she saw what else had been on the saddle.

It had been strapped along the near side, under the flap, in a long case of oiled canvas. He had laid the saddle down with that side uppermost. The wet canvas had fallen open at the end. There was a foot of dark wood showing, and beyond the wood, blue steel.

She had been taught to shoot on the sea wall when she was ten. She knew what it was.

"What is that for?" she said.

He did not look round. He went on with the mare.

"Tom. What is the gun for?"

"Vane," he said.

* * *

It was only the one word. He did not raise his voice. He might have been telling her the name of a field.

She had known. She had known at the window. But it was different to see it there, on the stone trough, with the candle on the barrels.

"My brother."

"I've a thing to ask him. He'll not answer it for me without. He never answered a Garrow in his life but to tell him what he owed." He threw down the leaves and took up more. "I'll not hurt him, if he tells me. I want him to have that to look at while he does."

"What do you want to ask him?"

He was silent for so long that she thought he would not say. The mare sighed, and shifted her weight.

"My father talked, at the end," he said. "The last night. He'd not said twenty words to me on the telephone in twenty year. I got there the Monday. He was propped up in the kitchen, in the chair, he'd not go to bed. He knew me. He said, 'You've took your time.' Then he never spoke till about three in the morning."

He was rubbing the mare's near foreleg, bent, so that she could not see his face.

"He said he'd stood on the wall that night with the lantern. From one o'clock. He'd the horse saddled, the mare's dam. He saw her light leave the house. Your mother's. He said he knew it for hers the way it moved; she walked quick. He watched it come down onto the Wade and out. He said it was the longest quarter of an hour of his life, and the best. She'd said he wasn't to come to meet her. She'd said, I'll walk off that island on my own feet and you'll stand and watch me come."

"Yes," Imogen whispered. "She said that."

"She got three parts over. She was past the Rill, past the Perch. He could near enough see her face. He said he'd his hand up to call to her." Tom straightened. He stood with the wet leaves in his fist. "And there come another light. From the house. Fast. It come down onto the Wade and out after her like something let off a chain. Dad said he knew that one too. He said there was only one man on the Ness ran like that, with a hitch."

Imogen had put her hand on the cold iron of the stove pipe.

"It caught her up. A hundred and fifty yards from where Dad stood. He heard voices. He couldn't hear words, the wind was wrong. He said a man's voice, loud, and hers, low. He started down the ramp. And he stopped, because she'd told him. *You stand and watch me come.* He thought, she'll deal with it. She'll send the boy home and come on."

"They stood there," Imogen said. "The two lights. They stood a long time."

His head came round.

"He said an hour. He said he stood on that ramp an hour with the lantern held up, so she'd see where he was. He said the tide turned. He felt it turn. He shouted then. He said he shouted till he'd no voice. And the two lights stood there, with the water coming. And then hers turned round."

He stopped. His jaw was working.

"It went back. Toward the house. Away from him. The other one went with it. He watched her light go all the way back to the Rill, and there it went out. And the water come over the road. He stood there till it was up to his knees on the ramp."

"Tom—"

"He never knew. That's what he said to me. He said, 'I never knew, boy, if she turned back of herself or was turned. I never knew if she thought better of me at the last, with the water coming, and chose the house. Or if that drunken young devil took hold of her and dragged her.' He said he'd lain awake on it twenty year. He said he'd sooner she'd been dragged, God forgive him, because then she'd still have been coming." Tom's voice had gone rough. "He'd got hold of my wrist. He'd no strength in him and I couldn't have broke that grip. He said, 'Find out, Tom. You go over there and you ask Edmund Vane which it was. And you make him tell you.' That was the last thing he said to me that had sense in it. He went about six."

The rain ticked on the glass. Up in the roof a dead leaf let go and came down, turning, through the candlelight.

"So that's what the gun's for," Tom said. "I've come to ask him. I buried Dad Thursday. I come back from the church and there's a paper from your brother's lawyer to say we're to be off the ground by Lady Day, a hundred and eighty year, for caravans. I stood in Dolly Pask's kitchen with that in my hand and I thought, well, that's plain enough. He's took the woman off my father, and now he's took the land, and he's never once had to stand in front of a Garrow and say why."

He looked at her. His eyes were as she remembered them, grey-blue, steady, with the lines cut deep round them now.

"I came for Vane," he said. "I'll not lie to you. I never have. I didn't know you were in the house. I put the mare at that water tonight to find your brother, wherever he's hid himself, and make him tell me how your mother died."

* * *

She had waited twenty years for this, and dreaded it. She had put on a dead woman's dress for it.

"I can tell you how she died," Imogen said.

He did not move.

"The second light was Edmund's. Your father was right. I saw it too. I saw both of them, from here. I was sitting on that pot." She pointed. Her hand was quite steady; she noticed it with surprise. "I watched my mother's lantern go down to the Wade, and I watched my brother's go after it. I saw them meet and stand. And then I fell asleep. I was twenty-four and I had cried until I was sick. When I woke it was light, and he was walking up the lawn, wet to the neck."

"You saw him come back."

"At six in the morning. He went past that door. He told them at breakfast that he'd slept in the stable, and I sat at the table and let him say it." She made herself go on. "I've let him say it for twenty years. I've let my father believe that his clock killed her. I've never told a living soul what I saw."

"Why?"

It was the question. She had known that he would ask it, in just that way.

"Because of why he went," she said.

She told him. She did not soften it. She told him about the jewel case on the bed, and what she had said to her mother. She told him about the plan, the four of them in his father's kitchen. Her voice shook once, there, and she steadied it. She told him about the tea table, and the quarrel over a horse.

"It was Mab's dam. Edmund said your father had no business breeding a mare of that quality on our grazing, and that the foal by rights belonged to the estate. I was so angry. I was so angry on your account. And I had it in my mouth, the one thing that would hurt him more than anything on earth, and I said it. *Mother's going to Amos Garrow tonight. She's leaving. Ask her yourself.*" She shut her eyes. "He adored her. She was the only person who ever looked at him. I knew that. I used it."

"Imogen."

"Let me finish. I have to say all of it." She opened her eyes. "I was to walk with her. I'd promised. I came out here at eleven, to wait, and I sat in the dark and thought about what I'd done. And at one she came through that door with her lantern, in her stockings. She called me. She said, 'Immy? Are you there? It's time.' I was six feet from her. I was behind the vine."

She could not look at him now. She looked at the candle.

"I didn't answer. I held my breath. I couldn't face her. I couldn't face you. She waited. She called again. Then she said, 'Never mind, my darling. Come over in the morning.' And she went by herself. If I'd gone with her, Tom, there'd have been two of us on the Wade when Edmund came. I could have held him. I could have stood in front of him while she went on. She was a hundred and fifty yards from your father's hand."

The tears had come. She let them.

"That's why I wouldn't see you. It wasn't your father. It wasn't that I couldn't bear the sight of a Garrow. You stood in that yard in the rain for two hours, and I stood behind a curtain and watched you. I'd my coat on. I thought, if I go down, I shall have to tell him that I told. And that I hid, and let her walk to her death alone, because I was ashamed. I'd see his face change. I could not have borne that."

She stopped. She had said it. It had taken perhaps three minutes, and it was out.

The orangery was very quiet. She heard the mare breathe. She heard the wind come in at a broken pane and move the leaves along the floor.

She waited for him to speak. She thought that she had known every kind of fear there was. She had not known this one.

He put down the handful of leaves. He did it carefully, on the edge of the trough, beside the gun. He wiped his palms on his wet coat.

"You were twenty-four," he said.

"So were—"

"I was twenty-three. I know what I was. I'd not have known what to do with a thing like that either." He came a step toward her. "Twenty year. Twenty year I've thought it was him. Dad. I thought you'd looked across at that farm and seen the man your mother died going to, and seen his son. I thought every time you looked at me you'd see her on the mud. I never blamed you. I'd have felt the same."

"It was never that."

"I see it wasn't." He was quite close now. She could smell the wet wool and the horse, and the salt. "I went to the other end of the world on account of it. I got on a boat because I thought my face was more than you could stand. And all the while you were up at that window thinking yours was more than I could."

"I told Edmund," she said. "Don't you understand? It was my doing. If I'd kept my word—"

"You said a thing at a tea table in a temper. You were a girl. You never took hold of her on the Wade. You never kept her standing there an hour with the tide making." His voice was low and rough. "If I'm to hate somebody for a hard word said in a temper, I'd best begin with myself. I said one or two to my father, the day I left, that I'd give this arm to have back."

"You don't hate me."

"Hate you." He said it as though she had spoken a language he did not know. "Imogen. I've carried a bit of your writing inside my shirt for twenty year. I had it on me when I wed. I told Jeanie what it was; I'd not deceive her. She said, keep it. She said she'd sooner have a man that could love like that than one that couldn't, even if it wasn't her."

He put his hand inside his coat. He brought out something flat, wrapped in a square of oilcloth. He unfolded it on his palm, under the candle.

There was a stiff blue paper, folded small, with a solicitor's name printed at the head. And under that there was a half sheet of cream writing paper, gone soft and brown at the creases, and worn through in one place. She saw her own hand on it, the hand she had written at twenty-four, round and confident.

*O, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you.*

"It was in the same pocket as the notice," he said. "I never thought. I put the one in on top of the other. I've been carrying your brother and you against my chest all day, and didn't know which was the heavier."

She could not speak.

"I said I came for Vane." He folded the oilcloth over. He put it back. "That's true. I got on the mare for that. I told myself so the whole road down to the water. And then she lost her feet in the Rill. We went under. I'd the reins in one hand and her mane in the other and the sea in my mouth, and I thought, that's it, that's the finish. And I'll tell you what I thought of. I didn't think of your brother. I didn't think of Dad."

He stopped. He had always been a man who could not say things.

"I thought, I'll not see her. I've been home a fortnight and I've stood and looked at that house every day like a dog at a gate, and I'll go down in this water and never have seen her. That's what I thought." He looked at her with those steady eyes. "So I'll say it straight, since we're saying things. I came for you. I've been coming for you for twenty year. I only never knew it till I was drowning."

She went to him. She did not know that she had moved. She was against the wet canvas of his coat, with her face in his neck, and his arms had come round her as slowly and completely as they had on the tenth of July under the vine. He was shaking. So was she. The sea water came through her mother's silk and she did not feel it.

He kissed her. It was not as it had been at twenty-three. He kissed her like a man who has been a long time in an empty country and has come to a house with a light in it.

Behind them the old mare turned her head, and looked, and blew softly through her nose.

* * *

It was some time before either of them spoke.

They were sitting on the two pots. He had put his coat round her shoulders, wet as it was, and the saddle blanket over that. He had her hands between his. He was looking at them.

"You've not got it on," he said.

"The ring? It's in Edinburgh. In my workbox. I've kept it oiled."

"Have you?" He turned her left hand over. "And nobody's ever put another there."

"Somebody tried. I gave it back."

"Why?"

"It was gold," she said. "It wasn't iron."

He laughed. It was the first time. It took years off him.

"Will you come away?" he said. "Now. Tonight."

"You can't cross. Not even you. Not till—"

"Twenty to four. By my watch. She can do it then; there'll be three foot on the Rill and falling, and I'll lead her through. I'll have you at Saltcote by four." He held up his wrist. He had a big steel watch on a leather strap. "It's twenty past one now."

"It's twenty past twelve. I heard it strike."

"That's your father's time. That's Compline. It's twenty past one in England." He almost smiled. "I'd forgot. Dad always said the Vanes even kept a different hour from other folk."

She looked at the watch. She had not worn one since she was a girl. She thought of a hundred and eleven clocks, and an old man in a cellar who had given his wife the wrong time.

"I can't come yet," she said.

His hands tightened.

"Not because I don't mean to. I mean to. I'll come across that water behind you if I have to swim it." She held his eyes. "But I have to go into the house first. At one o'clock by the hall, my father opens the door. It's the Hour. My mother made it; it's when we're supposed to say what's true. Twenty years ago I was sitting here on this pot when I should have been in that hall. I'm going to stand in it tonight. I'm going to tell my father what I saw, and what I did. Before I leave his house."

"In that?" He touched the grey silk at her shoulder.

"In this."

"He'll think he's seeing her."

"Perhaps. I don't know. I only know I can't go to you from behind a curtain a second time." She freed one hand and laid it against his face. The stubble was rough and wet. "An hour, Tom. Give me till two by the house. Then I'll come back here, and you'll put me up on that mare. I won't look round."

He was silent. She saw him set it against the thing that he had come for.

"And your brother?"

"I don't know where he is. Nobody ever does, on this night. He goes to ground."

"I'll find him. I've a notion where he's bound for. There was a man in the Plough at dinnertime, an oysterman, talking louder than he should about a job of work at the Hythe tonight, at the top of the tide." He turned his head and looked at the gun on the trough. "I've an hour of my own to fill, it seems."

"Tom. Leave it here."

He said nothing.

"Please. Ask him. Make him tell you; you've the right, and so had your father. I'd have told you myself, only I don't know what happened out there, I only know what I saw. But leave that here. He's my brother. And whatever he did on the Wade, he did because I sent him."

"I said I'd not hurt him if he told me."

"And if he doesn't tell you? If he laughs? He does laugh. It's what he does when he's frightened." She took hold of his sleeve. "I know you. You've never raised your hand to a living thing. You'd not know what you were until you'd done it, and then you'd have to carry it. You've a child."

His face changed at that.

"Dolly told you."

"She said a little girl. Nine. Dark."

"Wren." He said the name as he had said the mare's, low. "Lorraine Wren, after her mother's mother. She's nine and three-quarters; she'll tell you so. She's at Dolly's cottage now, asleep, with old Vi. I went to the door at dusk and Vi wouldn't have her woke. She said she'd gone up at seven with her notebook."

"What is she like?"

"She watches." He looked at Imogen. "She don't say a lot. She sits and she looks at a thing till she's got it. She's like you, that way. I've thought it before. I used to see her looking at a horse, with her head on one side, and think, now where've I seen that." His voice dropped. "She's all I've got that's any good. Her mother died two year back, in the winter. It took eight months. Wren sat with her. I'd find her on the bed with a book, reading out loud, and Jeanie asleep."

"Then for her," Imogen said. "Leave the gun."

He looked at it for a long moment. The candle was burning down. Across the yard, thin and clear, the small bell on the tower rang three times. A quarter to one. She had fifteen minutes.

He did not say that he would. She noticed that. He was a man who never said what he was not sure of. He stood up, and drew her up with him, and put his mouth for a moment against her hair, on the white place.

"Go and say your piece," he said. "I'll be here at two by your father's clocks. Or she will." He nodded at the mare. "If I'm not, you get up on her and give her her head. She'll take you home."

"You'll be here."

"I've come three thousand mile and through seven foot of water," Tom Garrow said. "I don't reckon to miss you by an hour."

She gave him back his coat. She went to the garden door in her mother's dress, with the wet marks of his arms on the silk. At the door she turned.

He had gone back to the mare. He was standing with one hand on her neck and his head bent, the way he had stood in a yard in the rain. He was not looking at Imogen. He was looking at the long shape on the edge of the stone trough.

She had asked him. She could do no more. She went in.

## Chapter Five

She got as far as the garden passage, and there her courage left her.

It was a narrow stone corridor that ran from the garden door to the back of the hall. At its far end was a baize curtain, and through the curtain came candlelight, and voices. She could hear Fenn. She could hear Octavia Prowse demanding champagne. She stood ten feet from them in the half dark, in the grey silk, and could not go on.

She had been so sure, in the orangery. With his hands round hers it had seemed a simple thing. She would walk into the hall and say it. *Papa, I am Imogen, and there is something I must tell you about the night Mother died.*

Now she thought of his face. She thought of every one of them turning to look.

There was an old mirror on the wall of the passage, spotted, in a black frame. She saw herself in it by the light from the curtain. The damp had darkened the silk on her shoulders. Her hair had come down a little on one side. There was a dead vine leaf caught at her waist.

She looked like a woman who had come in from the sea.

The garden door opened behind her, and the wind came in, and someone with it.

It was Celia. She was in her green dress with a man's waxed jacket over it, far too big, and gumboots. She had a rubber torch in her hand. Her fair hair was plastered flat to her head and running with wet, and her face under it was the colour of ash.

She shut the door and leaned on it. She had not seen Imogen. She stood with her eyes closed, breathing through her mouth, like someone who has run a long way. Then she began to get out of the jacket, with slow clumsy movements, and kicked off one boot, and looked up.

She made a sound that was hardly a sound at all. She went back against the door as though she had been pushed.

"Celia. It's only me."

"Oh, my God." Celia put her hand flat on her chest. Her eyes went from the grey silk to Imogen's face and back. "Oh, my God, Imogen. I thought—" She stopped. She began to laugh, without any breath in it. "No. Why not? Why shouldn't she? It's the night for it. I've just seen worse."

"What have you seen? Where have you been? You're soaked."

"I went out for some air."

"In that? Celia, what's happened? Where's Edmund?"

"I don't know where Edmund is."

She said it too quickly. She had got the other boot off and was standing in her stockings on the stone. She took a pair of evening shoes out of the jacket's deep pockets, and she put them on, holding the wall. Her hands were shaking so that she could hardly manage the straps.

"He's asleep, I should think," she said. "Somewhere. He's had a great deal to drink. He always turns up." She went to the spotted mirror and looked at herself. She took a comb from somewhere and dragged it through her wet hair, and pressed her lips together, and pinched her cheeks, hard, with finger and thumb. Imogen had seen her do that in the wings of a village hall, thirty years ago, before going on as Lady Bracknell. "There. Shall I do? I've got to stand where everybody can see me."

"Why?"

Celia met her eyes in the glass. For a moment the trained face slipped, and what was under it looked out. It was not an actress. It was a frightened woman of forty-eight who had done something and could not undo it.

"Because I've been told to," she said. "By a man who knows about these things." She turned round. She looked at Imogen's dress again, more steadily, and at her face. Something came into her own that was almost tenderness. "You've been with him. Haven't you? The Garrow boy. You've got it all over you. I saw a light on the Wade from my window and I thought, that's either the devil or a man in love, and nobody else would be such a fool."

Imogen said nothing.

"Good," said Celia. "I'm glad. I mean it. One of us should." She took a step toward the curtain, and stopped, with her back turned. "Don't go in yet. Not in that. Let him open his door first. If Leo sees you coming at him in that dress before one o'clock, he'll think the Hour's begun without him, and he will never forgive you."

"I wasn't sure that I could go in at all."

"Oh, you'll go in. You're a Vane. You'll stand about for a quarter of an hour feeling sick, and then you'll do it, with your chin up. It's the one thing you're all good at." She put out her hand to the baize. "Immy."

"Yes?"

"Whatever you hear. Tomorrow, or after. About tonight." Celia's voice was very low. "I only wanted him to stay. That's all it was. You of all people might understand that. I only wanted him not to go."

She lifted the curtain and went through into the light, like a woman walking onto a stage.

Imogen stood in the passage. She did not understand. She thought that she would ask, in the morning. In the morning she was at Saltcote, and Celia was on a ship.

* * *

She waited, as she had been told.

The clocks began. She heard them through the curtain, the hurried silver one and the cracked one and the deep slow one by the stairs. She heard them finish. She heard her father's voice say, "Now," and the iron bolt go back, and the two leaves of the great door groan.

The wind came down the passage and laid the baize against her legs.

"Come in, then," her father said. "You're late."

Far off, across the yard, the tower began to tell the quarters.

She stood with her hand on the wall. She was counting, as she had as a child, lying in bed, when the Hour was something the grown-ups did downstairs. Four chimes. Then the great bell.

It struck.

And on the stroke, as though the bell itself had burst, there were two shots.

She knew what they were. She had been taught on the sea wall. A twelve-bore, both barrels, the second on the heel of the first, and close; they had come from the yard.

She did not hear what the hall said. She heard a woman cry out, and a laugh, and Octavia's voice. She was not listening. She was already running.

She went back along the passage and out at the garden door, into the wet. The moon was out. She ran down the brick path in her mother's sandals, with her skirts in her fists, and wrenched at the door of the orangery and fell through it.

The candle had burned out. There was the lantern still, turned low, on the floor by the trough. It showed her the mare. Mab was standing where he had left her, tied to the stove pipe by her halter rope, with the saddle blanket over her back. She had her head up and her ears pricked toward the yard.

There was no one with her.

The saddle lay on the edge of the trough. Imogen went to it. She knew before she touched it. The long canvas case hung open and flat along the flap. It was empty.

"Tom!"

Her voice went up into the dead vine. A leaf came down.

She ran out again. She went along under the wall of the house, on the grass, to the corner, where one could see the front. She stopped there with her hand on the stone.

The gravel lay white under the moon. It was empty from end to end. The front door of the house stood wide, pouring yellow light, and the wind was taking the candle flames. Across the yard the stable block was black, and the tower stood up out of it. Under the little roof she could see one of the figures, with its arm lifted.

Nothing moved anywhere. There was no man with a gun. There was no one lying on the stones.

She stood and shook. The wind went through the silk as though she had nothing on.

He had not left it. She had asked him, for his child's sake, and he had looked at it, and said nothing. And when she was gone he had taken it out of its case and gone to find her brother.

*I'll not hurt him, if he tells me.*

*And if he laughs?*

She thought: I must find them. She took three steps out onto the gravel.

Where? The shots had come from the yard, but the yard was empty. He might be in the stables. He might be on the sea wall, or the Hythe. She did not know this island by night any longer. She had no lamp. And if she found them, in the dark, with a loaded gun between them, what would she do? She had had her chance to stand between Edmund and someone else on a dark night. She had sat on a pot.

She stopped. The gravel was sharp through the thin soles.

It came to her slowly, and it was the coldest thought she had ever had. She was doing it again. In the house behind her the door was open and the Hour had begun, and she was running away from it. Twenty years ago she had hidden in the orangery. Tonight she had a better reason. There was a man out there whom she loved, with a gun. But she was still about to spend the Hour out in the dark, and she knew what her father would be asking.

*Is Margot down?*

If Tom had done it, it was done. She could not change it by finding him ten minutes sooner. If he had not, if he had fired into the air, or at a shadow, then he would be at the orangery at two, as he had said. He was a man who did not say what he was not sure of. *I don't reckon to miss you by an hour.*

She had one thing left that she could do. Nobody else could do it.

She turned round. She went back along the wall. In the orangery she stopped by the mare and laid her face for a moment against the warm white neck.

"Wait for him," she said. "I'll come back."

Then she went in at the garden door. She did not go to the baize curtain. She went up the back stairs.

* * *

She knew how it must be done. She had watched it every year of her childhood, through the banisters, in her nightgown.

Her mother had never been in the hall when the door was opened. She said that it was Leo's moment. He liked to stand there alone with his clocks and let the world in. She went up after the music and took off her shoes, and lay on her bed for half an hour with a book. And when she heard the tower strike one, she got up, and put her shoes on, and came down.

She came down the main staircase, slowly, in the grey silk, with one hand on the rail. Papa would be standing by his chair. He would look up. Every year he looked up as though he had not expected her. She would say, from the fourth stair, "Well, Leo? Have you got your hour?" And he would say, "I have it, Margot. Come and help me spend it."

Then they would dance. It was the only time in the year that he did. And after that she would stand in the middle of the hall and clap her hands and say, "Now, my darlings. The truth. Who is going to begin?"

Imogen came out at the top of the back stair, into the gallery.

She did not stop under the portrait. She walked the length of the long floor, past the dark windows. She came to the head of the main stairs and stood there, out of sight of the hall, in the shadow.

She could hear them below. A young man's voice was saying something loud and cheerful about ice. There was a silence. There was a murmur, and her father's voice, mild and exact. She could not hear the words.

She waited. She heard him speaking again, for a long time. She heard him say Fenn's name. She stood with her hands gripped together and her eyes shut. She thought of Tom. She thought of a white gravel yard with nobody on it.

Then there was a hiss, and a crackle, and music.

It was the waltz. It was "Gold and Silver." He had asked for it.

She opened her eyes. She put her hand on the rail. And she went down.

* * *

She saw the hall as one sees a painting, all at once, before any part of it.

It was full of candles. They were on every ledge, on the stairs, along the tops of the clock cases. All the brass was shining. She saw the long pendulums going. She saw the Font on its table, and beside it a thing on a grey blanket that she knew at a glance. It was the Thorne. No. She had cleaned pictures for twenty years; she knew the look of a surface that had not lived long enough. It was Papa's Copy. It was standing on the hall table like a guest who had arrived at the wrong party.

So that had been Edmund's arrangement. And it had gone wrong.

She came down another step, and they saw her.

She had not thought of them. She had thought only of her father. She saw Octavia Prowse heave herself up out of her chair, and her big plain face break. She heard her say a name. She saw Kit at the gramophone with his hand out, and Fenn bow his head. She saw the little nurse go back against the wall and slide down it to the floor.

She saw Celia, under the tall clock, quite still, with her hand at her throat.

None of them said, *Imogen.* She understood then what she had done. She had put on a dress to keep a promise to the dead. She had not known that she was putting on the dead.

She very nearly turned. She had her weight on her back foot. She thought, this is wicked. I must go up and take it off.

Her father had risen.

He stood by a chair near the open door, with the night behind him. The rug had fallen from his knees. He was looking up at her, on the fourth stair.

She had seen his face in every state. She had seen it bent over a bench, absorbed. She had seen it puzzled and mild, lost in the middle of a sentence. She had seen it at her mother's grave, like a shut door. She had never, in forty-four years, seen it as it was now.

He looked at her as a man looks who has waited on a railway platform for twenty years, every day, meeting every train, and one day she gets down from a carriage.

"You came back," he said. "Margot. You came back."

She had her sentence ready. *Papa, it is Imogen.* She had rehearsed it in the passage, and on the stairs. She had come into this hall, in this dress, for no other reason than to say something true at last.

She crossed the floor to him. She saw his eyes. They were pale and clear and they were not confused. That was the thing that undid her. He was not wandering. He knew quite well that it was 1994, and that he was eighty-one. And he knew that his wife was coming toward him across the hall, in her grey gown, as she had every year.

He held both those things. He had made room for both.

*Papa, it is Imogen.* It was the truth. And she saw that if she said it, now, in front of them all, he would hear it, and his face would change. It would go back to what it had been for twenty years.

The girl who sat with him at night told him the truth, straight out, every time. Imogen had honoured her for it. She had thought, I could never be so brave.

She found, standing in front of him, that there were two kinds of courage, and that the one she had come for was not the one that was wanted.

She put out her hand.

"Yes, Papa," she said.

It was not enough. She saw that it was not. He had not been waiting twenty years to be called Papa.

She took a breath. She let her mother's name for him come into her mouth. She had heard it ten thousand times, across this hall, in that light amused voice.

"Yes, Leo," she said. "I came back."

* * *

He took her hand. His own was dry and cool. He set his other hand at her waist, exactly, as a man sets a hand who was taught to do it in 1930. He stood a moment listening for the beat.

Then he danced with her.

She had been afraid that he would fall. He was so thin; she could feel his shoulder blade under her fingers like the handle of a spoon. But he did not falter. He led her down the length of the hall in the old slow waltz, turning, and she followed, as she had seen her mother follow. Her body knew it. She had stood on his feet for this, at five years old, in her nightgown, on Christmas Eve.

The clocks went round them. The candles went round. She saw faces, and lost them. His eyes were closed.

"I had it wrong," he said.

He spoke low and quickly, close to her ear. It was the voice he used at the bench, when he was explaining a difficult thing.

"I had it wrong for you, the last time. I put the hall clocks back before dinner. To save a scramble. I never told you. And you looked at the regulator and saw two, and it was three out there, and the tide goes by out there. I gave you an hour that you hadn't got. I have known it every day since."

"Leo—"

"Let me say it. I've had it ready for twenty years, and I shall lose it if I stop." His hand tightened on hers. "High water tonight was at eight minutes to one. I have that from the Thorne. I went and looked. The Wade will not carry you on foot before half past four. You're not to try. Do you hear me? Not on foot."

She could not see. The candles had run together.

"But a horse may go at twenty minutes to three. Not a minute before. He must swim at the Rill; there will be three feet there and a strong set to the north, and he must be let to find it himself. The Garrows' horses always could. That is by this house, Margot. By our clocks. Not by any watch that anyone shows you."

Twenty minutes to three. By the house.

She heard Tom's voice, in the orangery, an hour ago. *Twenty to four. By my watch. There'll be three foot on the Rill and falling.*
