It was the same minute. Her father, who had not left the house, who did not know that there was a man on the island or a horse, had given her the hour of her crossing as exactly as the man who had been born on that shore and could smell it.

He had worked it out for his wife. He had gone into the library that afternoon, an old man with a failing mind, and read the tide off a clock. He had carried the figures in his head all evening, through the dinner and the speech. He wanted to be sure that tonight, if she came, he would have them right.

"Do you hear me, Margot?"

"I hear you, Leo."

"You'll not go on foot."

"No."

"You'll wait for the horse."

"I'll wait."

"Then you will get across," her father said. He let out a long breath, and she felt his whole frame ease, as if a spring that had been held wound for twenty years had been let gently down. "You'll get across, my dear. That is all I wanted. I don't ask you to stay."

Her father danced with her, and called her by her mother's name, and told her the hour of the tide.

She understood that it was the only way he had ever known of saying the other thing. He could not say *I love you.* He could not say *I knew that you were unhappy,* or *forgive me.* He was not made so. He had found a thing that he could give her that was exact and true and would bring her safe to the other side, even though the other side was another man's kitchen. He had got it right to the minute. And he had told her that she might go.

*I don't ask you to stay.*

Her mother had waited thirty years to hear that he saw her. She had stood behind him at a clock in July. *If he had turned round and asked me one single question.* Imogen did not know that those words had ever been written. She knew only that something in the grey silk seemed to loosen, and that she was crying as she had not cried since she was a child, without any sound.

She had come to tell him that it was not his clock. She tried. She owed him that.

"It wasn't the clock, Leo," she whispered. "It wasn't your doing. I knew the time. I swear to you, it was never the clock."

She did not know that it was true. She believed that her brother had done it, on the Wade. But she said it as her mother, and it came out of her with a certainty that she could not have explained.

"You're kind," he said. "You were always kind to me, at the last. It was how I knew." He turned her, at the end of the hall, under the tall clock. "It doesn't signify now. I have got it right. One ought to be allowed to do a thing over, if one has it right the second time. I've built something that lets me. I'll show you, when you come home."

"Yes."

"You will come home? Not to stay. I don't ask it. But to see the clocks."

"Yes, Leo. I'll come and see the clocks."

"Good." He was smiling. "The gallery one is still gaining. Four seconds a week. I never have accounted for it. I think that you used to move the hands on, to tease me."

"I did," Imogen said. She did not know whether it was true. She found afterwards, from Dolly, that it was. "Every Sunday. While you were at church."

He laughed. She had not heard her father laugh aloud since she was a girl.

The music ran down. The needle hissed in the groove. He brought her to a stop in the middle of the floor and stood holding her.

"There," he said. "There, my dear. You see. It's quite all right. We had the time after all."

* * *

She kissed him on the forehead. She took his face between her hands. It was all bone, and his eyes were open now, looking into hers, very clear.

She did not know whom he saw. She has thought about it a great deal. She thinks that at that moment he saw them both, and knew it, and was content.

"Goodbye, Papa," she whispered. It was so low that no one else could have heard.

"Go along, my dear," her father said, as softly. "You've a man waiting with a lantern. You mustn't keep him standing on that wall."

She stared at him.

He patted her cheek. Then his eyes went past her, mild and tired, and he looked about for his chair.

She let him go. She turned. The hall swam. She saw Octavia with her hand over her eyes. She saw Kit standing at the gramophone with the tears running down. She walked toward the garden passage, quickly, and she did not look at any of them.

By the open door the little nurse was sitting on the floor against the wall. Her face was turned up, as white as paper, with enormous eyes. Imogen looked down at her. She thought: this is the one who tells him the truth. I have just told him the largest lie of his life, in front of her, and she has seen what it did.

She nodded to her. She meant, *I leave him with you.* She meant, too, *Forgive me. I could not do it your way.*

Then she was through the baize, and in the cold stone passage. She stood there holding the wall.

She had gone into that hall to say her piece. She had not said one word of it. Her father did not know that she had told Edmund, or that she had hidden. He did not know that she had seen her brother come up the lawn. She had given him her mother instead. She had stood up in front of her family in a dead woman's dress and answered to a dead woman's name.

It was the kindest thing she had ever done. It might also be the worst. She did not know which. She thought that her mother, who had made the Hour, would have known. And she seemed to hear her mother's voice then, very clearly, light and dry, in the dark of the passage.

*Darling. Don't be solemn. He asked for me, and you were the nearest. Now go and get on that horse.*

The clock in the morning room, through the wall, struck the half hour. Half past one. She had thirty minutes.

She went out to the orangery.

## Chapter Six

He was there.

He was sitting on one of the upturned pots with his elbows on his knees. The lantern stood on the bricks between his boots. The mare was behind him, dozing, with a hind foot tipped.

The gun lay across his knees. It was open at the breech. On the floor beside the lantern there were two short brass-ended cylinders, side by side, standing up like chessmen.

Imogen stopped in the doorway. All the way along the brick path she had been telling herself that he would be there, and that it would mean he had fired into the air. Now she saw his face.

He looked up. He did not get to his feet. In the low light he was grey to the lips, and his eyes had gone back in his head.

"You've been in the house," he said. "You've said your piece?"

"I've been in the house."

"That's good." His voice had no colour in it. "I'm glad you did that. I want you to have done it." He looked down at the gun. "Imogen. There's a thing I've to tell you. You'd best hear it before you come any nearer."

She looked at the two spent cases on the floor.

"You found him," she said.

"I found him."

"Did he tell you? What your father wanted to know?"

"No."

It was one word. She heard everything that was in it. Her heart seemed to stop and go on.

She came in. She shut the door behind her on the wind. She found that she was calm. It was the calm that she had felt once in the studio, when a solvent took hold too fast and she watched an inch of sky lift off a panel under her swab. One did not cry out. One put the swab down and thought very clearly about what could still be saved.

"Tom," she said. "Is he—"

"I'm trying to tell you. I never asked him. I never got to ask. He was up—"

"No."

She had crossed the floor. She was on her knees in the dead leaves in front of him, in her mother's dress, and she had put her hand over his mouth.

He stared at her above it.

"Don't," she said. "Don't tell me. Not now."

He took her wrist and moved her hand away, quite gently.

"You've got to hear it. You'll not want to come with me when you have. I'll not take you over that water on a lie."

"It isn't a lie if I don't ask." She was speaking fast and low. "Listen to me. My mother made a rule. From one o'clock to two, by this house, on this night, nothing that's said is to be held against the one who says it. It's put back with the clocks. I've thought all my life that it was a game. But I went into that hall just now to tell my father the truth, and I found there was something he needed more, and I gave him that instead. I don't know if it was right. I know it's done. And I know this. If you tell me now what you did with that gun, I shall have to know it. I shan't be able to put it back. And I shall not be able to get on that horse."

"That's why you ought to hear it."

"That's why I won't." She took his face between her hands. It was cold. "I hid from you once because I couldn't bear what you'd think of me. I lost twenty years by it. I'm not going to lose the rest because of what I might think of you. Whatever it is. I'll hear it in daylight, on the other side, in your father's kitchen. Not here. Not in this house. Do you understand me? I have waited twenty years to go across that road, and I'm going. I'll not be turned back halfway."

He looked at her. She saw him weigh it. He was a man who did not lie, and she was asking him for something very near it.

"It's not a thing that'll keep," he said. "It's a thing they'll come for me about."

"Then they'll come to Saltcote, and I shall be there."

"You don't know what you're saying."

"No. I don't. That's the point." She let go his face. "Is there anything to be done? Now? Tonight? Anyone to be fetched?"

He was silent a moment. His eyes went to the dark glass, toward the stables.

"No," he said. "There's nothing to be done. I went round and looked. There's nothing there to do anything for."

She shut her eyes. She thought of her brother at eighteen, on the sea wall, with his arms round her, holding a gun to her shoulder. *Squeeze it, Immy. Don't pull. Like shutting your hand on a bird.*

She thought: I will not know this. I refuse it. I'll know it tomorrow.

It was the worst thing she had ever done, and she did it with her eyes open. She has never pretended otherwise.

"Then we go at twenty minutes to three," she said. "By the house. My father's given me the time."

"Your father?"

"He told me while we danced. High water at eight minutes to one. A horse at twenty to three, and not before; three feet in the Rill and a set to the north." She saw his face change. "It's the same as you said. To the minute."

"How'd he know there was a horse?"

"I don't know. He thought I was my mother. He thought he was sending her to Amos." Her voice broke at last. "He said, 'I don't ask you to stay.' He said, 'You've a man waiting with a lantern.' Tom, he knew. I think he's always known. He was giving her leave."

Tom Garrow put the gun down on the bricks. He put it away from him, with the flat of his boot, into the leaves. He bent forward and laid his forehead against hers.

"God help the pair of us," he said. "I come over here to kill a Vane, near enough. And the old man's give me his daughter and his blessing, and never knew I was on the place."

* * *

She could not cross the Wade in grey silk and kid sandals. That was plain. She would be thrown off by the cold before they reached the Rill.

"I must go in again," she said. "For a coat. Boots. Ten minutes."

"I'll saddle up." He had stood. Some of the colour had come back to him, now that there was a thing to do with his hands. "Bring something for your head. And nothing you can't carry in front of you. She'll have the two of us and the sea; I'll not ask her to take a trunk."

"I've nothing to bring. I never have had, from this house."

She went by the kitchen yard. It was the nearest way to the back stairs and her own room. The moon was high, and the wet cobbles shone. From the tower, as she crossed, the great bell struck twice.

She stopped. She listened for the quarters. There had been none. Only the two heavy strokes, out of a silent sky.

Two o'clock. The Hour was over. Whatever was said now would count.

The back door of the kitchen stood open. There was a lamp burning within. She went along the stone passage past the scullery, in her sandals, quickly. Her mind was on a tweed coat and a pair of gumboots.

"That's a Vane walking," said a voice from the kitchen. "I can tell by the feet."

She stopped dead.

She knew the voice. She had known it all her life.

She stood in the scullery passage with her hand on the cold wall. A door closed, somewhere up the kitchen stairs. A chair scraped. Then there was the sound of an uneven step on the flags, and the light from the kitchen doorway was blocked.

Edmund was standing in the scullery passage at twenty past two with a candle, as alive as she had ever seen him, and she said to him the one thing she had promised herself she would never say.

But first, for the space of a breath, she could say nothing.

She had thought him dead. She had knelt on a brick floor not half an hour ago and refused to be told it, and she had believed it all the same. *There's nothing there to do anything for.* She had walked across the yard carrying that, like a stone in her chest.

And here he was. He filled the low doorway. He had his dinner jacket on and his collar open and no tie. His hair was wet and standing in spikes. There was a swelling on his forehead, on the left, as big as an egg and nearly black, and the eye beneath it was half closed. The side of his neck was all over small dark spots, and his collar was soaked red. He held a candle in a kitchen saucer, and in the other hand the leg bone of a goose.

He was grinning at her. One side of his face did not move as well as the other.

"Good God," he said. "It is you. I thought I'd got to the stage of seeing things. Toby said you'd come down in the grey, and I thought he was drunk." His eyes went over the dress, the bare shoulders, her hair. The grin went. "Immy. You look—"

"Don't."

"I wasn't going to say like her. You do, but that's not it. You look like yourself. I haven't seen you look like yourself since you were twenty-four."

She found her voice.

"What have you done to your head?"

"Fell over my own feet. As usual." He touched the swelling, lightly, and winced. "And down some steps. And out of a wheelbarrow, if you'll believe it, but that's a long story and reflects no credit on the cook."

"And your neck? That's blood."

"Some idiot letting off at the duck. I was up the tower. I caught the edge of it." He hitched his left shoulder. "It's nothing. A few pellets. I've had worse from Father's gun at a pheasant shoot."

She put her hand on the wall again. She thought her knees would go.

*I never asked him. He was up—*

Tom had fired at a man on the tower. He had seen him fall, and gone round, and found nothing. So he had sat on a pot in the orangery for half an hour believing that he had killed her brother. And she had stopped his mouth, and he was sitting there now, saddling a horse, still believing it.

And her brother was standing in the scullery passage eating goose.

The relief was so great that it came out of her as fury. She had not known that it was there. She had kept it under the floor for twenty years, and all at once the floor was gone.

* * *

"You're alive," she said.

"So I'm told. People keep remarking on it."

"You're standing there. With a bone. Making jokes." Her voice was shaking. "Do you know what tonight has been? Do you know what I've—Papa thought I was Mother. I let him. I danced with him and let him tell me the tide, because he's spent twenty years believing that he gave her the wrong time and killed her. He's built his whole life round it. He was so happy, Edmund. He said, 'I've got it right now.'"

Edmund said nothing. He had put the bone down on the scullery shelf.

"And it was never his clock. Was it?"

"No."

"You know that. You've always known it. And so have I."

He looked at her. The candle shook a little in the saucer.

"I was in the orangery," Imogen said. "That night. I was there from eleven. I was supposed to walk across with her and I hadn't the courage, after what I'd said to you at tea. I sat behind the vine. I saw her lantern go down to the Wade. And I saw yours go after it."

"Yes."

"I saw them meet. Past the Perch. She was nearly over. Amos Garrow was standing at the far end with a light and she was a hundred and fifty yards from him. And you caught her."

"Yes."

"I saw the two of you stand there. An hour. More. I fell asleep watching. And when I woke it was six in the morning and you were walking up the lawn, past the orangery door, as close as you are to me now. You were wet to the neck. You had no lantern."

"I didn't know you were there," he said. It was very low. "I've sometimes thought so. I never knew."

"You went in and changed. You came down to breakfast and said you'd slept in the stable. I sat across the table from you and heard you say it. Then Pask came up from the saltings."

She had to stop. She had not known that she could still see it so clearly. The toast, and the marmalade spoon, and her father looking up.

"I've never said it. Not to Papa. Not to the police. Not to you. For twenty years I've come down here twice a year and sat at that table and passed you things. I let Papa think it was his clock, because if I'd told him it was you, I'd have had to tell him why you went. I'd have had to say that it was I who told you." Her voice rose. "I've hated you for that. Do you understand? Not only for what you did. For what you made of me. You made me a liar to my own father for twenty years, to cover us both. I couldn't see Tom Garrow because of it. I've lived in a cold flat mending other people's pictures because I couldn't bear to look at anything of my own."

"Immy."

"You went after her. You stopped her on the Wade. You kept her there, talking, shouting, I don't know what, a drunk boy who couldn't stand to be left, until the tide came. And then you got yourself out. You got out, and you left her. And you have let that old man wind a hundred and eleven clocks every week for twenty years and tell every one of them that it was his fault."

She was crying with rage. She wiped her face with her bare wrist.

"I said I'd never say it. I promised myself. I thought, if I ever once begin I shall not be able to stop. Well, I've said it. And it's gone two; I heard it strike. It isn't the Hour. It isn't going to be put back. I want it to count. I hope you never have another night's sleep as long as you live."

* * *

The scullery passage was quiet. Somewhere a tap dripped.

Edmund had not moved while she spoke. He stood in the doorway with his big shoulders against the jamb, holding the saucer. He had kept his eyes on her face the whole time. She had expected him to look away. He always had.

"Yes," he said.

She waited.

"Is that all?" she said. "*Yes?*"

"It's all of it that's true. I went after her. I caught her past the Perch. I kept her standing on that road for an hour and a quarter with the tide making, because I couldn't bear it, and I was drunk, and I was thirty-two years old and had never in my life been told no." His voice was quite steady. "That's true. You've had that right for twenty years. I'm sorry you had to keep it. I didn't know that you were."

"And then you saved yourself and left her."

He was silent.

"Didn't you?"

"That's the part you've got wrong," Edmund said. "It's worse than what you think, Immy. And it's better. I don't know which you'd say."

"I don't want to hear it."

"You ought to. You've a right. I told Father, an hour ago, up the tower. I'd have told you first if I'd known what you'd been carrying. I told that little nurse this afternoon that I'd tell the pair of you in the morning. She's got a book of Mother's, did you know? Her diary, for that year. It was in the clock that doesn't go."

"I don't want it."

She heard her own voice. It was hard and thin, like a child's.

"I have carried what I saw for twenty years. I saw two lights, and I saw one man come home. I don't want your account of it. I don't want to be told that it was more complicated, and that you suffered. I'm sure it was. I'm sure you did. I am not going to stand in a scullery at half past two in the morning and take that on as well."

"It isn't that. It's what she did. At the end. You ought to know what she did."

"She drowned," Imogen said. "That's what she did. A hundred and fifty yards from a man who'd waited for her for ten years. I'll not hear another word."

She saw it go home. He shut his eyes for a moment, as he had in the gunroom.

It is the thing that she has had to live with. He was trying to tell her. He had it ready. He had told their father an hour before, and he would have told her then, in two minutes, by a candle. She stopped him. She had refused to hear Tom, for love. She refused to hear her brother, for anger. She has thought since that there was not much to choose between the two.

"All right," Edmund said. He opened his eyes. He did not seem angry. He looked, if anything, relieved, and very tired, and oddly gentle. "All right, Immy. Another day. I've said it once tonight, and it nearly finished me. Father's got it now. He'll tell you. He won't remember that he knows it, but he'll tell you all the same, one morning when you're not expecting it. It'll come out with the tide tables."

He set the saucer down on the shelf beside the bone. He looked at her dress again, at the wet marks on the shoulders.

"You're going," he said. "Aren't you? Tonight. I can see it on you."

"Yes."

"With Garrow."

"Yes."

"He's on the island? How in God's name did he—" He stopped. He began to laugh. It hurt him; he put a hand to his neck. "The duck. Oh, my Lord. Of course. It was Tom Garrow letting off at me from the yard. I shouted at him. I couldn't see who it was; I said something about getting off my land." He leaned his head back against the door frame. "Well. I can't say I didn't have it coming. Is he a good shot?"

"He thinks he killed you."

"Does he? Then I shouldn't tell him otherwise till you're over the water. It'll make him mind the mare." His eyes had lit, the old wicked light, that she had not seen for twenty years. "No. That's unkind. Tell him he missed. Tell him he's a rotten shot, and that I said so, and that he can have the farm."

"What?"

"Saltcote. He can have it. Father's given it to them. He told me so himself, up the tower; he did it in the hall an hour ago, in front of Fenn. Freehold. *To Amos Garrow or his heirs.* So there'll be no caravans. I've been outbid by my own father." He was still smiling. "I find I don't mind. I find I don't mind anything tonight. It's a most peculiar feeling."

She did not know what to say to him. She had come into that passage with twenty years of hatred and had spent it all in three minutes. He had stood and taken it, and said yes. And now he was giving her a farm.

She thought: he has been hit on the head. He is not himself.

She thinks now that he was more himself, in that passage, than he had been since he was a boy.

* * *

"Wait," he said. "Before you go."

He was feeling in the pocket of his waistcoat. His fingers were clumsy. He brought something out and held it on his palm, under the candle.

It was a ring. It was a plain gold band, worn thin, such as every married woman of her mother's age had worn.

Imogen looked at it. She looked at his face.

"That's Mother's."

"Yes."

"She was buried in her ring. Papa said—"

"Papa never looked. He couldn't. Dolly laid her out. Dolly knew it was gone and never said. I've sometimes wondered what she thought." He turned his hand a little, and the gold caught. "She gave it to me. That night. Out there. She took it off her finger and put it in my hand and shut my hand on it. She said, 'Give that to your father.'"

Imogen could not breathe.

"I never did. I've had it in my pocket for twenty years. Every day. I've changed it from one waistcoat to another every morning of my life." His voice had dropped. "I couldn't give it to him without telling him how I came by it. So I kept it. That's what I am, Immy. I couldn't even carry a message."

He held it out.

"Take it. Give that to Father."

"Give it to him yourself. In the morning. You said you were going to tell him the rest."

"I've told him the rest. I forgot this. It was in my pocket and I forgot it; I was looking at his face." He took her hand, the left, and turned it over, and put the ring in her palm, and closed her fingers on it as his own had once been closed. His hand was very cold. "You do it. You'll make a better job of it. And I've an idea I shan't be about in the morning. I never am, after this night. I go to ground. Ask Dolly."

"Edmund—"

"You gave him Mother tonight. I heard. Toby says the old man was dancing. I've not been able to give him anything in twenty years but copies." He let go her hand. "Let him have that from you. Tell him she sent it. It's true."

She stood with the ring shut in her fist. It was warm from his waistcoat.

She should have asked him then. *How did she come to give it you? What did she do, at the end?* He would have told her. He was waiting to.

She was too proud. She had said that she would not hear another word, and she would not go back on it. And there was a man in the orangery, saddling a horse, who thought that he had done murder. And the tide would not wait.

"I must get my coat," she said.

"There's Mother's old tweed on the peg in the gunroom. And her boots. They've been there since. Nobody liked to move them." He stood aside from the door, to let her by. "Take those. She'd laugh."

She went past him. In the doorway she stopped. He was so close that she could smell the whisky and the blood.

She had told him that she hoped he would never sleep again. She wanted to take it back. She did not know how. She had no practice.

"You should have that head seen to," she said. It was all that she could find.

"I will. In the morning." He smiled at her. It was not the easy smile. It was a boy's, crooked, the one he had had before he learned the other. "Go on, Immy. Don't look back. She looked back."

She did not understand him. She thought that he meant their mother had looked back at the house, on the Wade, and wavered, and been lost. She thought that he was telling her not to hesitate.

She did as he said. She went through the kitchen and up the stone passage to the gunroom, with the ring in her hand. She took down the tweed coat from its peg. It still smelled of horse. She put her feet into her mother's boots. The game book lay open on the bench, with its pencil on a string, and she tore a leaf from the back of it and wrote a line, so that Dolly should not have the creeks dragged for her. *Gone across to Saltcote. Don't wait luncheon. I.* She left it under a cartridge.

She did not look back. She has been sorry for it every day of her life.

* * *

Tom was standing at the mare's head when she came into the orangery. He had her saddled and the lantern hung. He had not put the gun in its case. It lay where he had kicked it, in the leaves.

He looked at the old coat, and the boots, and the grey silk showing between. He looked at her face.

"What is it?" he said. "What's happened?"

"I've seen Edmund."

He did not move.

"He's in the kitchen. He's eaten half a goose. He's a lump on his head the size of an egg, and a few of your pellets in his neck, and he says to tell you that you're a rotten shot."

Tom Garrow stood with his hand on the bridle. She watched it reach him. His mouth opened. He put his other hand out behind him, feeling for the stone trough, and sat down on the edge of it as though his legs had been cut.

"He's on his feet," he said.

"He's on his feet and making jokes."

"I saw him go off the back of that tower. I saw him fall, Imogen. With his arms out. Into the fleet."

"I don't know what you saw. I know what I've just spoken to." She came and stood in front of him. "You didn't kill anyone. Do you hear me? You didn't."

He put his face in his hands. His shoulders shook. She thought that he was weeping, and then she saw that it was something else, a kind of long silent shudder, like a horse that has been ridden too hard. She put her arms round his head and held it against her mother's coat.

"I asked him for you," she said. "What your father wanted to know. He said yes. He went after her. He kept her on the Wade an hour and a quarter. That's what he said."

"Then she never turned back of herself."

"He said there was more. He wanted to tell me. I wouldn't hear it." She shut her eyes. "I was too angry. He said, another day."

"Another day." Tom lifted his head. His face was wet, and ten years younger. "I'll go to him another day. I'll go in daylight, by the road, with my hat in my hand and no gun, and ask him civil. I've done enough tonight on my father's account. He'd not have thanked me for the half of it."

"There's something else. Papa's given you the farm."

He stared.

"Saltcote. Freehold. He dictated it to Fenn in the hall, in the Hour. *To Amos Garrow or his heirs.* Edmund told me." She found that she was laughing, and that the tears were running into her mouth. "There'll be no caravans. You came over here with a gun to get your father's ground back, and he gave it to you in the middle of a waltz without knowing you were there."

Tom looked at the gun in the leaves. He looked at it for a long time.

Then he got up. He picked it up, and broke it, and looked through the empty barrels at the lantern. He put it in its canvas case. He buckled the case, slowly, and strapped it under the saddle flap.

"I'll not leave it lying in your father's glasshouse," he said. "But I'll tell you this. It's the last time I carry that anywhere but after rabbits."

He turned to her. He took her left hand. She had forgotten that it was shut. He opened her fingers.

The ring lay on her palm.

"What's this?"

"It was my mother's. Edmund had it. She gave it to him that night, on the Wade, for Papa. He's carried it for twenty years." She closed her hand again. "I'm to give it to my father. I can't now. I'll bring it across to him on Sunday."

He looked at her fist, and at her face.

"That's a queer thing for a woman to do," he said slowly. "That's about to leave a man. To send him back her ring by her son."

"Yes."

"That's not a woman being dragged."

"No."

They looked at each other. Neither of them knew what it meant. It would be thirty years before anyone told them.

Outside, the wind had dropped altogether. The moon stood over the broken roof. From the tower the bell did not ring; there was nobody now to ring the quarters. But Tom looked at the big steel watch on his wrist.

"Twenty-five past three," he said. "By England. That's twenty-five past two by your father."

"Then we've a quarter of an hour."

"We'll walk her down. I want her warm when she meets the water." He untied the halter rope. He stood a moment with the mare's white head against his shoulder. "You're sure? There's no going back over it tonight, once she's in. And I've a damp house and a child you've never seen and a hundred and forty acres of mud."

Imogen put the ring into the pocket of her mother's coat. She buttoned the coat to the neck.

"I held your lamp in May," she said. "I've been waiting since to be asked what for."

## Chapter Seven

They went down through the orchard. He led the mare, and Imogen walked at his other side with her hand in the crook of his arm. The grass was long and soaking. The apple trees stood about them, black and bent, with a few late fruit still hanging, and the moon came through the branches and lay in pieces on the ground.

Neither of them spoke. There was the sound of the mare's feet, and the creak of leather, and ahead of them, growing, the sound of water.

The orchard ended at the sea wall. There was a gap in the bank there, with a gate, and beyond the gate the ramp where the Wade left the island. She had come up that ramp on the Friday night with a bag in her hand.

There was no ramp now. The sea began at the gate.

It lay in front of them, flat and bright, from their feet to the far shore. The moon had laid a track across it, a long road of white light, straight as a rule, that ran out from the gatepost and went away over the water to the black line of the mainland. On either side of the track the two rows of withies stood up out of the tide. Only their tops showed. They went off into the distance like the masts of a drowned fleet.

"That's a foot and a half down on what I came through," Tom said. He had stopped at the edge. He was not looking at the water. He was looking past it, and up, and she saw his nostrils move. "The wind's gone round north-west. That'll hold the ebb back a bit in the Rill. Your father said three foot?"

"Three feet, and a strong set to the north."

"He's not far out. I'd have said three and a half." He glanced at his watch, and then, with a half smile, at her. "Eighteen minutes to four. He said twenty to. I'd not like to tell him he was two minutes slow."

"He'd say that you were two minutes fast."

"Likely he would." He turned to the mare. He ran his hand down her neck and along her back, and bent, and felt each of her legs to the hoof. He spoke to her under his breath. Then he stood up and looked at Imogen.

"Can you ride astride in that?"

She gathered up the grey silk in both hands, above her knees, under the tweed coat. "I rode astride before I could read."

"She's no saddle to speak of for two. You'll go up in front, in the seat, and take the reins. I'll walk at her head as far as I can, and get up behind you when it deepens. At the Rill I'll get down again."

"Get down? In that?"

"I'll swim it with her. She'll carry one through that set, with the tide falling. She'll not carry two. I asked it of her once tonight and that's enough." He said it quite simply. "You'll have nothing to do but sit still and hold her mane. Don't pull at her mouth. Don't try to steer. She'll go down and be carried, and you'll think she's lost it, and she'll come up on the road again thirty yards on. If you feel her go right under, you slide off on the upstream side and keep hold of the stirrup. I'll have you."

"And if you're carried?"

"I'll not be. I've swum the Oldman in spring with a calf across the saddle." He put his hands at her waist. "Up."

He lifted her as though she weighed nothing. She found the stirrup and swung her leg across. The saddle was a strange one, deep, with a high horn in front, such as she had only seen in films. It held her like a chair. The mare stood like a rock.

She was a long way up. She looked down at him, at his wet dark head.

"Tom."

"What?"

"If I don't—if anything—"

"You will. Your father's give you the time, and I've give you the horse. Between the pair of us, we ought to get one Vane woman over that water." He took the rein under the mare's chin. "Don't look at the sea. Look at the far wall. There's a light."

She looked. Half a mile off, low down, at the end of the moon's road, there was a small yellow point.

"I left the lamp in the kitchen window," he said. "It's where Dad stood."

He led them in.

* * *

The water was so cold that she felt it through her mother's boots as a kind of burning. It came over the mare's fetlocks, and then her knees. Tom walked ahead, to his thighs. He did not hurry. He went as he had always gone at anything, a step at a time, feeling for it.

The ramp fell away under them and they were on the Wade.

She could feel the road beneath the mare's feet. It was firm and ribbed, and the mare knew it. Her ears went forward. She put her head down and walked into the sea, like an old horse turning for home.

The withies went by on either side. The water rose. It was at Tom's waist, and at the mare's belly, and it pulled. Imogen felt it take hold of the horse and lean on her from the left. The mare leaned back against it and kept on.

"She's all right," Tom said. He had not turned his head. "That's only the top of it. That's nothing."

He stopped her, and came back along her side. He put his foot on Imogen's in the stirrup and his hand on the horn, and was up behind her in one movement, with the sea pouring off him. His arms came round her and took the reins. His chest was hard and wet against her back, and she could feel his heart.

"Now sit down in the saddle and let your legs hang," he said in her ear. "We'll have ten minutes of this, and then the Rill."

They went on. She had never been on the Wade at the flood. No one had. She had lived beside it for twenty-four years and had only ever seen it as a road or as the sea. She had not known there was a time between, when it was both. The stones were under them, and the water over, and the moon lay on the top like a skin. It was a world with two floors.

She thought of her mother.

She had been thinking of her all night. But that had been in a house. This was the place. It had been on this road, in this hour, twenty years ago, that her mother had come walking with a lantern, in her stockings, quickly, toward a light on a wall.

She had been past the Perch. She had been as far as this. Further.

And then a voice behind her, shouting. A second light. Her son.

Imogen had seen it from the orangery as two small stars. She had never before been where it happened. She looked at the black water sliding by, north, toward the sea. She thought of what it had been to stand on this road and feel it begin to rise round one's ankles, and to argue.

*It's what she did. At the end. You ought to know what she did.*

*She drowned. I'll not hear another word.*

She had the ring in the pocket of the coat. She could feel it against her hip, through the tweed, small and hard.

"There," Tom said.

She looked up. In front of them the two lines of withies seemed to sink. The water between them was darker, and it was moving in a different way. It had a kind of smooth swift shine on it, like oil, and little creases, and it made a sound.

And to the right of it, twenty yards off, standing up black against the moon, on its four tall legs, was the Perch.

* * *

She had not known that it would be so near. The tide was halfway up its posts. She could see the ladder going down into the water, and the little door, shut, and the tarred roof with the moonlight on it.

It was the nearest that she had ever been to the place where her mother died.

Tom had reined in. The mare stood with the sea streaming round her chest, blowing, looking at the deep water with her ears flicking. He sat still behind Imogen for a moment. Then he slid off.

He went in to the armpits. He gasped, once, and got his breath. He waded to the mare's head and took hold of the bridle by the cheek strap.

"Hold her mane," he said. "Both hands. Shut your eyes if you like."

"I'm not going to shut my eyes."

"No. You never would." He looked up at her. The moon was on his face. He was up to his neck in the North Sea in October, at four in the morning, and he was smiling. "I'll say this now, in case I've no breath for it after. I'd go through this every night for another twenty year, and count it cheap."

He turned, and said one word to the mare, and walked off the edge of the road.

It went from under them. She felt it go. One moment there was stone beneath the horse's feet and the next there was nothing, and the whole great warm body dropped, and the sea came up over the saddle and over Imogen's knees and into her lap. The cold took her breath. She had her fingers wound in the white mane. She saw Tom's head, dark and sleek as a seal's, a yard in front, with one arm stretched back to the bridle.

The mare was swimming. Imogen could feel it, the great shoulders working, the legs striking. But the Rill had her. It took her sideways, as it had taken the light that Imogen had watched from the window. The withies went away to the left. The moon's road slid out from under them. They were being carried north, down the gut, toward the open flats and the sea.

The Perch went by.

It went by so close on the right hand that she could have touched one of its legs. She saw the weed on the post, and the rusted heads of the bolts. She saw the ladder. She looked up at the black box over her head, with its shut door.

And she thought, quite clearly, in the middle of that water, with the cold at her waist: *Someone was in there.*

She did not know where the thought came from. It was like a voice. She saw nothing. She heard nothing but the sea. But it came to her with entire certainty that on the night her mother died, someone had been in that box. Someone had sat up there in the dark, above the tide, and been safe.

She had seen one person come home.

"Hold on!" Tom's voice, half choked.

The mare's feet struck. Imogen was flung forward on her neck. There was a scrabbling, a heave, another. The water fell from the saddle to the girth, to the knee. The old horse stood, shuddering, with her head down and her sides going like bellows, and under her feet there was stone.

They were on the road. They were thirty yards north of the withies, on the far side of the Rill, and the bottom was hard and ribbed and rising.

Tom came up out of the water at the mare's head, on his hands and knees. He stayed there a moment, coughing. Then he got up. He put both arms round the white neck and laid his face against it.

"That's my girl," he said. "That's my beauty. That's the last time. I'll never ask it of you again."

He looked up at Imogen. He could not speak for a moment.

"You're over," he said. "That's the deep of it. There's nothing between here and the wall now but a walk."

She was shaking so that her teeth rattled. She had lost one of her mother's boots. The grey silk was a sodden rope round her legs. She looked at him, standing in the sea to his waist, with the moon behind him, and she began to laugh, and found that she could not stop.

"I've crossed it," she said. "Tom. I've crossed it."

"You have."

"Twenty years. It took me twenty years to walk half a mile."

"You've not walked a yard of it," said Tom Garrow. "You've been carried the whole road, by a horse you named yourself. Now sit still. I'm coming up."

* * *

He was behind her again, with his arms round her. The mare went forward at a walk. The water sank to her knees.

It was then that Imogen looked back.

She had been told not to. Her brother had said it, in the scullery. *Don't look back. She looked back.* She had obeyed him in the house. She had gone down through the orchard with her face to the sea and had not once turned her head.

But they were over. The lamp in the farm window was large and yellow in front of them. She thought that it could not matter now. And she wanted to see it. She wanted to see Compline, from this side, from the back of a Garrow's horse.

She turned in the saddle and looked over Tom's shoulder.

The island lay black on the bright water. She could see the line of the trees, and the long roof, and the chimneys. She could see the tower. There was one lamp burning, in the porch, the one that her father had lit at dusk every night of his life, since he held that a house with a tide in front of it owed the traveller that much.

And there was another light.

It was very small. It was low down, at the water's edge, where the orchard gate was and the Wade began. It was not yellow, like a lantern. It was whiter and thinner, a mere point, like a glow-worm. As she looked, it moved. It came down a little way toward the sea, and stopped, and came on again.

She thought: that is Edmund.

She was sure of it. He had followed them down through the orchard with his candle in its saucer. He had come to the gate to watch them over. He had said that he would not be about in the morning. This was his way of seeing her off.

Her eyes filled. She had said such things to him. She had said that she hoped he would never sleep. And he had put their mother's ring in her hand and told her to go, and now he was standing at the edge of the tide, alone, with a lump on his head and shot in his neck, holding up a light.

She lifted her arm. She waved to it, a wide slow wave, as one waves from the deck of a ship.

"Who are you waving at?" Tom said.

"My brother. He's come down to the gate. Look."

Tom turned his head. He looked for some time. She felt him go still against her.

"That's a queer little light," he said. "That's low down, for a man."

"He's carrying a candle in a saucer."

"Is he." He was frowning. "It looks to me as if it's out on the Wade. It looks to be coming this way."

"He wouldn't. Not on foot. He knows the tide better than anyone."

"No. You're right. Nobody would." But he looked a moment longer. "There's three foot on the Rill yet. A man'd be off his legs."

A cloud went over the moon. The white road on the water went out. The island was gone, and the tower, and the little light with it. There was only the dark, and the lamp ahead.

When the cloud had passed she looked again. She could see the porch lamp. She could not find the other.

"He's gone in," she said.

"Likely." Tom shook the reins. "Come up, Mab. You can smell your stable."

The mare walked up out of the sea.

Imogen has gone back to that many times. She has stood on the wall at Saltcote, on other nights, and looked across at the place. She saw a light at the edge of the tide and gave it her brother's name. She waved to it. Then she turned her face to the shore and did not look again.

She does not know what else she could have done. She asks herself, all the same.

* * *

The kitchen at Saltcote was low and warm and smelled of wood smoke. There was a range, with the fire banked. There was a deal table, scrubbed white, and a dresser with blue plates, and a clock on the wall with a painted face. On the sill, in the window that looked toward the island, stood an oil lamp.

Tom carried her in. She could not have walked. He set her down in a high-backed wooden chair by the range. It was an old man's chair, with a cushion flattened to the shape of one body. He knelt and pulled off the one boot. He took her feet between his hands.

"They're like ice," he said. "Don't move. I've the mare to see to. I'll be ten minutes. There's a blanket."

He was gone twenty. She heard him in the yard, talking, and the sound of straw. She sat in Amos Garrow's chair with a horse blanket round her and looked at the lamp in the window.

It was where he had stood. Tom had said so. The old man had gone out to the wall with the lantern, that night. But this had been the house's light. It had burned in this window for a woman who was coming to live here.

She was the wrong one. She was twenty years late. But she had come.

She put her hand into the pocket of the wet coat. The ring was there.

When Tom came in he had a dry shirt on and his hair was rubbed up on end. He put the kettle on the range. He found a towel, and a pair of his own thick socks, and a flannel shirt that came down to her knees. He turned his back while she got out of the grey silk. It took her some time. The hooks had swollen.

She held it up, when it was off. It hung from her hands, dark with sea water, heavy as a drowned thing. It had been painted in 1956. It had been worn to twenty Hours. It had been left on a hanger for twenty years, and tonight it had crossed.

She did not know what would become of it. She found, later, that salt water does less harm to good silk than one would think. She had it cleaned by a woman in Colchester who did church vestments. In January she carried it back over the Wade, in a box, and hung it on its padded hanger at the end of the rail, and locked the door.

"Tea," Tom said. He put a mug into her hands. It was thick and white, and the tea was nearly black. "There's whisky in it. Dad's. He'd want you to have it."

She drank. The heat went down into her like a hand.

He sat on the edge of the table, facing her. He looked at her in his shirt and his socks, with her hair coming down.

"I ought to go and look at Wren," he said. "I've never left her a night before."

"Go."

"I'll not wake Vi at this hour. She's eighty-three, and deaf as a post, and she'll think it's the Germans." He rubbed his jaw. "I'll go at seven. She'll be asleep. She sleeps like the dead, that child, once she's off. I'll carry her home and you'll see her when she wakes."

"What will she think of me?"

"I don't know." He was honest, as always. "She'll look at you a good while before she says. She did me, when I come back from a month on the range once. She was four. She sat on the step and looked for an hour, and then she said, 'You've got a different hat.'"

Imogen smiled. She looked down into the mug.

"Tom. In the Rill. When we went past the Perch."

"Ay?"

"Did you feel anything? As if—" She did not know how to say it. "As if somebody had been there."

He was silent for a time.

"I've felt that all my life," he said. "Every Garrow has. Dad would never pass it without he touched the post. He said it was for them that had sat in it." He looked at the window, and the lamp. "It's a queer old thing. Your brother's let it go. Them bottom rungs wouldn't bear a child."

She thought of her brother. She thought of a small white light at the edge of the sea.

"I'll go across on Sunday night," she said. "By the road. I've a ring to give my father. And I'll find Edmund. I said some things to him that I'm going to unsay. And then I shall make him tell me the rest."

"I'll come with you. I've a question of my own."

"Without the gun."

"With my hat in my hand," Tom Garrow said.

* * *

She did go across on the Sunday. She walked over at the evening ebb, in a borrowed skirt, with the ring in her glove.

The house was upside down. Celia had gone. Edmund had not been seen since the night. Kit met her on the gravel, grey in the face. They had found the Jack in the outfall that morning, he said, in Grandfather's old dinner jacket, and for a minute they had thought—

She went up to the Admiral's room. Her father was in bed, propped on pillows. The nurse got up from her low chair and went out without a word.

"Imogen," he said. He knew her at once. "They said that you had gone over to the farm."

"I have, Papa. I'm going to stay there. I'm going to marry Tom Garrow."

"Are you? That is very suitable. I gave them the ground last night; you'll be on your own freehold." He nodded, pleased. "I ought to have done it thirty years ago. One puts things off."

She took off her glove. She opened her hand.

He looked at what lay in it. He fitted the glass into his eye. He took the ring from her palm, between finger and thumb, as he would have taken up a pivot, and turned it to the lamp.

"That is Margot's," he said. "I had it made by a man in Hatton Garden. Twenty-two carat; it wears, you see, it has worn to a wire. Where was this?"

"Edmund had it. She gave it to him. That night, on the Wade. She told him to give it to you." Her voice shook. "He's carried it ever since. He asked me to bring it."

Her father was quiet. He closed his fingers on the ring.

"Yes," he said. "That would be so. He told me. In the tower, last night. She turned back, you know. She had got nearly across, and she turned round on the Wade and came back. He was there. He saw. She was coming home." He looked up at her, mild and certain. "I thought for twenty years that she drowned going away from me. She was on her way back to this house."

Imogen stood by the bed. She looked at his face, so peaceful.

She thought: he has made it into the story that he needs. Edmund told him something, up there, and he has turned it round until it will bear his weight. She *turned back*. Amos Garrow had said it, dying. *I never knew if she turned of herself or was turned.* And here was her father, sure that she had turned of herself, and toward him.

She did not correct him. She had learned something in that hall, about truth, and when to give it. She thought that she understood exactly what her father had done with what he was told.

So she bent, and kissed him, and said, "Yes, Papa. She was coming home."

It was the third time that night and day that she had been offered it. Tom had tried to tell her one thing in the orangery, and she had stopped his mouth. Edmund had tried in the scullery, and she would not hear. And now her father had given it to her in plain words, from his pillow. She smiled at him, and thought him confused.

Her father slipped the ring onto the smallest finger of his left hand. It went on easily; he had grown so thin. He was buried in it.

They found her brother on the Monday.

* * *

She has written this as a love story. It is one. She was married to Tom Garrow in April, in St Botolph's, a month after her father died. She wore a blue coat. The ring was a horseshoe nail, bent round, with the head beaten flat. She had sent to Edinburgh for it. She has kept it oiled.

Dolly Pask cried all through. Octavia Prowse gave her away, since there was no one else left to, and said in the porch that it was about time one of them got something out of that family. There was a small dark child in a new frock and gumboots, who held the bride's flowers upside down and watched everything.

Afterward they walked down to the yard. The old mare was looking over her door. Tom had plaited a ribbon into her mane.

She has been happy. She is not going to pretend, for the sake of anyone's feelings, that she has not. She has lived for a long time in a low damp house with a lamp in the window, among sheep, and has learned to smell the tide. She has had a daughter given to her whom she did not bear and could not love more. She has had a man who cannot say things, and who shows her.

That was what she got, on the night of the twenty-second of October. She went into her father's house with twenty years of silence in her, and came out on a grey horse, across the sea, by moonlight. She was told the time by the one man and carried by the other.

She had her Hour. It was given back to her, as her father always said it was, and she was let do the thing over. This time she crossed.

And on the same night her brother, whom she had told that she hoped he would never sleep again, went down to that water by himself.

She does not know why. She has an idea. It is the idea that anyone would have, who had said what she said. He had put his mother's ring into her hand like a man clearing his pockets. He had said, *I've an idea I shan't be about in the morning.*

She saw a light at the edge of the tide. She waved to it.

She has never told her husband what she said in the scullery. He has never spoken again of the two spent cases on the orangery floor, and she has never asked. There is a paper in a drawer, from a coroner, that mentions shot. They have been married a long time and are very close. There are two rooms in the house that neither of them goes into.

The publishers of this book have asked for a happy ending. They are quite right. It is what the form requires. And she has one to give them, with a good conscience.

Here it is. On an evening in May, in the year after, she was standing on the sea wall above the farm. The tide was making. It came in over the flats in long bright sheets, without a sound, the way it does. The larks were going up.

Tom came and stood beside her. He had the child by the hand.

"Watch," he said to the child. "It'll stop."

"It won't. It's the sea."

"It will. In a minute. It stops at the top and thinks."

They watched. The water came up the stones of the wall. It came to within a foot of their boots. It slowed, and spread, and lay flat from the wall to the island, with the sky in it.

And it stopped. The whole of it. As if someone had laid a hand on it.

"There," Tom said. "That's the slack. That's the tide thinking better of it. You've a few minutes, then, when nothing's coming and nothing's going. You can get a boat anywhere. You can do near enough what you like."

The child looked at the still water for a long time, with her head on one side.

"What does it think about?" she said.

Nobody answered her. Across the bright flood the house stood on its island with every window shut. It was very quiet there now. Somebody had stopped the clocks.

Imogen put her arm through her husband's. She did not look at a watch. She had never worn one.

Then, slowly, with a small sound like breath, the sea turned and began to go out.

# PART FIVE {.part}

::: {.parttitle}
Saltcote

*as told by Tom Garrow*
:::

## Editor's Note {.note}

Thomas Garrow never wrote anything down that was longer than a stock return. He left school at fifteen. From 1974 to 1994 he worked cattle and shod horses on the eastern slope of the Rockies in southern Alberta, and from 1994 until he died, in the winter of 2021, he farmed a hundred and forty acres of Essex marsh. He was the least talkative man I have ever known.

But he told this. He told it over a number of years, in pieces, to one listener, usually late and usually out of doors. He told it always in the same words, as people do who have gone over a thing many times in their own heads, and he would stop if he was interrupted and go back to the beginning of the piece. I have set it down in those words as nearly as I am able. I am confident of most of them. I heard them often enough.

Two things about the telling I have kept, because I do not think the account is his without them.

He never said *I*. Not about that night. He would say *I* about anything else: the price of hoggets, what he had for breakfast. But when he came to the Saturday he said *the man*, and went on saying it until the story was done. I asked him once why. He thought about it for some time and said that it hadn't felt like him. I think that he had spent twenty years in a country where a man with a horse and a grievance and a gun is a kind of person that everybody recognises, and that on that one night he found he had become it, and that it was easier to look at from a little way off.

And he did not report speech as other people do. He would not put on a voice, or say *he said* and then the words. He ran it all in, flat, what was said along with what was done, as if talk were only one more thing that happened, like weather. I have left out the quotation marks accordingly. You will find that you do not miss them.

His times are from his own wristwatch, which he had set by the wireless that morning. He was never inside the house and never saw one of its clocks. So he is the only witness of the seven whose midnight is England's midnight. When you set him beside the last account, you will see what that does.

He believed until the end of his life that he had killed Edmund Vane. He did not put that in the story. He said it to me once only, in a hospital, and by the time I had told him what I knew he was past hearing it.

## 1. The Burying

The man came back to that country on a Monday in the fall of the year, with a child, in a hired car.

He had been gone twenty years. He drove out from the railway town through the flat land in the afternoon with the rain coming in off the sea. It was a small land after where he had been. There were hedges. The fields were the size of a horse pasture and every one of them had a ditch around it with water standing. He had forgotten how wet it was. He had forgotten that the sky came down so low a man could feel it on his hat.

The child sat beside him with her face to the glass. She was nine years old and had not seen the sea. She had asked him on the airplane what it looked like and he had said it looked like the prairie only it moved. She had thought about that for some time. Then she had got out her notebook and written something down.

Is this where you were a kid, she said.

Near enough.

It's all one colour.

It is today.

They came through the village. It had not changed. There was the church and the public house and the row of cottages with their doors on the street. An old woman was standing in a doorway and she looked at the car as it went by and he saw her know him. He lifted one finger off the wheel. She did not lift anything.

Past the last house the road went up onto the sea wall. He stopped the car on top of it. He had not meant to.

The tide was out. The mud ran away grey and shining to the edge of the sky. Across it lay the Wade with its two lines of stakes, and at the far end the island, low and black, with the trees leaning. He could see the roof of the house. He could see the tower.

He sat with his hands on the wheel. The engine ran. The wipers went across and back.

What is that, said the child.

That's the Ness.

Who lives there?

People called Vane.

Do we know them?

He put the car in gear.

No, he said. We don't know them.

* * *

The farm lay under the wall on the landward side. It was a long low house of tarred boards with a tile roof gone green, and barns to the north and east of it built the same, and a yard between. There had been Garrows on it since his great-great-grandfather came home from the French wars with one arm and took the lease. None of them had ever owned a foot of it. They paid the rent on Lady Day and Michaelmas, in the estate office, with their hats off.

He drove down into the yard. There was nobody about. The stock was out on the saltings to the north; he could see the sheep, small and dirty white, strung along a creek. In the home pasture by the barn a grey mare was standing with her tail to the rain.

He got out. The child got out on her side and stood looking.

The mare had lifted her head. She was old. She had gone white all over, the way greys do, white as a bone. She looked at him across forty yards of wet grass. She did not move for as long as it would take to count twenty. Then she walked to the fence, slowly, and put her head over it.

He went to her. He stood with his hand on her face.

He had pulled her out of her mother with his own arm, on the saltings, by a lantern. He had been twenty-three. A girl had held the light.

Hello, old lady, he said.

The mare breathed on his shirt.

Is she yours, the child said. She had come up beside him. She was a horseman's daughter and she stood where the mare could see her.

She's my dad's.

What's her name?

Mab.

That's a funny name.

It's out of a poem.

You don't know any poems.

No, he said. I was give it.

A woman had come out of the house. She stood on the step with her arms wrapped in her apron. She was broad and grey and he did not know her at first, and then he did. It was Dolly Pask from the cottage. She had been a young married woman when he left, with a tongue like a rasp. She cooked at the big house.

She looked at the hat. He had not thought about the hat. He had worn it for twenty years and it was only what went on his head.

Well, she said. Tom Garrow. You'd best come in. He's been asking the time since Thursday.

* * *

The old man was in the kitchen in his chair.

It was the chair he had always sat in, by the range, with the high back. They had put a pillow behind him and a blanket over his knees. He had been a big man, wide, with hands that could span a ewe's back. The hands lay on the blanket now like a pair of gloves someone had left there. His face had gone in. His breath came and went with a sound in it like a wet rope running through a block.

His eyes were open. They were the same.

The man took off his hat. He stood in the door with the rain running off his coat onto the bricks.

The old man looked at him. He looked at him for a long time. He looked at the grey in his hair and the lines on his face and the coat, which was a stockman's coat of oiled canvas with a cape to the shoulders. The clock on the wall ticked.

You've took your time, the old man said.

I came when they sent.

I never told them to send.

No. Dolly did.

She would. The old man's eyes moved. Who's that?

The child had come in behind. She stood by the man's leg and looked at the old man the way she looked at everything.

That's Wren. That's your granddaughter.

She's dark.

Her mother was dark.

Where's her mother?

She died. Two years back. I wrote you.

Did you? The old man was quiet. I don't recollect. I don't read them. I can't see to. He looked at the child again. Come here, girl.

She went. She stood in front of the chair. The old man lifted one of his hands off the blanket, an inch, and let it fall.

She's a look of your mother, he said. About the jaw. Can she ride?

She can ride, the man said.

Can you ride, girl?

Yes sir.

Sir, the old man said. He made a sound that might once have been a laugh. They've learned her manners out there. That's more than I ever done for you.

He shut his eyes. He did not speak again that afternoon.

Dolly Pask gave them tea. She said the doctor had been at noon and had said it would be the night, or the next. She said the old man had not been to his bed in a week. He would not lie down. He said if he lay down he would not get up and he had a thing to do first. She did not know what thing.

She took the child home with her to the cottage across the yard to sleep. The child went without a word. At the door she looked back.

Is he going to die, she said.

Yes.

Like Mom.

Not like that. He's old. It's different.

How is it different?

He's ready, the man said. He did not know that it was true. He found out in the night.

* * *

He sat with his father.

He built up the range and pulled a chair to the other side of it. He took off his boots. The rain stopped about ten and the wind went down, and through the wall he could hear the tide come in over the flats. He had not heard it in twenty years. In the place where he had been living the nearest salt water was six hundred miles off and the only sound at night was the wind in the grass and sometimes coyotes. He had lain awake his first year there listening for the sea.

The old man slept and woke and slept. His breath caught and went on. The man watched the blanket rise and fall.

He thought about the last time he had sat in that kitchen. It was the fourteenth of November in the year 1974. He had a cardboard suitcase and a ticket. His father had been sitting where he sat now, with a face like a shut gate. He had not looked up from the fire.

I'm going, then, the boy had said.

Go.

I'll write.

Do as you like.

Dad. It's no good my stopping. She'll not see me. There's nothing here for me.

There's a hundred and forty acre and thirty score of sheep.

That's not what I mean.

I know what you mean, his father had said. You mean a Vane. Well, I had one. You've seen what come of it. You go on to Canada and find a girl that'll have you and forget you ever looked at that house. I wish to God I had.

The boy had stood there. He was twenty-three and he had lost the girl and he did not know why. He had found out only the week before, from the talk in the village, what his father and Mrs Vane had been to each other. He had learned it standing in the public bar with a glass in his hand. He had said nothing to anyone. He had come home and looked at his father across the table and his father had looked back and neither of them had spoken of it.

You might have told me, he said. He had not meant to say it. All that summer. You knew where I was going nights. You might have said.

What was I to say?

That you was doing the same.

His father had turned his head at that.

It wasn't the same, he said. Don't you ever say that. You was a boy after a girl. I waited ten year for that woman. I'd the lamp lit for her. She was a hundred and fifty yard from that door. He stopped. His jaw moved. Get out, Tom. Go and catch your boat.

So he went. He walked up onto the wall with his suitcase. At the top he had turned and looked across at the house on the island, at one window. Then he walked the four miles to the bus.

He had written at Christmas for twenty years. He had sent a photograph of the wedding and one of the child. He had never had a line back. Dolly Pask wrote, twice a year, in pencil. *Your father keeps well. He has the mare still. He don't say much.*

The clock on the kitchen wall said three.

Tom, the old man said.

* * *

His eyes were open. They were clear. He had hold of the arm of the chair.

I'm here.

I know you're here. I'm not daft. Give me your hand.

The man got up and went to him. He knelt on the bricks. He put his hand on the blanket and the old man's fingers came down over his wrist and closed.

There was no strength in the rest of him. A child could have lifted him. But the man could not have broken that grip without breaking the bone.

I've a thing to tell you, his father said. I've held on for it. I'd have told that woman from the cottage if you hadn't come, but she cooks for them, and it's not for them to hear.

Tell it.

You'll let me say it through. I've not the wind to say it twice.

I'll let you.

The old man shut his eyes. When he spoke again his voice was low and even, with the wet sound under it. He might have been telling the points of a horse.

It was the night they put the clocks back. You'll remember. You was here. You was sat in this kitchen with your good boots on, waiting, same as me.

I remember.

She'd said one o'clock. She'd said she'd tell him to his face at half past twelve and leave at one, and I wasn't to come to the house nor yet to meet her. She said, I'll walk off that island on my own two feet, Amos, and you'll stand on your wall and watch me come. She was a proud woman. I liked that in her. I'd liked it for ten year.

He breathed. The man waited.

I went out at half past twelve. I'd the big lantern. I'd the bay mare saddled, this one's dam, in case she was tired. I stood on the top of the ramp. It was a clear night with a bit of moon and the tide was right out. I could see the house. And at one o'clock, to the minute by the church, I see a light come out of the garden door.

It was her. I knew the way it moved. She always walked quick, like she was late for something. It come down across the grass and through the orchard and out onto the Wade. And it come on.

I never took my eyes off it. I thought, that's her. That's Daisy. She's done it. In a quarter of an hour she'll be stood here, and I'll never have to watch her go back across that road again.

The old man's fingers tightened.

She got past the Rill. She got past the Perch. I could see her shape. I could near enough see the colour of her coat. I put my hand up to shout to her.

And there come another light.

It come out of the house like something let off a chain. It was running. It come down onto the Wade after her, and it was going up and down, up and down, and I knew what that was. There's only ever been one on the Ness that runs like that. He'd broke his knee at football when he was a boy and it never set right.

Edmund Vane, the man said.

Young Edmund. He'd a skinful. I could hear him before I could see him. He was bawling her name. Not her name. He was shouting Ma. A man of thirty-two.

He caught her. A hundred and fifty yard off from me. I could have thrown a stone. And they stood.

* * *

The range ticked. A coal fell.

I started down the ramp, the old man said. I'd took three steps. And I stopped.

Why?

She'd told me. You stand and watch me come. I thought, if I go out there, I'm the tenant, and he's the squire's son, and drunk, and there'll be blows. And she'll not thank me for it. She'd deal with him. She'd dealt with him all his life. I thought, she'll send the boy home with a flea in his ear and come on.

So I stood. I held the lantern up over my head, so she'd see where I was.

I stood there an hour.

I could hear them. I couldn't hear words. The wind was off the land. I could hear him, loud, and then her, low, and then him again. It went on and on. Once I see his light go down, like he'd sat on the ground. Then it come up.

And the tide turned. You know how you feel it. I felt it in my feet. I looked down the creek and it was running in.

I shouted then. I shouted, Daisy. I shouted, the water. I shouted till I'd no voice. I don't know if she heard. I'd say she did. I see her light move. It come toward me. It come ten yard. Twenty.

Then it stopped. And it turned round.

The old man opened his eyes. He was not looking at his son. He was looking at the window, where the lamp stood on the sill.

It went back. Toward the house. Away from me. The other one was ahead of it, going the same way, all over the road. I watched her light go back along the Wade as far as the Rill. And there it went out.

The water come over the road about ten minutes after. I stood on the ramp till it was at my knees. I'd have gone in. I've thought since that I should have. But I'd no boat and I can't swim, and the mare wouldn't face it.

They found her on the mud at nine.

The man knelt on the bricks. His wrist had gone numb in the grip. He did not try to move it.

I've lain awake on that for twenty year, his father said. Every night. I've lain in that room up there and gone over it. Why'd she turn?

She'd got by him. She was coming to me. She'd twenty yard on him and he was too drunk to run. She'd only to keep on. I'd have had her up on the bay and off that ramp before the water was over her shoes.

And she turned back.

So I've asked myself, was she turned? Did he get hold of her? Did that drunken young devil lay hands on his mother and drag her back toward that house, to stop her, and the tide caught the pair of them, and he got out and she never? I've thought that. God forgive me, Tom, I've hoped it. I've prayed it was that.

Because the other is this. That she stood out there an hour with her son crying at her. And she looked at my light on the one hand and that house on the other. And at the last, with the water coming, she thought better of it. She chose them. She'd picked up her feet to come to me and she put them down again the other way.

His voice had gone to almost nothing.

I never knew which. That's all. I never knew if she was coming or going when it took her. I've farmed this ground twenty year since and paid my rent to that family, and looked at that house every morning. I've never once been able to ask.

You could have asked him.

A Garrow, ask a Vane? Go up to that door with my cap in my hand and say, Mr Edmund, sir, did you kill your mother or did she change her mind? He'd have had me off the farm by the quarter day. And I'd not leave it. Not while she was in that churchyard. I'd my reasons to stop.

He turned his head on the pillow. He looked at his son. It was the first time he had looked straight at him since the hat.

You'll ask him.

Dad.

You've nothing to lose by it. You've a place out there. You've no rent to pay. He's nothing to you. You'll go over to that house when I'm in the ground, and you'll stand in front of Edmund Vane, and you'll say, which was it. And you'll make him tell you.

How do I make him?

That's your affair. You've been twenty year among cattlemen. I'd think you'd have learned something. The old man's mouth moved. There's my gun in the corner. He always minded a gun. He was gun-shy as a boy; I've seen him flinch at a rook-scarer.

And when he's told me?

Then you'll know. One of us will. He shut his eyes. That's all I've stopped for. I'd like one Garrow to know if she was coming.

* * *

He did not speak again that had sense in it. Toward five he said a name, twice. It was not the man's name or his mother's. It was Daisy.

He went about six. It was getting grey in the window. The man was still on his knees. He felt the grip on his wrist go, a finger at a time, like a knot working loose. He stayed where he was a while after.

Then he got up. His legs had set. He went to the window and turned down the lamp on the sill. It had burned there all night. He supposed it had burned there every night for twenty years, though the old man had never said so, and Dolly had never written it.

He looked out. The tide was in. It lay from the wall to the island, flat and grey, with the first light on it. The house stood on the other side with its chimneys.

He stood and looked at it.

He had a thing now that he had not had the day before. He had carried one question out of that country in 1974, and it was why a girl had stood behind a curtain. He had thought he knew the answer. He had thought it was his father. He had gone to the other side of the world to get away from it.

Now he had another, and it was not his own. It had been put on him. He could feel it on his wrist where the fingers had been.

He was not a man who had ever looked for trouble. He had worked for wages on other men's ranges. He had stood a good deal from foremen. He had seen men in that country settle things with their hands and once with a rifle, across a fence line, over water, and he had thought them fools.

But he looked at the house and he thought about a lantern held up for an hour. He thought about a man of thirty-two bawling for his mother on a road with the tide making. He thought about twenty years of rent.

Somebody came into the kitchen behind him. It was the child. She was in her night things, with a coat over, and her feet bare. She stood and looked at the chair.

He's dead, she said.

Yes.

She came and stood by the man at the window. She did not cry. She had done her crying two years back and she was careful with it.

Is that the house where the lady drowned, she said.

Who told you that?

Mrs Pask. I asked her. She said a lady went out on that road and the sea got her. She said it was a long time ago and I wasn't to go on it by myself.

That's right. You're not to.

Did you know her? The lady?

To look at.

Did Grandpa?

The man put his hand on the child's head. Her hair was thick and black and it had not been brushed.

Yes, he said. He knew her.

* * *

They buried him on the Thursday.

It was a clear day with a cold wind. There were forty people in the church. They were farm people and village people, in their dark clothes, and they looked at the man sideways when he came in. He had no suit. He wore what he had come in, and he had the hat in his hand. The child walked beside him in a blue coat that Dolly Pask had found.

He carried the coffin at the head end. It weighed nothing. The other three were men he had been at school with. One of them said, at the lych gate, low, You're back, then, Tom. He said, For this. The other said, You'll have heard about the farm. He said he had heard nothing.

He found out what the man meant when he got home.

They put the old man down on the north side, under the wall. The vicar read the words. He was a soft pink deaf old man and he read them well. The man stood with his hat against his chest. He was looking at the next grave but two.

It was a plain stone, grey, with moss in the letters. *Marguerite Vane. 1920 – 1974.* There was nothing else on it. Somebody had put flowers there, not lately. They had gone brown in the jar.

His father had bought the plot he lay in the year after. Dolly had told him so. He had gone to the vicar and paid for it in notes. He had wanted to be near.

When it was done the people went away down the path. A few shook his hand. The child had gone ahead with Dolly. He stayed.

He stood at the foot of the two graves. The churchyard wall was low there, and beyond it the ground fell to the marsh. He could see across the flats. The tide was out and the Wade lay bare and brown. He could see the island.

He looked at the house. He stood with his hat on now, since the wind was cold, and his hands in the pockets of his coat. He looked for a long time. He was looking at one window on the upper floor, on the west side. It had a curtain. He knew that it was foolish. She was four hundred miles off. Dolly had said so.

There was somebody on the sea wall of the island.

He saw it after a while. It was a figure, small with the distance, standing on the bank at the place where the Wade came ashore. It was a man. He was big. He stood with his feet apart and one hand up to his face, and something winked in the hand. He had a glass.

The man in the churchyard did not move. He stood by his father's grave and let himself be looked at.
