It came thin across the gravel. It was a fiddle tune, slow, and sweet as treacle, off a gramophone. He knew the kind. They had played such at the harvest suppers when he was small, for the old people.

It was a waltz.

He stood with his dead man's blood on his hands, as he thought it, and listened to the Vanes dance.

He has said that it was the strangest quarter hour of his life. He was more afraid in it than he had been in the Rill. In the water he had only been going to drown. Here he had done murder, in the open, with noise. And the house had looked out, and seen, and gone back to its party.

He thought, they know. That was the old man in the door. He saw his son fall. And he turned and went in and called for a tune.

He thought of twenty years of rent, paid to those people, in notes, with a cap in the hand. He had thought them hard. He had not thought them that.

He did not understand then about the house. He was never in it. He did not know that it kept its own hour and its own rules. He knows now that there were eleven people in that hall and that only two of them had been looking out of the door. One was a nurse who thought she had seen a ghost, and the other was an old man who thought he had been paid a debt. He has been told so since, by one who has read what they wrote.

It makes no odds. He stood in the yard, and nobody came. A man who is ready to be taken and is not finds that he has nowhere to put himself.

He looked up, once more, at the tower.

She was there. The wooden woman. She had her arm lifted. The moon was on her painted face. She was looking down the length of the yard, over his head, through the open door, at the hall where they were dancing.

He thought that she had seen it all. He thought, she's the only one that has.

He closed the gun. It was empty. He put it under his arm and walked out of the yard, along under the wall of the house, on the grass, to the glasshouse. The mare lifted her head. He sat down on the upturned pot. He laid the gun across his knees and took the two spent cases out of his pocket, and stood them on the bricks by the lantern, side by side, where he could look at them.

He looked at his watch. It was twenty-five past two.

She had said two by her father's clocks. That was three by his. He had thirty-five minutes to think how he would tell her that he had shot her brother.

## 7. Riding Out

She came at half past two by his watch. He heard her on the brick path. She was early.

He did not get up. He sat on the pot with the gun across his knees and the two cases at his feet. She stood in the door. She was still in the grey gown. Her face was wet, and it was shining, the way a face does that has been crying for a good reason.

He saw her look at the cases.

You've been in the house, he said. You've said your piece?

I've been in the house.

That's good. I want you to have done it. He looked down at the gun. There's a thing I've to tell you. You'd best hear it before you come any nearer.

She asked if he had found him. He said that he had. She asked if he had been told what his father wanted to know. He said no.

He began to tell her. He got as far as the tower. *He was up—*

She would not have it. She came across the floor and knelt in the leaves and put her hand over his mouth.

He will not say much of that. He says that she asked him not to tell her, not then, not in that house. She said she would hear it on the other side of the water, in daylight. She said that if she knew it she would not be able to get up on the horse, and she had waited twenty years to cross that road.

He told her it was a thing they would come for him about. She said, then they will come to Saltcote, and I shall be there.

He has turned that over since, more than any other part. She did not know what he had done. She would not let him say. But she knew that it was bad. She had seen the cases, and his face. And she said that she would come.

He did not think that he had a right to it. He took it. A man who has just gone through what he had will take a thing he has no right to.

She asked was there anything to be done. Anyone to be fetched.

He thought of the sluice, and the water going out.

No, he said. There's nothing there to do anything for.

She shut her eyes. He saw her make up her mind not to know. It was a hard thing to watch. He has thought since that it was the bravest thing he ever saw anyone do, and that it was also wrong.

She told him then what the old man had said. She had danced with her father, in the hall, and he had given her the hour of the tide. *A horse at twenty to three, by the house. Three feet in the Rill, and a set to the north.*

That was twenty to four. It was the hour he had reckoned himself, by the feel of the water, standing at the orchard gate. The old man had never left his house. He was eighty-one and they said his mind was gone. He had got it to the minute.

How'd he know there was a horse, the man said.

She did not know. She said that her father had taken her for her mother. He had thought he was sending her to Amos Garrow. *He said, I don't ask you to stay.*

The man put the gun down on the bricks and pushed it away with his boot.

He had come over that night with his father's gun, to settle for his father. He had settled nothing. He had shot a man who might have told him. And across the yard, in a hall full of candles, the old man he had never spoken to had stood up and given him his daughter and the time of the tide.

He did not know then about the land. That came after.

* * *

She went to the house for a coat. He saddled the mare.

He was a long time about it. His hands would not work. He dropped the cinch twice. The mare stood and let him. She had eaten some of the dead vine leaves and seemed none the worse.

He left the gun where it lay. He could not bring himself to touch it.

He thought about what he would do. He would get the woman across. That first. He would put her in his father's chair by the range. Then, when it was light, he would walk up to the village and knock at the constable's door. He would say, I'm Tom Garrow of Saltcote. I shot Mr Edmund Vane off his stable tower at two this morning with a twelve-bore. You'll find him on the saltings north of the Ness, or down the river.

He would ask to see the child first. He thought they would let him.

He did not think beyond that. He had seen the inside of a gaol once, in Fort Macleod, fetching out a hand who had been drinking. He thought of the smell.

He heard her feet on the path again. She was running.

She came in at the door. She had on an old tweed coat, a woman's, too wide in the shoulder, and a pair of gumboots. The grey silk showed between. She had something shut in her left hand. She stopped in front of him. She was out of breath, and she was laughing, and the tears were running into her mouth.

I've seen Edmund, she said.

He stood with his hand on the bridle. He did not take her meaning.

He's in the kitchen. He's eaten half a goose. He's a lump on his head the size of an egg, and a few of your pellets in his neck. He says to tell you that you're a rotten shot.

He heard the words. He could not make them into anything.

He's on his feet, he said.

He's on his feet and making jokes.

I saw him go off the back of that tower. I saw him fall. With his arms out. Into the fleet.

I don't know what you saw. I know what I've just spoken to. You didn't kill anyone. Do you hear me? You didn't.

He felt behind him for the stone trough. He sat down on the edge of it. His legs had gone.

He will not say what that was like. He says that there is no way to say it. He had been a dead man for an hour and a half. He had stood in a yard and waited for them to come. He had planned what he would say to the constable. And she had walked in out of the dark in her mother's coat and told him it was not so.

He put his face in his hands. She held his head against her.

Later he asked himself what he had seen. He has asked it ever since. He had looked up that tower and seen a white face with a wound on it. He had seen a black coat with its arm coming down. He had fired at the coat, and the coat had gone over into the fleet and out through the sluice. He had stood on the bank and watched a white cuff go under the arch.

And Edmund Vane was in his kitchen with a goose bone.

He learned on the Sunday what it was. They dug it out of the outfall and carried it up to the house on a hurdle. It was a thing of oak, two hundred years old. It struck the quarters. The young people had put a dinner jacket on it for the party.

He had shot the Jack. He had come through seven feet of sea with his father's gun, and stood in a yard, and with both barrels at thirty yards he had killed a clock.

He laughed when he was told. He laughed until the woman came in from the dairy to see what ailed him. And then he stopped. He had remembered the second barrel. It had gone left and high. He had been told about the pellets in the neck.

* * *

She had asked her brother for him. In the scullery, with a candle. She told him so in the glasshouse while he sat on the trough.

She had said to Vane what she saw, twenty years ago, from behind the vine. Two lights on the Wade. One man walking up the lawn at dawn. She had said, you went after her. You kept her there.

And he had said yes.

That was the answer. The man had come for it, and it had been got for him by a woman in a passage, in three minutes, without a gun.

*I kept her standing on that road an hour and a quarter with the tide making.* She gave him the words. Vane had said them straight out. He had not laughed.

Then she never turned of herself, the man said.

He said there was more. He wanted to tell me. I wouldn't hear it. She shut her eyes. I was too angry. He said, another day.

The man thought about that. He thought about his father, in the chair, with the wet sound in his chest. *I'd like one Garrow to know if she was coming.*

She had been coming. Vane had said it. He had kept her on the road. So she had been dragged, as near as made no matter; she had been held there by a drunk son till the water was round them. She had not stood and looked at Amos Garrow's lamp and chosen the house.

It was what the old man had prayed for. God forgive me, he had said, I've hoped it.

But there was more. Vane had said so. *It's worse than what you think. And it's better.* And the woman opened her left hand. There was a ring in it, plain gold, worn thin. Her mother had taken it off on the Wade that night and given it to her son. *Give that to your father.*

The man looked at it on her palm.

That's a queer thing for a woman to do, he said. That's about to leave a man. To send him back her ring by her son.

Yes.

That's not a woman being dragged.

No.

He did not know what it meant. He turned it over the whole of that winter. A woman who is being hauled back toward a house by force does not stop to take off her wedding ring and send a message. That is a thing done by somebody with her mind made up, and a little time.

So there was more. And he would go for it. He said so to the woman. He would go across by the road on the Sunday or the Monday, in daylight, with his hat in his hand, and ask Edmund Vane civil for the rest. He had done enough on his father's account with a gun.

He did not go. On the Monday they found Vane on the Ray Sand.

He never asked. He had one answer, got by someone else, and it was half. He has had to make do with it. He would say to the one who listened, when he came to this place: That's all I ever had. I had, he kept her. And a ring.

He would look at the range for a while.

I'd have liked the rest, he would say. For Dad.

* * *

She told him about the ground as he was strapping the gun under the saddle flap. He had picked it up after all. He would not leave it in the old man's glasshouse.

Papa's given you the farm, she said.

He did not understand her.

Saltcote. Freehold. He dictated it to Fenn in the hall, in the Hour. *To Amos Garrow or his heirs.* Edmund told me. There'll be no caravans.

He stood with the buckle in his fingers.

He had the lawyer's paper inside his shirt. It had gone through the Rill with him. *Vacant possession. The twenty-fifth day of March.* He had read it standing, in a kitchen, with the child watching. He had thought about three hundred ewes going up a ramp.

A hundred and eighty years they had paid rent for that ground. They had gone up a stair twice a year with their hats off. And the old man had given it away in a night, to a dead tenant, between a speech and a dance. He did not know that the tenant's son was eighty yards off in his stable yard with a loaded gun.

The man does not know why he did it. He has heard what was said in that hall. *There is something I owe across the water. I can't pay it to the man. I'll pay it to his name.* He thinks that the old man knew more than they gave him credit for. He thinks he had known for twenty years where his wife was walking to, and had never said. And on the last night that he kept, he paid.

The paper came in April. It was from the same firm, on the same blue sheet, signed by the same hand. It conveyed the freehold of the house, buildings and land known as Saltcote Farm to Thomas Garrow, son and heir of Amos Garrow deceased, in consideration of one peppercorn. The lawyer had written a line at the foot, in ink. *I am glad to have lived to draw this.*

The man put it in the biscuit tin, on top of the rent books.

He has a way of telling that. The one who set this down has heard it many times, and has argued with him.

He says: He took his father's ground back that night with a gun.

He says it flat. It is how he ends that piece of the story. He will say, I rode over there with Dad's twelve-bore under the saddle, and I rode home with the farm.

He has been told it was not the gun. It was an old man with a pen. The gun did nothing but spoil a carving and put eleven pellets in a man's shoulder. He would have had the farm if he had stopped at home that night by the range.

He knows it. He will hear you out. Then he will say it again the same way.

I asked him once why. He was a long time answering.

Because I'd have took it, he said. That's what I can't get by. I never knew the old man had give it. I stood in that yard and I'd a loaded gun, and Vane up there laughing, saying I'd no land. If he'd come down them stairs, I don't know what I'd have done to get it. I think I'd have done anything. I found that out. He was looking at his hands. So I'll not say it was give me. It was give me, and I'd have took it, both. I went over to take it. That's what I carried over, and the farm's what I carried back. A man ought to say what he set out to do.

* * *

He does not tell the crossing at any length. He says that it was a still night by then, with a moon, and the ebb running. He put the woman up in the saddle and led the mare in at twenty to four.

He swam the Rill at her head. There was three and a half feet on it and a set to the north that carried them down past the Perch. He had hold of the cheek strap. The mare went through it like a ship. She came up on the bank thirty yards down, where she had landed the first time, and stood, and he got up out of the water on his hands and knees.

That was the last time he asked it of her. She lived six years more and never went into salt water again above the fetlock.

He will tell one thing about it.

When they were over the deep, and he was up behind the woman with his arms round her, she turned in the saddle and looked back. She said that her brother had come down to the gate with a candle to see them off. She lifted her arm and waved.

The man looked.

There was the porch lamp. And there was another light, at the orchard gate, where the Wade came ashore. It was small and white. It was very low down.

He has said that he did not like it. He did not know why. A candle is yellow, and a man holds it at his chest. This was thin and pale, like a glow-worm, and it was not three feet off the ground. And it moved. It came down to the water, and it seemed to him that it came on, out along the road.

That's low down for a man, he said.

She said that Edmund was carrying it in a saucer.

It looks to be coming this way.

She said he would not. Not on foot. He knew the tide better than anyone.

That was so. There were three feet in the Rill. Nobody who knew that water would walk into it. The man told himself that it was the moon on a wet stone, or a lamp set down on the gatepost.

A cloud came over. When it had gone by he looked again and could not find it.

He turned the mare's head to the shore. He had a woman in front of him who had not slept, and was wet to the waist, and shaking. He had a horse of twenty who had swum the Rill twice. He had a lamp in a kitchen window to steer by.

He did not look back again. He rode up out of the sea at Saltcote at five minutes past four by his watch, on the Sunday morning, with Imogen Vane before him on the saddle.

That is where he stops.

* * *

He will go on, if he is asked. He does not count it as part of the telling.

He carried her in and set her in the chair. He saw to the mare. He rubbed her down for an hour, and gave her a warm mash, and stood with her until she had stopped shivering.

At seven he went across the yard to the cottage for the child.

The old sister opened to him. She looked ill. She had her hand at her throat. She said, Tom, I've a thing I ought to tell you, and then Dolly Pask came round the end of the cottage at a run, with her skirt hitched. She had left her van up on the wall with the door hanging open. She had come off the island as soon as the road was dry. She was grey in the face and there were cobwebs in her hair.

She stopped. She looked at the old woman, and at him.

Is she here, she said.

Is who here?

The child.

She's abed. Vi's just this minute telling me.

Dolly Pask shut her eyes. She stood with her hand on the wall. Then she pushed past him, and past her sister, and went up the stairs. He heard her boots overhead, and a door.

She came down slowly. She sat on the bottom stair.

She's asleep, she said. She's in her bed, asleep. Her voice was not steady. You'd best take her home, Tom. She'll have had a bad night. There was a wind.

He went up. It was a slip of a room under the thatch, with one window. The child lay on her side with her knees drawn up and the blanket over her head. He turned it back.

She was sound asleep. Her face was white. Her hair was soaking.

He thought that she had sweated. She did, sometimes, since her mother. She would wake in the night crying and wet through.

He lifted her. She did not stir. She was in her vest and drawers. Her clothes were not on the chair. He saw her shoes by the bed. They were the canvas ones with stars on the soles that he had bought her in Lethbridge. They were dark with wet, and there was weed in the laces.

He thought, the dew. She has been out in the yard at first light looking for me.

He did not think more than that. He has said so, when he was asked. He had not slept. He had been in the sea twice. He had killed a man and been told that he had not. He had a woman in his kitchen that he had waited twenty years for. He looked at a pair of wet shoes on a cottage floor and he thought, I must tell her not to go out without her coat.

There was something pushed in under the bed. It was a bundle, black, rolled tight. He saw the edge of it. He took it for one of old Vi's shawls.

He carried the child down, and across the yard, and into the house. She woke as he came through the door. She looked up at him, and then round the kitchen. She saw the woman in the chair by the range, in his shirt, with her hair down.

She looked for a long time.

You're the lady, she said.

Which lady, the woman said.

From the house. You were on the road, Friday. You touched the box.

Yes.

Did you come on Mab?

Yes.

In the dark?

Yes.

I'd be scared.

I was, the woman said.

The child considered it. She had her head on one side. Then she put her face against the man's neck. He felt her go heavy. She said one thing more before she slept. She said it into his collar, so low that he hardly had it.

Is the man all right?

What man?

She did not answer. She was gone.

He thought she had been dreaming. He put her in his own bed and she slept till four in the afternoon.

* * *

They found Vane on the Monday. A policeman came to the farm on the Tuesday. He was a young man, an inspector, and civil.

He asked if the man had a shotgun. The man said every farm on that shore had one. He asked to see it. He looked through the barrels. He said that the deceased had some pellets in him, number five, fired from below.

The man said nothing.

The inspector asked where he had been on the Saturday night.

He would have told. He had it ready. He was not a man who lied, and he had made up his mind in the glasshouse to walk to the constable's door. He had only been stopped by being told there was nothing to confess.

There was something now. Edmund Vane was dead. He had been drowned. But he had gone into the sea with shot in his neck and shoulder, and the man knew whose.

He opened his mouth.

He was here, the woman said.

She was standing at the range with her back to it. She had on a skirt of Dolly Pask's and the iron ring that she had sent to Scotland for.

He was not on the Ness that night, Inspector, until twenty to four in the morning. I can tell you so, because I was standing at the orchard gate, and I watched him come out of the sea on that mare to fetch me. He never got down from the saddle. He turned her round and brought me straight back. I'm Imogen Vane. We are going to be married.

The inspector looked from one to the other. He wrote it down.

It was the only lie the man ever heard her tell. She told it without a tremor, looking the law in the eye, and she never spoke of it afterwards. Nor did he.

He let her. That is the part he does not forgive himself. He stood in his father's kitchen with his mouth open, and let a woman lie for him. He let it go. He had the child. He told himself that.

There was an inquest. He sat through it beside her with his hat on his knee. A doctor read out how Vane had died. He said drowning. He said a blow to the head, hours before. He said a second blow. He said chloral. And he said eleven pellets of number five shot in the left shoulder, the neck and the ear, from a distance, from below.

The coroner said that he hoped somebody's conscience would one day supply what the evidence did not. He looked along the benches.

The man looked at his hat.

He has done the sum since. He does it most nights. Vane was hit on the head by somebody; he does not know who. He was doped; he does not know why. Then he climbed a tower, hurt, and stood in a lamp, and the man put a charge of duck shot into the side of his neck from thirty yards. An hour and a half later he was sitting in a kitchen making jokes. Two hours after that he was in the sea.

A man bleeds from the neck. He may not feel it. He may sit and eat and say that it is nothing, and all the while it is running down inside his shirt. Then he stands up, and walks down to the water to see his sister off, and he is light in the head. He goes dizzy. It takes him at the edge of the tide.

The man saw a light at the orchard gate. It was low down, for a man.

He has thought, he was on his knees.

That is what he believes. He does not tell it. It is not in the story; the story stops when the mare comes out of the sea. But he said it once to the one who set this down, a few weeks before the end, in a white room, with a tube in his arm. He said, I never killed him on the tower. I've known that near thirty year. But I put the shot in him that took him down to the water. He'd have been alive in the morning, but for me. He'd have told Imogen the rest. He'd have told me.

He said, I've had the farm. I've had her. I've had the girl. I got the whole of it, that night, everything a man could ask, and I got it with his blood on it.

He said, I never asked him the question.

He was told that it was not so. He was told there was another account.

He did not hear. They had given him something for the pain.

# PART SIX {.part}

::: {.parttitle}
A True Relation of the Experiment at Compline

*by Leopold Vane, F.B.H.I.*
:::

## Editor's Note {.note}

Leopold Vane dictated this to Hester Quaile on forty-one evenings between the first week of December 1994 and the end of February 1995. She took it down in longhand in six exercise books, of the same make as the three she later filled herself. He would not have a typewriter in the house; he said that it sounded like a clock with a broken tooth.

She has told me how it was done. He sat in the wing chair in the drawing room, or latterly lay in his bed, and spoke slowly, with his eyes shut, in complete sentences. He never went back to correct one. Where he broke off, she left a line. Where he said a thing twice, she wrote it twice. Where he asked her a question in the middle of a paragraph, such as whether his wife had come in, she put down the question and her answer in the margin, and those margins are a document in themselves. I have not printed them. They are hers.

He meant it as a scientific paper. He had read a great deal, as a young man, of the kind of book in which a gentleman of private means builds an apparatus in his own house and afterwards relates, soberly and in the first person, what came of it; and when he came to set down the most important thing that had happened to him, that was the form he had. He numbered his sections. He stated his method. He was careful, as you will see, to separate what he observed from what he inferred.

I ought to say something about his mind, and I shall say it once. He was eighty-one and he was ill. There were days on which he did not know the year. Miss Quaile's account, which you have read, shows what that was like from the outside. This is what it was like from within, and I would ask you to notice that from within it does not look like confusion. It looks like a man moving, without warning and against his will, between rooms that are all equally real to him. He had a word for it. He called it leakage.

He believed that he had built a machine that returned to him one hour. I have a professional interest in that claim, of a kind that I will explain in its place, and I have been through his reasoning with some care. I can find no error in his arithmetic. His premises are another matter. But I will say this for the old man: the hour that he was waiting for did come back, at the instant he had calculated, to every clock in England. It comes back every year. He was quite right that nearly everyone is asleep.

His times are the house's. He would have been insulted to be told that there were any others.

## I. Of Time, and of the Act

§ 1. I, Leopold Vane, of Compline House in the County of Essex, horologist, being in my eighty-second year, and of sound hands if not always of sound recollection, desire to set down a true relation of an experiment which I conducted in my own house on the night of the twenty-second of October last, and of its result.

I do so for three reasons. The first is that the result was positive. The second is that I am aware that it will not be believed, and I should wish there to be a record made by the experimenter himself, while the particulars are fresh, against the day when some better-furnished person may repeat it. The third reason I shall give at the end, if I have not by then forgotten it.

I am dictating this to Miss Quaile, who attended me on the night in question and was a witness to the greater part. I have asked her to write down what I say and nothing else. She is a truthful young woman. She does not believe that the experiment succeeded. I have told her that she is not required to believe it, only to spell it correctly.

§ 2. I should begin by stating what I am, since the reader is entitled to know what kind of instrument has made the observations.

I was born in this house in the year 1913. My father kept the clocks here, as his father had, and at the age of fifteen I was sent to Clerkenwell, and afterward to Le Locle in Switzerland, to learn the trade properly. I have worked at the bench for sixty-six years. I have restored, I suppose, some four hundred clocks and watches of the first rank, among them nine by Tompion and the Thorne Sidereal, of which I shall have more to say. I have made forty-three of my own, all copies, since I had never any gift for invention and knew it. I am a Fellow of the British Horological Institute and was for some years on its council, until I found that I could no longer follow the minutes.

I mention these things without vanity. I mention them in order that it may be understood that I am not a philosopher, nor a mathematician, nor any sort of visionary. I am a mechanic. I have spent my life persuading small pieces of brass to do the same thing at the same rate for as long as possible. If I now put forward a claim that sounds extravagant, I should like it to be remembered that it is put forward by a man whose whole training has been against extravagance, and who would not accept a quarter-second's error in a going train without knowing the cause.

§ 3. I must also state a defect.

My memory is no longer continuous. I have been told that this is a disease of the vessels of the brain, and I have no reason to doubt it. I do not experience it as a disease. I experience it as follows. I shall be in a room, engaged upon some ordinary matter, and without any interval I shall be in another room, or the same room in another year. I am not remembering that year. I am in it. The light is as it was. I can read the date on a newspaper. Persons who have been dead for a long time come in and speak to me about the business of that day, and I answer them, and find that I know what to say.

Then I am back. Miss Quaile will be looking at me. She tells me that I have been silent for a minute or two, or that I have called her by another name.

I call this leakage. I use the word in its workshop sense. In a clock, power is meant to pass from the spring through the train to the escapement, by one path, tooth by tooth. Where a pivot is worn, or a wheel is out of depth, some of the power escapes sideways and is lost. The clock goes on. But it no longer keeps its place in time. I am an old movement, and my pivots are worn. Something in me which ought to hold each hour in its proper order, one tooth after the next, has begun to let them slip past one another.

I state this for two reasons. It will explain certain gaps in my relation, which I shall mark honestly where they fall. And it has a bearing upon the experiment itself, as will appear. For it was in consequence of this infirmity that I first came to consider whether the order of the hours is so fixed a thing as I had been brought up to think.

§ 4. I now come to the question of what time is. I shall be brief, since I do not understand it, and nor does anyone.

A clockmaker has a view of the matter which differs from the common one. The common person supposes that there is a thing called the time, which flows of itself, evenly, like a river, and that a clock is a kind of window through which one looks at it. We in the trade know better. A clock does not show the time. A clock makes it. There is a spring, or a weight, which would run down all at once in a rush if it were let. There is an escapement, which stops it; and lets it go by one tooth; and stops it again. Tick. And tock. Each of those is a small quantity of power, released and arrested. The hands go round because they are pushed. What you read upon the dial is not a view of anything outside the case. It is a count of how many times the thing inside has been let go.

It follows that there is not one time. There are as many as there are escapements. I have a hundred and eleven in this house, and I can say upon my honour, having regulated every one, that no two have ever agreed for an entire day together. I have had them within a second. I have never had them the same.

Which, then, is right? The question was put to me by Mrs Edmund Vane on the afternoon before the experiment, in my hall. I am told that I answered, They are all right. I do not recollect it. But it was a good answer. They are each of them a faithful record of their own letting-go.

§ 5. There is, however, one clock that we did not make.

The earth turns. The sun comes to the meridian of a place, and that is noon at that place. It is the oldest escapement and the only one that no man can regulate. All our brass is an attempt to keep step with it. A good clock is one that says twelve when the sun stands due south over the roof under which that clock is going, and says it again after one turn of the earth, and so on.

That is the true time. I say so without apology. It is the time of the place. It differs from Greenwich to Bristol by ten minutes, and from my bench to the church at Thorney by about two seconds, and in the days before the railways every town in England kept its own and was right to. I do not say that it is convenient. I say that it is true, in the plain sense that it corresponds to something which is the case.

The sun, I should add for completeness, is not himself an even timekeeper. He runs fast in some months and slow in others, by reason of the shape of the earth's path and the tilt of her axis, so that the noon of the sundial and the noon of a well-regulated clock may differ by as much as sixteen minutes. That difference is called the equation of time. It is tabulated for every day of the year. The Thorne Sidereal shows it upon a subsidiary dial, by a kidney-shaped cam which the maker cut by hand, and which I spent the winter of 1957 learning to copy. I mention it here because I shall want it later. The reader should hold in his mind that a regulator and a sundial may stand side by side, and disagree by a quarter of an hour, and both be perfectly correct.

§ 6. I come to the Act.

In the year 1916, when I was three years old, Parliament passed a measure by which every clock in the kingdom was to be advanced one hour upon a certain night in spring, and put back one hour upon a certain night in autumn. It had been urged for some years by a Mr Willett, a builder, of Chislehurst, who was fond of riding before breakfast and was grieved to see the blinds drawn in the houses that he passed. He desired that his fellow countrymen should have more of the morning. As they would not rise earlier of their own will, he proposed that they should be deceived into it.

I wish to be fair to Mr Willett. He was, I believe, a kindly man, and he died before his scheme was adopted. But I ask the reader to consider what it is that he did.

He did not add one minute of light to the day. No Act can. The sun rose and set exactly as before. What was changed was only the number that men agreed to call it. From the last Sunday of March, forty million people look at the sun standing at eleven and say with one voice that it is noon. They know that it is not. There is not a clock in the country that agrees with the sky. And they have consented to this, year upon year, so readily that most of them have forgotten that it is being done.

I have been called obstinate upon this point. My wife called me so. I do not think it is obstinacy to decline to say a thing that one knows to be false, merely because one's neighbours have agreed to say it. But I did not always decline. I should set that down. For fifty-eight years I kept the Act in this house, as a good citizen. I changed the clocks, all of them, twice a year, with my own hand. My wife made a festival of the autumn change, of which I shall speak. I held my tongue and moved the hands.

§ 7. I ask the reader now to attend closely, since it is from this that the whole experiment proceeds.

When the clocks are advanced in spring, an hour is passed over. The hands go from one to two. The hour between is not lived. No one in England has an appointment in it, or is born in it, or dies. If you look in a parish register you will find no entry against it. It is left out.

When the clocks are put back in autumn, an hour is had twice. The hands go from one to two, and are returned to one, and go to two again. A child may be born at half past one and his twin brother forty minutes later at ten minutes past. It has happened. The registrars have a form for it.

Now I am a mechanic, and I was brought up to believe that nothing is had for nothing. If I take a tooth off a wheel, the train loses by exactly that tooth. If I let down a spring, the power that was in it has gone somewhere. I cannot make a movement that gives out more than was put in. Nobody can.

So I asked myself a question. It took me, I am ashamed to say, until I was sixty-one years of age and had a reason to ask it. *Where is the hour kept?*

It is taken in March. It is given back in October. For seven months it is not upon any dial. But it is given back; that is not in dispute; every clock in the kingdom receives it. A thing cannot be returned which has ceased to exist. It follows that between March and October the hour is somewhere. It is held over. It is, if I may use a term of the counting-house, on deposit.

I put this to my solicitor, Mr Fenn, some years ago. He said that it was a manner of speaking. He said that an hour was not a thing, and that one could not owe it or bank it; that it was only a convention about numbers.

I asked him whether he would say the same of a pound.

He did not reply. But I have thought since that it was a fair question. A pound is also a convention about numbers. One cannot hold it in the hand, nor say where it is when it is in a ledger. Nevertheless it may be lent, and owed, and held over, and paid back, and a man may be ruined for want of it. I do not see that an hour is less real than a pound. I have found it a good deal more so.

§ 8. I must now speak of a private matter. I do so with reluctance and only because the experiment cannot be understood without it.

My wife's name was Marguerite. I called her Margot. We were married in the spring of 1948, and I had the keeping of her for twenty-six years, and did not keep her well.

She was a person of great life. I am not. I have often thought that it was like housing a bird in a clock case. She was patient of it. She made the house laugh. She had a way of teasing me about my accuracy which I pretended to mind. I have learned since her death that she used to move the hands of the gallery clock forward a little every Sunday while I was at church, in order to watch me try to account for the gain. I spent eleven years upon that movement. I took it down four times. I am told that she would stand in the door of the Shop with her hand over her mouth.

I should give a great deal to be so deceived again.

It was she who made the Hour. I must explain that. On the night of the autumn change, when the hour came round the second time, she held that it was a gift, and that it was bad manners not to use a present. She said that the first time through was for the world and the second was ours. She gathered us in the hall, the children when they were old enough, and whoever was dining. She would have me open the front door upon the stroke, to let it in. And then she laid down a rule, which was that for that hour anyone might say to anyone else whatever was true, and it should not be held against them afterward. It was to be put back with the clocks.

I thought it a game. I thought that she did it for the children. I see now that she did it for me. She had married a man who could not be told things. She made one hour in the year when I might be, and stood in the middle of my hall and waited. I never once asked her anything in it. I danced with her. I was pleased with the precision of the arrangement.

§ 9. In the year 1974 the change fell upon the night of the twenty-sixth of October.

I shall set down what I did that day without excuse. It was a labour to alter the clocks; there were by then a hundred and four in the house. It had been my custom to do it at the Hour itself, with the family helping, each taking a room. That year I was tired. I had a movement on the bench which I wished to finish. I thought that I would get the business over. And so in the afternoon, between four and six, I went through the house by myself and put every clock back.

I told my wife. I recollect it. I went into her room, where she was dressing, and said that I had done the clocks already, to save a scramble. She looked at me in her glass. She said, 'Oh, Leo. You would.' I took it for one of her jokes.

So that from six o'clock that evening this house stood upon winter time, one hour behind the rest of England, which would not change until two in the morning.

At some time in the night my wife left the house and went out upon the Wade. I did not see her go. I had opened the door at the hour and had waited for her to come down the stairs, as she always did, and she did not come. I supposed that she was tired. I went to my bed.

They found her on the mud at nine in the morning.

The road had closed that night at a quarter past three, by the summer clocks that the tide tables are printed in. That is a quarter past two by the clocks of this house as I had set them. She was found a hundred yards from the refuge. She had been upon the road when the water came.

I worked it out. I am a mechanic; I work things out. She had looked at the regulator in the hall, which I had put back at four in the afternoon. It said two. She had thought, I have an hour and a quarter. She had no more than a quarter of an hour. She went out to cross a causeway of half a mile with what she took to be ample time, and the hour that she was relying upon was one that I had taken from her that afternoon with my own fingers, to save myself trouble.

I did not then ask why she was crossing. I did not ask for a long time. That is another defect and I shall come to it.

§ 10. I stopped the clock in her room. I did it with my hand, at twenty-five minutes to four in the morning of the twenty-eighth, when they had brought her home and I had seen her. I have not started it since.

And I made a resolution, which I have kept. I resolved that no clock in this house should ever again be altered for the Act. The house had been upon winter time when she died. It should stay there. In the spring, when the rest of England put its hands forward, Compline would not. In the autumn, when they came back, they would find us where they had left us.

I was told that it was madness. Edmund said so. The tradesmen could not understand our appointments. For seven months of each year my family have been obliged to add an hour in their heads to every dial under this roof, and guests give up their watches at the door. I am aware that it is a great inconvenience. I meant it to be.

For I had found that I could not bear to hear a clock in this house tell the false time. Every one of them, if it had been put forward in March, would have been saying, for seven months, the thing that killed her. I preferred that they should say what was true, and that I should be reminded each time I looked at one of what I had done. A hundred and eleven of them say it now. I have not been out of the sound of it for twenty years.

§ 11. It was some while before I perceived what followed from this.

The house had not taken the hour in the spring of 1975. It has not taken it in any spring since. It followed that the house was not owed it in the autumn. Each October, upon the night, the hour that had been held over since March was paid back to every clock in England; and it was not paid to Compline, since Compline had lent nothing.

I thought of that, at first, only as a just consequence. We had stood out of the transaction and had no claim upon it.

But I continued to keep the night. I did so for my wife's sake. Each year I opened the door at one o'clock by this house, which was two by the world; and stood there; and each year I had the same sensation. I do not ask the reader to give weight to a sensation. I record it. It was that something went past. One feels it upon a railway platform when an express goes through without stopping: the air moves, and there is a sound, and one's coat is pulled. I felt that at my own front door, twenty times, upon the stroke of one, with my family behind me in the hall. Something very large went by in the dark outside, going toward the rest of England, and did not stop for us.

It was in the fourteenth or fifteenth year that I understood what it was. It was the hour. It was being delivered.

And I thought: it passes my door. It comes as near as that. For the space of one stroke of the bell it is neither in March, where it was taken, nor in the houses where it is to be spent. It is in transit. And the world's clocks at that instant stand at two, and mine at one, and in the next instant they will stand together. There is a moment at which the difference between the false time and the true is exactly one hour, and is in the very act of being closed.

I am a maker of escapements. I know what it is to catch a thing in the instant of its letting-go. It is the whole of my art.

I began to ask whether a movement could be made which should take up that hour as it went by.

§ 12. I should say what I wanted it for. A man does not spend five years upon a piece of apparatus without an object.

I did not want an hour in general. I am eighty-one, and one hour more or less of the ordinary kind is of no consequence to me. I wanted that one. I wanted the hour between one and two upon the night of the twenty-sixth of October, 1974, as it stood upon the clocks of this house. It was the hour in which my wife went down the stairs in her stockings and looked at my regulator.

I wanted to be standing in the hall when she did. I had the words ready. I have had them ready for twenty years; I say them over at night. *Margot, the clock is wrong. I put it back before dinner. It is three, not two. You have a quarter of an hour. Do not go on foot.*

That is all. It is nineteen words. It would take me perhaps ten seconds to say them. I did not ask to have her back for good. I knew by then, though I did not allow myself to know it, that she had been going to another man, and I had no right to prevent her. I asked only to be let to tell her the time correctly. It was the one thing in the world that I was fitted to do for her, and on the night that it mattered I had done it wrong.

I state the object plainly so that the result may be judged against it. The experiment was designed to return to me one particular hour in order that I might give my wife the true state of the tide.

§ 13. I must here record a leakage, since it bears upon what follows, and since I have undertaken to mark them.

It occurred in September last. I was in the long gallery, at about four in the afternoon, regulating the clock beneath my wife's portrait. I had the hood off and my glass in my eye.

Without interval I was in the hall. It was night. The door stood open upon the gravel and the wind was coming in. All the candles were lit. I was wearing evening clothes, which I had not had on a moment before, and I was a much heavier man; I felt it in my shoulders. My son's wife was at the foot of the stairs in a yellow frock that I had forgotten. She was twenty-eight. My son was by the fire with a glass in his hand, flushed, and he was not looking at the stairs. He was looking toward the garden passage.

I knew the night at once. I looked at the regulator. It said five minutes past one.

I thought, I am here. It has happened of itself. I have been let back.

I went to the foot of the stairs. I looked up. I said, I believe aloud, 'Margot!' I had the nineteen words in my mouth.

She was not there. The stairs were empty. And I recollected, standing in that hall in 1974, what I had not known in 1974: that she had already gone. She had not come down to the hall that year at all. She had left by the garden door while I stood at the front with my hand on the bolt.

I had been returned to the night, and I had been put in the wrong room.

Then I was in the gallery, with the hood of the clock in my hand, and Miss Quaile—no. It was before she came. It was Mrs Pask, who had brought up my tea. She said that I had been standing so for some minutes and had shouted.

I set this down carefully because of what I concluded from it. I concluded two things. First, that the thing could be done; for I had been there, in the flesh, in the hour, and had felt the draught from the door. I do not accept that it was a dream. I know the difference. I have dreamed of my wife on most nights for twenty years, and in dreams I am never able to read a dial. I had read the regulator. It was five past one, and the seconds hand was moving.

And second, that it was of no use to be carried back by leakage. A leak has no direction. It had put me down in the hall at five past one, when I wanted to be at the garden door at one precisely. If the thing was to be done, it must be done by a proper train, with a known ratio, so that I should arrive where I meant and at the minute I meant, and in possession of my faculties.

I went down to the Shop that evening and began to draw.

It was on the same afternoon, or the next, that I opened the long cupboard to look for a pattern, and found that eleven of my copies were not in it.

## II. Of the Engine

§ 14. Before I describe the apparatus I must give some account of the instrument upon which it was founded, and of how I came by it. The reader who has no interest in clocks may pass over this section. I should be sorry if he did.

In the spring of 1951 I attended a sale at a farmhouse some miles out of Norwich. The owner had died, an old bachelor, and the contents were being cleared. I had gone for a lantern clock that proved to be a marriage. In the yard, among the outside lots, there was a tea chest of scrap brass, fire irons and a broken fender, which was to be sold by weight.

I turned it over, as one does. At the bottom, under the fender, there was a plate.

It was about eleven inches by nine, of thick brass, black with tarnish, and pierced with a great number of holes. I knew what it was before I had it out of the box. It was the back plate of a movement. And along its lower edge, engraved in a round hand under the dirt, I could make out letters. I wet my thumb and rubbed. *Isaac Thorne. Colchester. Fecit 1771.*

I ought to explain that name. Thorne was a clockmaker of Colchester of whom almost nothing is known. He left perhaps a dozen ordinary long-case clocks. But there is an entry in the minutes of the Board of Longitude for 1773, which I had read as a young man and never forgotten. It records that a Mr Thorne of that town had submitted for the Board's inspection a table regulator of his own design, showing at one view the mean time, the sidereal time, the equation, the age and place of the moon, and the state of the tide at a named bar upon the Essex coast; and that the Astronomer Royal had examined it for a month and found no error. The Board gave him twenty pounds for his trouble. The clock was never heard of again. It was supposed to have been broken up.

I bought the tea chest for eleven shillings. The auctioneer asked whether I wanted the fender.

There was more of it in the house. I found the dial in an attic, serving as the lid of a meal bin. I found the moon work, complete, in a drawer of nails. Over the next four years I traced the frame and two of the trains to a marine store in Great Yarmouth and a dentist's widow in Diss. About a third of it was gone for good. That third I made.

It took me nine years. I do not say that with complaint. They were the best of my working life. To restore a movement by a man of that quality is to keep his company. One learns his hand. Thorne cut his teeth a shade deeper than the fashion of his day, and left his pivots long. He was left-handed; one sees it in the turning. And he had a habit, where he was pleased with a piece of work, of scratching upon it, in some place where it would never be seen, a small device like a sprig of blackthorn. I found it upon the back of the moon disc and under the left foot of the dial. I found it nowhere else. I took it that those were the two parts that he was proudest of.

I finished it in the autumn of 1960. I set it going on the table in the library window on the evening of the twenty-first of September, at the equinox, when the equation is small. It has not stopped since. It has not, in thirty-four years, been out by one minute from the sun, nor by five from the tide upon Compline Bar, which is the bar that Thorne made it for. I had not known that when I bought the plate. I found the name engraved upon the tidal dial when I cleaned it. He had made it for this water.

My wife said that it was the only clock in the house that told you something you needed to know.

§ 15. I made a copy. I began it in 1962 and was eight years about it.

I did so for the reason that I have always made copies, which is that I do not understand a thing until I have made it. I wished to cut every wheel that Thorne had cut, in the order that he cut them, and to find out at each step why he had done it so. I wished also to have something upon which to teach.

For I had by then a pupil. My son Edmund came into the Shop when he was nine years old. He stood beside the bench for an hour without speaking and then asked whether he might hold the file. I have had some gifted apprentices sent to me in my time, from the trade schools. I never had one to compare with that boy. He had it in his fingers. He could feel a thousandth. At fourteen he cut a scape wheel that I could not have bettered.

I did not tell him so. I record that against myself. It was not the custom of the trade, as I learned it, to praise; one looked at a piece of work, and if it would do, one said that it would do. I thought that he understood. I see now that I never asked.

He cut the lunar train of the Copy. It is the most delicate part. He was sixteen when he began the original with me, and thirty-one when he finished the same train for the Copy, by himself, in eleven weeks, and brought it up to show his mother before he showed it to me. It is a better piece of work than Thorne's. I say so now. I did not say so then. I looked at it through my glass and said that it would serve.

I have had that sentence in my ears a good deal lately.

He never came into the Shop again after his mother's death. He did not say why. He put down his tools on the Monday of that week, in their rack, in order, and I do not believe that he has touched a file since. I supposed that it was grief. I let him alone. One does not ask.

The Copy is exact. I will stake my reputation upon it. There is no measurement that would distinguish it from the original. It differs in two respects only. I did not scratch Thorne's device upon it, since it was not his. And I cut the cock that carries the moon work somewhat too light, in the winter of 1964, and have always meant to do it again. It will not bear being laid upon its side.

§ 16. I return to September last, and the long cupboard.

I kept my copies there, in the Shop, upon shelves, each under a cloth, with a ledger. There were forty-three. I opened the cupboard to look for a pattern, as I have said. I lifted a cloth and there was nothing under it. I lifted the next.

I counted eleven empty places.

I am not, I think, a suspicious man. My first thought was that I had moved them myself and forgotten. I do forget. I spent a day searching the house. On the second day I was winding the month-going clock in the hall, which is by Tompion, and I looked at the dial, as I had looked at it every month for forty years.

It was mine.

I knew it as a man knows his own handwriting. The silvering was mine. The engraving of the chapter ring was a little more upright than Tompion's; I have never been able to get his slope. I opened the door and looked inside for the signature upon the back plate, and it was clean brass.

Somebody had taken my copy out of the cupboard and stood it in the case. And had taken Tompion's away.

I went round the house. I shall not describe that afternoon. I found ten more.

§ 17. I considered the matter as a mechanic considers a fault. One asks what must be true for it to have occurred.

It must be someone with the freedom of the house. It must be someone who knew that the copies existed, and where, and which answered to which; that is, someone who had read my ledger. And it must be someone with the skill to take a movement out of its case and put another in, and set it to time and in beat, so that I should wind it for a year and observe nothing. That last is not a small matter. I do not think that there are thirty men in England who could do it to my satisfaction.

I had trained one of them. He lived in my house.

I did not wish it to be Edmund. I say that as a fact about the investigator, which the reader should allow for. I turned over every other possibility. I thought of my daughter, who knows a copy from an original at sight and might have been shown the rest. I thought of my son's wife, who has not been happy, and of my grandson, who has good hands and no money. I am ashamed to say that I thought of the cook.

And I found that I could not go on with it. Each time I had the reasoning complete, it leaked away. I would wake in the morning knowing that there was something that I had resolved to do, and not what. I wrote it down, and lost the paper. I began to be afraid that the thief was relying upon exactly this, and need only be patient.

So upon a day when I was clear I wrote to Fenn. I told him to find me a man who could look at people. I told him that I might not remember having written, and that he was to act regardless.

I am informed that he did so, and that a person came. I have no recollection of him whatever. Miss Quaile says that he was a heavy man with a tired face who dined with us and was struck upon the head. It seems a hard return for his trouble.

§ 18. But I did one thing more, and that I do remember, since it was a matter of the hands.

The eleven had been taken from the less regarded cases. Whoever it was had begun with the small things and was working upward. It was plain to me where that must end. There is one clock in this house which is worth more than all the rest together. I had only to ask how long it would be before he came for the Thorne.

I resolved that when he did, he should not get it.

I went into the library on a night in the middle of September, when the house was asleep. I took the Thorne out of its glass. I carried it down to the Shop. It weighs thirty-one pounds and I was two hours upon the stairs. I took the Copy from its place in the long cupboard and carried that up, and stood it in the library window under the glass, and set it to time, and covered it with the baize as I do each night.

I was aware of what I was doing. I was laying a bait. And it was not only that I wished to save the original. I shall be honest. I had a second purpose, and it was not a kind one.

I wished to see whether he would know.

If it was Edmund, he had cut the lunar train of that Copy with his own hands. He had helped me to restore the original when he was a boy. There was no one alive but myself who was better placed to tell the one from the other. He had only to turn it over. He had only to look beneath the left foot of the dial for a sprig of thorn. If he looked, he would see that I had found him out, and would know that I had stood my own work in the place of honour and was waiting.

And if he did not look? If he carried off my Copy for Thorne's clock, in the dark, in a hurry, without once putting a glass to it?

Then I should know something else. I should know that the best hands I ever trained had forgotten what they were for.

I am not proud of that test. A father ought not to set such a thing for his son. But I had told him once that his work would serve. I think I wished to learn whether he had believed me.

§ 19. I now had the true Thorne in my Shop, and nowhere to keep it. It could not stand upon the bench; my son's wife comes down, and the girl who dusts.

I thought of the tower.

No one goes up the tower but I. It is a hard climb. There is in the clock chamber, in the corner, a tall cupboard of deal, built against the wall, where my grandfather kept his oil and his spare lines. It has a lock. I carried the Thorne across the yard that same night, wrapped in a blanket, and up the ladder. I do not know how. I rested upon every rung. I stood it upon the shelf and locked the door.

And there, standing in that chamber at four in the morning, with my heart going, I looked from the cupboard to the frame of the turret clock, a yard away, and I saw the engine entire.

I had been drawing it for a week and could not get the ratio. I saw it then as one sees the answer to a sum upon waking.

§ 20. I shall describe it in terms that a layman may follow. The trade will want more, and I have left the drawings in the top drawer of the bench.

The difficulty was this. I required a movement that should, at one instant, take account of two times together: the false time, which the world keeps, and the true, which this house keeps; and should at the moment of their coming together gather up the difference.

Now I had in that chamber, by the accident of that night, the two best timekeepers that I own. The one is the turret clock. It was made in 1790 by my great-great-grandfather and it has a pendulum of fourteen feet and a bob of two hundredweight. It is not fine. But it is the house's own; it has told Compline time for two hundred years, and all the others are set by it. It is the true time made in iron.

The other is the Thorne. And the Thorne, the reader will recollect, shows upon one of its dials the equation of time, which is to say the difference between two noons. It has within it a differential: a pair of wheels so mounted that the motion of a third is the difference of their motions. Thorne put it there to subtract the mean sun from the true. It is the most beautiful piece of gearing that I have ever handled. It is, in plain terms, a machine for reckoning how far two times disagree.

I had only to couple them.

I cut two rods of brass, a yard long and a quarter-inch in section. I bored the side of the cupboard. I carried the motion of the turret clock, from the arbor of its hour wheel, by the one rod, to the Thorne. I returned the motion of the Thorne's equation work, by the other, to a cage of four wheels of my own design which I clamped upon the frame. The cage is the heart of it. I shall call it the take-up. It runs free, doing nothing, so long as the two inputs keep their proper relation. But let the one fall back upon the other by a known quantity at a stroke, and the take-up is wound. It stores the difference. It is in effect a fusee. And what is wound into a fusee may be let out again.

I called it the Reconciler. The name was Miss Quaile's, though she does not recollect having given it. She said, upon the first night that I showed it to her, that it looked like a thing for making two people agree.

§ 21. I worked upon it through the last of September and the first three weeks of October. I worked at night, since by day I was watched. Miss Quaile came to me upon the first of the month. She found out within a week where I went, and thereafter she came with me and held the lamp.

I must record my debt to her. She told me plainly that she did not believe the thing could be done. She told me also, each time that I asked it, that my wife was dead. I had been told for twenty years that Margot had gone up to change. I cannot convey what a relief it was to have by me one person who would not manage me. I found that I could think. I had not been able to think for some years, among so much kindness.

She held the lamp for eleven nights while I cut the last pinion of the take-up, which has seven leaves and is three thirty-seconds of an inch across. I am eighty-one. I did not break one.

§ 22. There remained the setting.

A fusee lets out what it has taken up. But it lets it out along the line on which it was wound. It was not enough that I should be returned one hour; I have explained that. I wanted a particular one.

Here I shall be candid. I am upon ground where I can no longer show the working.

The Thorne carries a calendar. It knows the day of the year, since without it the equation cam would have no meaning. I had only to consider what the equation was upon the night of the twenty-sixth of October in the year 1974, and what the age of the moon, and the state of the tide upon the bar. Those three together are a kind of address. There is no other night in a century upon which the sun, the moon and the water stood in just that relation. I have the figures. I had them by heart before ever I thought of the engine.

Upon the afternoon of the twenty-second of October last I went up the tower at noon, when they supposed me at the bench. I disengaged the Thorne from its own going train. I turned the moon by hand to her age upon that night: she was eleven days old. I set the equation cam to sixteen minutes and three seconds, sun before clock. I set the tidal dial to low water at twenty-eight minutes past midnight.

I set her, in short, to the hour that I wanted. And I engaged the rods.

I looked at her for some time. She was telling a night twenty years gone, to the minute, and beside her through the wall the old turret clock was telling this one. Between them the take-up stood ready, slack, with its click resting upon the first tooth.

I thought: at one o'clock tonight the world falls back upon us. An hour is paid. It will go by my door, as it has gone by for twenty years. But this time there is something set to catch it. And when it is caught, it will be let out along the line that I have laid. I shall stand at my door, and it will be the same door, and the same hour. And she will be coming down the stairs.

I ask the reader to believe that I knew how this sounded. I was not at that moment leaking. I had my faculties. I said to myself, Leopold, you have spent sixty-six years refusing to believe anything that you could not measure, and you are now proposing to travel through time by means of two brass rods and a tide dial.

I answered myself as follows. I said: I have measured it. I have stood at my door upon twenty nights and felt it pass. I do not know what an hour is. Nor does the Astronomer Royal. But I know that it is given back, at a stated instant, to every clock that lent it; and I know that I have here the only house in England that stands outside the account, and the only instrument ever made that can reckon the difference between two times. If it cannot be done here, it cannot be done.

And I said one thing more. I said: if I am wrong, I shall have lost nothing but a night's sleep. And if I am right, I shall have given my wife the tide.

I locked the cupboard. I went down and let them dress me.

§ 23. I must note here a second leakage, which took place upon the ladder as I descended. I note it because of a thing that I learned in it.

I had my foot upon the fourth rung. Without interval I was standing in a yard, in sunlight, among a crowd of farmers, with a brass plate in my hand, wet where I had rubbed it with my thumb. I was thirty-eight. The auctioneer was saying that he was bid eleven shillings.

It was the Norwich sale. I had not thought of it for years. I looked down at the plate. I read the name again. And I turned it over, there in the sunshine, as I had turned it then, to look at the back.

I had forgotten what was on the back. It is covered now by the frame, and I have not had the movement down since 1960.

There is a line scratched there, very small, in Thorne's left-handed script. I read it in 1951 and thought it a workman's memorandum. It says: *Made for M. that she may know when to cross.*

I stood in the yard with the plate in my hand and the sun upon it. I understood it. I had not understood it at thirty-eight. He had made the clock for a woman. He had put the tide upon it for her sake, at that bar, so that someone whose name began with that letter should be able to look at a dial and know whether the road was open.

I do not know who she was. I do not know whether she crossed.

Then I was upon the ladder again, holding the rung, and Miss Quaile was calling from below to ask whether I was ill.

I said that I was perfectly well. I came down. I did not tell her what I had seen. But I record it here, since I think that it has a place in the evidence. That instrument was made by a man who wished to give a woman the hour of the tide. It lay in pieces for a hundred and eighty years. It was put together again, in this house, by another such man, who had failed to. And upon the night that I asked it to do the same thing over, I do not think that it was being asked to do anything outside its nature.

## III. Of the Dinner

§ 24. I shall now relate the events of the evening in their order. I have the first part of it clearly. I am less sure of some of the faces. I shall say where.

It was the twentieth keeping of the night since my wife's death. I had determined that it should be the last, whatever the result. If the experiment succeeded there would be no further need. If it failed I did not think that I should care to stand at that door again.

I was dressed at six. I went down upon Miss Quaile's arm. They were assembled in the hall, as they have been each year, with the fire lit and the candles, and the Font upon its table.

I should explain the Font. It is a pewter basin, of the time of Henry the Eighth, which came out of the ground when my grandfather drained the orchard; it is supposed that the monks used it. Since 1975 I have required every guest who enters this house upon the night to put his watch into it. I do not do this to be disagreeable. I do it because a watch that has been advanced under the Act is an instrument set wrong, and I will not have forty of them going about my hall contradicting the house. There is besides a practical reason, which bore upon the experiment. I did not know how the take-up would behave in the neighbourhood of a large number of escapements keeping the false hour. I wished them all in one place, and still.

I looked into the basin. There were nine or ten. I stirred them. I do not care for wrist watches as a class; the movements are stamped out by the thousand, and jewelled for show. But there was one among them which pleased me. It was a plain pin-pallet lever in a tin case, with a mouse painted upon the dial whose arms served for hands. It was the only article in that basin which made no pretence. I asked whose it was. A tall young man put up his hand, a grandson of my sister Dorothea, with her wrists. I saw at once that he had come to ask me for money and that he had broken something.

I shall say how I knew, since it has a bearing on my method throughout. I do not read faces. I have never been able to. My wife said that I should not notice if a person's nose fell off, provided that he continued to hold his fork correctly. But I have looked at hands for sixty-six years. A hand cannot dissemble; it has not the muscles for it. That young man was holding his right hand flat against his coat pocket, with the fingers a little spread. It is the posture of an apprentice who has snapped a pivot and put the pieces where he hopes the master will not look. I have seen it a hundred times at the bench.

I told him to ask me at one. I did not think that it could be anything of consequence. It jingled.

§ 25. I then made some remarks upon the Act, which I make every year, and which I shall not repeat, having given the substance above.

And I asked whether my wife had come down.

I must be exact about this, since I am told that it distresses people. I knew that she was dead. I had been told so by Miss Quaile at about a quarter past one that morning, as on most mornings, and I had retained it. When I asked whether Margot was down, I was not wandering. I was enquiring, as an experimenter, into the state of the apparatus.

For it had occurred to me, standing at the Font, that if the Reconciler was to return that hour at one o'clock, there might be some sign of it beforehand. A spring that is about to be let go will sometimes tremble. I thought that the house might already be leaning a little toward the other night. And I looked up the stairs, and for an instant I was quite sure that someone was dressing in the room at the end of the gallery, and would be late.

So I asked. It was my daughter who answered. She said, 'She'll be along, Papa.'

I looked at Imogen's hands as she said it. She had them clasped in front of her, the right over the left, very tight. It is how she stood as a child when she had said a thing that she wished were true.

§ 26. We went in to dinner at eight.

I have always had my wife's place laid. I know what is thought of it. I ask the reader to consider it as I do. A place at table is a kind of clock. It says that a person is expected. If I had left hers off, upon the first night after, I should have been saying that she was not; and I was not prepared to say so, and am not now. It is laid at my right hand. The girl serves it. I do not ask that anything be eaten.

I do not see her there. I should like that to be written down plainly. I am not so far gone. I have never, in twenty years, seen my wife at that table, nor heard her voice with my ears.

But I am a man who has lived all his life among clocks, and I will say what I do perceive. If you are sitting in a room, and there is a clock going in the next, with the door shut, you do not hear it. And yet you know that it is going. You would know at once if it stopped. There is a pressure of it, upon the mind, that is not sound. I perceive that the chair at my right hand is occupied in that sense. Something there is going.

And I know what she would say. That is not the same as hearing it. I lived with her for twenty-six years. When the girl with the cropped head announced that she did not eat anything with a face, I knew, as surely as I know the count of a train, that Margot was delighted, and had said, 'Leo, give the child what she wants; she has more sense than the rest of us.' So I said it for her.

I carved. I am told that I do it well. It is only a matter of seeing where the joints are.

§ 27. I must now record the observations that I made at table, since they were the last that I was able to make with a quiet mind.

I had in the house, by Fenn's arrangement, a person whose business it was to discover who had been taking the clocks. I had by that hour entirely forgotten his name and which of the guests he was. I knew only that he was there and that he was to tell me before one. I mention this because I see that it has been thought comic. It did not seem so to me. I have been made to depend, in the last years, upon arrangements that I have set up in my better hours and cannot afterward recall; it is like leaving a clock wound for another man to find.

But I did not rely upon him wholly. I looked for myself, in the only way I have.

I looked at their hands.

My son's wife was at the foot of the table. She has a wedding ring that has grown loose. She turned it, the whole of dinner, with her thumb, round and round. That is not guilt. That is a person winding something up. She was getting ready to do a thing.

My grandson sat with his hands under the table. When he brought them up to take his glass, they were white at the knuckles. He is a pianist, and keeps his hands like a surgeon's. He was frightened; but he kept looking toward his father, and I judged that it was for him.

My daughter held her fork and did not use it. Her eyes went more than once to the west window, where there is nothing to see after dark but the water. She was not thinking of clocks at all.

The young nurse had her hands in her lap. Her right kept going to the pocket of her dress and coming away. She had something there. I did not suppose it mine.

The solicitor had his fingers together.

There was a heavy man opposite my son, whom I did not know, who ate steadily. He had the hands of a policeman, thick, with the nails cut square. I see now that that will have been Fenn's person. At the time I took him for something to do with drains.

And there was Edmund.

He sat upon my right, the second place beyond his mother's. He was drinking. He has drunk for twenty years, and I have watched his hand grow less sure, each October, until I could hardly bear to see it lift a glass. A hand that could feel a thousandth of an inch.

It was steady.

I noted it particularly. He filled his glass four times while I watched, and raised it, and set it down, and there was no tremor in it whatever. I have seen that in a workman once or twice. It comes when a man has been dreading a thing for a long while and learns at last that it is to be that day. The dread goes out of the fingers. He had the hand of someone who has been waiting to be caught, and has just been told the hour.

I knew then. I did not need Fenn's man. I think that I had known since I lifted the cloth in the long cupboard.

§ 28. I rose for the toast before the sweet. We drink it each year. It was my wife's, and she meant it lightly. *To absent time.* She meant the hour that we should not have again until the spring. I have kept it, though for twenty years it has meant to me something that she did not intend.

I had prepared a few words upon the anniversary. When I stood, they had gone. I said so. I have found that it is best to say so at once; people are embarrassed if one hunts.

And then I did a thing that I had not planned.

I said that one of them had been robbing me.

I have considered since why I said it there, at my own table, before strangers. I had meant to wait. I had meant to hear from Fenn's man, and then, in the Hour, to take the person aside. I think that it was the hand. I looked down the table and saw my son's hand lying beside his glass, quite still, that had been the best I ever trained. I thought of it lifting my Tompion out of its case. And I found that I could not sit and eat a syllabub.

I told them what had been done, and with what. I told them that I knew my own work from another man's blindfold, and I pointed, without turning my head, to the two in that room which were mine. I heard somebody draw breath. I do not know who.

I told them that I did not know which of them it was. That was not true. It was the first deliberate untruth that I have told in this house since my wife died, and I told it at her table, with her at my elbow. I knew what she would say of it. She would say, 'Leo, that is the first sensible lie of your life.'

For I did not want to name him. I wanted him to come to me. I had set the Copy in the library as a test of his eye. I set this as a test of something else. I said that I should know by one o'clock, and that then it would be the Hour, and that whoever it was might come and tell me why. I said that I should not want anything more. Not the police, nor the money. Only the reason.

I said, 'I have not got so many hours left that I can afford to waste the odd one.'

I had not meant to say that either. My voice was not steady. I sat down.

I asked what was upon my plate. I am told that I asked my wife whether we had ordered it. I do not recollect that. I recollect only that I looked along the table at Edmund, and that he was not looking at me. He was looking at the heavy man with the policeman's hands, and smiling.
