I have turned this over. I am inclined to think that an hour, like a tide, will find its own way out. If I had not provided a means of release it would have made one.

I have the Jack upon trestles in the Shop. He can be mended. I had a baulk of the same oak, that was his brother's.

§ 70. Upon the Sunday evening my daughter Imogen came across from the farm.

She told me that she was to marry young Garrow. I was glad of it. I had given them the ground the night before, and it is as well that someone should have it who knows what to do with sheep.

She brought me a ring.

It was my wife's wedding ring. I had it made in Hatton Garden in the spring of 1948, by a man called Abrahams, of twenty-two carat gold, which is too soft, and wears. It had worn to a wire. I knew it by the mark inside.

I had believed that she was buried in it. I did not look, at the time. I could not.

Imogen said that Edmund had given it to her, in the scullery passage, after two o'clock that morning. He had told her that their mother took it from her finger, upon the Wade, on the night of her death, and put it into his hand, and said, 'Give that to your father.' He had carried it, Imogen said, for twenty years.

That was the thing that he had not given me. He had said so in the tower. *There's a thing I've not given you.*

I put it on. It goes upon the smallest finger of my left hand. I have it there as I dictate.

I enter it under the results, and I shall say why.

My wife took off that ring upon the Wade, in the Odd Hour of 1974, and sent it to me. It did not arrive. It was kept back, by the messenger, for reasons that I understand, in a waistcoat pocket, for twenty years. And upon the night of the experiment, within one hour of the reversal, it was let go. It came to me by way of a woman who had crossed the same water, in the same gown, at an hour that I had given her.

The reader may call that a coincidence. I am a mechanic and I do not believe in them. When I find two wheels turning at the same rate I look for the arbor that joins them.

It took her twenty years to come back across that hall. It took her ring a day longer. But both came.

§ 71. I come to the entry that I have been putting off.

Upon the Monday afternoon Fenn came into the drawing room and shut the door. He told me that my son was dead. He said that he had been found that day upon the Ray Sand, by a man digging bait, and that he had been drowned.

I told him that he was mistaken.

I am aware of how that will read. I ask to be heard. I did not say it from weakness. I said it as I should say it to an apprentice who brought me a movement and told me that it had stopped, when I could see the scape wheel turning.

I had killed my son. I recorded it, with the time. I then passed through the hour again, and found him living. I had my hand upon his face. I counted his pulse. He spoke to me for a quarter of an hour, in sentences, and wept, and made a joke about rats. He put a key into the pocket of his coat. All this was after the stroke. It was upon the second passage, which is the one that stands.

A man cannot be dead who has been made not to have died. It is a matter of sequence.

Fenn told me again. He is an old friend. He was very much distressed. Then he went out, and Miss Quaile came and knelt by my chair and told me the same thing, in her own way, which is without ornament. She said that he had been alive when I saw him, and had died afterward.

I asked of what.

She said that he was drowned.

I asked why he should be drowned. He had no reason to go near the water. He had told me what he meant to do: to see his sister, and to watch a boat. He was to come to me in the Shop.

She could not tell me.

§ 72. I have had that conversation, I am informed, a great many times since. Miss Quaile says that I ask her where my son is upon about one morning in three. She tells me. I am grieved; and then I recollect the tower, and I correct her. She does not give way and nor do I.

I should like to set down, while I have it clear, what I think is the true account of the matter. I have reached it slowly.

I said at the beginning that nothing is had for nothing. I believed, upon the night, that the price of the hour had been the Jack. It was a comfortable belief. He is of oak.

But I see now that I was careless in my reckoning. I did not ask for one thing of that hour. I asked for two.

I had set the engine to give my wife the tide. That was the purpose for which it was built, and that was granted. A woman crossed.

And then, at ten minutes past twelve, with my son lying dead and the girl's wrists in my hands, I asked for a second thing. I asked that the blow should be taken back. I had not designed for it. I put it upon the engine as an afterthought, as a man throws another parcel upon a cart that is already loaded.

That was granted also. I found him living.

Two things were given. A crossing upon the Wade, safe. And a life.

I do not think that a wooden figure pays for that.

I have gone over it as I should go over a train that will not run true, wheel by wheel. And I find that the account balances in only one way. A woman was sent across that water who, in the hour as it first stood, was not to have crossed. And a man went into that water, before morning, who was not to have gone.

It was the same water. It was the same night of the year. He was her son.

I do not say that I understand it. I say that it is what the figures show. I asked the hour to give me back a wife from the Wade, and it did; and the Wade was owed one. I asked it to give me back a son, and it did; and I had him for a quarter of an hour, which was the first quarter of an hour that I ever had him. And then the difference was taken up.

I told him that a man is not hanged for what is done in a passage that has been gone through again. I was wrong. Nothing is forgiven. It is only moved.

§ 73. I shall be asked whether, knowing this, I would do it again.

I have thought about that upon a number of nights. I have the ring upon my finger while I think.

Before the experiment I had a wife who had drowned leaving me, by my own clock, and a son who had not spoken to me in twenty years.

After it I have a wife who turned back; and a son who told me why, and wept, and let me put my hand upon his head. I have a daughter across the water with a man who can tell the tide by the smell. I have paid Garrow. I have said that the train was better than Thorne's.

And my son is drowned. They tell me so.

I do not know how to weigh those. I am not a man who has ever known how to weigh such things. I can tell you the mass of a pendulum bob to the grain.

I think that if he were asked he would say that it was a fair exchange. He said in the tower that he had been waiting twenty years for somebody to hit him. I think that he had been waiting for more than that.

But I should not do it again. I record that. I should let the hour go by my door.

§ 74. Miss Quaile reminds me that I have not said what became of the Thorne.

It is in the tower still. He was to have brought it down upon the Sunday and looked to the moon cock. It is in the cupboard, with the one rod hanging. It has not been wound since the eighteenth of October and will have stopped upon the twenty-sixth.

I cannot find the key. I have looked in my waistcoat.

I gave it to someone. I gave it

§ 75. It is very cold in the workshop at Le Locle before the stove is lit. Monsieur Jeanneret comes down at six and looks at each of our benches before he will speak. He has put my lever escapement under his glass. He says nothing. Then he says, *Ça ira.* It will serve. I am eighteen and I have worked upon it for nine weeks. I think that I should like to go home.

Miss Quaile says that I was speaking French. I have asked her to leave it in.

§ 76. I must put on record that the gallery clock has ceased to gain. I timed it against the regulator through the whole of November. It keeps within two seconds in the week.

It gained four seconds a week for thirty years. I never found the cause. Now it does not.

I asked Mrs Pask whether anyone had touched it. She said that nobody had, and then she sat down upon the stairs and put her apron over her face.

§ 77. I am not certain of the date. Miss Quaile says that it is the nineteenth of January. I have been in bed some days.

I wish to enter a correction to § 9. I stated there that I told my wife I had put the clocks back, and that she said, 'Oh, Leo. You would.' I have recollected the rest.

She was at her glass. She had the grey silk on, and was putting up her hair. She looked at me in the mirror. She said, 'Oh, Leo. You would.' And then she turned round upon the stool, which she did not often do, and looked at me directly. She said:

'Is there anything that you want to ask me? Before we go down?'

I said that I did not think so. I said that I had the Dent to finish.

She said, 'No. Well.' She turned back to the glass.

I have had that for twenty years and did not know that I had it. It was under the other. I think that the engine shook it loose.

That was the Hour, do you see. She had brought it upstairs. She was giving it to me early, by myself, at six o'clock, in her own room, where nobody should hear. She had her hand out.

I had the Dent to finish.

§ 78. Is Margot come in?

Miss Quaile says no. She says that she is dead, and was drowned, and that she had turned back.

Yes. I had that. I thank her.

§ 79. I wish to say something about the child.

I have recorded her twice as an anomaly. I have been thinking of her. I do not sleep a great deal now, and I go over the observations.

She was seen by me in the yard at eight minutes to twelve, upon the first passage. She was seen by my son in the stable at about a quarter to one, and gave him a handkerchief. She was heard, I believe, in the weight closet at five minutes to two. She was of nine or ten years, dark, in a coat too large. She did not speak to me. She looked at what I had in my hand.

There is no such child. I have enquired of everyone.

I have a hypothesis. I put it forward with diffidence.

When a movement is running, there is at each instant one tooth of the scape wheel that is neither locked nor free. It is upon the edge of the pallet, in the act of dropping. We call it the tooth in action. Everything else in the clock is either before or after. That one is now.

I think that an hour which is gone through twice must have, somewhere in it, something that is gone through only once. There must be a fixed point for the rest to turn about, or there could be no saying that it was the same hour. Something must stand in the yard and see both passages, and not be changed by either.

I think that she was that. I do not know what she was otherwise. But I think that when I came out of the ice house upon the first passage, with what I had done upon my hand, there was required to be someone who saw it; who would go on having seen it, whatever the engine did afterward. Else I should have got off too lightly.

She was not afraid of me. I remarked that at the time. She was afraid for him.

If there was such a person, I should like her to know that I am sorry she was made to look.

§ 80. Edmund has not been to see me.

I asked Miss Quaile whether he was away. She told me.

I said that it could not be so. I said that I had been through it twice.

She said, 'Yes, Mr Vane.' She did not say it as the others say it. She has stopped arguing with me upon that head. She says that I found him in the tower, alive, and touched his face. She says that she believes it.

I asked her when she had begun to.

She said that she did not know.

§ 81. I am going to dictate this section slowly. I have asked Miss Quaile to write it large. It is the twenty-third of February and I am clear. I have been clear since six this morning, and I think that I shall not be so again for very long together. I can feel the pivots.

I said at the head of this paper that I had three reasons for making it and that I should give the third at the end.

I shall first say what I know. I have not said it before, and I do not wish it thought that I did not know it.

I know what the Act is. It is a rule about the numbers upon a dial. I know that at two o'clock in the morning of the twenty-third of October every clock in England was put back by its owner's hand, or would be when he woke, and that nothing whatever was reversed but some millions of pieces of brass. I have said so myself for fifty years, in this house, to anyone who would listen. No hour was taken in March. None was returned. Mr Fenn was right. It is a manner of speaking.

I know that two brass rods and a tide dial do not make a road into the past. I cut them. I know what they are. A differential subtracts one rate of turning from another, and that is all that it does.

I know that the woman who came down my stairs was my daughter. I knew it when she said 'Papa.' She is a brave girl. She did for me what I had not the courage to ask of anyone, and she has not once reproached me with having let her.

And I know that I struck my son upon the head with a piece of lead, in an ice house, because he laughed at me. I know that he fell, and that I left him there for dead and pulled the gate shut. And I know that he lived through it by the thickness of his skull, and by the kindness of a cook and a young fool with a wheelbarrow, and by no engine of mine. He was not given back to me. He had never gone. I found him in the tower because he had climbed there, upon his own legs, with his head broken.

I have known all this upon certain days. I knew it, I think, upon the Tuesday after. I have known it on perhaps one day in four. Miss Quaile will bear me out that upon those days I have been very quiet.

On the other days I have known the other thing.

§ 82. I have set down the other thing. I have dictated it upon forty evenings, as carefully as I could, with numbered sections. I have not altered a word of it today, though I might.

I shall say why, and then I have done.

I told the reader, at § 5, that a regulator and a sundial may stand side by side and disagree by sixteen minutes, and each be right. The one tells the time that we have agreed upon, which is even, and useful, and by which the trains run. The other tells where the sun is. The difference is called the equation of time. It is not an error in either instrument. It is a real quantity. It can be tabulated.

There is an account of that night by which the trains run. It is the one that I have given in the section before this. A sick old man struck his son; a daughter put on a dress; a clock was moved from a library to a tower; somebody fired a gun. I do not dispute a line of it.

And there is the other account, which is this paper.

I have asked myself which of them is true. I have been a servant of the true time all my life. I stopped my house for it.

And I find that I cannot say that the first is true and the second false. For consider what the first leaves out.

In the first account, my wife is dead, and did not come down the stairs. But I gave her the tide. I said the words. I had carried them twenty years, and they are not in me now; I have looked. They were said, and something received them.

In the first account, I never struck my son a second time, since there was no second time. But I knelt in front of him in the tower, and I had the weight of what I had done upon me, entire, and he was within reach of my hand. I put the hand upon his head. I do not know what else to call that but a passage gone through again, and done differently.

In the first account no hour was returned. But I had from one o'clock until two, that night, in which I said four things that I had not said in a lifetime. Where did I get it? It was not upon any of my clocks. I have a hundred and eleven of them and they had none of them shown it to me before.

I think that my wife knew what the Act was as well as I did. She was not a fool about time. She knew that the clocks were only put back. And she stood in my hall, every year, and told her family that an hour had been given to them. She said it so that they would behave as though it had. And when they did, it had.

I think that is the equation. I think that there are two times in a house: the one that the regulator keeps, and the one in which a man may turn round and ask his wife a question. They do not run at the same rate. For most of the year they are sixteen minutes apart, or sixteen years. And upon certain nights, by an old custom, or the kindness of a woman, or the accident of somebody else's gun, they stand for an hour together, and what is done in the one is done in the other.

I did not build an engine that does that. I see that today. But I built something, with a great deal of labour, that made me believe for one night that it could be done. And believing it, I did it.

So I shall let the relation stand as I dictated it. It is not what the world's clocks would say. It is where the sun was.

§ 83. The third reason.

I said that I should give it if I had not forgotten. I have not forgotten. I have held on to it today with both hands.

I have made this paper for my son.

I am aware that he is dead. I am clear today, and Miss Quaile has told me, and I recollect Fenn's face. I know also that tomorrow, or the day after, I shall ask where he is, and wonder that he does not come.

That is the reason. I shall not always know it. And I find that I cannot bear that there should be nowhere in this house, when I have gone, where it is written down in my hand that I said what I said to him in the tower. He may not have believed me. He had not much cause to believe a kind word from that quarter. I gave him a quarter of an hour, after fifty-two years, and he went from it into the sea.

So I put it here, at the foot, where it cannot leak.

Edmund Vane cut the lunar train of the Copy of the Thorne Sidereal between the last week of November 1973 and the eighth of February 1974, in the Shop at Compline, with his own hands, unaided, at the age of thirty-one. I have examined it under a glass of ten diameters. It is better than the original. It is the finest piece of wheel-cutting that I have seen in sixty-six years at the bench. I was his master. I said at the time that it would serve.

I was wrong, and I knew it, and I say so.

I ask whoever comes after to see that the Copy is found. Mrs Edmund Vane took it away with her, I am told, in a motor car, and sold it. I do not want it back. But if it is ever opened, I should like the person who opens it to look at the moon work, and to know whose it is.

§ 84. I have some instructions.

The Thorne is to go to the Museum, as in my will. The key is lost. A new one may be cut; there is a drawing in the bench, top drawer, left.

The Jack is mended. He is upon the trestles. He is to be put back upon his pin when the weather is fit. It wants two men and a rope. I do not like to think of her striking by herself.

When I am dead the clocks are to be stopped. All of them. I should be obliged if Miss Quaile would do it; she knows where they are. The pendulums are to be held with the hand and not with a feather. They need not be started again. I have been listening to them for a long time.

To Miss Quaile I leave nothing, since I have nothing that she would want, and Fenn tells me that I gave the best of it away in one night. But I record that she did not lie to me, except three times, and that I knew of each, and that upon consideration I think that she was right in all three.

§ 85. One thing more, for whoever reads this.

The hour is given back every year. I have said so, and I have said also that I know it is not. Take it in whichever sense you can.

It comes in the small hours, upon the last Saturday night of October. You will be asleep. Nearly everyone is. You will wake in the morning and find that you have been given something, and you will put the kettle on.

I should advise you to be awake for it. Open a door. There will very likely be somebody in your house to whom you have not said a thing that you ought. You need no engine. I spent five years upon one, and it was shot to pieces at the first stroke, and I got through the whole of what I had to say without it.

Ask the question. Whatever it is. She is standing behind you at the gallery clock. She has been there five minutes.

Turn round.

§ 86. Is Margot come in?

# PART SEVEN {.part}

::: {.parttitle}
The Secret of Compline House

*by Wren Garrow, aged 9¾, and 39*
:::

## 1. The Seventh

I said that I would not offer you a note on the author of the last account. Here she is instead.

My name is Wren Garrow. I am thirty-nine. On the night of the twenty-second of October, 1994, I was nine years and nine months old, and I was in Compline House from a little after nine in the morning until ten minutes to four the next. Nobody was supposed to know that. For thirty years almost nobody did.

You have met me several times already. I was the voice in the dumb waiter that Mr Pargeter was so polite to. I was the white face at the corner of the stable. I left the drawing on the nursery floor, and the footprints with stars in them. Hester Quaile heard me sing, and cry out, and she put her hand in the place where I had been lying and found it warm. Leopold Vane saw me in the yard with the rain on me and took me for his daughter. He decided later that I was a kind of fixed point, put there so that somebody should see. He was nearer than he knew.

I was the child that Tom Garrow left at a cottage door with an old woman, and made promise not to go on the road. I am the one who set down his telling. He was my father.

And I was the small white light at the orchard gate, low down, that Imogen waved to from the back of a horse. She thought it was her brother holding a candle. It was a red plastic torch from a gas station in Lethbridge, and I was holding it. I saw her wave. I waved back. I thought she was telling me to come on.

So that is who has been talking to you between the parts. I am sorry to have kept it back. I did not do it to be clever. I wanted you to read the six as I had to read them, without knowing what the seventh person knew. If I had told you at the beginning that there was a child in the house, you would have gone through every page looking for her, and you would not have listened to them.

They deserved to be listened to. Each of them carried that night alone for the rest of their lives, and each of them was wrong about what it was.

* * *

I should tell you what I do, because it has a bearing, and because I promised the old man's ghost that I would explain my professional interest.

I work at the National Physical Laboratory, at Teddington, in the group that keeps the time. That is meant literally. There is a room there with caesium fountain clocks in it, and hydrogen masers, and between them they generate the United Kingdom's time scale. It is sent out by radio from a transmitter in Cumbria, and down fibre, and it is what your telephone agrees with. If you have ever heard the pips, you have heard a thing that my colleagues and I are responsible for.

The clocks I look after would lose or gain a second in something like a hundred and fifty million years. I mention the figure because Leopold Vane would have wanted to know it. I think he would have taken his glass out of his eye and been silent for some time.

I did not choose the work by accident. I knew that at nineteen, when I chose it, though I could not then have said why. I had been a child in a house with a hundred and eleven clocks in it, all an hour out, on a night when everything depended on what time it was and nobody could agree. I wanted to spend my life in a place where they could.

I will tell you one thing about my trade that the old man would have liked. He believed that an hour was taken from the country every March and given back every October, and that in between it was held somewhere on deposit. He was told that this was a manner of speaking.

It is a manner of speaking. The time scale that I help to keep does not change in March or October. It is called Coordinated Universal Time, and it has no summer. It runs straight on, second after second, through the night the clocks go back, and nothing whatever happens to it. What changes is a label. At one o'clock by my clocks on the last Sunday morning of October, a rule comes into force which says that the civil time of this country is no longer to be reckoned as my time plus one hour, but as my time exactly.

So Leopold Vane had it precisely right about his own house, and I should like that recorded by somebody who is qualified to say so. Compline kept Greenwich time the year round. It kept, to within the error of a turret clock, the same time as the caesium fountains. It was the rest of England that went away in the spring and came back. On that one night in October, at the instant he opened his door, the country's clocks rejoined his. He was the only man in Essex who was already there.

He was wrong that an hour came in at the door. Nothing came in. But I have stood in the room at Teddington at one in the morning on that night, watching the count go by, and I have thought of fifty-odd million people who are at that moment being handed sixty minutes they did not have. They are asleep. He was right about that as well.

* * *

Now I have to tell you why I said nothing for thirty years. It is the part of this that I am least able to forgive, and I have had to forgive six other people a good deal in the course of putting this book together.

I shall give it in the order that it happened to me.

I was nine. My mother had been dead two years. I had one parent, and I had watched what it was to lose the other, a day at a time, for eight months. I do not think that I can make anyone understand who has not been that child what my father was to me. He was not only the person I loved. He was the only thing between me and nothing.

On the Friday he had taken me by the shoulders, which he never did, and made me promise that I would not set foot on the Wade. *Not if the Queen of England was to call you from the other end.* I had promised. I had said the words back.

And on the Saturday night I heard his voice in the stable yard at Compline, forty feet below me, shouting a man's name. I heard what he asked. I heard the man laugh at him. Then I heard my father's gun.

I knew that gun. I had watched him clean it at the kitchen table that afternoon—no. I had not. I was in the nursery at Compline that afternoon. I knew it because it was my grandfather's, and had stood in the corner of the kitchen at Saltcote, and I had been told not to touch it. And I knew my father's voice as I knew my own heartbeat.

The man beside me in the clock room went backward into my arms with blood coming out of his neck.

That man was dead thirty-six hours later. He was found on a sandbank. I heard them talking about it in the kitchen at Saltcote, my father and the lady who had come on the horse, in low voices, when they thought I was asleep on the settle. I heard the word *pellets*. I heard my father say, *They'll come for me, Imogen.* I heard her say, *They will not. I've told them where you were.*

I was nine years old and I had been reading detective stories for a year. I knew what it meant when a man has been shot at and is afterward found dead. I knew what they did to the person who had fired. I had it, I am ashamed to say, from a book in which it was done with a rope.

I believed that if anyone found out my father had been on that island with a gun, they would take him away and hang him. And there was exactly one person in the world who could put him there. It was not the lady. She had only seen the empty cartridges. It was me. I had been in the tower, and seen the flash in the yard, and tied my handkerchief round the place where the shot went in.

That is the first reason. I kept my mouth shut to save my father's life. I would do it again.

The second reason was Mrs Pask.

She found me at seven that morning, in bed, at her cottage, with my hair wet. I will tell you about that in its place. She sat on the edge of the bed. She was grey in the face; she had been all night looking for me in a house with a sea round it. She took hold of my two wrists, and she said:

"You were never there. Do you hear me, Wren Garrow? You were never in that house. You were here, with Vi, all night, in this bed. If they find I took you over, I'll lose my place, at my age, and your father'll never speak to me again; and that's the least of it. There's been something done in that house last night that I don't know the half of. There's a policeman been. If you say one word about where you were, they'll have you in a room with a lady in a hat, asking you questions, and then they'll have your dad. And they'll take you off him. They do that. They'd say he wasn't fit, a man on his own, leaving a child. They'd put you in a home."

She did not mean to be cruel. She was a good woman, and frightened, and she loved me. She had no idea what I had seen. She thought that I had been wandering in the passages and had heard a quarrel.

"Swear," she said.

I swore. I swore on my mother.

So I had made two promises that week, and broken the first in the worst way that it could be broken. I was not going to break the second.

The third reason is the simplest and the worst.

The man had given me a message. He gave it to me at about ten minutes to five in the morning, in the dark, from the water, and he made me say it back to him twice. It was for three people. One of them was his sister. One was my father. The third he corrected himself about; he had already told that one.

I could not deliver it. To say what he had told me, I should have had to say where he told it. I should have had to say, *I was on the Wade. I went on the road. He came in after me.* And then there would have been the questions, and the lady in the hat, and my father.

I told myself that I would do it when I was older. I told myself that when I was twelve, and when I was sixteen. By the time I was old enough to understand that no one was going to hang anybody, I had been not telling for so long that I could not find the place to begin. My father had married Imogen. They were happy, in that low house, with the lamp in the window. I thought, they have put it behind them. I thought, if I speak now, I shall be the one who brings it back.

I did not know what they were each carrying. That is the thing I ask you to believe. I did not know that my father went over that night most evenings of his life, doing a sum about blood. I did not know that Imogen thought her brother had walked into the sea because of what she said to him in a scullery. They never spoke of it to me, or to each other. There were two rooms in that house that neither of them went into, she wrote. I lived in it for nine years and never knew the rooms were there.

Edmund Vane had lived for twenty years with a secret that would have set three people free, and had told no one, because he was ashamed of his own part in it. He told it to a child, on the last night of his life, and asked her to pass it on.

And the child grew up and did the same as he had. For thirty years.

I work with clocks that do not lose a second in the lifetime of a continent. I was half a lifetime late with nine words.

* * *

My father died in December of 2021, in a hospital in Chelmsford. He was seventy. It was his heart.

I have put in his own part what he said to me there. I had gone in every day for three weeks, and for most of that time he could not talk. On the last afternoon but one he was awake, and clear, and he began, without any warning, on the tower.

I had never heard that piece. He had told me the crossing a hundred times, and the ewe, and the Rill. He always stopped when the mare came out of the sea at Saltcote. He had never once said what he believed came after.

He said that he had put the shot in Edmund Vane that took him down to the water. He said that the light Imogen saw at the gate had been low down for a man, and he had thought ever since that Vane was on his knees. He said, *I got the whole of it, that night, everything a man could ask, and I got it with his blood on it.*

He said, *I never asked him the question.*

I was holding his hand. I had held it at nine years old, walking the boundary.

I said, "Dad. He didn't die of that. I know how he died. I was there."

He did not turn his head.

I said it again. I said, "The light at the gate was me. It was my torch. I went on the road. He came in after me and put me up the Perch. He told me what happened to her. She turned back for him, Dad. She'd left. She was coming to Grandpa. She turned back because Edmund had fallen in the Rill."

His eyes were shut. They had given him something an hour before, for the pain. His hand was slack in mine.

I do not know whether he heard any of it. I have told myself that the hearing goes last. A nurse said so. I sat there until it was dark, and said it over, the whole thing, from the nursery to the cottage bed, to a man who was breathing eight or nine times a minute.

He died the next evening without having woken.

So one of the three never had it. He was the one it was first meant for; it was his father who had asked. I shall not get past that. I have had to learn to carry it, as they all learned to carry theirs, and I have this advantage over them, that mine is at least the right weight.

* * *

I could not tell Imogen. Not then. She had just buried him. She was seventy-one, and thin as a rail, and she went about the farm that winter in his coat.

I told her in the March of this year.

She was dying by then, and knew it. It was her lungs. She had moved her bed down into the kitchen at Saltcote, by the range, where she could see the window. She would not go to a hospital. She said that she had seen what they did to Tom.

I had come down from Teddington for the week. On the Tuesday evening she asked me to fetch something from the bottom drawer of her desk. It was a parcel in brown paper. Inside were six paperback books with a rose on the spine, and a typescript.

"I wrote that," she said. "In 1998. Nobody knows. Not even your father knew. I want you to read it. There's a chapter in the typed one that isn't in the book; they made me take it out." She was looking at the lamp on the sill. "I want somebody to know what I said to my brother. I've never told a soul. I think that I killed him, Wren. I think that he went down to the water because of me."

I read it that night, by the range, while she slept. I read the sixth chapter three times. *I hope you never have another night's sleep as long as you live.*

At about four in the morning she woke and saw my face.

"You've read it," she said.

"Yes."

"Well? You needn't be kind. I've had thirty years of people being kind."

I got down on the bricks by her bed. I do not think that I have ever been so frightened, not even on the Wade.

"Immy," I said. "He didn't. It wasn't you. I've got to tell you something, and I should have told you when I was nine, and I'm so sorry."

I told her. I told her all of it. It took until it was light. She did not interrupt me once. She lay with her eyes on the ceiling and her hands on the blanket, and when I came to the Perch, and what he said there about their mother, I saw the tears begin to run back into her hair. She did not make a sound.

When I had finished there was a long silence. The clock on the wall ticked. It was the old painted one.

"She put him up the ladder," Imogen said.

"Yes."

"And he put you."

"Yes."

"And she gave him the ring from the water. With her hand up." She shut her eyes. "I held that ring. He put it in my palm and I said, *give it to him yourself.* He tried to tell me. Twice. *It's what she did, at the end.* And I said, *she drowned, I'll not hear another word.*" Her voice cracked. "Oh, Edmund. Oh, my poor boy."

"He said to tell you that she turned back for him. Not from Amos. Those were the words. He made me say them twice."

"When you were nine."

"When I was nine."

"On a post in the sea, in the dark."

"Yes."

She began to laugh. It was dreadful to hear, with her chest as it was. She laughed and coughed and held on to my arm.

"Thirty years," she said. "Oh, my Lord. We are a family of people who cannot deliver a message. Mother gave Edmund a ring to carry two hundred yards and it took him twenty years. He gave you nine words and it's taken thirty. And Papa waited twenty to tell her the time." She wiped her eyes with her wrist, as she always did. "And I sat behind a vine. And then behind a curtain. And then I wrote it all down in a book with a rose on it and changed the names."

"I thought they'd hang Dad."

"Of course you did. You were a child." She took my face between her hands. Hers were so thin. "I am not angry with you. Do you understand me? I should be the last. I looked back from that horse and saw your torch, and I gave it my brother's name, and waved. You were walking into the sea, nine years old, and I *waved* to you. If Edmund hadn't been standing at that gate—"

She could not finish.

After a while she said, "Does anyone else know?"

"Nobody."

"Tom?"

I told her about the hospital.

She was quiet for a long time. I thought that she had gone to sleep.

"Then you'll have to tell the rest of them," she said.

"The rest of whom?"

"All of them. Everyone who was there." She opened her eyes. They were her mother's eyes; I have seen the portrait. "You've read mine. I've thought for thirty years that I did it, with my tongue. Your father thought he did it with a gun; I always knew that he thought so, though I never let him say. And they're not the only ones. I've had letters."

"What letters?"

"The little nurse wrote to me, in 'ninety-five, from a hospital. She'd had a breakdown. It was a strange letter. She said she had done a thing in the hall that night which she would answer for. She wouldn't say what. Toby Pargeter sent me his ridiculous book, with a page turned down, and wrote on the flyleaf, *I think you should know that it was me.* I never answered him. I thought he meant the pudding." She was breathing with difficulty. "And there was a policeman. Fenn told me before he died. He said the man had gone to his grave believing that he'd helped Celia get away with murder. And Celia. God knows what Celia thinks. She's in Portugal. She sends a card at Christmas with a tram on it."

"Immy, rest."

"I'll rest presently. Listen." She had hold of my wrist. It was my father's grip, at the last, and my grandfather's. "They all think they did it. Don't you see? Every one of us. We each of us had our own piece of that night, and nobody ever laid them side by side. Edmund said it himself, to that policeman, across the dinner table; the man wrote it down. *Everybody in the house has their own idea of who did it, and they're all wrong.*"

"I know. I've read it now."

"Then you know what you've got to do. You're the only one who can. You saw all of it." Her eyes were very bright. "Have them to the house. On the night. In October. Mother's rule. You'll be thirty years late, but that's nothing, for a Vane. Get them round that table and tell them. Not kindly. Exactly. You're good at exactly. Tell each of them what they did, and what it came to. And then tell them what he did."

"I'm not a Vane."

"You're the nearest thing that's left," said Imogen. "And you've got her habit of standing in doorways."

* * *

She died on the eleventh of April. She left me Saltcote, which was hers, and Compline, which had come to her from Kit, who had never wanted it. She left me a horseshoe nail on a ribbon. And she left me a list, in pencil, of names.

I spent the summer finding them.

Some of it was easy. Mr Pargeter's book was on her shelf. Miss Quaile I wrote to, at an address on the Yorkshire coast. She took a week to answer. Then she wrote, in a small clear hand, that she had been waiting thirty years for somebody to ask. She sent me nine exercise books by registered post: three of her own, and six that she had taken down from an old man's dictation and kept, since no one else had wanted them. She put in with them a small red diary and a child's drawing in wax crayon. She said that she thought the drawing must be mine.

It was mine. I had not seen it since I dropped it.

The policeman took me longest. I had only a surname and the word *Leigh*. I found him in the end through Mr Pargeter, who had once bought him a whisky. He had been dead five years. The manager of the nursing home had kept his box. She gave it to me across her desk and said, "He used to type at night. We could hear him. He said he was writing up a case." I read it on the train home. When I got to the last line I had to get out at Shenfield and sit on a bench.

*Edmund Vane was dead at a quarter past one by my watch. I'd swear to it. I've sworn to worse.*

My father's I had already. I had had it since I was ten years old, a piece at a time, on the sea wall. I wrote it out in August, in the kitchen at Saltcote, in the evenings. I did not need notes.

And then I had six piles on a table.

I did to them what a person of my training does. I have told you. The lining paper, the ruler, the tide tables. I had a seventh pile as well, a very small one. It was a school notebook with a spiral binding, the cover gone soft, that had been in a biscuit tin under my bed since 1994. On the front, in capitals, in felt pen, it says THE SECRET OF COMPLINE HOUSE. And underneath: CLUES.

I had never been able to open it. I opened it that August.

It took me eleven weeks to lay the seven together. I had an advantage that nobody else could have had. I knew the answer. But I want to say that knowing the answer is not the same as seeing how it fits. I knew where Edmund Vane had been at five o'clock in the morning. I did not know, until I had Mr Cade's watch in one column and the kitchen clock in another, how he had got there through six people who each believed they had stopped him.

When it was done I looked at the sheet for a long time. It was nine feet of lining paper, pinned to the wall of my stepmother's kitchen. Every statement that any of them had made was on it, in its square.

There was not a lie anywhere. There was not one square that I had to cross out.

I wrote to them all in September. I said who I was. I said that I had something to tell them about the night of the twenty-second of October, 1994, and that I would rather tell them together, in the place, on the anniversary. I said that I knew it was a great deal to ask. I gave the times of the tide.

They came. I am going to tell you about that. But first I have to give you the seventh account, since it is the one they came for. It begins at nine in the morning, in the back of a van, under a sack.

## 2. Clues

The notebook is a spiral-bound school one with a blue cover, bought at a drugstore in Pincher Creek, Alberta. I had begun it on the aeroplane. The first six pages are about the Atlantic Ocean, which I could not see, and a list of what my father had told me about England, with ticks against the things that turned out to be true.

On the seventh page I started again. I am going to give you what is written there. I have not corrected the spelling, and where I have left something out I say so. I was nine. I had a wristwatch that my father had set that morning by the wireless, a Casio with a light in it, of which I was very proud, and I had lately read eleven books about a girl who solved mysteries. That is all the equipment I had. It turned out to be more than anyone else in the house.

**THE SECRET OF COMPLINE HOUSE**
**by Wren Garrow age 9¾**
**Saturday Oct 22**

*9.04 a.m. In Mrs Pasks van. Under a sack. It smells of goose. Gail says if I sneeze she will sit on me. We are on the sea road. I am not on it. I am IN A VAN on it. That is diffrent. I did not set foot.*

I want you to notice that. I had been made to promise the evening before, and I was a truthful child, and I spent the whole of that crossing working out whether I was breaking my word. I decided that I was not, and wrote it down so that I could show my father if it came up.

I should say how I came to be under the sack. Mrs Pask has had some hard things said about her in this book, by implication, and I would like to put her side.

She had agreed with my father that her sister would mind me. But Vi was eighty-three and deaf, and the week before she had put a kettle on the gas and gone to sleep in her chair, and Dolly had come home to a kitchen full of it. Dolly was to be on the island from nine in the morning until the road dried on Sunday. She stood in her yard that morning with the van loaded, and looked at Vi, and looked at me, and I saw her change her mind.

"I can't leave her with you," she said to her sister. "Not for a day and a night. I'd never forgive myself."

"Eh?" said Vi.

"Get in the back," Dolly said to me. "Under that. Quick, before your dad looks round."

She meant it for the best. She thought that she would put me in a room at the top of a big house, with a plate of food and a rocking horse, where nobody went, and that I should be safer there than with an old woman and a gas stove. She told Vi what to say if my father came. She did not think that he would come. She thought that he would be at the lawyer's all day and asleep by nine.

She could not tell him, you see. That was the difficulty. He would have asked where I was to be, and she would have had to say *at Compline*, and he would have said no. And she could not have told the Vanes that she had brought a Garrow child into the house. Mr Edmund had sent a notice to the farm that week. There was bad blood. She had her place to think of. She was sixty-three.

So she hid me. It was a small deception by a tired, decent woman, to get through one difficult day. I have put her name on a stone in St Botolph's churchyard, next to her husband's, and I take flowers.

*9.31. We are there. Up the back stairs with a box on my head so Im a parsel. Mrs P says NOT A SOUND WREN GARROW. There are 4 flights. A room at the top. It has BARS on the window like a jail. There is a rocking horse with a red saddle and most of his hair gone. A bed. A cubbord with animals painted. It smells of mice.*

*RULES (Mrs P):*
*1. Stay in this room.*
*2. Not a sound.*
*3. If anybody comes, under the bed.*
*4. She will bring my dinner.*
*5. Tomorrow when the sea goes down she will take me home and DAD IS NOT TO KNOW.*

*I asked why its a secret. She said becos the people here and the Garrows dont speak and if they found one in their nursry she would lose her place. I said what did we do. She said its not what you did, its what was done. Then she locked the door.*

*She LOCKED it. I heard.*

*9.50. I am a PRISONER in a house on an island and nobody knows I am here exept the cook. This is the best thing that has ever happened to me.*

I am afraid that is exactly what it says.

* * *

I shall go through the day more quickly than the notebook does. There are fourteen pages before dark. A good deal of it is about the rocking horse.

*10.15. CLUE NO. 1. There is a clock in this room. It says 9.15. My watch says 10.15. I thot it was broke. But I can here another one thru the floor and I counted when it struck and it struck 9. So thats TWO and they are BOTH an hour wrong THE SAME WAY.*

*That is not broke. If they were broke they would be wrong diffrent. Somebody has done it ON PURPOSE.*

*WHY would you make all your clocks wrong?*

I had it in the first hour. I had it before the detective sergeant had got his loupe out. I do not say that to boast. He was looking for something complicated. I was looking at a clock. And I had not been told by a solicitor to expect it, or by a cook to put my watch back. I simply had two times in front of me and wanted to know which was lying.

I never did put my watch back. I kept it on Alberta habits: you set it by the radio and you leave it alone. So the times in this notebook are the same as Mr Cade's, and my father's. They are the rest of England's. I was the only person inside that house, apart from a detective with a Tissot in his sock, who knew all night what time it really was. And I was the only person anywhere who wrote down both.

*11.02. I am OUT.*

*It was easy. Its in my book (The Clue in the Old Mill). She left the key in the lock on the OUTSIDE. There is a gap under the door. You get a peice of paper and push it under so its flat on the floor outside. Then you poke the key out with a pencil from inside. It falls on the paper. You pull the paper back. The key comes with it.*

*It worked FIRST TIME. I did not think it would. In the book it takes her 3 goes.*

*I am going to put it back after so she wont know. I am only going to look. I will not make a sound.*

*11.10. There is a little door in the wall on the landing with ropes in. I looked down. It is a LIFT but tiny. For dinners. It goes all the way down. I can FIT.*

I could. I was small for nine. I rode in that dumb waiter, I should think, fifteen times in the course of the day. If you pull on the one rope you go down and on the other you go up, and it stops at three places: the nursery landing; a little serving pantry behind the dining room, with a hatch that looks into it; and the larder off the kitchen. It was slow, and it creaked, and it was the most wonderful thing I had ever been in. I thought of it as mine.

It was through the hatch in the serving pantry that I watched the dinner. It was in the larder, at five past one in the morning, that the rope jammed and I spent what I told Mr Pargeter was ages. I had been in there eleven minutes. I have the time.

*11.40. This house is FULL of clocks. I have counted 31 and I have only done 2 floors. They are all an hour wrong. They all tick but not together. It sounds like a lot of people wispering about you.*

*There is a long room with windows and a pictur at the end of a lady in a gray dress. She is looking at you. I went from one side to the other and she still was. She looks like she knows a joke. I like her. I think she is the lady who drowned. Under her is a clock that goes cuh. cuh. like it has a cold.*

*There is a door next to her that is locked. No key in it. I looked thru the keyhole. A bed. SHOES on the floor. Nobody in.*

*12.05. Had to hide. A man came. I got behind a curtin.*

*He is not from here. He has a raincoat over his arm and a magnifing glass and a lot of photos. He goes up to a clock and opens it like hes scared of it and looks INSIDE at the back. Then he looks at a photo. Then he writes in a book. He did 4 while I watched. On 2 of them he shook his head.*

*He has shoes like the police have. I think he is a DETECTIVE in disgize. So there is a CRIME. I knew it.*

*What is he looking for at the back of the clocks?*

I followed Mr Cade for most of an hour. He never saw me. He was, I think, the best-trained observer who was ever in that house, and I walked behind him through four rooms. It is not that he was careless. It is that there are some things a grown man looking for a thief does not look for, and one of them is a child of nine standing very still behind a curtain. He was right about what a detective is worth. You see everything. You could pass an examination on it. He simply had not been told that I was on the paper.

I worked out what he was doing by going back afterwards to a clock that he had shaken his head at, and one that he had not, and opening them myself. I had to stand on a chair.

*12.30. CLUE NO. 2. I looked where he looked. In the ones he liked there is a NAME cut in the metal at the back. Tho. Tompion Londini. In the ones he didnt like there is NO NAME. Just smooth.*

*So some of the clocks are REAL and some are FAKES and he is finding out which.*

*Somebody has been taking the real ones and putting fakes. That is the CRIME. Its like in The Hidden Staircase only with clocks.*

I have that in my handwriting, at half past twelve in the afternoon, eight hours before Leopold Vane stood up at his own table to announce it. I had no idea that it was a secret. I thought that everyone must know.

* * *

*1.30 p.m. Mrs P came with bread and cheese and 3 little oranges. I was back in time. I had put the key back in the outside and shut the door and I was on the horse. She said have you been good. I said yes. She said have you made a sound. I said no. Both true.*

*She said theres a lady going about, a nurse, pale, in a blue dress, and if she comes up here I am to be SILENT AS THE GRAVE becos she notises things.*

*I said who else is in the house.*

*SUSPECTS (from Mrs P and from looking):*

*1. MR EDMUND. Big. Limps. Drinks. He is the son. Mrs P says he is to be pitied. She would not say why. He sent the paper to Dad. So he is the VILLAN, probly.*

*2. THE DETECTIVE (I am not ment to know). Mrs P says he is from the insurence. He is not.*

*3. MRS EDMUND. Fair hair. Pretty but old. Mrs P says she was on the stage.*

*4. THE OLD MAN. Mr Vane. He is 81. He made all the clocks wrong. Mrs P says he is not right in his head but she says it like she likes him.*

*5. MISS IMOGEN. The daughter. She is the lady who touched the box on the road. I saw her on the stairs. She has a white bit in her hair like a skunk. She looks like the pictur.*

*6. KIT. He is the grandson. He plays piano. He has a girlfreind with NO HAIR.*

*7. THE NURSE. Have not seen yet.*

*Mrs P said there are more coming for dinner. A vicar and a lawyer and a Dame. I said what is a Dame. She said a lady who has shot more foxes than you have had hot dinners.*

*She said there will be 13 at table and one of them a ghost. I said WHAT. She said never you mind, and went.*

*She forgot to lock it this time!!! No she didnt. I heard. But she took the key.*

*That is all right. I have the lift.*

I did not need the door after that. I went down the shaft.

I am going to pass over the early afternoon, except for one thing. At a little after three by my watch I was in the long gallery, on my stomach, with my ear against a place where the floorboards did not meet. The library is underneath. I had been listening to the clock down there, which had more ticks in it than any of the others, when two people came in.

*3.10. In the libary under me. The nurse (I think, a little quiet voice) and the Big Man. I cant here all.*

*She said I should like to speak to you. He made a joke. She did not laff.*

*She has a BOOK. She found it in a clock. He said have you read it. She said yes. He said all of it. She said to the end.*

*Then she said DID YOU FOLLOW HER.*

*He did not say anything for ages. Then he said YES.*

*Thats a CONFESSION. But I dont know what to. Who is her?*

*He said he would tell his father tomorrow. He said after breakfast. He said if I am not there you tell him EDMUND SAID HE WAS SORRY AND IT WASNT THE CLOCK.*

*What wasnt the clock???*

*He sounded sad. Villans in books do not sound like that.*

I underlined the last sentence twice. I can see where the pencil went through.

It is the first place in the notebook where the case stops being a game. I did not know it then. I only knew that I had gone down on that floor to listen to a man who had sent my father a paper, and had heard somebody who sounded as my father had sounded, by the range, the night my grandfather died.

* * *

*4.55. I was singing. I FORGOT.*

*I was on the horse and I was singing Four Strong Winds, just the start becos its all I know, and I heard FEET on the stairs. Fast.*

*I got off. I got against the wall by the door where the keyhole cant see. The horse was still going.*

*Somebody tried the door. Then knocked. A lady said is someone there. I didnt breathe.*

*Then Mrs Pask came up. She was out of breath. I heard it all. The lady said she herd a child singing in the chimney. Mrs P said its the WIND. The lady said there is no wind. Mrs P said theres always wind at Compline.*

*The lady said the horse was rocking. Mrs P said its the draft.*

*The lady said I SMELT ORANGES.*

*I had just eaten the last one. The peel is on the table.*

*Mrs P said she has a box in the kitchen. That is a LIE. She gave them all to me. I have never heard a grownup lie that good.*

*She said THERE IS NO CHILD AT COMPLINE. She said it like in church.*

*The lady went. Mrs P waited. Then she said thru the door very quiet: Wren Garrow. I will skin you.*

That was Hester Quaile. She has written about that afternoon herself, and I have compared the two. She says that she smelled oranges on the landing, and I had the peel on the table. She says that the rocking horse was moving as a horse moves after someone has got down. I had got down four seconds before.

She believed Mrs Pask. She says so. A sensible woman of sixty-three, with flour on her arms, told her to her face that there was no child, and she went downstairs and lay on her bed and told herself that the flue sang.

I have thought about what that cost her. She came to Compline as a nurse, with a rule about telling the truth and a trained eye. She heard a child. She was right. And she was told, by someone she had every reason to trust, that she had not; and from that minute she could no longer be sure what in that house was real. Eight hours later she stood on a landing and watched a woman in grey come down the gallery, and she had already been taught that afternoon that her ears could not be relied upon.

I do not say that Dolly Pask made Hester see a ghost. But she did take away the ground Hester was standing on, and I was the reason.

*5.15. I have drawn the tower. You can see it out the back window on the stairs. There are 2 people on top. Wooden. A man who hits the little bell and a lady who hits the big one. The boy with the piano and the girl with no hair went up and put CLOTHES on them. A black jacket on the man. A scarf on the lady. They were laffing.*

*The lady is gray like the pictur. She has her arm up all the time waiting. She doesnt look at the bell. She looks at the house.*

That is the drawing that Hester found on the floor. I had written under it what she copied down. I dropped it at five to one in the morning, when I came back into that room running, and did not know that it was gone.

* * *

I shall give you two more entries from the daylight, since they both come into it later, and then the dinner.

*6.30. Nearly CAUGHT. I was in a blue bedroom looking at the clock in there (No. 44) when the big girl came in with towels. I got under the bed. It has a frill. She went. I was coming out when ANOTHER one came in.*

*He is new. Very tall, pink, wet. He was holding his shoes. He took off his sweater and knocked the clock off the table with his elbow. It rolled RIGHT UNDER THE BED. It stopped by my foot.*

*He came under after it.*

*I thot thats it. I pulled my legs up. There is an old suitcase under there and I was behind it. He was on his tummy. He got hold of the clock. He sneezed. He banged his head. Then he put his KNEE on it.*

*It went crunch. A bit flew out.*

*He said OH I SAY.*

*He sat on the floor and looked at it for ages. He looked like he was going to cry. Then he put ALL THE BITS in the pocket of a black jacket that was hanging on the door.*

*He never saw me. I was 2 feet away.*

*I dont think he is the theif. A theif would not break it. He is just an accident. But he has HIDDEN THE EVIDENSE so I am putting him down.*

*8. TALL PINK MAN. Broke clock no. 44. Hid it in his pocket. Not on purpose.*

I have had that entry open in front of Toby Pargeter. He read it standing, in the hall at Compline, with his reading glasses on the end of his nose. He was fifty-nine. He went the colour he says in his memoir that he went, and then he sat down on the stairs and laughed until his wife had to fetch him a glass of water.

"Two feet," he said. "Two feet away. I've told that story for thirty years. I've done the budgerigar at weddings. And there was a small Canadian under the bed the whole time, taking notes."

And the other.

*6.50. CLUE NO. 5. The Detective has a room on the 1st floor at the back. I looked thru the keyhole.*

*He was sitting on the bed. He took his WATCH off. He looked at it. Then he pulled up his trouser and put it DOWN HIS SOCK.*

*Why would a person put a watch in their sock?*

*7.05. I know why. I watched from the top of the stairs. Everyone who comes in has to put their watch in a big bowl in the hall. The fair lady holds her hand out. The Dame threw hers. The Pink Man had a MICKEY MOUSE one (!!) and the Old Man picked it up and said it was honnest.*

*The Detective said I DONT WEAR ONE.*

*That is a LIE. Its in his sock.*

*So he is the only one in the house (exept me) who has a watch that says the real time. The rest have only got the wrong clocks.*

*He wants to know what time it REALLY is. Good. So do I.*

I had not then seen what it would come to. But I had seen the thing itself. There were two times in that house, an hour apart, and from seven o'clock that evening every person in it except two had been separated from the true one. They would be told the hour, all night, by a hundred and eleven dials that were all agreed with one another and all, as far as the rest of England was concerned, wrong. And they would each remember, afterward, what the dials had said.

I wrote one more line under that entry. I had drawn a box round it.

*If somebody says something happened at 1 o clock, you have to ask WHICH 1 o clock.*

It took the adults thirty years.

* * *

*9.10 p.m. (8.10 by the house). DINNER. I am in the little pantry behind the dining room. There is a hatch. If you open it a crack you can see the whole table. I am in the lift with my knees up so if anyone comes I can pull the rope.*

*There are 12 people. I counted. But 13 PLACES.*

*The emty one is next to the Old Man. They put soup at it. Then they took the soup away. Then goose.*

*He talks to it. He turns his head and says something and waits.*

*That is the ghost. That is the lady who drowned. It is her chair.*

*I am not scared. He isnt. He looks at it like Dad used to look at the door when Mom was in the hospitel and it was time for her to come back from the tests.*

I am not able to say anything about that entry. I will only point out that the others who sat at that table have each described the chair, and that none of them describes it as I did. The detective says it was doing most of the talking. The young man in love counted the table and got thirteen and was uneasy. The nurse says that it was cold on that side of her. Imogen kept it at the edge of her eye.

I was nine, and I had seen a person look at a door. So I knew what the chair was for. It was the only thing in that house which I understood better than anybody.

*9.40. The Old Man stood up. He said TO ABSENT TIME. They all said it.*

*Then he said ONE OF YOU HAS BEEN ROBBING ME.*

*!!!!!!*

*I WAS RIGHT. Its the clocks. He said somebody has been taking them and leaving copies. He said he made the copies himself. He said he could tell blindfold.*

*He said I dont know which of you it is. He said I shall know by one o clock.*

*This is a REAL CASE. It is not in a book. I am in it.*

*WHO LOOKED GILTY:*

*Pink Man went white and held his pocket. But I know what is in his pocket and its only No. 44.*

*The fair lady looked at Big Man.*

*The piano boy looked at Big Man.*

*The nurse looked at her lap.*

*The skunk lady looked at the emty chair.*

*The Detective did not look at anyone. He was eating.*

*BIG MAN LOOKED AT THE DETECTIVE AND SMILED.*

*That is the one. You dont smile if its not you. And you smile at the detective if you KNOW he is one.*

*So: it is MR EDMUND. Suspect No. 1. I said so at 1.30.*

*But he is the one who was sad in the libary. He is the one who said yes.*

*I dont like this as much as I thot I would.*

There is one more line on that page. It is in a different pencil, blunter. I wrote it at five past ten, by my watch, in the nursery, when I had gone up to fetch my coat and had looked out of the barred window at the dark where the road had been.

*10.05. The sea is over the road now. Nobody can get on or off. In the books that is called a CLOSED CIRCLE and it is when the murder happens.*

*I dont want there to be a murder.*

*I am going to watch Suspect No. 1 and see he doesnt do anything.*

I had the wrong person down as the one who needed stopping. Everybody did. But I ask you to notice what a child of nine resolved to do, at five past ten, on the top floor of that house. Mr Cade was hired by a wife that night to stay near Edmund Vane. Hester Quaile loved him. His father followed him with a piece of lead and his sister with twenty years of anger. My own father came for him through seven feet of water.

I was the only one of them who actually did stay near him. I was behind him, or beside him, or above him, with a notebook, from twenty-five past eleven until five o'clock in the morning.

It is why he is dead. I am going to show you that. I am going to show you also that it is why none of the others killed him.

## 3. Which One O'Clock

After the lights went out there is much less in the notebook. I had the torch, but I did not dare to use it where anyone might see, and I wrote most of what follows crouched on the back stairs, by feel, in letters an inch high. Some of it I cannot now read. I shall give what there is, and fill in the rest from memory. I have not forgotten any of it. I could not if I tried.

*11.20. All the lights went out. The piano stopped and then went on. I was behind the curtin in the long room. It is VERY dark. All I can here is clocks.*

*11.24. Suspect No. 1 has come out of the room with the fire. He has a lamp. He is going to the libary.*

I went down the main stairs behind him on my hands and seat, a step at a time. The hall was empty. He had left the library door open.

He had set his lamp on the table in the window. There was a wooden box on the floor that I had not seen before, a tea chest, with a blanket in it. He took the green cloth off the big clock. He opened the glass.

He did not lift it out at once. That is what I remember. He stood in front of it for quite a long time, with his arms hanging. Then he put out his hand and laid it flat against the dial, the way you would touch the face of somebody who was asleep.

He said something. I was at the door and could not hear it.

Then he was quick. He had it out, and into a pillowcase, and into the blanket, and the lid on, and a cord round. I watched him tie the knot. I have never seen hands move like that. They did not seem to belong to the rest of him, which was swaying.

He put the cloth back over the empty glass. He picked up the box. I got behind the hall table.

*11.30. He has TAKEN THE BIG CLOCK. In a box. He went out the side door. The girl with no hair held it open for him. He said thank you Celia. She is not Celia. She has the same DRESS as Celia. I notised that at dinner. There are 2 green dresses and I dont think the grownups have counted.*

That is in the notebook. I want it on the record, since a detective sergeant of the Metropolitan Police went to his grave not having put it together. I had it by half past eleven. I was not cleverer than Mr Cade. I had simply not been hit on the head yet, and I was at the height where one notices boots.

I followed Edmund Vane out into the rain.

It was the first time I had been out of doors. The wind nearly took me off the step. I had my blue coat, that Mrs Pask had found for the funeral, which came down past my knees, and my canvas shoes. I kept the torch in my pocket. He had a lamp, and I had only to stay behind it.

He went along the front of the stables, with the box against his chest. I heard the little bell on the tower ring twice over my head, and I looked up, and saw the two wooden people in their clothes, and did not like them.

He went down a track into some trees. There was a hump there, with a door in it. He went in. I stood behind a trunk.

And I saw that I was not the only one.

*11.36. There is SOMEBODY ELSE. Under a holly bush. A man with a hat. He has a lamp but its turned right down. It is the DETECTIVE. He is following Suspect No. 1.*

*So it goes: Suspect. Then Detective. Then me.*

*He doesnt know Im here.*

I have Mr Cade's account of those five minutes. He says that he had rain down his collar and a twig in his ear, and that he had spent some of the best years of his life like that. I was eleven feet behind him. I could see the back of his neck.

Edmund came out without the box. He stopped on the track and looked back at the house. He said, "Sorry, Ma."

I heard that. The detective heard it too; he has written it down. He could make nothing of it. I could not either, then. I thought only that it was a queer thing for a thief to say.

When Edmund had gone the detective went into the hump. He was in there a long time. I crept to the gate. There was a passage, and a lamp at the end of it, and I could see him on his knees with the lid off the box, looking in. His face was lit from underneath. He looked for a moment like a man who is very hungry and has been shown food. Then he put the lid back. He tied the cord again. He did it badly.

He came out, and I got behind the mound. He went off through the trees toward the sea.

I went in myself, when he had gone. I had the torch. It was colder in there than any place I have ever been, and there were steps going down into the dark. I tried to lift the box. I could not move it an inch.

*11.50. The box is in an ICE HOUSE (it has ice in). I cant lift it. I am going to tell Mrs Pask in the morning where it is so she can tell the Old Man and he can have his clock back.*

*That is the case SOLVED. Suspect No. 1 did it and I know where the loot is.*

*I am wet. I am going in.*

I thought that it was over. I went back to the house quite pleased with myself.

* * *

There is a thing that happened next which belongs to somebody else, and I have asked his leave to tell it.

I went in by the side door. I was in the passage by the gunroom, taking my shoes off to carry them, when the door banged open behind me and someone came in out of the rain, running.

It was the boy who played the piano. I flattened myself against the coats.

He did not see me. He would not have seen a horse. He was as white as paper, and his mouth was open, and he was making a sound in his chest like a dog that has been running. He got as far as the gun rack and held on to it. Then he was sick on the floor.

A door opened further up, and the girl with no hair came down the passage with a candle. She said, "Kit? Kit, what is it? Where've you been?"

He said, "I've killed him."

"Killed who?"

"The man. Sears's man. The one with the face. He was in the tack room. He was waiting for Dad." His teeth were chattering. "I hit him with my bat. From school. It was on the wall. I only meant to—he went down, Sass. He just went down. There's blood. He isn't moving."

"Oh my God."

"I told him to leave Dad alone. And then I ran." He put his hands over his face. "I've killed a man with a cricket bat."

She got hold of him. She was a year or two younger than he was, with a ring in her eyebrow, and she took charge of him as though he were six. She said that he was not to tell anyone. She said that they would go and look, together, in a minute, when he could stand. She took him away up the passage with her arm round his waist.

*12.14. The piano boy says he has KILLED A MAN in the stable with a bat. He thinks it was a bad man come for his dad. I think it was the DETECTIVE.*

*I am going to look.*

I know that I should not have. I was nine. But I ask you to consider what I had been reading for a year. In those books, when somebody says there is a body, the girl goes to see. And I had a reason that was better than the books. If the detective was dead, there was nobody left who knew about the box but me.

I put my shoes on again. I went back across the yard.

There is a door at the foot of the tower. It was open. Inside there was a strong smell of paraffin and something else, sharp. I shone the torch.

He was lying on his face on some horse blankets. His hat was beside him. There was blood on the back of his head, and a lamp on the floor, broken. A cricket bat lay just inside the door.

I had seen a dead person. I had seen my mother. I knew that you cannot tell by looking.

I knew what to do. It was in the fourth book. You hold something shiny to their mouth. If they are alive it goes misty.

I had my watch. I took it off. I got down on the floor and held the glass of it under his nose, with the torch on it.

It went misty. It cleared, and went misty again.

*12.22. He is NOT DEAD. I did the mirror test with my watch. He is breathing. He is asleep with a bump. He smells of wisky.*

*I put a blanket on him. I cant do anything else. He is too big.*

*The piano boy has NOT killed anybody. Somebody should tell him.*

Nobody did. I should have run after the pair of them. I was afraid of being caught.

Kit Vane went back to that harness room twenty minutes later with the girl, to look at his dead man, and found a broken lamp and some blood, and no one. Mr Cade had got up at a quarter to one and walked out. Kit did not know what to think. He came into the hall for the ceremony with hay in his hair, holding on to the stairs. He watched the baize door open, and a young man come through it carrying a box, and he thought that it was the body.

He spent the whole of that night not knowing whether he had killed a moneylender's man or not, or where the corpse had gone. In the morning he asked the girl who waited at table, three times, whether the gentleman from the insurers had been at breakfast. When she said that Mr Cade had driven off at six with his mother, he sat down on the stairs and laughed until he cried. Hester saw him do it, and could not think why.

He told me this himself, in the hall at Compline, thirty years later. He is fifty-four. He writes music for films, in Berlin, and has a way of keeping his hands in his pockets.

"I've never hit anyone since," he said. "Not once. I can't even kill a wasp."

I showed him the page. *I did the mirror test with my watch.* He read it twice.

"You were nine," he said. "You went into a dark stable by yourself to see if a man was dead. And you thought to check that he was breathing."

"It was in a book."

"There was a detective sergeant on that island," Kit said. "There was a trained nurse. There were about fourteen adults. Do you know how many of us, that night, came on a body and bent down to see whether it was breathing?"

I did know. I had the sheet of lining paper.

"One," I said. "Toby. And he only did it because Hester had told him how."

* * *

I am coming now to the thing I saw. I have been a long time getting to it.

I went back into the house. I meant to go up to the nursery and stay there; I had had enough. I had got to the first landing when I heard voices below, in the room with the fire. A man's voice said that he was going to have a look at the generator.

It was Edmund.

I thought: he is going for the box. He does not know the detective has been at it. He does not know the detective is lying in the stable with a bump.

I thought: I said that I would watch him.

There are two ways down from that landing. The main stairs come out in the hall, in the light. The back stairs come out by the gunroom. To get from the one to the other on that floor you have to go the whole length of the long room with the picture.

I ran. I ran down it in my socks, with my shoes in my hand, as hard as I could go, past all the clocks, to the far end where the lady was. I did not think about who was underneath.

Two women in the drawing room heard me. One of them was sure that it was a ghost, and went upstairs to meet it. The other went and put on a dead woman's dress. I have had to get used to that. A good deal of what happened in that house after half past eleven happened because a child ran along a floor.

*12.33. He has gone out the side door. I am behind him. It has stopped raining nearly.*

*12.34. THE OLD MAN HAS COME OUT TOO.*

I had not expected that. I had got out of the door and into the shadow of the wall, ten yards behind Edmund's lamp, and I heard the door open again at my back.

He came out slowly. He had no coat and no hat. His hair was white in the dark. He walked straight past me, a yard away, and never turned his head. He was looking at the lamp ahead.

He was carrying something in his right hand. It hung down by his knee on a short string. I put the torch on it for one second, behind my fingers. It was a round metal thing about the size of a tin of beans.

I did not know what it was. I thought it might be a lantern that had gone out.

So there were three of us again, going across the yard. The son in front. Then the father. Then me. Nobody was following me, I am fairly sure, though by that point I would not have been surprised.

They went down the track. Edmund went into the hump, and a minute later the old man went in after him.

I did not go to the gate. I do not know why. I think that I had begun to be frightened. I stood among the trees, a little way off, where I could see the arch.

I could hear them. It was only voices at first, one low and one loud. I could not make out any of it. Then the loud one got louder, and I began to catch words.

*12.44. They are having a FIGHT. In the ice house. Not hitting. Shouting. It is the Big Man shouting. The Old Man is quiet.*

*He said IT WILL SERVE. He said it twice like it was a bad word.*

*He said SHE WAS LEAVING YOU.*

*The Old Man said something.*

*Big Man LAFFED. It was horrible.*

*He said IT WAS NEVER THE*

That is where the entry stops. The pencil goes off the edge of the page.

I heard the laugh. I have heard it described by a nurse who never heard it and a father who heard it too well, and by my own father, who heard another like it an hour later from the top of a tower. It was not a happy sound. It went on and on. And through it I heard him shout. *It was never the clock. It was never the bloody clock.*

Then there was a small noise. It was like somebody knocking once on a door.

The laughing stopped.

There was a crash, and another, a wooden thing falling. Then something else fell. It was heavier, and it went on for longer. I could count it. It hit, and hit, and hit, twelve times, and then it was quiet.

I stood under the trees with the notebook against my chest. I knew that sound. A year before, in a rented house in Pincher Creek, my mother had got up in the night, when she ought not to have, and had fallen down the stairs. There were nine of them. I was in bed. I had counted.

Nothing happened for what seemed a very long time. I heard water dripping.

Then I heard the old man's voice. He was calling a name. He said it over and over, quite gently, as you would to somebody you wanted to wake.

Nobody answered him.

A light came toward the arch, and went out. I heard him feeling along the wall. He came out through the gate. He turned, and took hold of it, and pulled it shut behind him, and it made a clang, and a click.

He stood there. He lifted his right hand and looked at what was in it.

I ran. I ran up the track ahead of him. I got as far as the corner of the stable wall and my legs would not go any further. I stood against the bricks.

He came up out of the trees. He was walking very slowly. He came round the corner, and he saw me.

I have his account of that. He says that I was looking at what he had in his hand. I was. The moon had come out. It was a grey metal weight on a string, and one side of it was dark, and shining, and wet.

He says that I was not afraid of him. That is true as well. I do not know why I was not.
