He was a very old man with white hair, in evening clothes, in the rain, and he had just done something at the bottom of some steps. But he looked at me with such a puzzled, gentle face. He looked like somebody who has lost his way in his own house.

He said, "Go in, Immy. You will catch cold."

He thought that I was his little girl.

I could not speak. I wanted to say, *you have to go back, he's hurt, you have to fetch somebody.* It would not come out. I turned round and ran.

* * *

I do not remember crossing the yard, or the stairs. I remember that I was in the nursery, with the door shut behind me, and that I had my back against it, and that something was coming up through my chest that I could not stop.

It came out. It was one sound. I got the eiderdown off the bed and pushed it against my mouth with both hands, and stood there, and shook.

*There is no child at Compline. I heard a child cry out in the old nursery at five minutes to twelve.*

Hester has that right to the minute. It was five to one by my watch. I looked, afterward.

She has written that it was not a cry of pain, nor for a mother. She says that it was the sound a child makes who has seen a thing done. She was a nurse, and she had it exactly.

But she thought that she knew whose voice it was. She knelt on that floor, with my drawing in her hand, and decided that it was a boy who had slept in that iron bed forty years before, and had seen something, and was still crying about it. She was wrong about the child. But I have often thought since that she was not very far wrong about the boy.

I heard her on the stairs. She was coming up fast, and saying, "I'm coming, I'm coming."

I did not want to be found. I had sworn, and there was Mrs Pask's place. And I had just seen an old man come out of a hole with blood on a weight. I could not have told it to a stranger in a blue dress. I wanted the only grown-up in that house who knew my name.

I was out of the door and across the landing before she reached the top. I had the hatch open and was in the lift with my knees under my chin. I pulled the rope. I went down into the wall, in the dark, as she came through the nursery door with her lamp.

She says that when she came out again the ropes were trembling. They were. I was on the end of them.

I went down three floors. I was going to the kitchen. I was going to tell Mrs Pask.

And the lift stuck.

* * *

*1.08. I am STUCK in the lift. It is between the pantry and the kitchen. The rope has gone crooked. I have been here for ages.*

*Somebody opened the little door at the bottom. A man. I said Hello. I said please could you pull the other rope.*

*He said IM VERY SORRY I CANT HELP YOU. YOU ARENT THERE.*

*I said I am tho.*

*He shut the door.*

*It was the Pink Man. I know his voice. Why did he say I wasnt there???*

I have read Mr Pargeter's version of that conversation a number of times. It is one of the few things in this entire business that I can think of without any pain at all. He was polite to me. He says that one is not frightened by a thing that is simply not so. He had had a great deal to drink, and a vicar had died on him and risen again, and he had fallen in love on a staircase. When the wall spoke to him, he declined, courteously, to believe it, and went and asked the cook whether the lift generally did.

She came. I heard the bolt. The hatch opened and there was her face, with a candle under it.

I have never been so glad to see anyone. I began to cry properly then.

"Not a sound, I said," Mrs Pask whispered. She was working at the rope. "What did I tell you? Not a sound. And you're talking to the gentry out of a cupboard. Wait till I get you home."

"Mrs Pask—"

"I'll skin you. I'll skin you and hang you on the line. That nurse has been up to the nursery. She's found your orange peel."

"Mrs Pask, please. There's a man."

"There's a dozen men, and none of them's to know you're here. Hold still." She had got the lift down level with the hatch. She put her arm in and felt me all over, quickly, as she would a hen, to see that I was whole. "You're soaked. You've been outdoors. Wren Garrow, you have been out of this house."

"The old man hit Mr Edmund."

She stopped.

"What?"

"The old man. With the white hair. He hit Mr Edmund with a thing on a string. In the ice house. He's fallen down the steps. He's at the bottom and he isn't moving." It came out of me all in one piece. "He called him and he didn't answer. The old man shut the gate and came away."

I could see her face. It had gone quite still.

I had expected her to shout for somebody. I had expected her to run. That is what I wanted. I wanted a grown person to hear what I had seen and take it from me.

"You never saw that," said Mrs Pask.

"I did. I did see it. I heard him fall. I counted."

"You saw nothing. Listen to me." She had hold of my chin. Her hand smelled of goose fat. "There's things go on upstairs in this house that I've made it my business for forty year not to know. I'm not going to start with what a child tells me out of a lift at one in the morning. Mr Vane's eighty-one. He's never raised his hand to a creature in his life. He couldn't hit a clock."

"He had blood on it."

"That's enough."

"But Mr Edmund's lying in the cold!"

She shut her eyes. I saw her breathe.

I understand her now. I did not then, and I hated her. She had been in that house since 1952. She had put that old man's dinners in front of him for forty-two years. She had picked his son up off the Wade, crying, and walked him home, and never told. Everything in her was made for keeping what went on above stairs from coming down. And here was a child she had smuggled in against every rule, telling her that the master had killed his heir with a clock weight.

If she believed me, she would have to raise the house. She would have to say how she knew. *A little girl told me. A Garrow. I hid her in the nursery.* And it would all come out together.

But she could not leave him there. She was not that kind of woman. If there was one chance in fifty that I was telling the truth, Edmund Vane was lying on wet straw at the bottom of twelve steps in a place as cold as a grave.

She opened her eyes.

"He'll be drunk," she said. She was not speaking to me. "That's what it'll be. He's drunk every year on this night. He'll have gone down them steps on his backside and he'll be sat at the bottom singing." She let go of my chin. "It wants somebody to look. That's all. Somebody that can go there natural, and find him, and no questions."

"I could show you."

"You'll show nobody. You'll go up in this lift to the nursery and you'll get in that bed and you'll stay in it, or as God's my witness I'll tan you so you can't sit." She was already pulling the rope. "I've the ice to send for. I've had it out there since the lights went. It wants fetching for one o'clock."

The lift went up. Her face went down below me, and the light with it.

I heard her go back into the kitchen. I heard her say, in quite a different voice, loud and comfortable:

"There. All it wanted was a firm hand. Now then. If you've nothing to do but sit there eating my stock, you can run me an errand."

* * *

That is why Toby Pargeter was sent for the pudding.

He has wondered about it. He says in his memoir that she looked up at the clock on the wall, and then at him, and that he saw her come to some decision; he thought that she wanted him out of the kitchen. She did. But she wanted him somewhere in particular. She gave him her own keys, with the red wool on the one for the gate. She told him to mind the steps. She told him that the box would be at the bottom.

The bombe had been in the ice since half past ten. She had no need of it for forty minutes. Gail could have gone, when she had her shoes on.

She sent him at twenty-five past twelve by the kitchen clock. That clock was eight minutes fast. It was seventeen minutes past by the house, and seventeen minutes past one by my watch. I had told her at eleven minutes past.

She took six minutes to think of a way. That is all. In six minutes she had found a means to get a man down those steps with a candle, on an honest errand, who would come back and tell her what was at the bottom. She did it without leaving her kitchen or admitting that she knew a thing. And when he came running back to say that Mr Edmund was lying there with a lump on his head, she untied her apron and went for the wheelbarrow.

Mr Cade had been at that gate two minutes before. He had put his arm through the bars with a lighter, and looked for the best part of a minute, and gone away to find the wife. He was trained. He was the only person on the island whose job it was. He looked at a man lying on straw and made up his mind, from the door, as he had learned to do in twenty years of looking at the dead.

And a child told a cook, through a hatch in a larder. The cook did not believe her. But she sent a young man with a spoon.

Toby got down those steps and heard him snore. He turned him on his side. He and Dolly Pask got sixteen stone of him up twelve steps and into a barrow and under a horse rug, in the dry.

A doctor told me, years afterward, what would have become of a man with that much chloral in him and a fractured skull, left on his back, head down, on wet straw, in a brick chamber full of ice, for four and a half hours until the road opened. I had not told him why I was asking. He said that the cold alone would have done it by three.

So I am going to claim that. I have little enough to my credit in this story. I saw a man struck, and I ran away, and cried into an eiderdown. But I went down a shaft in the dark to tell somebody, and I made her hear me, and because of it he was lifted out.

Edmund Vane did not die in the ice house. He did not die of his father's blow, or of his wife's bottle. He was carried out of there alive at twenty-three minutes to two in the morning, by a wine merchant and a cook.

It was the first time that night that he was saved. I did not go up to the nursery. I got out of the lift at the little pantry behind the dining room, and went through the dark house to the side door, and followed the young man with the spoon.

## 4. The Fixed Point

I saw Toby Pargeter go into the ice house with a candle in a saucer. I heard him yell. I heard a spoon ring on brick.

I was in the trees. I waited for him to come out and shout for help. He did not come out. I waited what seemed a very long time, and by my watch was four minutes. Then he came through the gate at a run, without his candle, and went past me up the track toward the kitchen with his long legs going like a foal's.

He had left the gate open. The cook's keys were hanging in it.

I went in.

I did not want to. I had heard that fall. I stood on the landing with the torch in both hands, and it was shaking so that the light went all over the dome. Then I made it go down the steps.

He was at the bottom. He was on his side now, with his cheek on his arm, and somebody had pushed straw under his head. There was a candle burning on one of the steps. Beside him, tipped over in the wet, was the box.

He was making a noise. It was a long slow rasping breath with a click at the top.

I have told you about my mother. She had made that noise. Not at the end. Before the end, in the weeks when they gave her the strong medicine, she would sleep in the afternoons with her mouth open and breathe like that, and I would sit on the bed and read to her. I knew what it was. It was a person a long way down.

I went down the steps on my seat. I got my watch off. I held the glass under his nose.

It misted.

*1.26. Suspect No. 1 is NOT DEAD. I did the test. He is breathing slow like Mom did. He has a big lump on his head and its bleeding. The Old Man DID hit him. But not dead.*

*The Pink Man found him and put him on his side. That is the right thing. They did that with Mom.*

*I am staying with him till somebody comes.*

I sat on the bottom step. I did not touch him. I looked at his face. It was the first time I had seen it close. I had been calling him the villain since half past one that afternoon.

He did not look like one. He looked like a big tired man who had been hit. There was grey in his hair. He had long eyelashes, like a girl's, and one of his eyes was half open with the white showing, and the other was swelling shut.

He said something. I bent down.

"Ma," he said.

I said, "She isn't here."

I do not know why I answered him. He could not hear. But I had said the same word in my sleep for two years, and been told the same thing, and I thought that somebody ought to tell him.

There were voices outside, and a squeaking. I got behind the ice.

* * *

I watched them take him up. I was crouched behind a heap of wet sacking with my torch off.

It was the cook and the pink young man. I have read his account of it and I can tell you that he has left nothing out and added nothing. He went up those steps backwards on his seat, one at a time, with sixteen stone in his lap, and Mrs Pask pushed from below with her shoulder. On the seventh step the man they were carrying spoke. He said, "Is it over?" She said, "Nearly, Mr Edmund. You go back to sleep."

Toby came down again for the box. He looked for his spoon. He passed within a yard of me. He blew out his candle and left it on the step.

When they had gone I came out. I picked up the spoon. I do not know why. I put it down again in the straw. Mr Cade found it there twenty minutes later and held it up to a torch, and it made him think of a moneylender.

I followed the barrow.

It went up the track with the cook between the shafts, in a man's cap, leaning. Edmund lay in it on his back with his legs hanging over the front. He had the box on his stomach. His hands had been folded on top. I walked behind, in the dark, along the wall.

At the corner of the stables I put my head round. That is when Toby saw me. He has written it down: a small white face, at the height of his waist, there for two seconds. He put it with the lift.

I saw what happened at the mounting block.

He has told you. I can only confirm it. Mrs Pask was taking the barrow in a wide curve, slowly. He said, "Here, let me, do let me." He stepped in and took hold of one handle. The wheel went down between two stones.

I saw the barrow go over. I saw him let go and catch the box. He caught it beautifully.

I saw Edmund Vane go out on the other side, head first, and I heard the back of his head meet the corner of the stone.

I put my hand over my own mouth. I had made one noise that night already.

And he said, "Ow."

I want to tell Toby this, and I have told him. I was ten yards away. I heard what the man said, and how. It was loud, and cross. He put his hand up to his head. He said a bad word. He opened both his eyes and looked at the young man standing over him against the moon and asked who it was, and what he was holding. When he was told that it was the pudding, he said, "Good. Well done." Then he turned over on the cobbles of his own accord and went back to sleep.

A person who has been killed by a blow to the head does not do that. I am not a doctor. But I have since asked two, with the pathologist's report in front of them, and they both say the same. It was a contusion. It bled. It did not break the bone. The fracture was on the other side, at the front, and it had been there for forty-five minutes already when the barrow tipped.

Toby Pargeter has believed for thirty years that he gave his cousin the injury that sent him dizzy into the sea. He called a book after it. He did give him a cut on the back of the head, by trying to help. He also heard him snore, and put him on his side, and carried him up twelve steps out of a place that would have killed him by three. If you set those two things in a balance, I do not think that it comes down on the side he supposes.

* * *

They put him in the end loose box and covered him. Mrs Pask tucked the rug in at his neck. I watched her through the gap in the door. I had not known that her hands could be like that.

They went. I heard the little bell on the tower ring three times as they crossed the yard. It was a quarter to two by my watch.

I went in.

It was warm in there, after the ice house, and it smelled of hay. They had left no light. I sat down in the straw beside him with the torch between my knees, pointing at the wall.

I do not know what I thought I was doing. I had said that I would stay with him till somebody came, and somebody had come, and gone again. Mrs Pask had told me twice to get into the nursery bed. I could not have gone back up to that room for anything in the world.

I think that it was only that he was asleep, and hurt, and by himself. I had sat by somebody like that before.

I got out the notebook.

*1.48. They have put him in a stable in the straw. The cook and the Pink Man. In a WHEELBARROW. The Pink Man dropped him on his head by accident but he woke up and said ow so its OK.*

*I am with him. I am gaurding.*

*CASE NOTES. I have to think.*

*The Old Man hit him. But the Old Man is not bad. He looked lost.*

*The Big Man took the clock. But he said sorry Ma. And he was sad in the libary.*

*The fair lady*

That is as far as I got. He moved.

He drew his knees up, and groaned, and put a hand to his forehead. He lay still. Then he opened his eyes, both of them as far as they would go, and looked straight up into the dark.

"Where the devil am I?" he said.

I had the torch on the wall. He turned his head toward the light. He saw me.

He looked for quite a long time. I sat perfectly still, with the notebook on my knee.

"Am I dead?" he said.

"No."

"Are you sure?"

"I did a test. With my watch. Twice."

"Did you?" He seemed to think that over. His voice was thick and slow. "That was thorough. What are you? Are you a ghost?"

"No."

"You're in the nursery. I've seen you there. You were on Dapple."

"I was this afternoon. How did you see?"

"I didn't. I mean a long time ago." He shut his eyes and opened them. "No. That was Immy. You're not Imogen."

"I'm Wren."

"Wren." He said it carefully. "That's a bird."

"It's after my mom's mom."

"Is it? I'm after nobody. I was supposed to be after my father, and it didn't take." He was trying to get up on his elbow. He got halfway and stopped, and went grey. "Oh, Lord. Somebody's hit me."

"The old man did. With a thing on a string. I saw."

He looked at me.

"You saw that."

"I was outside. I heard you fall. I counted the steps."

"How many?"

"Twelve."

"That's right," said Edmund Vane. "There are twelve. I counted them too, on the way down. I remember thinking, that's the lot." He put his fingers to the back of his head and looked at them. "And I've another at the back. Did he hit me twice?"

"No. That was the Pink Man. He tipped you out of the wheelbarrow. He didn't mean to. He caught the pudding instead."

He stared. Then his face did something. It began at the corners of his mouth. I saw that he was laughing, without any sound, and that it hurt him.

"The pudding," he said. "Oh, my God. Toby. With the—I was holding a church." He wiped his good eye. "Whose are you, Wren? You're not one of ours. You talk like the pictures."

"I'm not allowed to say."

"Aren't you? Who says so?"

"I'm not allowed to say that either."

"I see. You've been well trained. You'd do for this family." He had got himself sitting, with his back against the manger. He was shivering. "What time is it? Have you really a watch? Nobody's got a watch in this house."

I held it up with the light on.

"Ten to two."

"Is that by us, or by the world?"

"It's the real time. I set it by the radio. All your clocks are an hour wrong."

"So they are," he said. "So they are. You've noticed that. It's taken some people years." He shut his eyes. I thought that he was going to sleep again. Then they came open, quite wide. "Ten to two. The real time. *God.* The boat."

* * *

He got up. I do not know how. He hauled himself up the manger hand over hand and stood holding it, with his head hanging and his breath coming hard.

"I've got to tell the boat to go," he said. "It's waiting. I was to bring the box. If I don't come they'll walk up to the house, and my father's standing at the door." He took a step, and his knee went, and he caught the wall. "A light. From the tower. That was the arrangement, if it was off. Three swings."

"You can't. You're hurt. You've had medicine in your drink; the nurse said."

"How do you know what the nurse said?"

"I was in the lift."

"Of course you were." He was working his way along the wall to the door. "Listen, Wren-after-your-grandmother. I've done a great many stupid things tonight, and I'm about to do another, and I shall very likely fall off the ladder. You needn't watch. Go back to wherever it is that you're not allowed to say."

I went after him. I had said that I would.

He got into the harness room. He stopped. There was the broken lamp, and the smell.

"Somebody's had a party in here," he said.

"The piano boy hit the detective with a bat. He's not dead either. I did the test."

"Kit did?" He turned and looked at me in the torchlight. "Kit hit that policeman? What for?"

"He thought he'd come to hurt you."

He stood there. I could not see his face well.

"Did he," he said. It was very low. "The young fool. For me." He took a lantern down off a nail, and got a match to it, with hands that would hardly do it. "I must speak to that boy. I've not spoken to him properly since he was ten."

The ladder goes up in the corner. He put his foot on the bottom rung and his hands on the sides, and nothing happened. He could not make the other foot come.

I got underneath. I took hold of his ankle with both hands and lifted it onto the next rung.

"What are you doing?"

"Helping."

"I'm sixteen stone."

"I'm only doing your foot."

We went up like that. He pulled with his arms and I moved his feet, one and then the other, fourteen times. He says, in what he told Toby afterward, that he got up those stairs on his hands and knees. That is nearly right. He had forgotten whose hands.

* * *

The clock room is a wooden box at the top of the tower, with a great iron frame in the middle and a pendulum as long as a man swinging through a slot in the floor. It was bitterly cold. The moon came in through the slats.

*It goes TOCK. Then nothing for ages. Then TOCK. It is the biggest clock I have ever seen. You can see all the wheels.*

*There is a cubbord in the corner with 2 gold rods coming out of the side going to the big clock. The door is not quite shut. I looked.*

*THERE IS ANOTHER ONE.*

*The same as the one he put in the box. The same faces. The same moon. EXACTLY.*

*There are 2 big clocks. Like there are 2 green dresses. He has stolen one and the other is UP HERE.*

*Which is the real one?*

I wrote that by the light of his lantern, sitting on the floor, while he got his breath. It is the last thing in the notebook that is written in sentences.

I did not tell him. I have gone over that. He was six feet from the Thorne Sidereal, the real one, with its door ajar, and he never turned his head. He had not looked at a clock in twenty years. I could have said, *There's another one in that cupboard.* He would have gone and put his glass on it, and seen the thorn. He would have known that the box in the ice house was not worth the price of the boat.

I was nine, and I was not sure what I was looking at, and he had other things on his mind.

He opened the small door in the wall. The night came in.

There is a ledge out there, a few feet wide, with a low parapet, and a little roof over. The bell hangs in the middle. On the far side of it stood the wooden lady, as tall as he was, grey, with her arm up. On the near side, close to the door, with his back to us, was the wooden man.

Somebody had dressed him. He had a black jacket on, buttoned, and a white front, and a bow. He had a hammer in his fist.

Edmund went out past him with the lantern. He held on to the wooden man's shoulder to do it, as you would hold on to a friend. He stood at the parapet, between the Jack and the bell, and lifted the light, and swung it.

I stayed in the doorway. I could see over the edge. A long way off, down by the water, there was a small white light, and two people standing.

"There," he said. "That's Ostler. He's seen it. Who's that with him?" He leaned out. "That's not—who the devil is that?" He swung the lantern again. "Go on, man. Go home. It's off."

I looked at my watch. It was two minutes to two.

And a voice came up out of the yard.

* * *

"Vane."

It was right underneath. It was not loud. Then it was.

"VANE."

I knew it before the second one had finished. I would have known it at the bottom of the sea.

It was my dad.

I cannot tell you what that was like. I had left him at Saltcote at half past seven in the morning, shoeing a mare. There was six feet of water between that farm and this tower. I had seen it out of the nursery window. He could not be there. He had made me promise about the road, and he never broke a rule that he made.

I very nearly shouted. I had my mouth open. I was going to lean over that parapet and yell, *Dad, I'm up here.*

I did not. I have asked myself why a thousand times. I think it was two things. One was the promise. I was in the last place on earth that I was supposed to be, and he was underneath, and I knew how he would look at me. And the other was his voice. I had never heard it like that. He had never in my life spoken above the level of a man talking to a horse. I did not know that he could make that sound. There was something in it that kept me where I was.

Edmund had turned. He brought the lantern round, and the light fell down the tower.

"Who's that?"

"Garrow."

"Who?"

"Tom Garrow. From Saltcote. You looked at me Thursday through a glass."

I heard Edmund laugh. It was short and broken. He asked how he had got over. My father said that he had swum it.

"You swam the Rill? At the flood? Then you're a bigger fool than I am." He was holding on to the wooden man's arm. He turned his head, and he was not looking at me, or at the Jack. He was looking across the bell at the grey lady. "He's swum the Rill, Ma. Did you hear that? Old Amos's boy. He's come for his rent."

He was talking to her. He was drugged, and had been hit twice on the head, and he had climbed forty feet. He looked at a figure of painted oak in a wet shawl, and he saw his mother.

My father has told you what he said next, and I can tell you that he has it word for word. He said that he had a thing to ask. He said that it was from his father, who was dead, and had held on a week to give it him.

"Not now," Edmund said. "Not *now*, man. Can't you see I'm busy? I've a boat." And then, louder, in a voice that frightened me: "Get off my land. You've no land. Fenn's sent the paper. Go home to your bloody sheep."

He laughed. My father says that it rang down the tower. It did. I was beside him. I could see his face, in the lantern, and I can tell you what my father could not see from the yard. He was not laughing at anyone. He was hanging on to a wooden man with one hand, forty feet up, with his eyes rolling. I do not think that he knew what he was saying. He was frightened out of his wits and he made the noise that he always made.

Then my father asked his question.

"Was she coming or was she going?"

I heard it. I did not understand it. I heard him say that my grandfather had stood on our wall with a lamp, and seen her light come three parts over, and another go after. That he had stood an hour. That hers had turned back.

"Did she turn of herself? Or did you turn her?"

Edmund stopped laughing.

I was looking straight at him. I shall never forget it. Everything went out of his face. The drink, and the drug, and the fear. He looked down into that yard at a man standing in the light with a gun in his hands, and I saw him understand who it was, and what he was being asked, and that he had been waiting twenty years for it.

"You tell me," my father said. "You'll tell me now. I've come through the sea for it."

Edmund's mouth opened.

He was going to answer. I am as sure of that as I am of anything. He had it. He had told a nurse that afternoon that he would say it in the morning. Somebody had come across the water at night and asked him to his face, which no one had ever done, and he was going to tell a Garrow, there, from the top of his own tower, what had become of Marguerite Vane.

He said one word. I was a yard from him. I heard it. Nobody else could have.

He said, "Both."

And the clock struck.

* * *

There was a whirring in the room behind me, and a clank. The floor shook. Over my head a rod moved.

The wooden man lifted his arm.

I had not known that he could. I had drawn him that afternoon from a window, hitting a bell, and it had not come into my mind that he would do it while I was standing next to him. His whole arm came up from the shoulder, stiff, with the hammer in the fist. The black sleeve rode back from a white cuff. It came up, and over, and down.

*Ting.* And on the other side, a smaller hammer on a wire. *Tang.*

He swung out as he struck. That is how he is made. He stands on an iron pin, and when the rod pulls he turns a little toward the bell, and leans, and his arm comes down past the edge of the roof. From the yard, with a lantern behind him, he would have looked like a man stepping forward to the parapet and levelling something at whoever stood below.

He did it four times. Edmund had let go of him and was holding the bell frame. They were shoulder to shoulder, the two of them, in their dinner jackets. The light was swinging.

Then the lady moved.

She was on the far side. I saw her arm go back. It went a long way back, slowly. It came down.

The big bell went off like the end of the world.

I had my hands over my ears. I did not hear the gun. I saw it. There was a red flash down in the yard, and another, so close together that they were nearly one.

The wooden man jumped. That is the only way I can put it. Something hit him in the chest, and his white front burst open, and there were splinters. He rocked on his pin. There was a crack. He went over backward, quite slowly, with his arm still up, and his black jacket, and he fell off the far side of the tower into the dark.

I heard him hit the water.

In the same instant Edmund cried out and clapped his hand to his neck. The lantern flew out of his fingers. It went over the parapet. He came backward through the little door as if he had been thrown, and landed on me.

We went down together on the floor of the clock room. Something whined over us and smacked into the cupboard in the corner, a lot of small things at once, like hail on a tin roof. There was a twang. One of the gold rods jumped and hung loose.

Then it was quiet. The pendulum went on. *Tock.*

* * *

He was lying across my legs. He was very heavy.

"Are you hit?" he said.

"No."

"Are you sure? Feel. All over."

I felt. "I'm not."

"Thank Christ." He rolled off me. He was holding the side of his neck, and something dark was coming between his fingers. "I am, I think. A little. He's given me the edge of it." He took his hand away and looked at it by the moon. "Oh, well done, Garrow. That's what I get for standing next to a better-dressed man."

I got my handkerchief out. It was one that my mother had bought me, in Lethbridge, with red maple leaves on it. I had been keeping it clean. I folded it and put it against his neck, where the wet was, and held it there.

"Press," I said. "You have to press. For ten minutes."

"Who taught you that?"

"The nurse at the hospital. When Mom had the tube out."

He put his own hand over mine. It was a big hand, and cold, and it was shaking.

"You're a useful sort of person to have about," he said. "Wren." He lay back on the boards. "Did you see what he shot?"

"The wooden man."

"The Jack. In my father's dinner jacket. Both barrels. He's gone into the fleet." He began to laugh, and stopped, because of his neck. "He thinks it was me. He'll have seen it go over. He's standing down there now thinking he's done murder."

I said nothing.

He turned his head on the floor and looked at me. The moon was in bars across his face. One eye was shut tight and the other was very bright.

"Who is that, down there?" he said. "You know. I saw you, when he called. You nearly went over the edge."

I did not answer.

"You're not allowed to say."

"No."

"You talk like the pictures. And Tom Garrow's been twenty years in Canada." He was quiet. "Dolly Pask's been taking plates up the back stairs all day for a cat. We haven't got a cat."

I held the handkerchief.

"You're Garrow's child," Edmund Vane said. "You're old Amos's granddaughter. In my nursery. On my rocking horse." He shut his eye. "Oh, Dolly. You old fox."

"She'll lose her place."

"She will not. Not while I've breath." He was silent for a moment. "That's your father."

"Yes."

"Does he know you're here?"

"No. He made me promise. He'll kill me."

"He's just had a fair try at me." He was nearly smiling. "Don't cry. He won't. I know that sort. He carried a ewe on his back once, when he was a boy, a mile and a half, with a broken leg; I watched him from the wall. I thought, that's a better man than I'll ever be." He moved his hand on mine. "Listen. I ought to put my head over that parapet and shout down that I'm alive. But I can't stand, just at present. And if he sees a face come up over the edge, after what he thinks he's done, he'll either drop dead or let off the other barrel. And you're up here."

"He's only got two."

"So he has. You do count things." He breathed. "Let him think it for an hour. It'll do him no lasting harm. It'll keep him out of the house, which is the main thing; my father's in there, and my sister. I'll go down directly and find him. I owe him an answer. He asked me a fair question and I'd got as far as one word."

"You said both."

"Did I? Did you hear that?" He looked at me with something like respect. "Yes. Both. She was coming, and she was going. I'll tell him. I'll tell him the whole of it, as soon as I can walk. I've said that to three people today. It gets easier."

We stayed there. I held his neck. I did not have a watch on; I had put it in my pocket after the test. I counted instead. I had got to four hundred and something when I heard the music.

It came up from the house, very thin. It was a waltz.

"That's my father," Edmund said. "He's dancing. He does, in the Hour. With nobody." He listened. "No. Not with nobody. Somebody's come down for him. Who'd have the nerve?"

He did not know. I did not either. I know now. My father was standing in the yard, underneath us, at that minute, with an empty gun, waiting to be taken. In the hall a woman in grey silk was being told the tide. And forty feet up, a man with shot in his neck lay on the floor with his head in a child's lap and listened to "Gold and Silver."

I must have slept. I was nine, and it was half past two in the morning. I do not remember lying down.

* * *

I was woken by his hand over my mouth.

"Hush. Somebody's on the ladder."

He had me up, and across the room. There is a closet there where the weights go down, with a slatted door. He put me in it. There was just room, standing, beside a thing like a sash-weight as big as I was.

"Not a sound," he whispered. "Whatever you hear. It's my father. He's not to see you; he'd think that he'd gone mad, and he's near enough already." He shut the door.

I looked through the slats.

A candle came up through the floor. Under it there was white hair, and a long face, and a magnifying glass swinging on a string. It was the old man. He climbed up into the room as slowly as a spider. He stood, and held the candle out, and looked at the cupboard with its broken rod.

Then Edmund said, "Who's that?"

I am not going to give you what was said in that room. The old man would not set it down, and he was right. It was said in their Hour, and it was theirs. I heard all of it. I was standing two yards from them, in the dark, with my hand over my own mouth. I understood perhaps a third.

I can tell you what I saw.

I saw a man of eighty-one go down on his knees in front of his son, and put a hand on his face, and keep it there. I saw him count something at the angle of the jaw, with his lips moving.

I heard him explain about an hour that had been given back. I heard him say that he had killed his son and then had not. And I watched Edmund's face while he listened. He did not laugh. He looked as I think I must have looked when my father told me that the prairie was like the sea, only it didn't move. He knew that it was not so, and he saw that it was being said to him by someone who loved him, in the only words that person had.

He said, "All right, Father. I was dead, and now I'm not. I'll not argue."

Then he told the old man what had happened on the Wade.

It took about two minutes. I have said that I understood a third. I understood the box on legs, since my father had shown it me. I understood that somebody had been put up the ladder, and that somebody had not. I did not then understand who.

I heard the old man say, "Then she didn't leave me." He said it six times. I counted.

And I heard him say the thing about the wheels. He said that the ones Edmund had made were better than the ones the first man had made. He said that he had known it on the day, and had said that they would serve.

Edmund put his arm over his eyes.

That is when I sneezed. There was twenty years of dust in that closet. I had been holding it for a long time.

The old man said, "What is that?"

"Rats," said Edmund.

He looked straight at the slats when he said it. I saw his one eye. I have never before or since been lied for so well.

The old man gave him something small, out of his waistcoat, on a ribbon. He told him to put it in his coat pocket and not the waistcoat. I saw Edmund put it away. It was a key.

There was a voice from below then, a woman's, calling up. Edmund put his finger to his lips. He would not let his father say that he was there. I thought it strange. I had watched that nurse all day; I knew how she looked at him. I thought that she would have been glad.

He told me why, afterward, on the ladder. He said, "She'd have had me in bed. And she'd have found you. And then there'd have been questions, and Dolly out of a place, and your father brought up to the house with every Vane in it looking at him. I'd one night left to do some things. I couldn't spend it having my temperature taken."

The old man went down. I heard her take him away across the yard.

And right beside my head, on the other side of the wall, the lady brought down her arm.

It struck twice. I thought that my skull would split. There was no little bell before it. There was nobody now on the left of the bell to ring one.

When the sound had died, the slatted door opened.

"Come out, rat," Edmund said.

I came out. I had dust all over me. He was standing, holding on to the iron frame, and his face was wet.

"You heard that," he said.

"Yes."

"All of it?"

"Yes."

"Did you understand it?"

"Some."

"That's about what I'd have said myself." He let out his breath. "Well. Keep hold of the part you did. I may want you to remind me. I've told it once now, and I didn't die of it, which surprises me." He put his hand in his coat pocket and felt the key there. "He said they were better than Thorne's. Did you hear him?"

"I heard."

"Thirty-nine years I've waited for that. Since I was thirteen, and played the Schubert." He wiped his face with his sleeve. "Come on. Help me with my feet. There's cold goose in the kitchen, and I've a sister to find. And you, madam, are on the wrong side of six feet of water from your bed."

## 5. Both

We came down the ladder the way we had gone up, with me doing his feet. At the bottom he sat on the corn bin for a while with his eyes shut and the handkerchief against his neck. The bleeding had nearly stopped. He said that it was only the edge of the pattern, and that he had been peppered worse by his own father at a pheasant shoot in 1966.

Then he took me across the yard by the hand, in the moonlight, in full view of every window on that side of the house. I said that someone would see. He said that by this hour of the Odd Hour everyone in that house was looking at something else. He was right. Nobody saw.

He took me in by the kitchen yard. The kitchen was empty. He put me in the larder, among the hams, and gave me a leg of goose off the carcass and told me to eat it and be quiet. Then he sat on the kitchen table, as Toby has described, with his own goose and a tumbler of the cooking brandy, and his feet on a chair.

I have the notebook entry. It is in very large letters, written by feel, in the dark of the larder, and most of a page is taken up by the one line.

*3.15. I AM IN A CUBBORD EATING A GOOSE.*

Toby came down the stairs. I heard everything that he has written: that he was engaged, that Edmund nearly broke his hand, that he should not wait for the right time because there was not one in that house. I heard Edmund say, "I've just had a talk with my father." I heard him say, "You were only a boy," and laugh, and say that he had been thirty-two.

I heard the step in the scullery passage, and Edmund send Toby away.

And I heard Imogen.

I am not going to give it again. She has written it, and she has written it straight; she did not spare herself. I sat on the floor of that larder with a goose bone in my lap and listened to a woman tell a man that she hoped he would never sleep again as long as he lived. I had not heard a grown person speak like that to anybody. I had heard my parents quarrel, once or twice, at the end, about the hospital. It had not been like that.

I heard him say yes. I heard him try to tell her. *It's what she did, at the end.* I heard her say that she would not hear another word.

I heard him give her something and say, *Go on, Immy. Don't look back. She looked back.*

Then she was gone. He stood in the passage for a long time. I could hear him breathing.

When he opened the larder door he had a candle in the kitchen saucer. He looked at me on the floor among the hams, and I saw that he had forgotten I was there, and was trying to remember.

"Did you hear that?" he said.

I nodded.

"All of it?"

"Yes."

"Well," said Edmund Vane. "She's quite right. You'll find that people mostly are, about me. It's only that they're right about the wrong thing." He held out his hand. "Come on. My sister's going across the water with your father, on a horse. I think we should go and watch. One ought to see a thing like that, if it's to be had."

* * *

I want to put down exactly what happened at the orchard gate, because it is the one thing in this whole history that I have had to piece together from my own memory alone, and because I am the reason for it.

We went out by the garden door. He did not go by the orangery; he went round, by the wall, slowly, with his hand on my shoulder. I think that it was to lean on. The moon was very bright. There was no wind at all now. At the bottom of the orchard there was a gap in the sea wall with a gate in it, and beyond the gate the ramp went down into the water, where the Wade had been.

We stood behind the gate, in the shadow of the last apple tree. He set the saucer on the gatepost.

They were already in the sea. They were a long way out. I could see a white horse, up to its chest, with the moonlight all along its back, and a lady sitting on it with her hair coming down, in a dark coat. And at the horse's head, walking in the water to his waist, with one hand on the bridle, was my father.

I knew him by the way he walked. I would know him by that at a mile.

I said, "That's Dad."

"Yes."

"He's going home."

"He's taking my sister home. To your house. She'll be there in the morning when you get back. I shouldn't wonder if she's there for good." He was quiet. "I hope you'll like her. She's better than she sounds. She's had a bad night."

I did not hear any of that properly. I heard only that he was going home, across the sea, and I was on this side of it. I was not supposed to be there. Nobody but a cook and a drunk man with a hole in his neck knew that I was there. He was going home to Saltcote with a lady, on the horse, and he thought that I was asleep in Vi Pask's bed. And he would get there, and go across to the cottage, and look in, and the bed would be empty.

I had promised him that I would not set foot on the road.

I stood behind that gate and watched him wade away from me into the moon, and I could not breathe.

Edmund said, "Ah." He put his hand to his forehead. "Wren. I'm going to sit down for a minute. I've gone rather peculiar." He sat down on the grass with his back to the gatepost, quite slowly, and put his head between his knees. "It's nothing. It's the head. It goes round. Give me a minute and I'll be right."

I looked down at him. Then I looked out at the water.

They had come to the place in the middle where the road went down. My father had got up behind the lady. I saw the horse stop, at the edge of something. I saw my father slide off into the sea up to his neck. And then the horse went down. It went right down, and the lady with it, and I saw them carried away sideways, and I heard myself make a noise.

They came up. They came up a long way off to the left, and the horse was standing, and my father was holding on to its neck.

The lady turned round in the saddle. She looked back at the island. She looked straight at our gate, at the place where I was standing, with the candle on the post beside me. And she lifted her arm, and waved to me. It was a long slow wave, the whole arm, the way you wave from a train.

I have thought about that wave more than about anything else in my life, more than about the Perch. I know now what it was. She thought it was her brother. She thought he had come down to see her off, after what she had said to him, and she was saying goodbye, and she was sorry.

I did not know who she was. I knew that she was on my father's horse, going to my father's house, and that she had seen me, and waved.

I thought that she was telling me to come on.

* * *

I had my torch in my coat pocket. I had not used it all night where anyone could see. I took it out and I switched it on.

I opened the gate. I did not look at Edmund. I think that I knew that if I looked at him I should not go. I went down the ramp into the water.

It was so cold that it did not feel like water. It felt like being bitten. It came over my shoes and up my legs and I went on. I had the torch up in front of me, pointing at the horse. I could see the white of it, a long way off, going up out of the sea on the other side.

I was not on the road. I mean that I did not think of it as the road. I thought of it as the way to my father. I had made a promise about the road on the Friday, to a man who was standing in a farm kitchen with a paper in his hand, and it had been about not going. It had not been about coming back. He had not thought to make me promise anything about coming back.

He says that in his own part. He says it twice. I think that he knew.

The water came to my knees, and then to my middle. It pulled at me from the side. I held on to one of the sticks that line the road and went from one to the next. I could not see the horse any more; there was a cloud. There was only the torch, making a little yellow road of its own across the black, and the sticks coming up out of it one at a time.

I heard Edmund behind me. He was shouting my name.

I did not stop. I have been asked why. I do not know. I was nine. My father was on the other side.

Then the bottom went.

I had come to the place where the road goes down. I did not know it was there. My foot went forward and there was nothing under it, and the water closed over my head.

I do not remember much of the next part. I remember that it was dark and very loud and that I was being turned round and round. I remember that I still had the torch. I remember thinking, quite clearly, that it was like the time I fell off the pony into the creek at home, only colder. I remember that I could not find which way was up.

Then something had me by the collar of my coat.

It hauled. My head came out. I got a breath of air and half the sea with it. I was against something big and warm that was swimming, and swearing, and a voice was in my ear saying, "I've got you. I've got you. Stop kicking, you little devil, I've got you."

He had come in after me. He had been sitting on the grass with his head between his knees, drugged, with a broken skull and a hole in his neck, and he had seen my torch go down the ramp, and got up, and come in.

He has his account of the Rill from 1974; I am coming to it. He knew that water. He knew that it set to the north and that there was nowhere to land below the bridge but the tail of the bank. He let it take us. He held me against his chest with one arm and swam with the other, across the current, as my father's mare had done twice that night. Something came up out of the dark over us. It was black, with legs.

He got hold of it. He got hold of one of the legs of the Perch with his free hand and he held on, with the whole of the Rill trying to pull us off it.

"Ladder," he said. "On the other side. Round the post. Can you hold on to me?"

I held on round his neck. He went round the post hand over hand, with me on his back. He found the ladder with his foot.

"Up," he said. "Go up. I'm behind you."

I got on to it. I put my foot on the bottom rung that I could reach under the water, and stood up, and put my hand up to the next.

It came away.

* * *

I have Toby Pargeter's account of what he did to that ladder at five o'clock on the Saturday afternoon. He pushed the bottom rung back into its socket, with the nail sticking out, because it seemed rude to leave it.

It was not his fault. I want that understood. It was one rung among nine, and I have been told since by a man who builds these things that every rung on that ladder below the high-water mark had been rotten for ten years. Edmund had been going to see to it since Kit was at school. Every Garrow who passed had touched the post. Nobody had looked at the rungs.

The second rung came away in my hand, and the third came away under my foot when I put my weight on it to get past. I went down into the water again to my chest. Edmund caught me.

He did not say anything. He reached up past me into the dark. He found the fourth rung and pulled on it, and it held. He found the fifth.

"Right," he said. "Listen to me. Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"I'm going to lift you up as high as I can reach. You put your hands on that rung, there, and you climb, and you don't stop till you're inside the box. It's dry in there. There's a door. Will you do that?"

"What about you?"

"I'll be along."

He took off his jacket. He did it in the water, holding on to the ladder with one hand and getting out of the sleeves with the other. It was the black one, with silk on the front. He folded it into a bundle, very fast, the way you would fold a flag, and pushed it inside the front of my coat and buttoned the coat over it.

"That's for in there," he said. "Put it on. It's warm. It's got a key in the pocket; don't lose that. It's not mine."

Then he got his hands round my middle and lifted me up out of the sea, straight up, as high as he could reach, at arm's length.

I got the rung. I climbed. There were four more, and they held. I came to the little door at the top, and it was not locked, and I fell through it on to a wooden floor, and lay there.

When I put my head out he was still in the water at the foot of the ladder.

He had his arms round the post. The sea was up to his chest, running past him, and pulling at him, and he was holding on to that tarred leg with both arms and his cheek against it, like a man holding a tree in a flood.

"Come up," I said.

"I can't, love. The bottom's gone. I can't reach the first one that'll bear me, and I've not got the arms to pull up to it, not tonight." He said it quite calmly. "It doesn't matter. The water's on the turn. It'll go down. I'll hold on here till it does."

"How long?"

"An hour, perhaps. Less. Put the coat on."

I put it on. It came down to my ankles. It was wet on the outside and dry inside, and it was warm from him.

I lay on the floor of the Perch, in a dead man's jacket, with my head out of the door, and looked down at him. My torch was gone; I had dropped it when the rung broke. It was lying on the bottom under the water, still lit, I could see the glow of it. There was a moon. I could see the top of his head and his arms round the post and the water going by.

I said, "Are you cold?"

"Freezing."

"Are you going to die?"

"I shouldn't think so," said Edmund Vane. "I've had several tries tonight, and none of them took. Talk to me, Wren. Keep me awake. I've a tendency to drop off."

* * *

So we talked. For fifty minutes. I had my watch; I had put it back on after the tower, and it had a light. I looked at it a great many times.

I told him about Pincher Creek, and the Oldman River, and the chinook wind that comes over the mountains in January and melts the snow in an hour so that the whole town goes out in its shirtsleeves. I told him about my mother. I told him how she had read me the Nancy Drew books, and then I had read them to her when she was too tired, and I had found I liked them better than anything. I told him about the clues.

"What have you got in your book?" he said. "About tonight?"

So I told him. I told him that his father's clocks were all an hour wrong on purpose and that you had to ask which one o'clock. I told him that there were two green dresses. I told him that the detective had a watch in his sock. I told him that the pink man had broken clock number 44 and put it in his pocket.

He laughed so much that I was afraid he would let go of the post.

"You've solved it," he said. "You've solved the whole damned house. Two green dresses. My God. Celia will be livid."

I told him that I thought he had done it. I told him that he had been Suspect Number One since half past one in the afternoon.

"Quite right," he said. "I did do it. I took about thirty clocks. I've got a list."

"But you said sorry. In the trees. You said sorry, Ma."

He did not answer for a while.

"She's the other one," he said. "That's a different case. That's twenty years old. Nobody's ever solved that one, because there was only one witness, and he's a coward."

"Was it you?"

"Yes."

"What did you do?"

He told me.

* * *

I am going to give it here as nearly as I can in his words. I had it by heart by morning. I said it over all the way to the cottage. I have said it over most nights since.

"It was the same night as this," he said. "The night the clocks go back. I was thirty-two. My mother was leaving my father for a farmer across the water. Your grandfather. My sister told me so at tea, to hurt me, and it did. So I drank a bottle of port, and at one in the morning I saw my mother's lantern go across the lawn and out on to the Wade, and I went after her.

"I caught her on the far side of this. The Rill. Past this box. She was three-quarters of the way. I could see your grandfather's light on the wall.

"I got hold of her arm. I begged her. I did all the things that a drunk man does. I cried. I said that she couldn't leave me with him. I said I'd kill myself. She was very patient. She'd always been patient with me. She stood there in the dark with the lantern and let me say it all, and said, Edmund, darling, you're thirty-two, you have a wife and a little boy, you must learn to stand up without me watching.

"And she said that she was going. She kissed me. She turned round, and she walked on, toward his light.

"And I sat down."

He stopped. The water went by.

"I sat down on the road behind her, on the stones, like a child that won't walk. I thought she'd come back. She always had. And she didn't. She went on. I watched her light go ten yards, and twenty. And I thought, she's going. She means it. And I got up and went the other way. Back toward the house. I don't know why. I think I wanted her to see me go, and be sorry.

"I was so drunk. I didn't think about the water. It had turned while we stood there; I'd felt it round my feet and paid no attention. And I came to the Rill, here, going back, and it had filled. It was up to my chest and running like a mill race. I went in, and it took my legs, and I went under.

"She heard me. I must have shouted. I don't remember.

"She turned round."

He was quiet so long that I thought he had gone to sleep. I said his name.

"I'm here," he said. "She turned round, Wren. She was thirty yards from your grandfather's ramp, and he was standing there with his light up, and she'd done it, she'd got away. And she heard her son go into the Rill behind her, and she turned round and came back.

"She came into the water after me. In her stockings. She got hold of my collar. Just as I got hold of yours. She knew this water; she was born on this coast. She let it take us down to this post, and she got my hands on it.

"And the ladder was good then. Every rung. She got me on to it. She pushed me up it. I was sick and crying and too drunk to climb, and she got her shoulder under me and pushed, from the water, and I went up into the box, as you've done.

"And then she was at the bottom. Where I am. She had hold of the post. I put my hand down to her. She could have come up. There was room."

His voice changed.

"She had her hand up. Out of the water. I thought she was reaching for mine. She wasn't. She'd got her ring off. She put it in my hand and shut my fingers on it, and she said, Give that to your father. And she said, Tell him I'm sorry. And she let go of the post."

I did not say anything. I could not.

"I don't know why she let go. I've had twenty years and I don't know. Perhaps the water took her. Perhaps she was tired; she'd been in it a long time, getting me up. Perhaps she thought there wasn't room for two. Perhaps she'd made up her mind on that road that she was going one way or the other and she'd not go back to the house. I don't know. I put my hand down and she wasn't there. Her lantern was floating. It went out.

"I stayed up there till the tide went down. Then I walked home. It was getting light. I said at breakfast that I'd slept in the stable. My father said that he'd put the clocks back early and she'd misread them. And I let him. I let him for twenty years. I let my sister think I'd dragged her back. I let your grandfather think she'd changed her mind about him. I let them all think whatever they liked, so long as nobody knew the one thing, which was that she'd got away, and got clear, and come back into the sea for me. Because I'd sat down on the road and wouldn't walk."

The water had gone down. It was at his waist now. I could see more of the post.

"So that's the case," Edmund Vane said. "It was me. It was never the clock."

* * *

After a while I said, "She was coming and she was going."

"What?"

"You said it on the tower. My dad asked was she coming or was she going. And you said both."

"Did I." He sounded very tired. "Yes. That's it. That's the answer to his question. She was going to your grandfather. She was going, and she got there, as near as makes no matter. And then she was coming back. For me. Not from him." He breathed. "Not from him. That's the bit he never knew. He thought she'd turned away from him. She didn't. She turned toward me. It's not the same."

"You have to tell him."

"I meant to. I was going to, tonight. On the tower. Then he shot the Jack, and I lay down."

"You have to tell the lady."

"I tried. She'd not hear it. You heard her."

"You have to tell your dad."

"I've told my dad. That's done. That was the best quarter of an hour of my life, up that tower, with you sneezing in the cupboard." He was nearly laughing. "So that's one. There's two more. And I'm stood in the sea holding on to a post."

"I'll tell them."

He was silent.

"Will you?" he said at last. "Will you, Wren? I've no right to ask you."

"I'll tell them. What do I say?"

He thought about it. I could see him thinking, with his cheek against the post.

"Say she turned back for me," he said. "Not from Amos. Say that. To my sister, and to your father. Say she turned back for me, not from Amos Garrow. They'll know what it means. Say it."

I said it. *She turned back for me. Not from Amos Garrow.*

"Again."

I said it again. I counted it, the way I counted everything. It was nine words.

"Good girl," he said. "That's it. That's all of it. That's twenty years in nine words. I could have done it in a minute any time I liked, and I never did." The water was at his hips. "You're a better messenger than I am. I had a ring to carry two hundred yards and I've had it in my waistcoat since 1974."

"Where is it?"

"I gave it to Immy. An hour ago. In the passage. She'll give it to him. That's done too." He let out his breath. "There. I've cleared my pockets. I don't think I've been so tidy since I was nine."

* * *

It was a quarter to five by my watch.

His voice had got slower. He had stopped making jokes. I could see that he was shaking, all of him, the way the mare had been shaking in Tom's story, in long hard shudders.

"The water's going down," I said. "Look. It's only at your middle."

"So it is."

"Soon you can stand."

"Yes."

"Then you can come up."

"I don't think I'll need to," he said. "I'll walk. Listen, Wren. When it's down far enough you're to climb out and go to the lights. You see them? On the far side? That's your house. That's your father's kitchen. Go straight to it. Don't come back for me. I'll be behind you."

"I'll wait."

"No. Count to a thousand. Then come out and walk to the lights. Forward. Don't look back. People in this family look back, and it never does them any good. You're not one of us. You walk straight on."

"I want to wait for you."

"Count," said Edmund Vane. "Go on. Out loud. I want to hear you. One."

I counted. I lay on the floor of the Perch with my chin on the sill of the door and counted out loud into the dark. He said the numbers with me, for a while. Then he said them a little behind me. Then he only said every ten.

I got to two hundred and something. He said, "Good girl." I got to three hundred. I did not hear him.

I said, "Edmund?"

The water said nothing.

I put my head out. I could see the post. I could see the water going by it, lower now, below where his arms had been. The moon was on it. There was nobody holding on to it.

There was nobody anywhere.

I called him. I called him for a long time. I called him the way his father had called him in the ice house, over and over, gently, as you call someone you want to wake.

I did not go down. He had told me not to come back for him. And I was nine, and I was more frightened than I had been all night, and the ladder had no bottom.

I counted to a thousand. I did it because he had told me to, and because I could not think of anything else to do. I counted it all, out loud, with my teeth knocking together, in his jacket.

When I got to a thousand I looked at my watch. It was twenty past five.

I climbed out. I went down the rungs that were there and hung from the last one and let go. The water was at my waist. It was hardly moving. I could see the stones of the road under it, in the first grey of the light. My torch was lying on them, still on, very faint. I left it there. I did not look for him. He had told me not to.

I walked to the lights. Forward. I did not look back.

* * *

I was at the cottage door by ten to six. Vi Pask let me in. She was in her nightdress with a candle, and she looked at me standing on her step, soaked to the chest, in a man's dinner jacket down to my ankles, and she said nothing at all. She took me upstairs and dried me with a towel and put me in my vest into the bed, and took the jacket off me and rolled it up, and pushed it under the bed because she did not know what else to do with it.

She said, "Where have you been, child?"

I said, "I'm not allowed to say."

She looked at me a long time with her little bright eyes. Then she said, "No. I don't suppose you are." And she went down and sat in her chair by the cold grate until her sister came at seven, white, in her cobwebs, running.

I lay under the blanket with it pulled over my head and said nine words over to myself. I must have slept in the end, because I did not hear him come up the stairs. I half woke when he lifted me. I heard him say to Dolly, downstairs, that I would have had a bad night, that there had been a wind. I smelled the sea on him, and the horse. He carried me across the yard and into the farm kitchen, and there was a lady in his father's chair, in his shirt, with her hair down.

It was the lady from the horse. It was the lady who had waved.

I looked at her a long time. She asked me which lady. I said the one who touched the box, on Friday. I asked if she had come on Mab. She said she had. I said I would have been scared. She said she was.

And then I put my face in my father's neck, because I could not hold it any longer, and I asked the only thing I had left.

"Is the man all right?"

He said, "What man?"

And I understood that he did not know. That nobody knew. That Edmund Vane had gone into the Rill at a quarter to five in the morning, holding a post for a child that was not supposed to be on the island, and that I was the only person in the world who had seen.

I did not answer. I went to sleep instead. I slept until four in the afternoon. When I woke up, the policeman's car was at the end of the ramp, and I had already decided.

* * *

The coroner said that the palms of his hands were torn and the insides of his arms, with splinters of tarred wood in them, as though he had held on to something for a long time. He said that the deceased was in his shirt and trousers and braces and one sock, and no jacket. He said that he had been alive when he entered the water. He said that he could not find how he came to be in the sea.

They were all of them in that room, and they all looked down.

I was not in the room. I was ten by then, and at school in Thorney, and I knew nothing about inquests. But I have the report. And I have sat at a table this year with every one of them who is still alive, and asked them what they were looking down for.

Hester was looking down because she had cleaned the weight. Kit was looking down because he thought he had killed a man in the harness room and that the man had somehow become his father. Imogen was looking down because she had said a thing in a scullery passage. My father was looking down because he had put eleven pellets in a man's neck from below. Mr Cade was looking down because he had told a widow how to wash a glass and helped her sell a clock. Celia was not there; she was in Rotterdam, writing an affidavit, and she has told me that she did not sleep that night either.

Toby was not called. If he had been, he would have looked down too.

Not one of them had done it. Every one of them had a piece of it. Nobody but me knew which piece mattered.

The palms. The tarred wood. One sock. No jacket.

The jacket was under a bed in Wade Cottage, rolled up, and it stayed there until my father found it in the spring, clearing out Vi's things after she died. He took it for one of old Vi's late husband's and put it on the bonfire. I had got there first. I had taken the key out of the pocket in the November, and wrapped it in a page torn from the back of the notebook, and put it in the biscuit tin with the rest. My maple-leaf handkerchief I never saw again. Kit Vane picked it up off the boards of the clock chamber on the Sunday morning and asked whose it was, and nobody knew. He gave it back to me this year, in the hall at Compline. He had kept it in a drawer in Berlin for thirty years, he said, without knowing why. It is in my pocket now.

It is about three inches long, of steel, with a bow pierced in the shape of a sprig of thorn. Leopold Vane says that it fits nothing else.

He was wrong about that. He forgot what his own copies were.

## 6. Thirteen at Table

The clocks went back this year on the night of Saturday the twenty-sixth of October. High water at Compline Bar was at twenty-one minutes past eleven by the sun, and the Wade closed at a quarter to nine and opened again at ten past two. I had printed the times on the letters. I had printed them twice, once in Greenwich time and once in the time on people's telephones, and put a line between, and written underneath, in red: *please read to the bottom.*

They all came across before it shut. Toby Pargeter came first, at four in the afternoon, in a car that was not red, with his third wife, Philippa, who stayed in the car for the whole of the crossing with her eyes shut. Kit and Saskia came from Berlin by way of Stansted. Saskia is fifty-two and makes very large things out of steel and still has, in her left eyebrow, the hole where the ring was. Gail Thurlow drove over from Tiptree with a cake that she said her auntie used to make, and stood in the kitchen for ten minutes with her hand on the range without saying anything.

Hester Quaile came last but one, on foot, as she had come thirty years before, from the bus. I watched her from the gallery window. She stopped halfway, at the Perch, and stood a while. Then she put her hand on the post and walked on.

Celia Vane came last. She was seventy-eight. She came in a hired car from the airport, with a driver, and she got out on the gravel and looked up at the tower before she looked at the house. She had a stick, and she was very thin, and her hair was white. She stood in the hall in a camel coat and said to me, "You're the child."

"Yes."

"You're the one he said was under the bed."

"Yes."

She looked at me for a long time. She has grey-green eyes that look at something a little way behind you.

"Harry used to say," she said, "that in his trade, when the family hands you somebody in the first hour, you thank them and go on looking." She held out her hand, palm up. "I suppose you want my watch."

* * *

I did want it. I had put the Font on the hall table.

I had not opened the house for thirty years. Nobody had. Kit inherited it from his grandfather and never came; he let Imogen have it, and she kept it locked and aired and went over once a month with the key and a duster. The clocks were as Hester had left them on the morning of the twenty-sixth of March, 1995. Every pendulum still. Every weight down. A hundred and ten of them.

I did not start them. I want to say that. People have asked me why, since I could; it is my trade. I left them as she had stopped them, as he had asked. I started three clocks only, and the tower.

The tower I had seen to in the summer. I had found two men from Colchester who restore church clocks, and we went up together in August with a rope. The Jack was in the Shop on his trestles, where Leo had left him, mended. You can hardly find the join. It took the three of us a whole morning to get him up the ladder and out on to the leads and settled on his pin. When he was in place one of the men said, "There. She'll have someone to talk to." I had not told him anything.

So at five minutes to five on the twenty-sixth of October I stood in the yard with my guests and heard Compline tell the quarter for the first time since the night of the twenty-second of October, 1994. The little man lifted his arm. *Ting-tang.* Three times. Then he stopped, and the grey woman stood with her arm up, and waited for the hour.

Toby said, "Oh, Lord," and blew his nose.

The three clocks I had set on the long table in the dining room. I had laid it for thirteen.

* * *

I shall tell you how the table was laid, because they each noticed it when they came in, and each of them stopped in the doorway.

There were seven of us. There were thirteen places. I had put the six extra places in the order in which the accounts are given in this book, round the table, and at each of them, on the plate, I had set one of the manuscripts. Mr Cade's typescript in its Basildon Bond box. Toby's book, open at chapter eleven. Hester's three red exercise books. A paperback with a rose on the spine, and under it the typescript with the sixth chapter in. A sheaf of my own handwriting, which was my father's. Six more exercise books, in Hester's hand, with an old man's numbered sections.

At the head of the table, on the old man's right, I had laid the thirteenth place as it was always laid. Three glasses. A napkin like a bishop's hat. The chair drawn a little back. On the plate there was nothing. I could not think what to put there. In the end I left a small red diary beside the fork.

Hester sat down in front of her own exercise books, and then got up, and moved, and sat in front of Leo's.

"I took them down," she said. "He'd want someone there who could read his hand."

Celia stood behind the chair with Mr Cade's box on it for some time. Then she sat in it.

"Somebody's got to sit with Harry," she said. "He'd hate it, being on his own at a party. He'd go and stand against the wall."

So we were thirteen, with the dead. We had soup. Gail served it. She put a plate at every place. Nobody said anything about it.

* * *

After the soup I got up, and took down the curtains from the long wall, and showed them the lining paper.

It is nine feet long and three feet high. It is ruled in pencil in a grid. Down the left side are the names of every person who was on Compline Ness that night, sixteen of them. Across the top are the hours, from nine in the morning of the twenty-second to six in the morning of the twenty-third, in ten-minute columns. In each square is every statement that anyone has made about where that person was and what they were doing, with a reference to the page.

There are four colours of ink. Black is the time on Mr Cade's watch, and my father's, and mine. That is the time of the rest of England, an hour ahead of Greenwich. Red is the time of the house. Green is the time of the kitchen clock, which Mrs Pask kept eight minutes fast, every Monday, and never told anyone. And blue is what I have not been able to time at all: things people did not know the time of.

On the table I had set the three clocks. One was a little radio-controlled clock of the kind you buy for twenty pounds, which takes its time from the transmitter in Cumbria that my laboratory feeds. It said seven minutes past nine. One was the kitchen clock off the wall downstairs, which I had started, and set, and put eight minutes fast. It said fifteen minutes past eight. And the third was the plain dark regulator from the hall, the Vulliamy, which I had carried through, with its weight.

I had cleaned the weight in the summer, very carefully, with a soft cloth. It did not need cleaning. Someone had done it before me.

It said seven minutes past eight.

"Those are the three clocks," I said. "Everyone in this book was reading one of them. Nobody knew there were three. Not even Mr Cade, who had two."

"Two?" said Celia.

"His watch, and the kitchen. He looked at the kitchen clock at about twenty to two, on his way through, and read it as true. He had no reason not to. It said twenty-two minutes to two. It was a quarter to two by his watch, and a quarter to one by the house." I touched the green one. "I think that clock may have made more trouble than the Act of Parliament."

"She did it for the dinner," Gail said. "So it'd come up on time. She told me when I was twenty. She said she'd done it since 1952 and nobody had ever noticed."

"Nobody did."

* * *

I am going to give the summation in the order in which I gave it, which is the order of the book. I had promised Imogen that I would tell them exactly, and I had promised myself that I would not be kind, because kindness was what had kept every one of them carrying the wrong thing for thirty years. But I found, once I had begun, that exact and kind were not so far apart as I had feared. Exact was what they wanted. They had each been waiting for somebody to say a thing that could be checked.

I began with Mr Cade, though he was not there, because Celia was sitting at his place.

"*By my watch it was a quarter past one*," I read, "*and Edmund Vane was lying at the bottom of the ice-house steps with his eyes open and the left side of his head the wrong shape. I have seen what dead looks like. It looks like that.*"

I put my finger on the lining paper, on the black square at one-fifteen.

"That's true," I said. "Every word of it. He was there. He was lying like that. His father had struck him on the left temple at ten to one by this watch," I touched the radio clock, "which was ten to twelve by that one," the regulator, "and he went down twelve steps and landed with his feet up. He was under a heavy dose of chloral and his breathing had gone to about eight times a minute. Toby counted it later. If you look at a man by a cigarette lighter, through a gate, from twelve feet, for one minute, you will see his chest move eight times if you know where to look. Mr Cade didn't. He saw the eyes. He was right about the eyes. They don't move."

Celia said nothing. She had her hands folded on the Basildon Bond box.

"*At a quarter to two the gate was open and the steps were empty.* That's true too. At seventeen minutes past one, by Mr Cade's watch, Mrs Pask had sent Toby out with her keys. She sent him because I told her. Toby looked at the kitchen clock as he went. He has told you it said twenty-five past twelve. It did. It was eight minutes fast." I touched the green clock. "So it was seventeen past twelve by the house, and seventeen past one by Mr Cade, and Mr Cade had just walked away from that gate two minutes before. Toby walked in at one twenty and found him snoring. They were three minutes apart in that wood and neither of them saw the other, because one of them was walking toward the house to find a widow and the other was walking away from it to find a pudding."

Toby said, "Oh, my *God*."

"And then Mr Cade wrote this." I read it. "*At two o'clock somebody fired a twelve-bore twice. At a quarter past, a man in a dinner jacket went down the fleet on the ebb, face down, in no hurry.* That's true as well. It was the Jack. He was wearing your grandfather's dinner jacket, Kit, that you and Saskia put on him that afternoon. My father shot him off his pin with both barrels from the yard. He went into the fleet on his face, and he rode high, because he was oak, and he went out under the sluice and fetched up in the grating at the outfall, where you dug him out on the Sunday."

Kit said, "I thought it was Dad. For a minute. In the mud."

"So did Mr Cade. For thirty years." I put my hand on the box. "He'd seen one man in a black jacket lying still, and then another going out to sea, an hour apart. He joined them up. He said himself that a detective is a man who can't leave two things lying next to each other. He'd been struck on the head at ten past twelve and he says in his own words that a knock on the head doesn't make you lose what you know, it makes you lose the string between things. He had everything. The candle in a kitchen saucer. The spoon. The one wheel in the mud. He stood in that kitchen at twenty to two with his hand on an empty pudding mould and felt the answer go past him out of the door."

"He knew that," Celia said. "He wrote that he knew it."

"He knew it was there. He never knew what it was."

I read the last one.

"*'I killed him,' she said. I believed her. I still do.*"

I looked at Celia.
